stories.Headline: CoreWeave raises full-year revenue forecast as quarterly revenue jumps 168%
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported its third quarter results on November 10, causing its stock to jump about 14 percent in premarket trading the next morning. This report helped other AI stocks like Nvidia, Nebius, Iren, and Oracle rise after a rough few weeks for the sector. The Nasdaq Composite had fallen 5.5 percent on November 5, leaving it about 12 percent below its October record high. CoreWeave, Nebius, and Iren had each fallen at least 40 percent from the peak reached on October 6. Nvidia also lost more than 400 billion dollars of market value during one two-day slide before its CEO departed.

The company reported third quarter revenue rose 168 percent year over year, and it raised its full year forecast to 13.0 to 13.3 billion dollars. Revenue backlog rose 138 percent to about 132.5 billion dollars, while debt doubled this year to 47 billion dollars by September. CoreWeave expects to collect 9 billion dollars in prepayments over three months and will not issue unsecured debt through 2027. Net interest expense was 846 million dollars in the third quarter, with a GAAP loss of 709 million dollars. The company is largely sold out through 2027, with demand being 10 times the available capacity through next year.

CEO Michael Intrator told analysts that the company is largely sold out and that scrutiny might slow industry construction but not CoreWeave. He stated that planned capacity additions over the next year will not be impacted by new regulations or increased costs. Management said that cash flow from existing contracts will cover debt repayments, addressing a main reason investors had been selling. Dan Sheehan of Telos Wealth Advisors said the earnings directly addressed the fear that had driven the recent market selloff. Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei called it the best quarter they could have asked for in a client note.

OpenAI, Perplexity, and Jane Street all expanded their relationships with CoreWeave, showing that customers are still willing to pay for computing capacity. Amazon expects 220 billion dollars of capital expenditures in 2026, and Alphabet expects its spending to increase significantly in 2027. However, Bernstein analysts warned that CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the computing capacity shortage eases. Senator Kevin Cramer called for Jensen Huang to step down following allegations about his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman and spy. Other affected stocks including Applied Digital, Oracle, Nebius, and Iren climbed between 6 and 14 percent following the report.

Borrowing costs climbed as the 10-year Treasury yield topped 5.3 percent in October, and U.S. producer prices rose 6.5 percent annually. SoftBank took a 3.7 billion dollar write-down on equipment for U.S. data centers, leading to a second quarter loss of 7 billion. Midterm elections saw Democrats win, with some candidates campaigning for tighter regulation and moratoriums on new data center construction in Texas. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia amid a crisis involving alleged chip shipments to China and a personal scandal. Nebius has surged 60 percent this year, while other neoclouds lost between 32 and 48 percent as of Tuesday.

Nvidia is set to report earnings after the close on November 17, which will be its first report since Huang stepped down. Investors will watch for growth metrics and management commentary to confirm if the demand for AI computing capacity remains strong. Nebius is also due to report its own financial results before the opening bell on Thursday. The articles leave open whether a path to sustainable profitability will form for heavily indebted companies like CoreWeave. It remains uncertain if the current rally will hold, though Nvidia alone stood to add nearly 100 billion dollars.

stories.Headline: Liquid C2 and Graphiant launch quantum secure networking for African enterprises
stories.Summary:
Bas Wijne, the CEO of APO Group, released a report on November 16, 2026, regarding artificial intelligence research in African markets. He used data from Africa Newsroom to highlight gaps in research conducted by European and United States organizations. On November 18, 2026, Cassava Technologies and Mauritius Telecom signed a memorandum of understanding at the Africa Tech Festival. This strategic partnership focuses on strengthening compute and model access for AI services and education across African markets. Both events took place in South Africa to address the growing role of technology on the continent.

The partnership involves using Cassava's NVIDIA-powered AI Factory in Cape Town, which is the most powerful supercomputer in Africa. It integrates Cassava's AI platforms and regional reach with the local language capabilities and operating experience of Mauritius Telecom. The companies will explore the CAIMEx platform and the myt AI Cloud to provide on-demand computing capacity for AI offerings. They will also assess opportunities for myt Learn, an AI education platform, starting in South Africa's public and private sectors. This follows a 2023 Reuters Institute count of ten countries that excluded African nations from AI news collection research.

Bas Wijne stated that a company's first impression in Africa depends on which local websites AI assistants are allowed to read. He explained that being found by AI depends on relationships with local news outlets in each specific African country. Ziaad Suleman of Cassava Technologies said that realizing AI's promise requires infrastructure, technology, and proven expertise for relevant services. Veemal Gungadin, CEO of Mauritius Telecom, said the goal is to make trusted AI useful and accessible for all. He noted that myt Learn is already supporting students and teachers within schools located in Mauritius.

The report notes that procurement leads in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, may use AI assistants in French to research new companies. Many publishers in the US and UK block AI crawlers, but only 12 to 14 percent do so in Senegal. In South Africa, the GIBS Media Leadership Think Tank found that 30 percent of 263 news sites block these crawlers. This affects companies that need their announcements to be found by AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and DeepSeek. Users in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa often access AI through Meta AI inside the WhatsApp application.

APO Group was founded in 2007 by Nicolas Pompigne-Mognard and operates across all 54 African markets as a communications consultancy. Its newswire, Africa Newsroom, reaches over 250 news sites and connects organizations with more than 450,000 journalists and analysts worldwide. AI crawlers visit Africa Newsroom 200,000 times daily, while Google AI draws about 62,000 impressions every month for the site. Microsoft's AI services, including Copilot, name an Africa Newsroom page as a source approximately 16,000 times per month. Tests showed AI assistants included news in 90 percent of cases across four different languages used across Africa.

Next, Bas Wijne will speak in Cape Town alongside leaders from Siemens Sub-Saharan Africa, Gold Fields, Microsoft, and Yango. The partners will jointly assess how to expand the myt Learn education platform into other markets served by Cassava. Companies are encouraged to use generative engine optimisation to ensure they are correctly cited by various AI assistants. The articles leave open who will write the content that forms the first impressions of companies entering African markets. It remains to be seen how many more African news publishers will choose to block AI crawlers over time.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh opens a San Francisco Fed conference on AI and productivity
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh opened a conference at the San Francisco Fed on Monday at 9 a.m. Pacific with 15 minutes of remarks. He then spent most of the morning leading panels with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Stanford economist Nick Bloom, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, per the published agenda. The topic was how artificial intelligence, which the Fed calls superintelligence, will change productivity and jobs. The conference took place as the S&P 500 stood at 7,543.60, down 0.82%, and the Nasdaq 100 at 27,848.80, down 1.68%. The Dow Jones stood at 52,277.00, down 0.13%, and the Russell 2000 at 2,785.83, down 0.64%.

The Fed lifted the upper bound of its target range to 4.00% in September, from 3.75%. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, above the 2% to 3% range considered healthy trend growth. In the week ending November 13, the 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.86% to 5.15%, and the 30-year reached 5.47%. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings were $11.26 in October, a preliminary figure, down from $11.38 a year earlier. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index fell to 48.1 in September, a level associated with recessions, and unemployment sits at 4.1%.

Warsh said at Jackson Hole in August that "We've come to a hinge point in history," and called AI "potentially a new factor of production." He asked whether it would "cause a significant, sustained rise in productivity across the economy," and who ends up with the gains: chipmakers, cloud providers, AI developers, other businesses, or consumers. At his October 28 press conference, he said "Productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust," while noting inflation has run above target "for close to six years." He asked whether AI would bring a rapid productivity miracle or gradual gains, and whether it would make price stability easier or harder to achieve.

Warsh said capital spending sits "at a historically high share of GDP," led by high-tech investment. Data centers could use up to 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, according to Energy Department projections. The independent market monitor for PJM Interconnection, which runs the largest U.S. power grid, concluded that "data center load growth is the primary reason" for its tight supply and high prices. Data centers compete with everyone else for power, chips, and electricians, which pushes prices up well before any productivity return. Households are already feeling the costs, and AI has not caused mass layoffs but has yet to show up in paychecks.

Warsh was sworn in as Federal Reserve Chair on May 22 under intense pressure from President Donald Trump to lower interest rates. The $31 trillion Treasury market is sending Warsh a signal, and bond investors are betting against an AI productivity miracle. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued on CNBC's Squawk Box that the U.S. economy can return to strong growth without driving prices higher with inflation, pointing to Alan Greenspan's 1990s playbook. Warsh went to Sintra and tied the entire future of interest rates to whether the AI capex wave actually delivers on its promises. The stock market has spent much of 2026 focused on artificial intelligence, record corporate spending, and a surprisingly resilient economy.

Warsh has said the task force's findings will inform future policy judgments, not dictate immediate decisions, so Monday is unlikely to bring a rate signal. Two things are worth tracking instead: whether Warsh presents strong productivity as a reason for patience on rates, and the next reading of core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, which rose 0.3% in September. Cooler readings alongside 3% growth would be the first real evidence of an AI productivity boom. If productivity rises fast enough to lower the cost of producing each unit, the Fed could hold or cut rates while growth stays strong. If spending keeps outpacing the efficiency gains, long-term yields above 5% could stick, putting pressure on housing and on stocks whose prices depend on low interest rates.

stories.Headline: Shenzhen prepares to host APEC leaders to discuss Asia-Pacific AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen prepares to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19 under a theme of prospering together. EngineAI Robotics Technology Co., Ltd. organized a robot fighting competition to test the movement capabilities of their humanoid robot designs. A Malaysian researcher suggested that these fighting robots could eventually guard orchards or perform agricultural tasks in the country of Malaysia. Yao Qiyuan, a co-founder of the firm, noted that these robots could harvest oil palm fruit and pollinate durian trees. He stated that expanding overseas involves developing new applications with local partners rather than just exporting finished products to other markets.

The city's core AI industry generated 220 billion yuan, or 33 billion U.S. dollars, in revenue during the year of 2025. More than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size operate in Shenzhen, and trade with APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan. This trade figure for the first half of 2026 rose 33 percent and accounted for nearly 70 percent of foreign trade. Shenzhen exported 8.27 billion yuan of 3D-printing equipment in the first half of 2026, which was a 127.5 percent increase. The city released an AI action plan for 2026 to 2028 in September to strengthen cooperation with ASEAN and others.

Hu Zhenyu from the China Development Institute said the AI industry is now bringing entire industrial chains to various overseas markets. He noted that demand for computing infrastructure and digital transformation in Latin America and Southeast Asia creates new growth opportunities for firms. Bai Xue of the Shenzhen 3D Printing Association said integrated supply chains and AI innovation boosted the competitiveness of Chinese printers. Shi Xiaoliang of SmartMore Corporation hoped APEC would allow his company to share China's practical industrial AI experience with global partners. Yang Qian of X Square Robot said open-source technologies are lowering barriers to technology access for small and medium enterprises.

SmartMore Corporation has served over 730 enterprises and deepened cooperation with partners in Southeast Asia, Japan, and the Republic of Korea. These partners work in sectors including precision manufacturing, new energy, and consumer electronics to detect defects too small for human eyes. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for over 97 percent of businesses and provide most private sector jobs in APEC. These smaller businesses generate about half of the private sector output and are affected by the digital transformation of AI. APEC's 21 member economies house 3 billion people and accounted for 61.6 percent of global real GDP in 2025.

The APEC Artificial Intelligence Initiative for 2026 to 2030 was adopted in 2025 to promote secure and reliable AI ecosystems. On July 23, ministers in Chengdu adopted the Chengdu Statement to promote AI transformation in agriculture, services, and the manufacturing sector. China announced in July that it would provide 5,000 opportunities for AI training and seminars to developing countries over five years. The APEC member economies possess capabilities across the AI value chain, including semiconductor production, manufacturing, and the development of models. Bambu Lab is a local manufacturer that currently uses AI for machine control and the monitoring of its printing processes.

China plans to establish a center in Qianhai, Shenzhen, to promote APEC cooperation regarding the flow of data across borders. This center will serve as an open platform for business services, regulatory alignment, and research into various regional policy issues. Eduardo Pedrosa of the APEC Secretariat said research and innovation in Shenzhen can benefit the entire region and the world. stories.Headline: Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi warns AI boom raises inflation and borrowing costs while diverting investment
stories.Summary:
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi warned in a post on X on Sunday that the artificial intelligence boom is driving up inflation and borrowing costs while pulling investment away from other parts of the U.S. economy. He wrote that AI has been a boon to economic growth and job creation, but that its rapid expansion is bringing significant side effects. According to Zandi, AI is adding to inflation by driving up electricity and consumer electronics prices, and AI investment is pushing up interest rates by soaking up capital to finance the build-out. He cautioned that the massive flow of money into AI infrastructure is coming at the expense of other investment.

Zandi said that since ChatGPT debuted four years ago, AI has gone from a rounding error to accounting for nearly two-thirds of the growth in investment. At the same time, he said, growth in everything else has slowed by more than half since mid-2024. He concluded with a warning about the returns expected from the technology, saying the bet on AI had better pay off in higher productivity because the rest of the economy is not investing enough to deliver it. The article also cited other economists and institutions who have raised related concerns about AI spending.

The Benzinga article reported that economist Peter Schiff warned last month that rising borrowing costs could weaken AI investment and expose broader economic vulnerabilities, while potentially benefiting gold and gold-mining stocks during an impending recession. Former Federal Reserve adviser Danielle DiMartino Booth also suggested a recession may already be underway. In September, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said AI infrastructure spending could reach $1 trillion in 2027, adding about 1% to GDP growth annually while potentially contributing to inflation, and he cautioned that it was too early to identify winners and losers in the AI boom. In July, the International Monetary Fund warned that weaker-than-expected AI productivity gains could trigger a pullback in technology investment and a sharp correction in highly valued tech stocks, while raising its 2026 global inflation forecast to 4.7%.

The second article, published by Foreign Affairs on November 18, 2026, under the headline about America's hidden AI advantage, appeared in the source material only as page code and styling, with no readable story text. Because that article provides no usable reporting, nothing further can be drawn from it, and the account above rests on the Benzinga article alone.

stories.Headline: FBI warns hackers use Artex AI tool to breach global networks in under three hours
stories.Summary:
The FBI warned that hackers are using the Artex AI tool to launch autonomous cyberattacks globally and across the United States. These malicious actors have targeted various industries in recent months, including government, defense, tech, law firms, and phone and internet companies. The agency issued a flash cybersecurity advisory on November 13, 2026, regarding the weaponization of this penetration testing framework. Cybercriminals and state-aligned groups used the tool to breach networks in under three hours from initial targeting to privileged access. These campaigns included a widespread hack of ConnectWise customers and several financial institutions located within the country of South Korea.

The tool connects to frontier large language models from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as non-U.S. and open-source models. It targets security flaws like exposed passwords and weak protections to steal data from databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. In South Korea, hackers stole personal data from at least 68,000 people due to a lack of multi-factor authentication. The tool breached ConnectWise, granting access to Microsoft 365 cloud environments for at least 2,250 customers, according to the FBI. Barracuda also suffered a breach after the tool found an exposed credential from a third-party vendor that was not revoked.

The FBI stated that AI makes sophisticated attacks faster, easier to automate, and potentially more difficult for organizations to detect. They noted that Artex intrusions are noisy and generate reams of traffic that may trigger a company's defensive alerts. Microsoft identified a China-aligned threat actor known as Storm-0940 as the group behind these specific Artex-assisted hacking campaigns. Arve Kjoelen, the chief information security officer at Barracuda, said defenders responding to malicious activity often arrive after attackers finish. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to requests for comment regarding the claims made by the FBI.

The attacks affected financial services, healthcare, and telecommunications, as well as the aforementioned IT management giant ConnectWise and the company Barracuda. Victims include thousands of downstream tenants and tens of thousands of individuals in South Korea who had their data stolen. Separately, malicious scripts were found on websites of 178 organizations, including international brands, through a vulnerability in Optimizely. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said banking outages at Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and JPMorgan Chase were not cyberattacks. He attributed those specific disruptions to ageing computer infrastructure and software bugs rather than the AI hacking tools.

Artex is an open-source framework designed for legitimate cybersecurity testing that first made its public debut in July 2026. Malicious actors have been using the framework since at least August 2026 to identify weaknesses in networks and applications. The tool uses AI agents to automate tasks such as scanning networks and testing security systems for various vulnerabilities. It allows attackers with limited technical expertise to carry out operations that usually require considerable and specialized professional knowledge. The developer later made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks after the tool was used in cyberattacks.

The FBI says the previous open-source version of Artex continues to circulate and remains widely accessible for use in attacks. Researchers recently found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online that were placed on the internet without any password. This includes the specific Artex system used to target South Korea, which was likely exposed by mistake or misconfiguration. Barracuda changed all customer credentials because its logs were not detailed enough to rule out access to customer systems. The articles leave open exactly how many customers were affected by the breach at the cybersecurity company Barracuda.

stories.Headline: OpenAI expands free AI access to 200,000 researchers after study shows productivity gains
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released a report on November 16, 2026, about how scientists use ChatGPT. The company studied 1,819 scientists who participated in a summer pilot program. These researchers used the AI tool for various tasks throughout the scientific process. The study analyzed over 580,000 messages sent by these academic participants. A survey of 251 participants also provided data for the report.

The pilot ran from August 20 to September 22, 2026, with surveys from September 30 to October 7. Participants estimated that work would take 1.9 times longer without AI. OpenAI is now expanding free access to more than 200,000 researchers worldwide. The study found 68 percent of scientists used the tool to develop research ideas. These users brought specific questions, asked for refinements, or requested new research questions.

The OpenAI Economic Research team managed the study using automated classifiers to protect privacy. They stated that the tool helps accelerate discovery and serves as a playground for scientists. The team noted that training is off by default for the academic researchers plan. They explained that they did not read underlying messages or the responses from ChatGPT. The researchers aimed to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.

About 98 percent of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed up discovery in their field. Some researchers reported that constraints on staffing, funding, and experimental capacity still limit progress. Users from niche directions like stomatology and organoids now have advanced computing capabilities. These scientists can describe goals in natural language to call protein design and analysis tools. This shift allows researchers without AI backgrounds to perform complex interdisciplinary exploration.

Scientific research often involves repetitive labor and long cycles that squeeze out time for creation. Some processes, like screening peptide molecules, used to take a year but now take two to three months. In the first ten months of 2026, over 80 domestic AI4S financing deals exceeded 200 billion yuan. Companies like Zhiyuan Shenlan, Keli Xinxu, and Yuancai Xinjie are now receiving significant capital. Deep Principle launched the Hydrogen-1.0 model to help with experimental design and material discovery.

Alibaba released Qwen4-Max on November 16 to design coolant molecules and call automated experimental platforms. Other models like Claude Fable 5.2, Mythos 5.2, and Hunyuan Hy4 solve problems in physics and math. Future progress depends on whether these expectations translate into actual faster discovery in the real world. The articles leave open how long it will take for AI to conduct research independently. It remains unclear how big the business of AI for Science will eventually become.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude Code team uses layered automated checks and risk-based human approval to review AI-written code
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has outlined how the Claude Code team handles code reviews as AI agents increasingly contribute to its codebase, according to an InfoQ article published on 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z. The approach relies on multiple layers of automated verification, AI-powered reviews, and risk-based human approval, aiming to reduce manual review time without increasing regressions or production incidents. Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt and Qing Wang described how the team's review process has evolved alongside the growing volume of AI-generated code. Between June and September, merged pull requests to the Claude Code repository more than doubled, while the proportion of changes requiring a revert fell by over 40%. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of code, about 90%, is written and reviewed by Claude, according to a claude.dev blog post published Nov 16, 2026.

Before opening a pull request, Claude runs tests, builds, and linters, while a separate agent reviews the changes in a fresh context. Every pull request then goes through several automated checks, and Claude-powered reviewers inspect code changes for potential bugs, with multiple agents independently investigating findings before another group verifies them. A separate security review can also block a merge if unresolved issues remain. Low-risk modifications, such as documentation updates or internal features behind feature flags, may require no human approval, while medium-risk changes require one person and high-risk modifications need two approvals. Changes to particularly sensitive areas, including CI workflows, always require human oversight.

Human reviewers remain responsible for architectural decisions, product direction, high-risk changes, and the final outcome, and the team emphasizes that the person directing an AI agent remains accountable for the code it produces. The people who own the code write the checks for it and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag, and when a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why. The team maintains a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10, so nobody has to memorize past outages. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes, and the team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.

One commenter asked whether code review is officially synonymous with testing now, whether the code review mechanism should be owned by the QA team, and whether there is still a QA team. The approach raises questions about the evolving boundaries between software engineering, testing, and quality assurance. Merged changes are typically released behind feature flags, tested internally, and gradually rolled out to users. Incidents and reverted changes are also incorporated into a growing evaluation dataset used to measure and improve the automated reviewers. The team tracks how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude's work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. The share of internal pull requests passing after one review and fix round increased from 65% to 78%, while the proportion requiring five or more rounds dropped from 8.9% to 1.5%. Review cycles are capped at three rounds before the author is asked to reconsider the implementation, and subsequent reviews focus on new changes rather than repeatedly examining the entire pull request. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human. The team has set up a commit gate with off, observe, and enforce modes, and if commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck.

The central idea is to optimize code review around the risks a change introduces rather than the amount of code a human has personally read. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude, and without them you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. The article recommends end-to-end tests, property tests, and differential tests, and notes that property libraries such as fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, and proptest for Rust generate thousands of inputs that try to prove a statement otherwise. Differential tests run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs, using randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic, and you normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes.

The team created a verify skill placed in a .claude/skills/ folder in the repo, as close to the relevant code as possible, and Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes. Claude can test the whole app using the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or by running the service locally for backend work. In observe mode, the commit gate will log what would have been blocked so the team can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted, while enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. The articles leave open how the approach scales beyond the Claude Code team and how the evaluation dataset will be used to improve the automated reviewers.

stories.Headline: Saskatchewan introduces bill letting courts order removal of deceptive AI content and award victims compensation
stories.Summary:
Saskatchewan introduced a bill on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, that would allow courts to order the removal of manipulative AI content and let victims seek compensation. The province said deceptive artificial media, often called deepfakes, exploit the public, undermine trust and create financial hardship. Justice Minister Tim McLeod told reporters after tabling the legislation that some individuals will use AI inappropriately. He said that if they attempt to deceive or target vulnerable individuals, the province wants a framework to hold them accountable. He said Saskatchewan is the first Canadian jurisdiction to provide a legislative framework on deceptive AI.

The bill would let people who have fallen prey to deepfakes seek legal action against creators of deceptive content in audio or visual formats. If creators are found guilty, they would provide compensation to the victim at a cost determined by the court. The court could also force creators to destroy the content and remove it from platforms. The bill would require disclosures in certain cases, and if content could reasonably be believed as authentic, creators would need to put clear markings that it is AI. The bill does not limit AI use for other content, including parody or satire, as long as it is not manipulative.

McLeod said policing agencies would enforce the law, and he said the legislation would also apply to AI-generated intimate images. Asked if the province is working to find out who is responsible for deepfakes using Premier Scott Moe's likeness to promote cryptocurrency schemes, McLeod said he cannot speak to any details. McLeod said that if the bill passes, people would still be able to express themselves freely using the technology. He said that if it is all meant in good fun and does not rise to the level of defamation or deception, those purposes will continue to be used safely. In a statement Tuesday, McLeod said that with new developments in this field emerging almost daily, Saskatchewan must be prepared to both take advantage of its benefits and safeguard against its misuse.

Rod McKendrick of the Saskatchewan Seniors Mechanism group told reporters there have been cases of grandparents receiving calls from scammers pretending to be their grandchildren and asking for money. McKendrick said the bill is another tool in that person's tool chest to use when something like that happens to them. He said this is happening, but there is nothing authorities are able to do because there is no legislation. The bill says those who have fallen prey to deepfakes could seek legal action against creators of the deceptive content. The articles say the bill would apply to AI-generated intimate images and to deceptive content in audio or visual formats.

Alberta has passed legislation that prohibits the creation of fake AI content of politicians and targets the use of AI for spreading intimate images. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe previously raised concerns about online deepfakes using his likeness to promote cryptocurrency schemes. The province said deceptive artificial media, often called deepfakes, exploit the public, undermine trust and create financial hardship. The bill said those who have fallen prey to deepfakes could seek legal action against the creators of the deceptive content, whether it is in audio or visual formats. The articles state that Saskatchewan says it is the first Canadian jurisdiction to provide a legislative framework on deceptive AI.

McLeod said that if the bill passes, people would still be able to express themselves freely using the technology. It would be up to policing agencies to enforce the law, McLeod said. Asked if the province is working to find out who is responsible for the deepfakes using Moe's likeness, McLeod said he cannot speak to any details. The articles do not say when the bill would be debated or voted on, or what penalties the court could set beyond compensation and destruction of content. The report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026, and was written by Jeremy Simes.

stories.Headline: Alecto raises $20m seed led by Insight Partners to expand its AI law firm beyond UK conveyancing
stories.Summary:
Alecto, a London-based AI law firm serving consumers, raised $20m in a Seed round led by Insight Partners, the company announced today. The firm was founded in September 2025 by Will Rice, who previously built fintech mortgage lender Gen H. Alecto said it reached $8m in annualised revenue within its first eight months of trading. The company said it has acted on more than $1.3bn in property transactions. Alecto began with UK conveyancing, the legal work needed to buy and sell property.

Firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group and law firm Mishcon de Reya also took part in the round. Angel investors include Simon Rogerson, founder and chief executive of Octopus Group, and John Reynolds, founder of SwiftKey. Alecto puts the UK conveyancing market at $3.3bn and the wider UK consumer legal services market at $23bn, with a global addressable market of several hundred billion dollars. The company said it aims to become the UK's leading provider of property legal services in 2027. Headquartered in Shoreditch, the business has grown from three people in January 2026 to 85, with what it says is more than 500 years of collective legal experience between them.

Will Rice, founder and chief executive of Alecto, said the legal industry has for too long expected customers to work on its terms, and that AI now presents the opportunity to put the consumer in control. Rice said people do not want to buy a lawyer's time but want results, and that Alecto exists to make the law accessible to everyone. He said the company is not building a law firm but replacing the traditional law firm. Rice said property is where Alecto proves the model, and that it is building the technology and operations to rapidly break into new countries and new areas of law. He said access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.

Alessandro Luciano, principal at Insight Partners, said consumer legal services represent a huge market opportunity as cost and complexity mean the necessary support is beyond the reach of so many people. Luciano said Alecto's approach redefines how those services are delivered, starting with one of the most important transactions in a person's life, buying a home. He said Rice brings deep knowledge of the property market to bear and the team's progress in such a short timeframe clearly demonstrates the pace of execution. Alecto argues that traditional legal services are constrained by the finite number of qualified lawyers and the hours they can work. The company said this leaves consumers facing high and often unpredictable costs, opaque processes, slow responses and unfamiliar industry language.

The raise follows other activity in legal AI this year. In March, legal AI firm Harvey signed Suits actor Gabriel Macht as a brand ambassador as competition in the market intensified. In May 2025, the Solicitors Regulation Authority authorised Garfield.Law, the first purely AI-based firm approved to provide regulated legal services in England and Wales. The regulator said named regulated solicitors remain ultimately accountable for that firm's professional standards. Rice spent six years building Gen H, a lender focused on helping more people get on the property ladder, and Alecto said the experience, industry knowledge and relationships he developed there underpin its initial focus on property.

The new funding will support expansion into additional areas of consumer law and new countries, with the first international launch planned for 2027, the company said. Alecto said it also sees an opportunity to serve people who currently go without legal support because of its cost or complexity. The company said it aims to build relationships with mortgage brokers and estate agents looking for better service for their customers and faster completion times. Alecto said its service is designed to move matters forward proactively and explain legal issues in plain language. The company said it combines AI with human expertise to deliver what it describes as a premium service at a mass-market price.

stories.Headline: DistroKid gives UMG and Sony data on AI music in Suno lawsuit
stories.Summary:
DistroKid provided data about AI-generated music on its platform to Universal Music Group and Sony Music after initially refusing, according to a Monday November 16 court filing obtained by Billboard. The subpoena sought numbers on how much music passing through the DIY distributor is thought to be made with Suno and other AI generators. UMG and Sony say the data is key to proving Suno-generated music eats into their market share and royalty distributions. DistroKid is not a party to the Suno suit. The distributor changed course and produced responsive documents, and the filing withdrew the subpoena petition.

The subpoena is part of UMG and Sony's copyright infringement lawsuit against AI music service Suno. Competition between AI songs and human music is a key part of the fair use inquiry, the test for whether Suno infringed by training on millions of unlicensed tracks. DistroKid initially refused, leading the labels to initiate legal action last month seeking to force compliance. Reps for DistroKid and Sony declined to comment on Tuesday November 17, and reps for UMG did not return a request for comment. UMG still has an ongoing lawsuit filed in September alleging DistroKid flooded streamers with mass AI-generated, SEO-optimized, and copyright-infringing slop.

In a statement when that lawsuit was filed, a DistroKid rep said the company takes copyright protection, fraud prevention and the integrity of the music ecosystem seriously, and works closely with digital streaming platforms, rightsholders and other industry partners. The spokesperson said DistroKid strongly disagrees with UMG's allegations and is disappointed UMG chose litigation rather than established industry processes. The spokesperson said DistroKid is confident in its practices and intends to defend DistroKid vigorously. In Boston federal court papers filed last Friday November 13, the labels argued a full pause could keep the second case frozen into 2028. The labels said Suno's 2025 and 2026 models and business conduct, including v6 launched in September, would be examined nowhere until at least 2028.

Suno asked Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV on October 30 to pause the second case until he rules on summary judgment in the first lawsuit, filed in June 2024. Suno argues training its AI on copyrighted recordings is lawful without a license, and said a ruling for it on fair use or on the YouTube stream-ripping claim could foreclose the labels' theories in the second case. The labels offered to postpone proving ownership of the more than 60,000 recordings at issue until Saylor rules. The second lawsuit, filed September 18, accuses Suno of copying 60,202 recordings without a license, and statutory damages capped at USD $150,000 per work give a theoretical maximum of just over USD $9 billion. The labels also ask the court to order Suno to stop further use of their recordings.

The dispute began in June 2024, when Universal, Sony and Warner Music Group sued Suno. Warner settled and struck a licensing deal in November 2025, and the case now covers 560 of Universal and Sony's recordings. In May this year the labels asked to add 61,026 more recordings after tracing them in Suno's training data, and Saylor refused on August 18, saying adding them will have obvious consequences of complexity and delay, steering the labels to a separate lawsuit. Suno launched its v6 models on September 9, nine days before the second suit was filed, saying they were built with Warner, BMG and Believe. Suno raised more than USD $400 million at a USD $5.4 billion valuation in June.

The labels say Suno's document handover in the first case largely stops at February 2025, and no witness has been put forward to explain how v6 was trained. The labels say they recently learned the engineer responsible for Suno's data scraping and training data acquisition has left the company. Suno said it is retaining relevant data under legal preservation obligations and that the first case's record will preserve testimony from past years. The labels proposed a partial stay with three parts, including evidence-gathering now on Suno's later models, licensing efforts, new businesses and finances. If Saylor opts for a broader pause, the labels want the first case's record usable in the second immediately and a joint status report due within 14 days.

stories.Headline: Nokia leads AIGF Northern consortium to build AI computing network across four Nordic and Baltic sites
stories.Summary:
Founding partners Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda announced on 16 November 2026 the formation of AI Gigafactory Northern, a European consortium developing trusted, distributed AI infrastructure through a federated, multi-site AI Gigafactory across the Nordic and Baltic region. The partners intend to submit a bid to build and operate AIGF Northern under the call for tenders for AI Gigafactory consortia published by the European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking. The consortium is led by Nokia and is named AI Gigafactory Northern (AIGF Northern). The group plans to develop a network of AI computing facilities across the Nordic and Baltic region. The project seeks to select and establish AI Gigafactory consortia, aligning with European efforts to expand domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Operating as a federated AI Gigafactory under European governance, the sites will combine large-scale AI computing infrastructure with sovereign cloud and AI platform services, high-capacity connectivity and decarbonised energy. AIGF Northern will connect facilities in Oulu, Finland; Iru, Estonia; Valmiera, Latvia; with the location of the Swedish site yet to be determined. The proposed network would span four locations: Oulu in Finland, the Tallinn region in Estonia, Valmiera in Latvia, and a site yet to be selected in Sweden. Through InvestAI, the EU aims to mobilise €30 billion for AI investment, combining €20 billion in private-sector funding with €10 billion from EU and national public sources. By distributing capacity across borders, the federated AI Gigafactory will reduce concentration risk and strengthen the resilience of Europe's AI ecosystem.

Mikko Hautala, Chief Geopolitical and Government Relations Officer at Nokia, stated that Europe's AI ambitions depend on infrastructure it can trust, control and scale. He added that AIGF Northern brings together the connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities needed to turn that ambition into reality. He said that by linking strengths across borders, Europe can build a more resilient foundation for European innovation, competitiveness and technological sovereignty. Markus Päivinen, Managing Director of Nscale Finland, said scaling AI infrastructure in Europe requires the right foundation of partners and experience in deploying large-scale AI computing infrastructure for customers. Päivinen said Nscale's role is to ensure the AI solutions it delivers are enterprise-grade, flexible and ready to support organisations across Europe as demand accelerates.

Taavi Madiberk, CEO and co-founder of Skeleton Technologies, said Europe is stepping up its AI investment but building lasting AI capacity requires more than compute alone. Madiberk said it also requires the energy and power infrastructure to support that compute efficiently, reliably and at scale, using technologies developed and manufactured in Europe. Anders Olsson, Executive Vice President and Head of Telia Sweden, said customers and the continent have a rapidly increasing need for scalable and trusted AI services. Michael Champion, Chief Information Security Officer at Verda, said Verda is proud to be a founding partner and that as AI becomes more integral to competitiveness and security, it is essential that Europe has its own strong infrastructure to support research, the public sector and wider industry. AIGF Northern will give businesses, researchers and public-sector organisations throughout Europe access to trusted computing, cloud and connectivity services at scale.

Nokia will supply network and connectivity technology, while Nscale and Verda will provide AI computing and cloud platforms. Telia, with its subsidiary Telia Cygate, will support connectivity, data transmission, infrastructure operations and cloud solutions. Skeleton Technologies will provide high power systems designed to improve data center efficiency and electricity grid stability, reduce strain on the electricity grid and support lower-carbon operations. Research organisations VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden are also supporting the initiative. The Nordic and Baltic region offers suitable conditions for sustainable AI infrastructure, combining reliable, decarbonised energy supply, advanced digital networks and a cool climate that reduces cooling demand.

Distributing capacity across these locations will allow the consortium to draw on multiple sources of decarbonised energy, expand computing infrastructure where capacity is available and reduce reliance on any single site or supplier. VTT brings capabilities in quantum computing, semiconductors, physical AI and photonics, and KTH contributes multidisciplinary expertise in AI research, education and skills development. Partners are engaging European and national stakeholders to refine the model and identify next steps for growth. The consortium aims to create value for industry, start-ups, research organisations and the public sector across Europe. The articles leave open the Swedish site's location and the outcome of the EuroHPC JU tender bid.

stories.Headline: Google reports that cyberattackers use AI frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that state-sponsored and cybercrime groups are increasingly using generative AI for cyberattacks. These actors used multi-agent offensive frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without any human intervention. This shift allows intrusions to occur at machine speed, which represents a paradigm shift in operational velocity. The reports were published in November 2026, following an analysis of attacks over a third quarter. These automated tools enable the chaining of complex attack paths to scale operations significantly.

The exploit_agent framework, found on an exposed staging server, compares patched and unpatched web application code to develop exploits. Attackers use Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to increase the velocity of multi-stage intrusions and weaponise n-day vulnerabilities. Artex is most used by Chinese-speaking groups, while Cairn targeted the US aerospace sector and PentAGI scanned Asia. Between August and October, hackers used a customized PentAGI platform for systematic reconnaissance across various organisations in Asia. Other tools include ZeroHollow for exploit development, Agent Zero for autonomous code execution, and HexStrike AI for experimentation.

Google and Mandiant stated that the adoption of these frameworks allows for the reverse engineering of patches at machine speed. They noted that the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that often fail. GTIG observed that a Chinese group is building its own automated attack framework, likely for espionage operations. They also found that Phishing-as-a-Service operators, like the Jieyou service, use LLMs for chatbot configuration. Google reported that LLMs improve the quality of long-running influence campaigns and help IPM networks scale political clickbait.

Matt Hartman, Merlin chief strategy officer, said that US critical infrastructure faces danger from attacks occurring at machine speed. He noted that water utilities, hospitals, and regional electric utilities cannot win this race if they struggle to patch monthly. Hartman stated that AI dramatically lowers the cost and expertise needed, putting powerful capabilities within reach of smaller groups. State-sponsored groups, including multiple Chinese APTs and Iran-linked APT42, have already adopted these large language models. Many cybercrime actors will continue using autonomous tools because increased reach compensates for any decreases in success rates.

The articles explain that attackers still use compromised credentials and target unpatched systems, but the scale has increased. Google first noted an increase in LLMJacking in November, where hackers hijack AI systems to resell usage tokens. This trend toward automation reached a critical inflection point, as reported by the Google Threat Intelligence Group. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 also found a Chinese-speaking threat actor using the open-source Cairn tool on many organisations. These frameworks rely on large language models and agentic frameworks to automate the heavy lifting of hacking.

Google anticipates that intrusions will become nearly fully agentic, leading to reduced human involvement and increased stealth and sophistication. Defenders currently have a small advantage because unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic and leaves behind distinct code-level traces. However, as agentic pen testing frameworks improve, attackers may no longer need to trade their speed for operational stealth. Matt Hartman suggests that defenders must nail cybersecurity fundamentals and accelerate the shift toward automated defenses to respond quickly. The articles leave open how defenders will successfully implement these automated responses to match the speed of AI.

stories.Headline: UH to predict invasive beetle spread with AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience are developing an artificial intelligence tool to predict where the invasive coconut rhinoceros beetle is most likely to spread. The project covers Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island and is dated November 17, 2026 in the university’s news release. Pascal Aigbedion-Atalor, an assistant professor in CTAHR’s Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences, leads the project. The $300,000 project aims to help field crews decide where to place traps and look for new infestations. The university announced the work through its news service and Big Island Video News and Hawaii News Now reported it the same day.

The team will use machine learning to analyze local conditions that help the beetle survive and map areas where it is most likely to spread. Researchers plan to test the predictions against field observations to improve the tool’s accuracy. The maps could help crews decide where to place pheromone-baited traps and focus their efforts to contain the beetle. Researchers could also adapt the approach to help protect Hawaiʻi crops from other invasive pests. Funding comes from the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research through its Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research program, with matching support from CTAHR.

Aigbedion-Atalor said knowing where the coconut rhinoceros beetle is likely to spread gives farmers and response teams a major advantage. He said the technology aims to help farmers and agriculture officials act early, target high-risk areas and protect valuable crops and landscapes. Kathy Munkvold, scientific program director at the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research, said stopping invasive pests before they spread is one of the best ways to protect American agriculture. She said the research gives farmers a head start against a devastating introduced pest, helping to protect crops, livelihoods and the future of Hawaiʻi’s agriculture. CTAHR Dean Parwinder Grewal said mitigating the CRB crisis cannot be accomplished by a single organization.

Grewal said it takes a combined effort, from state agricultural inspectors and federal biosecurity officials to private funders and everyday community members checking their backyards. UH researchers are working with state agencies, federal partners, private organizations and residents to help limit the beetle’s spread. The maps would support those efforts by showing crews where to focus their fieldwork. Last week, it was reported for the first time that a coconut rhinoceros beetle was discovered in the Puna district on Hawaiʻi island. The Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity said the live, male CRB was found in a trap in the Kurtistown area.

The university’s news release describes the project as a two-minute read and lists it under agriculture, AI, entomology and invasive species tags. The release names the College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience and the Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences as the units involved. Big Island Video News reported the story under a summary saying the tool will predict where the invasive CRB is most likely to spread in Hawaiʻi. Hawaii News Now reported that the project aims to help farmers and response teams identify high-risk areas on Kauai, Maui and Hawaii Island. Hawaii News Now also reported that UH officials said the technology could eventually be adapted to help protect Hawaii crops from other invasive pests.

Researchers plan to test their predictions against field observations, and the maps could help crews decide where to place traps and focus efforts to detect and contain new infestations. The articles do not say when the tool will be finished or when the maps will be available to field crews. The articles do not say how many traps would be placed or where on Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island the mapping would begin. The articles do not say whether the Kurtistown beetle find is connected to the new prediction project. The articles do not give the outcome of any testing of the predictions against field observations.

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure stocks plunge as investors reduce exposure before Nvidia reports results
stories.Summary:
AI infrastructure stocks faced a wave of selling on Monday, extending losses beyond chipmakers to companies supplying computing capacity and networking equipment. CoreWeave, Oracle, and Nebius all plunged as investors reduced their exposure to AI businesses before Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday. CoreWeave and Nebius each lost 7 percent, while Oracle dropped 4 percent during the morning trading session on that Monday. Other affected companies included Iren and Applied Digital, which also traded lower as the broader AI sector experienced significant market weakness. This decline follows a period of turmoil for neoclouds fearing that debt fueled data center expansion could backfire if demand slows.

Nebius reported third quarter revenue of 980.8 million dollars, including 325.1 million dollars in non recurring strategic partnership payments that raised questions. The company disclosed a 40 billion dollar capital spending plan for 2027, which rattled investors sensitive to the pace of infrastructure buildout. Applied Digital maintains a 36.2 billion dollar lease book, with CoreWeave holding 11 billion dollars and a hyperscaler holding 20.2 billion dollars. Iren has a 3.4 billion dollar customer relationship with Nvidia, while CoreWeave bonds currently yield above 17 percent in the market. Marvell proposed an all stock purchase of Lumentum valued at approximately 115 billion dollars, though analysts question if the deal proceeds.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters that greater scrutiny could slow data center construction, but he does not expect significantly altered plans. He stated there will be no impact to planned capacity additions over the next year and the company will avoid unsecured debt. Dan Sheehan of Telos Wealth Advisors said CoreWeave earnings addressed the fear that had driven the previous selloff in AI stocks. Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei noted that CoreWeave delivered a great quarter and addressed funding concerns with strategic moves. Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress is scheduled to hold a meeting with employees on Wednesday following the departure of Jensen Huang.

Bank of America flagged that Nebius guidance implies a sequential revenue decline in the fourth quarter due to third party data center delays. SoftBank took a 3.7 billion dollar writedown on non refundable equipment payments, contributing to a second quarter net loss of 7 billion dollars. Republican Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called for Jensen Huang to step down as CEO amid a company crisis. Applied Digital CEO Wes Cummins stated the company must still finance approximately 800 MW of capacity over the coming 12 months. Investors in Nebius, Iren, Oracle, and Applied Digital previously cheered gains between 6 and 14 percent after CoreWeave reported strong growth.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following allegations of a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who was alleged to be a spy for Beijing. This controversy escalated with allegations that the relationship aided multi billion dollar Nvidia chip shipments to China, causing the AI industry to reel. Democratic midterm sweep candidates campaigned for tighter regulation and moratoriums on new data center construction, specifically in the crucial market of Texas. Most AI infrastructure stocks lost 32 to 48 percent this year, although Nebius surged 60 percent before the recent market decline. U.S. producer prices rose 6.5 percent annually in October, marking the largest yearly increase in four years for the United States.

Nvidia is expected to pull back on AI investments and credit guarantees following the exit of Jensen Huang as the company CEO. Nebius was due to report results before the opening bell on Thursday, while Applied Digital reports fiscal second quarter earnings in January. The market is pricing in risks for Applied Digital, which trades under 5x forward sales compared to an 11x average multiple. Analysts warn that CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the crunch in AI computing capacity eventually eases. The articles leave open whether the Marvell purchase of Lumentum will proceed and how the Nvidia leadership transition will impact investments.

stories.Headline: Warsh says AI could lift growth and warns of job losses and market drops
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday that artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and bring faster economic growth, in remarks at the Fed's San Francisco branch. He acknowledged that AI adoption could also cause widespread job loss or a steep stock market drop if expected healthy returns on huge AI infrastructure investments do not materialize. His remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the San Francisco branch. He did not mention inflation, though many colleagues blame data center buildout for accelerating price increases. He did not comment on the Fed's next interest rate steps or on government data showing inflation accelerated last month.

Warsh said AI could supercharge idea generation and appears to be changing the method and speed of innovation, and that growth could be sustained substantially higher than the long-run average if idea generation broadens. The Fed calls AI super intelligence following an executive order by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Warsh said great opportunities rarely come risk free and the risks can be highly disruptive and economically costly. He said expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall after significant capital investment and stock market gains, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, and the conference was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on economic efficiency.

Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. He has long said, including before his nomination as Fed chair, that AI could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, enabling it to grow without worsening inflation, and the Fed could potentially lower interest rates under that scenario. He spent more time in his remarks considering AI's downsides than in previous speeches. He has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost efficiency. He did not address AI's impact on inflation, a top concern of many Fed colleagues.

Several policymakers last week expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics, and the government said last week that smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time even if inflation declines. Jefferson said permanently higher productivity growth may increase firms' desire to invest and their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates. Many of Warsh's colleagues on the rate-setting committee signaled support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December.

The government data showed inflation accelerated last month, leading many of Warsh's colleagues on the rate-setting committee to signal support for additional interest rate hikes. Warsh's generally optimistic outlook on the new technology is at odds with many of his colleagues. Meta data centers operate near Social Circle, Georgia, as shown in a file photo dated September 5, 2026. Warsh spoke at a news conference at the Federal Reserve in Washington on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. The conference was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency.

Warsh did not say what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates. He did not say anything about the recent government data showing inflation accelerated last month. The articles leave open what the Fed's next steps on interest rates will be and what Warsh would say about the inflation data. The articles leave open how the Fed staff's scenarios for AI's impact may play out. The articles leave open what the task force Warsh set up will conclude about AI and economic efficiency. The articles leave open whether the additional interest rate hikes that many colleagues signaled support for will occur at the December meeting.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO as the stock falls nearly 30% in a month
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia, and uncertainty over who will run the business has weighed on its valuation. Nvidia has been in a tailspin over the past week, and in just the past month it has declined by nearly 30%. David Jagielski, CPA, of The Motley Fool wrote the article, published on November 17, 2026. The article names Alphabet, Amazon, and Broadcom as AI stocks that may be more attractive options right now. The article says there are no guarantees things will get better for Nvidia in the weeks ahead.

Alphabet trades under the tickers GOOG and GOOGL, and its market cap of $3.4 trillion remains lower than Nvidia's $3.7 trillion valuation. Alphabet has a dominant position in online search through Google and in video sharing through YouTube, plus opportunities in robotaxis through Waymo and AI chatbots through Gemini. Alphabet trades at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of a little under 20, in line with the average S&P 500 stock. Amazon trades under the ticker AMZN at a $2.8 trillion market cap, and it reported 12% revenue growth for the September quarter. Amazon Web Services grew at a rate of 39%, Amazon offers Amazon Haul to appeal to price-conscious shoppers, and CEO Andy Jassy said its chip operation could bring in $50 billion in annual sales if it were a stand-alone operation. Amazon's forward P/E multiple is just 24, and Broadcom trades under the ticker AVGO with a forward P/E of 18.

Broadcom's most recent quarter ended on Aug. 2, when revenue rose by 86% year over year, totaling $29.6 billion. Broadcom's growth rate is expected to rise to 93% for the last quarter of its fiscal year. Broadcom's stock is down 2% this year, and it has fallen more than 30% from its 52-week high of $495. Jagielski wrote that he had not always felt Broadcom was a good buy because he felt its valuation was too inflated. Jagielski wrote that he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, and The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Amazon, Broadcom, and Nvidia.

The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team identified 10 best stocks for investors to buy now, and Alphabet was not one of them. The article says Netflix made that list on December 17, 2004, and a $1,000 investment at the time of the recommendation would have been worth $327,620. The article says Nvidia made the list on April 15, 2005, and a $1,000 investment at the time of the recommendation would have been worth $959,410. Stock Advisor's total average return is 802%, compared to 205% for the S&P 500, with returns as of November 17, 2026. The article was originally published by The Motley Fool.

A second article, by Leo Sun of Motley Fool for The Globe and Mail, published November 17, 2026, compares SK Hynix and Micron. SK Hynix trades under the ticker SKHY, is based in South Korea, and is the world's second-largest producer of DRAM and NAND memory chips after Samsung. Micron trades under the ticker MU, is based in the U.S., and ranks third in both markets. Both companies generate most of their revenue from DRAM chips rather than NAND chips, and both rely on HBM, a specialized high-density DRAM chip that supports Nvidia's data center GPUs in AI clusters. Both stocks soared as the AI boom fueled demand for HBM chips but pulled back sharply over the past two months.

SK Hynix became the first memory chipmaker to mass-produce HBM3 chips in 2022, started producing HBM3E chips in 2024, and started producing HBM4 chips in early 2026. SK Hynix still leads the global HBM market, while Samsung and Micron rank second and third. Micron completely skipped the HBM3 generation, started mass-producing its first HBM3E chips in 2024, and made the leap to HBM4 chips in early 2026. As the two companies allocate more capacity to HBM chips, they have less capacity for conventional DRAM and NAND chips, causing a shortage of other memory chip types. In 2025, SK Hynix's revenue surged 47%, its gross margin expanded from 48.1% to 60.3%, and its net income soared 117%.

For 2026, analysts expect SK Hynix's revenue to jump 275% and its net income to rise more than sixfold. In fiscal 2026, which ended in September, Micron's revenue more than tripled, its gross margin more than doubled to 80.7%, and its net income rose nearly tenfold. Analysts expect SK Hynix's revenue to rise 60% in 2027 and 17% in 2028, and Micron's revenue to soar 107% in fiscal 2027, followed by 16% growth in fiscal 2028 and nearly flat growth in fiscal 2029. SK Hynix trades at just three times this year's earnings, while Micron trades at four times this year's earnings. Inflation and elevated interest rates could curb AI spending and make it more difficult for smaller neocloud companies to expand, and construction of new data centers in the U.S. could be more tightly regulated in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia after the Democrats swept the midterm elections in early November.

Sun wrote that both stocks could experience significant volatility over the next 12 months. Sun wrote that if he had to pick one, he would stick with SK Hynix instead of Micron for three reasons: it is larger, it is growing faster, and it will remain the market leader in HBM chips. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team identified 10 best stocks for investors to buy now, and SK Hynix was not one of them. Sun wrote that he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, and The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Nvidia. The Globe and Mail states it has not reviewed, approved, or endorsed the syndicated content and may receive compensation for placement of the content on its site.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy proposes a one-year pause on city AI procurement
stories.Summary:
On December 3, the Portland City Council will hear a proposal from Council President Jamie Dunphy to establish a temporary moratorium on the City government's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. The proposal would pause new contracts and limit the expansion of AI use in City operations. The pause would last while the City implements enforceable privacy infrastructure and policy guardrails needed to evaluate AI technologies responsibly. The news was reported on November 17, 2026, by News Radio 1190 KEX and other iHeart stations. Dunphy said emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City.

The proposal would pause new contracts and limit expansion of AI in City operations while the City implements privacy infrastructure and policy guardrails. Dunphy said the City cannot go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code. He said his goal is to protect public privacy, security, and civil rights while the administration makes the City's Data and Privacy Office fully operable and adopts comprehensive legislative guidelines. AI is increasingly embedded in software and services sold to the government, including tools that generate content, analyze personal data, and support or automate decisions that affect the public. Dunphy said governments and broader society are being pushed to accept advanced AI as though it were an unavoidable inevitability, and he said they are not.

Dunphy said he understands private companies' desire to rush to adopt these technologies to reduce costs and increase efficiency. He said the government is not beholden to profit-driven shareholders and must move more intentionally. He said the job is to serve the best interest of the public, which means considering the impacts on real people. He said that is not being slow but taking time for critical thinking. Dunphy said his staff spent the last calendar year trying to get more information on the structural thinking behind the current internal process.

Dunphy said his staff found the guardrails and access to those guidelines unsatisfactory, considering the stakes of these choices and the vulnerability of community members to data leaks. A recent WIRED article quotes Yoshua Bengio, a computer science professor at the Université de Montréal considered a godfather of modern AI, saying pauses are our best bets to avoid the most catastrophic things. Bengio said it takes time for democracy to adapt. He said a pause would give more time to organizations to figure out how to solve the alignment problem, if it is solvable. Governor Kotek recently signed Executive Order 26-26, Establishing Responsible Artificial Intelligence Procurement Standards for State Government.

The order acknowledges the State must proceed with caution and clear parameters before implementing frontier AI models. Dunphy said the City's pause aligns with the Governor's leadership as the State takes time to weigh government-wide use of frontier AI. The City established a Data and Privacy Office, led by a Citywide Data Officer, through Ordinance 192143 on March 7, 2026. That office is not yet operable and cannot review technology contracts. Without this expertise and clear Code guidelines, the City does not yet have a holistic system of checks and balances to ensure good data governance.

By pausing approval of new AI, the policy commits to ensuring the office is operable and ready to evaluate the privacy, security, and civil rights risks of AI before procuring, piloting, or implementing expanded uses of AI. The articles do not say when the Council will vote on the proposal or how long the temporary moratorium would last. The articles do not say whether the proposal has enough Council support to pass. The articles do not name any other Council members or their positions on the proposal. The articles do not say what specific AI tools or contracts the City currently uses.

stories.Headline: DataMEDS AI interim co-CEO Gerald Commissiong authors Q4 outlook letter on cutting healthcare costs
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the healthcare company DataMEDS AI released a corporate outlook for the fourth quarter of the year. Interim Co-CEO Gerald Commissiong provided the details of this strategic update to the public. The company is listed on the NASDAQ exchange under the ticker symbol MEDS. This announcement was distributed through ACCESS Newswire from the company headquarters in Tampa, Florida. The letter outlines a plan to fix the broken American healthcare system.

The strategy integrates the EinsteinRx artificial intelligence platform and the PharmacyChain blockchain enabled smart contracts platform. DataMEDS uses the Health Lives Here mobile application from Tollo Health, LLC, and its subsidiary Corexa Health. The company also owns Helomics Corporation, a commercial clinical molecular diagnostics laboratory based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. This laboratory focuses on the ChemoFx Assay chemotherapy selection diagnostics test for oncologists. The plan involves working with a Florida based Health Maintenance Organization to manage member health journeys.

Interim Co-CEO Gerald Commissiong stated that the focus must return to helping both insured and uninsured patients. He said the business model aims to cut out middlemen to ensure payors pay fair prices. Commissiong believes leveraging patient data can rein in stakeholders who are currently overcompensated and gouging the industry. He noted that the company seeks to narrow the arbitrage between healthcare costs and actual results. He believes the company can improve outcomes and reduce costs through GLP-1 patient management.

The company believes that most patients are willing to allow their de-identified data to be used for treatment. Institutional payors are identified as the target clients who see potential value in this scalable business model. The company aims to provide a better alternative for long term repeat customers than current treatment options. Shareholders are also affected as the company seeks to create synergies to deliver value to them. The process involves using patient flow through delivery portals to create new data inputs for research.

The company was formerly known as Wellgistics Health, Inc., and is currently completing a turnaround started in the second quarter. A report from Menlo Ventures states that healthcare AI spend grew 2.5 times to reach 3.7 billion dollars. This report notes that AI for drug discovery spend jumped from 30 million to 700 million dollars. Clinical copilots grew 5.5 times to 550 million dollars, while patient engagement grew 4.5 times to 450 million dollars. Payer AI spend lags behind provider spend by a factor of 19 times.

DataMEDS has 5,724,857 common shares outstanding, with 2,745,900 shares deposited in the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation. Certain stockholders holding 1,333,930 shares are under lock up agreements for at least ninety days from the date. There are 80,826 cash warrants outstanding with a fixed exercise price of 35.00 dollars per share. The company plans to drive for scale in 2027 after generating proof of concept revenue. The articles leave open the actual success of the operational turnaround and the achievement of profitability.
