stories.Headline: ControlUp launches AI Visibility & Usage Insights for IT to track AI tool adoption
stories.Summary:
ControlUp announced AI Visibility & Usage Insights on November 17, 2026, a new capability giving IT a unified view of AI tools adoption, usage, and experience across the organization. The company said IT teams can see how employees use AI applications including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Notion AI, and others. ControlUp described itself as a company reinventing IT operations with its AI platform. The announcement was published by David Marshall on VMblog and by GlobeNewswire in The Manila Times. The capability is a new addition to ControlUp's product line for IT operations.

The capability includes a unified AI application inventory showing tools in use, including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Codex, and Notion AI, with application type, user counts, and top-used models. It offers adoption and usage insights tracking active employees, total usage, and average usage per user across devices and platforms. AI experience scoring gives an average AI score and per-application scores to highlight apps that may need attention. Platform and environment context shows which browsers, operating systems, and device groups employees use, such as how Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise usage varies by browser and operating system. Physical PC and remote desktop comparison contrasts AI usage and experience between employees on physical PCs and those on remote desktops, including virtual desktop infrastructure, desktop-as-a-service, and other remote environments.

PII risk visibility tracks and reports on sensitive data such as API keys and banking information that employees may expose through AI. Flexible filtering focuses on groups by app, browser, platform, operating system, or device tag. Gartner projects generative AI model spending will grow from $13 billion in 2025 to $139 billion by 2030, citing Forecast: AI Spending, Worldwide, 2025-2030, 3Q26, published October 7, 2026, by Kay Arnott, Jon Erensen, Amarendra ., Adrian O'Connell, and Arunasree Chepa. Bob Johnson, SVP Global Partnerships & Alliances at ControlUp, said employees are adopting AI tools faster than IT can track, leaving admins unable to answer basic questions about shadow AI, adoption, or spend. Johnson said the capability gives IT a clear picture of AI tool adoption to guide governance, plan training, and optimize AI investments based on real usage, not guesswork.

ControlUp said IT teams can drive AI adoption by seeing where licensed users are active and where adoption is lagging. It said teams can improve employee experience by spotting underperforming AI applications early. It said teams can plan investment with confidence by comparing adoption and performance to decide where to expand, consolidate, or add enablement. It said teams can establish usage guardrails with a shared, evidence-based view of the AI tools in use across the organization. The articles state that IT teams are being asked to manage spend and demonstrate value, yet many lack a clear picture of the AI application footprint, including which tools employees use, on which devices, and where more support would help.

ControlUp said AI adoption is accelerating across the enterprise as employees use a growing mix of AI assistants, coding tools, and embedded AI features. The capability gives IT a data-backed baseline and a clear view of the AI footprint in their environment. ControlUp described its platform as built on real-time data, intelligent decisions, and automated action to help IT teams detect, resolve, and prevent issues before they impact the business. The platform delivers Autonomous Endpoint Management, unifying Digital Employee Experience capabilities with agentic AI to move organizations beyond reactive troubleshooting toward proactive, intelligent operations at scale. ControlUp ONE integrates real-time signals with AI-driven decisioning and automated remediation to reduce operational complexity and consolidate fragmented toolsets.

Attendees can experience AI Visibility & Usage Insights live at the ControlUp booth #5257L at Microsoft Ignite, November 17, 20 in San Francisco. ControlUp experts will demo how IT teams can baseline Copilot adoption and extend that visibility across their AI landscape. AI Visibility & Usage Insights is offered as an add-on module available to all ControlUp for Apps and ControlUp for Desktops Advanced customers. ControlUp directed readers to request a demo at https://www.controlup.com/schedule-a-demo/. The articles did not state pricing for the add-on module or a general availability date beyond the announcement.

stories.Headline: Anthropic warns that current AI safety tests are too easy and fail to capture advanced model capabilities
stories.Summary:
The frontier AI lab Anthropic issued a warning about safety tests on Friday, November 17, 2026. The company stated that current evaluations for artificial intelligence models have become too easy. These tests fail to capture the full breadth of capabilities in advanced models. Labs have focused on measuring how models follow directions and remain safe. Anthropic believes that these safety evaluations now have a significant problem.

The lab suggests building testing teams with experts who can sample, grade, and analyze responses. Domain experts must cover realistic test cases, and safety tests should be run in a sandbox. Enterprises must match evaluation designs to specific questions and use nuanced simulations to ensure results generalize. Tests should be neither too easy nor too hard for the models to complete. This approach replaces single-turn tasks with more expansive multi-turn conversations to reduce saturation.

Anthropic said that a single headline number for harmless response rates provides only an honest summary. The lab noted that more nuance is generally needed to make the findings useful. They explained that humans extract harmful information through gradual escalation over several prompts. The company stated that user distress tends to accumulate across a conversation and changes context. They argued that frontier labs should focus on these realistic, subtle situations of villainy.

Many experts warned that current tests miss how persistent AI models are in achieving goals. These concerns affect frontier labs and enterprises that rely on these safety benchmarks for security. Some testers attempt to goad models into divulging blueprints for a nuclear weapon. Malicious users avoid direct requests because they know models are experts at denying them. These users instead keep conversations going to break safeguards by the fifth turn.

Benchmarks have come under scrutiny recently after rogue AI agents began going against their instructions. Models are now outgrowing benchmarks because their capabilities exceed what current safety evaluations can test. Single-turn evaluations on the Anthropic API consistently score between 94 percent and 98 percent. Multi-turn responses show a wider range of harmless behavior response rates than single-turn tasks. This background shows that models handle first messages well but may respond inappropriately later.

Anthropic and OpenAI have paused training on their models to strengthen safety and alignment guardrails. They are working to improve safety testing procedures to keep pace with advanced models. The lab intends to incorporate more multi-turn evaluations to give researchers a better idea of abilities. The articles do not state when the paused training for these models will resume. They also leave open how other frontier labs will respond to these safety warnings.

stories.Headline: Susanta Ghosh finds AI models need 90% less training data for accurate materials predictions
stories.Summary:
A collaborative team led by Michigan Technological University Associate Professor Susanta Ghosh found that artificial intelligence models need less data than previously thought to produce accurate predictions in the development of novel materials. The study was recently published in npj Computational Materials, and the work was conducted with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles. Developing new materials often starts with understanding their electronic structure, or how electrons are arranged and behave within them. Calculating these electronic structures typically requires expensive simulations in supercomputers, which led researchers to train artificial intelligence models on millions of simulated data points to make faster predictions. According to the recent study led by Ghosh in Michigan Tech's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, that much training data isn't necessary.

The research team found that AI models could discard 90% of their training data with virtually no loss in accuracy. Even after removing 99% of the training data, most predictions stayed highly accurate, while the models trained three or more times faster. The new findings apply to an expansive range of materials, including metals, water and complex alloys. Ghosh says the answer is by using a minimal dataset carefully selected by researchers that is sufficient to capture the diversity of the data. These findings challenge the necessity of extensive datasets for electronic structure predictions, and could make AI-driven materials development faster and less costly.

Ghosh is a faculty member of the Center for Artificial Intelligence in Michigan Tech's Institute of Computing and Cybersystems, and he believes this could have a large impact in the field of materials development and modeling. Ghosh said that much of the electronic structure data repeats the same information, and that a small, well-chosen sample captures nearly everything the AI needs to learn. He said that by identifying representative electronic-structure data and reducing training time by at least threefold, this work can accelerate AI-driven discovery of complex alloys across vast composition spaces. Ghosh's study was conducted in collaboration with a team led by Assistant Professor Amartya Banerjee from UCLA's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. The collaboration also included MTU alumnus Ponkrshnan Thiagarajan '23, who completed his Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering-Engineering Mechanics at Tech and is currently a postdoctoral fellow at the Hopkins Extreme Materials Institute.

Research was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, the National Science Foundation, and the University of California Office of the President. Michigan Technological University is an R1 public research university founded in 1885 in Houghton, and is home to nearly 7,500 students from more than 60 countries around the world. The university is consistently ranked among the best universities in the country for return on investment, and Michigan's flagship technological university offers more than 185 undergraduate and graduate degree programs. Those programs span science, technology, engineering, mathematics, computing, forestry, business, health professions, robotics, psychology, social sciences, humanities, and the arts. The rural campus is situated just miles from Lake Superior in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, offering year-round opportunities for outdoor adventure.

stories.Headline: OpenAI releases a free image classifier that detects child sexual abuse material and flags AI-generated CSAM
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material on November 16, 2026, according to its blog post. The tool is an image classifier that looks for visual signs of abuse in images. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. OpenAI said this is the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific signal indicating if CSAM may be AI generated. OpenAI also released product warnings in ChatGPT, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators.

The classifier is offered at no cost through the OpenAI API to vetted organizations, including child safety organizations and the broader industry. OpenAI trained and designed it with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, OpenAI estimated the new classifier would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool. Images flagged by the new classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse. In fal's testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier's high-confidence flags as novel CSAM, invideo AI's testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban, and SafetyKit's evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children found the classifier detected 90% of cases.

OpenAI said individual companies have a responsibility to prevent their technology from being exploited by predators to harm children. John Shehan, Senior Vice President at NCMEC, said technology has an essential role in helping identify CSAM and the children depicted in it. Shehan said the new classifier gives more organizations access to tools that can help detect previously unidentified CSAM and strengthen reporting. Thorn said protecting children requires more than any single solution or organization and commended OpenAI for working with organizations throughout the child protection ecosystem. OpenAI said it engaged the Tech Coalition and ROOST to help share access to the tool and recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program.

A Childlight analysis at the University of Edinburgh found AI-related reports of CSAM increased globally by more than 8,400 percent from 2023 to 2025. Last year NCMEC received more than 400,000 of these reports, compared with roughly 4,700 in 2023. The ChatGPT warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, OpenAI will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

OpenAI developed the warning approach with input from Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha of the University of Kent, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. OpenAI published CSAM guidance developed with input from the Tech Coalition, Thorn, NCMEC, and the Internet Watch Foundation. OpenAI worked with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems, recently published by the Tech Coalition. OpenAI said this guidance has led to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI said it already prohibits CSAM, trains its models to refuse requests for it, and takes action against accounts that violate its policies.

The first law enforcement tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material. The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences. Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through OpenAI's intake form, and OpenAI said it will continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

stories.Headline: OpenAI releases a free image classifier and 24-hour ChatGPT pause to fight child abuse material
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced new AI-powered tools on Monday, November 16, 2026, to combat child sexual abuse material on its ChatGPT platform, according to the company. The announcement took place at a press briefing in Washington, DC, where OpenAI unveiled an image classifier that detects potential child sexual abuse material, including AI-generated imagery. OpenAI released new guidelines for developers and a suite of tools for law enforcement agencies as part of the same initiative. The company also added new warning screens to ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualises children. OpenAI developed the classifier in partnership with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

The classifier scans images for visual signs of abuse and assigns a score to give reviewers an indication of content, and during early testing it flagged 48 per cent fewer images while detecting the same number of abusive images. Images flagged by the classifier were twice as likely to be CSAM, which reduces the workload for human reviewers. Select organisations like Tech Coalition and ROOST will initially access the classifier through its API without extra cost. When users attempt to prompt ChatGPT for CSAM or related content, they will see an alert directing them to specialised support, and their accounts will be suspended for 24 hours as a warning. OpenAI reports all identified CSAM on its platforms to NCMEC, and the public coverage does not establish the classifier's official product name, a release price beyond the free tier for vetted groups, technical accuracy, model specifications, training-data details, or how many organizations are receiving access.

OpenAI says the tool can tell AI-generated abusive imagery apart from authentic imagery involving children, a distinction that matters because investigators treat the two categories differently. The company frames the tool around efficiency, saying investigators spend much of their working week looking at disturbing images to decide which ones demand action. OpenAI says its Stop It Now helpline regularly hears from people who report that an AI chatbot sent them there, though the company has not published a count of those contacts. OpenAI says new ChatGPT warnings will interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and direct users toward specialist help, and when the warning triggers it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. The public coverage does not include a direct quote from an individually named OpenAI representative, and the wording reported is attributed to OpenAI as a company.

The messages and guidelines were framed in partnership with Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan, a researcher at the University of Tasmania. The Internet Watch Foundation, a UK hotline, reported 3,440 AI-generated CSAM videos in 2025, up from 13 in 2024, and classified 65 per cent of those videos, or 2,233, as Category A, the most severe tier under UK law. Childlight data reported on November 16, 2026 put referrals of AI-generated material to NCMEC at about 4,700 in 2023 and more than 400,000 in 2025, an implied two-year change of about 8,400 per cent. IWF also classified 30 per cent of those videos, or 1,027, as Category B. Small nonprofits and under-resourced police units stand to gain the most from free access, but only if the vetting process is quick enough for them to use.

Google and Microsoft have long offered hash-matching, content classifiers, and reporting or moderation tools, while Meta uses automated detection, hash databases, human review, and NCMEC reporting. Thorn's Safer platform gives trust-and-safety teams tools to detect, review, and report CSAM. A hash catches a file someone already identified but fails on a freshly generated image that no one has seen, while a classifier can flag new material, which is why synthetic abuse pushes the industry toward models. For most of the past two decades, the fight against online child abuse imagery rested on a shared database model in which platforms hashed known files and compared uploads. OpenAI's distinct move is the bundle, pairing a free classifier for vetted groups with developer guidance, police training, and user-facing warnings inside its own product.

OpenAI will provide law enforcement agencies with AI-powered child safety tools, including dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, and is offering investigators training sessions and a reference guide on AI use. Developers using OpenAI tools will receive guidelines to help them prevent, detect, and report CSAM content to NCMEC. The public coverage does not explain how removal of flagged conversations interacts with preservation for investigators, a detail to watch as law-enforcement groups start using the system. Whether the tool reliably separates synthetic from authentic imagery is the open question, because OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. Readers should expect child-safety groups to ask for a model card, an audit path, or both, and the sources reviewed for this story contain no evidence that either is public.

stories.Headline: Karnataka chief minister D K Shivakumar launches six AI and semiconductor initiatives at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026
stories.Summary:
Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar launched six initiatives at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, which opened on November 17, 2026, in Bengaluru. The summit runs from November 17 to 19 and is themed "AI & Beyond". The Karnataka AI Hub was officially launched at the summit and is established at IIIT-Bengaluru. The state government had earlier approved a ₹35 crore budget for the Karnataka AI Hub. The summit's exhibitors come from more than 75 countries, according to its official website.

The Karnataka AI Hub will focus on AI research, skilling, innovation and entrepreneurship, and is the first step towards the state's proposed AI University. BRAINZ, the Bengaluru Robotics and AI Innovation Zone, is an envisioned 9-acre facility in collaboration with ARTPARK at the Indian Institute of Science. BRAINZ aims to catalyse investments of ₹1,000 crore over five years. The state is supporting IISc's proposed 200-mm research and pilot-line facility under the 2D Innovation Hub, which includes a technology building of about 100,000 sq ft, a 15,000 sq ft cleanroom and 80 to 90 process, metrology and testing tools. The state is also supporting INFIfab, a proposed national facility for semiconductor fabrication, advanced packaging and technology translation, covering about 96,284 sq ft including a 20,000 sq ft cleanroom, with focus areas including MEMS, photonics, quantum technologies and neuromorphic computing.

K-HEAL is a Centre of Excellence for healthcare, medical and assistive technology, and a flagship programme of the Department of Electronics, IT & BT. Innoverse aims to support 35 growth-stage deeptech ventures over five years, including autonomous systems and technologies from underwater applications to space. Shivakumar said Karnataka laid the foundations of modern industry and technology through institutions of learning and research, strong public sector enterprises and the trust of global companies. He said some of India's most ambitious scientific and engineering projects have found a home in Karnataka. He said, "We will bring the talent, the policies and the partnership.

You bring your ambition." Shivakumar said Karnataka accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports. He said the state received $9.4 billion in foreign direct investment equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India's total inflows during the period. He said more than 1,000 global capability centres have established operations in Bengaluru, and the state is home to more than 100 fabless chip companies. He said three out of every five engineers working in India's semiconductor capability centres were based in Bengaluru, and global companies are investing more than ₹23,000 crore in semiconductor research and manufacturing facilities in Bengaluru and Mysuru.

The state is developing four electronics manufacturing clusters from Dharwad to Mysuru. The government announced proposed AI skilling programmes with Google, Salesforce, Pega Systems, Sarvam AI and Gnani.ai, targeting 63,200 engineering and diploma students and professionals. The programmes will cover generative AI, agentic AI, voice AI, cloud computing, data analytics and responsible AI, combining classroom instruction with practical exercises, industry tools, capstone projects and certification pathways. Under the ₹300-crore Nipuna Karnataka reskilling mission, more than 33,000 people have already become industry-ready through partnerships with technology companies. Karnataka is home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, with nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns originating from the state.

Through its ELEVATE programme, the government has supported nearly 1,500 startups with $41 million in equity-free grants over a decade, and under ELEVATE NxT, 33 deeptech startups have received ₹30 crore in grants since last year. The government has allocated ₹25 crore under its Government First initiative to procure innovative solutions developed by startups. Shivakumar said the state accounts for one-fifth of India's bioeconomy, valued at $39.2 billion last year, and the government plans to expand biotechnology into marine resources, agriculture and healthcare. The Karnataka AI Hub aims to develop a globally competitive workforce and facilitate the application of research in practical fields.

BRAINZ will bring together research institutions, industries and startups working in robotics, artificial intelligence and deeptech. The 2D Innovation Hub facility will serve as a shared platform for academic institutions and industry partners to undertake semiconductor research and development. K-HEAL will connect clinicians, researchers, industries and startups to identify unmet healthcare requirements, develop and validate technological solutions and facilitate their adoption. Innoverse will support Karnataka-based deeptech startups that have already developed and validated their technologies and are looking to expand their market presence and global operations.

The articles do not say when the proposed AI University, BRAINZ, the 2D Innovation Hub facility or INFIfab will be built or opened. The articles do not name the cost of BRAINZ, the 2D Innovation Hub facility or INFIfab. The articles do not say which company will run each AI skilling programme or when the training will begin. The articles do not say how the six initiatives will be funded beyond the ₹35 crore approved for the Karnataka AI Hub.

stories.Headline: SAP engineers contribute to Nvidia OpenShell as SAP embeds it in its Business AI Platform
stories.Summary:
SAP and Nvidia are deepening their collaboration to make autonomous AI agents in enterprises safer, more controllable and fully auditable, the companies said, with the open-source secure runtime environment OpenShell to be deeply embedded in the newly consolidated SAP Business AI Platform. Thomas Pfiester, Head of Customer Engagement and Adoption and a member of SAP's Extended Board, presented SAP's vision of the Autonomous Enterprise in a keynote at the 2026 DSAG Annual Congress in Cologne on Tuesday, October 6, and referred to the Nvidia partnership when asked how existing SAP customers keep AI agents under control. Andre Lamego, Senior Vice President and Chief Product Officer for the SAP Business AI Platform Fabric, provided the technical background, and E3 Magazine summarized and supplemented his comments. The announcement covers the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform and the widespread availability of Nvidia OpenShell, as previously announced at the SAP Sapphire customer conference.

SAP engineers are contributing directly to the Nvidia OpenShell codebase as part of the co-development effort, while the AI-centric development environment Joule Studio provides a complete execution and governance stack for enterprise agents and Nvidia's OpenShell handles secure deployment and execution within clear security boundaries. SAP's development work focuses on four specific core areas of the OpenShell project: at the platform architecture level SAP has driven the decomposition of the runtime environment into independently deployable components by separating the supervisor layer from the actual agent execution layer to enable isolated scaling. For native Kubernetes operation the contributions include operator support, the management of confidential access data known as image pull secrets for private container registries, customer-specific storage requirements called Custom Volume Claim Templates, and the orderly deletion of sandbox resources. SAP is also working to minimize the environmental and technical footprint of the gateway container image, expand driver support for heterogeneous computing infrastructures, and embed monitoring of the supervisor's operational readiness and structured logging in accordance with established observability standards.

At the governance level the Joule Studio runtime environment serves as the highest authority, checking business authorizations, role-based policies and the relevant process context before a request reaches the actual execution layer, while Nvidia OpenShell complements this with an isolated runtime sandbox that precisely controls what an agent is allowed to see and do and where inference data flows. The collaboration is supported by the goal of achieving FedRAMP and FIPS certifications for regulated industries and by participation in the newly founded Open Secure AI Alliance. SAP is making Joule Studio's runtime environment available to its customers and partners free of charge through the end of October 2026, after which, according to the article, usage-based billing relying on consumption-dependent AI Units, BTP Capacity Units and AI token prices will kick in. The article describes the free period as a classic bait-and-switch tactic common in the software industry and says existing customers fall for a costly illusion if they believe autonomous agents will remain free of charge indefinitely.

stories.Headline: Nvidia invests billions in supply chain partners to scale AI computing production
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 18, 2026, the American chipmaker Nvidia announced it is expanding manufacturing capacity with several supply chain partners. The company is collaborating with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries, and TSMC to meet long-term demand for artificial intelligence computing platforms. These partnerships aim to scale production across substrates, advanced packaging, wafer manufacturing, and contract manufacturing. This strategic move supports the growth of both current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms.

The expansion involves a multiyear agreement with Siliconware Precision Industries to grow advanced packaging operations in Taiwan by mid-2029. Kinsus Interconnect Technology received over $1 billion from Nvidia to increase advanced ABF substrate capacity at its Taoyuan facility by more than 3.5 times. Production at that site should begin in the second half of 2027, with more capacity arriving in the third quarter of 2028. Samsung Electro-Mechanics will optimize its existing factories, while Amkor Technology expands advanced packaging capacity in South Korea and Arizona.

Nvidia is responsible for these investments and stated that the expanded commitments will support the long-term growth of its AI platforms. Foxconn Chairman Young Liu explained that his company is deepening its collaboration on networking and GPU platforms. He noted that Foxconn will use its global manufacturing network across Europe, North America, and Asia to scale AI infrastructure. These efforts ensure a steady supply of critical components for the company's rapidly growing hardware ecosystem.

The company recently began volume shipments of Vera CPUs and Vera Rubin NVL72 for agentic AI during the third quarter. These specific products utilize CoWoS advanced packaging technology along with the 3-nanometre and 5-nanometre chipmaking processes from TSMC. This rollout marks a significant step in deploying next-generation hardware for complex AI tasks. The company continues to leverage these global partnerships to maintain its lead in the accelerated computing market.

stories.Headline: Cathie Wood's Ark buys Nvidia, CoreWeave and Archer Aviation and trims Palantir and Tempus AI
stories.Summary:
Cathie Wood's Ark Invest bought more Nvidia, CoreWeave and Archer Aviation and sold parts of its Tempus AI and Palantir holdings, Yahoo Finance reported on November 17, 2026. The Motley Fool's Marc Guberti wrote the article, published at 1:01 PM CST that day. Late last month Wood told a Bloomberg interviewer the AI trade is not in its first inning. She said the sector is "still in the parking lot before we entered the baseball game." She cited Palantir's 123% year-over-year U.S. revenue growth as evidence of the long-term opportunity in AI.

Most Ark Invest funds focus heavily on AI stocks, which have had a bumpy month but trended higher in recent years. Wood has put a lot of money behind her statement through Ark's exchange-traded funds. The article says AI demand will rise for chips, optical cables, liquid-cooling solutions and electricity. It says humanoid robots and self-driving vehicles are among the next big opportunities. Waymo leads the robotaxi space, and Tesla's Cybercabs are in limited production.

Wood is the founder of Ark Invest, and the article ties her bullish view to Palantir's 123% U.S. revenue growth. It says Palantir excels at agentic AI, which helps explain how the stock crushed the S&P 500 over five years. It says chipmakers keep reporting exceptional growth and enthusiasm for more AI growth in 2027 does not match recent stock performance. It says such setups create asymmetric risk opportunities but require accepting a lot of volatility. It says Wood's Ark Innovation ETF has had many downturns of 20% or more.

The article says the Ark Innovation ETF slumped more than 80% from its February 2021 peak to a December 2022 cyclical low. It says the fund is still down more than 50% from that peak despite promising periods in the intervening years. It says the fund has not recently had the upward momentum it enjoyed from the mid-2010s to 2021. It says the recent pullback in AI stocks has created a more compelling opportunity.

It says the Motley Fool holds positions in Palantir and Tesla and recommends both, and that Guberti has no position in any stock mentioned. The article says ChatGPT first had no connection to the live internet and could not take uploaded images, PDFs and other documents. It says Anthropic's Claude was similar early on but has become an autonomous digital coworker, and Claude Code can create entire apps and websites from a few prompts. It says new features will raise customer expectations, and in five to 10 years current versions of ChatGPT and Claude could look archaic.

It says Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots could become lucrative once AI robotics is ready for broad commercialization. It says 1990s investors underestimated the internet's impact, a pattern that may be taking shape with AI. The article says Stock Advisor's total average return is 802% against 205% for the S&P 500, as of November 17, 2026. It says $1,000 invested in Netflix on December 17, 2004 would be worth $327,620, and $1,000 in Nvidia on April 15, 2005 would be worth $959,410.

It says the Motley Fool's analysts named 10 best stocks to buy now and the Ark Innovation ETF was not one of them. It leaves open whether Wood's concentrated AI bet is still the right one. It does not give the size of the Nvidia, CoreWeave, Archer Aviation, Tempus AI or Palantir trades. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microsoft claims MAI Code 2 matches 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost
stories.Summary:
Microsoft unveiled a new lineup of specialized AI models at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, making a direct run at Anthropic and OpenAI in coding, cybersecurity and image generation. The company pitched models trained to do particular jobs at substantially lower cost instead of one chatbot that beats everyone at everything. The biggest claim involves MAI Code 2, which Microsoft says delivers 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance on common enterprise coding tasks for just 5% of the cost. Microsoft also claims 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the price. OpenAI also released GPT-6.2 on Tuesday, so Microsoft's Sol comparison already concerns an older generation.

Those figures average results from four evaluations focused on practical software development, including fixing code and completing multi-file changes. Microsoft ran three of the tests on its own evaluation platform, used outside results for the fourth, and calculated MAI Code 2's costs using a 50% promotional discount. A lighter Code 2 Flash model targets routine fixes and quick edits, with Microsoft claiming performance comparable to Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. Microsoft says MAI Cyber 2 Flash succeeded on 92.3% of CyberGym-E2E's evaluated vulnerability-discovery tasks, compared with 91.5% for GPT-6 Astra, at less than 2% of the cost per task. Microsoft excluded 92 of 905 tasks after identifying overlap between their source material and its training data.

Microsoft has not yet published a direct comparison against OpenAI's restricted GPT-6 Cyber model. Its security system will begin replacing an older MAI model for eligible MDASH customers in mid-December, building on the vulnerability-scanning approach Decrypt previously covered. Microsoft's own documentation says Code 2 is not yet optimized for fundamental scientific research or very long-running autonomous assignments. Microsoft quotes about $35 per 1,000 images for MAI Image 2.7 and $10 for its Flash version, versus roughly $211 for GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst at maximum quality in Artificial Analysis's comparison. Microsoft is also offering selected business customers the ability to customize and run its models' licensed weights inside Azure, reducing reliance on outside vendors without making the technology open source.

On Artificial Analysis's image-editing test, which asks people to choose between anonymously generated edits and turns those preferences into an Elo rating, MAI Image 2.7 currently leads with 1,215 points against GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst's 1,211. The four-point gap is small enough that their reported uncertainty ranges overlap, and the separate text-to-image generation ranking puts Microsoft in fourth place. Google's Nano Banana 2.1 is about $34 per 1,000 images there, while Nano Banana Pro is about $134, and actual bills depend on the provider, resolution and settings. Both coding models are already in GitHub Copilot, putting Microsoft's in-house technology directly into a product that has relied heavily on outside AI suppliers. Microsoft also announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash and which can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, and track decisions and extract useful information from Teams.

Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023 and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property. Anthropic competes in the cheaper end of the market with Haiku, not just its premium Opus models, so Microsoft is entering a race its rivals already understand. OpenAI has taken a related approach with its Mini and Nano models, letting cheaper workers handle routine tasks while larger systems tackle the exceptions. Our earlier testing of MAI Image 2 found excellent realism but frustrating limits on editing and output formats, and the newer release adds interactive editing through Microsoft's Canvas workspace, transparent backgrounds and broader access through Foundry. Microsoft says the numbers it is reporting use a 50% introductory discount, and the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided.

For the next test of its specialist strategy, Code 2 is already available in GitHub Copilot, and the Cyber 2 Flash rollout is scheduled to start in mid-December. Microsoft is touting that it is integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 and Fabric. The company has not yet published a direct comparison against OpenAI's restricted GPT-6 Cyber model. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests, and benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads.

stories.Headline: Google spends heavily on AI and rebuilds search as rivals challenge its dominance
stories.Summary:
In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report, and the company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day, the biggest single-day percentage decline since Google went public in 2004. The Planet Money newsletter asked whether Google had been caught in the innovator's dilemma. Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information, and a new generation of AI rivals is now challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was a scrappy startup working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined Google in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science, and became its 20th employee.

When Mayer interviewed at Google there were just seven people there, and by the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee. That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue, and by 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company, by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet, was generating more than $280 billion, a more than millionfold increase. Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results, monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb, and its search business became like an unstoppable money machine. In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water, but neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.

Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI, and in 2017 a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer, a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible. Mayer, now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism, saying this is not a technology that's happening to Google and that they helped invent this new technology. Today Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals, and it is overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links. The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the innovator's dilemma theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail. Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a disruptive technology, and he helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary long before it became a cliché.

Google's researchers made computers translate languages, recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go, and the company developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation, but they didn't release it. On Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore, and Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses. Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business, saying that from a search perspective you want to get the right answer 100% of the time and that these models were not near that bar. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text. Mayer questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI, saying the standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is, are fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer.

Benedict Evans, a widely read technology analyst previously a partner at the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, says that every 10 or 15 years or so a revolutionary platform shift shakes up the tech industry, giving newcomers a chance to challenge dominant companies, and that it happened with personal computers, then the internet, then smartphones, and now with AI. Evans says the whole table gets reset and the things that meant that they had won and you couldn't take them on suddenly don't matter anymore. The process toward monopolization began with Google building a better search engine than rivals, and then, Evans says, its success became self-reinforcing: more users gave Google more data to improve its results, helping it attract still more users, which economists call a network effect. Google also paid to make its search engine the default in browsers and on devices, deals that a federal judge ruled in 2024 had illegally helped maintain its search monopoly. Google runs the operating system on many of our phones, we use free Google services to send emails, write documents, find directions, and watch a stranger explain how to fix our washing machine, and many of us keep going back to Google search out of sheer habit or because we keep getting nudged to go there.

Google has fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich. The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant and as profitable in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search. Christensen warned in The Innovator's Dilemma that companies that keep disruptive technologies bottled up in their labs risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be. The articles leave open what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first, whether a Google chatbot would have taken off in the same way and given Google a first-mover advantage, or whether its flaws would have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect. The articles also leave open whether rival AI systems will borrow from Google's playbook and work to intertwine themselves into our lives.

stories.Headline: US chip export curbs disrupt Southeast Asian AI data centre growth
stories.Summary:
The United States government implemented new export restrictions on artificial intelligence chips on November 17, 2026, to stop China from accessing powerful technology. These curbs follow the sudden resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang last week after reports of several extramarital affairs. One of these relationships involved Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed, who American media identified as a suspected Chinese spy. Washington believes that Southeast Asian infrastructure was being used as a cover to funnel advanced chips into China.

These new regulations require data centre operators to license their existing remote compute services within a period of 90 days. The move comes as the United States probes Megaspeed while the broader industry faces immense pressure on supply chains. According to Bain & Company, the world needs nearly 150GW of new compute capacity by 2030, requiring an estimated US$6.5 trillion. Hyperscalers may spend over US$1 trillion in capital expenditures by 2028, while global electricity demand for data centres is expected to rise from 589TWh in 2026 to 1,228TWh by 2030.

Washington officials are working to contain the fallout from this scandal involving a former White House ally and industry leader. They claim the measures are necessary to close a back door that allowed the world's most powerful chips to reach prohibited destinations. The government is now scrutinizing the role of Singapore-based firms in facilitating these unauthorized technology transfers. These actions aim to protect national security by ensuring that critical AI hardware does not fall into the hands of foreign adversaries.

The industry is expanding rapidly, with critical capacity expected to grow by 20 to 30 percent over the next five years. However, the number of companies capable of manufacturing advanced logic nodes has dropped from 25 in 2002 to only four between 2020 and 2026. This shrinking supply of manufacturers makes the new US export curbs even more disruptive for Southeast Asian growth. Operators must now navigate a strained grid and a volatile supply chain that will likely remain under pressure until 2030.

stories.Headline: South Korea plans unannounced disaster alerts during exam to catch AI-assisted cheaters
stories.Summary:
The government is considering sending unannounced disaster alert messages during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, an interior ministry official said Wednesday. Authorities have been mulling measures to root out cheating during the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday following a recent cheating scandal in the certified tax accountant exam using AI. As part of anti-cheating measures unveiled Tuesday, the government said it would send an emergency alert message, designed to reach most mobile phones and sound a loud alarm even when muted, before the start of the exam to detect any unsubmitted devices. The official said the government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m.

President Lee Jae Myung said Tuesday he had instructed authorities to review sending additional alerts, even during testing, to catch cheaters. The government will send another disaster alert at an unspecified time during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, the interior ministry said Wednesday. While the first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m., just before the start of the test, the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones, according to the ministry. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed.

The education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday that it will allow test takers to only bring in pencils inside CSAT exam rooms, revising its list of permitted items, according to sources. Authorities earlier notified test takers that they were allowed to bring black marker pens, correction tape, erasers, pencils and mechanical pencil lead for the exam. Under the revised rules, stationery items, except for pencils, will be provided at the test sites. The move appears to reflect concerns of misconduct involving miniature cameras hidden inside personal items brought by test takers.

South Korea has recently been rocked by the recent confession of the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices. The incident has deepened worries of such cheating on the upcoming CSAT, widely seen as a major life event in South Korea, where the university one goes to can heavily influence career prospects. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's college entrance exam, a proposed reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) for tips. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hitachi validates agentic AI platform that cuts chiplet design candidates by over 90%
stories.Summary:
Hitachi's Research and Development Group announced on November 12, 2026, that it had completed and empirically validated a foundational design platform for semiconductor chiplet package design. The platform combines autonomous agentic AI with ultra-fast surrogate physics models to streamline advanced semiconductor packaging. The announcement followed preliminary technical disclosures presented by Hitachi researchers at the 35th IEEE Conference on Electrical Performance of Electronic Packaging and Systems, known as EPEPS 2026. That conference was held in Fort Worth, Texas, from October 18 to 21, 2026. In verification trials using a heterogeneous package with three distinct chiplet types, Hitachi demonstrated that its agentic AI pruned the candidate design space by more than 90%.

Engineers provide high-level targets, thermal design power limits, footprint boundaries and cost goals in natural language, and the agentic AI structures these prompts into formal design-for-manufacturing rules. The system integrates procurement constraints, bill-of-materials availability and vendor lead times to discard unviable component pairings early. The engine concurrently evaluates candidate layouts across electrical performance, thermal dynamics and mechanical stress using accelerated AI surrogate models. Electrical performance covers signal latency, return loss and power impedance, thermal dynamics covers hotspot dissipation and junction temperatures, and mechanical stress covers warpage and shear strain from thermal expansion coefficient mismatches. Hitachi also announced on the same day a technology that uses quantum-inspired CMOS annealing to create a supply-demand plan covering more than 500 generators up to 36 hours ahead in 60 minutes.

Hitachi's Research and Development Group is responsible for the platform, and the company positions it as a foundational technology within its Lumada 3.0 digital transformation framework under its One Hitachi initiative. Hitachi aims to provide edge AI semiconductor engineering services across mobility, energy and robotics. Hitachi plans to conduct Proof-of-Concept engagements with commercial chip vendors, fabless design firms and packaging OSAT providers through late 2026 and 2027. Research teams are also extending surrogate models to support higher die counts, emerging optical interconnects and standard specifications from the UCIe consortium. Both the chiplet technology and the annealing technology remain at the verification stage, and the company is moving toward practical application.

Writing for Mynavi TECH+ on November 13, 2026, technology writer Yukio Kobayashi emphasized that component volatility remains a critical obstacle in chiplet projects. Kobayashi noted that incorporating procurement availability into early automated screening directly targets a common source of project delays. Writing for EE Times Japan on November 16, 2026, semiconductor journalist Takatsuna Mamoto underscored the value of concurrent tri-physics analysis. Mamoto observed that optimizing trace latency often concentrates heat dissipation, generating coefficient-of-thermal-expansion mismatches that can crack solder microbumps. Japanese industry portal Dellows News noted on November 13, 2026, that the technology arrives as edge AI and automotive electronics shift rapidly toward modular silicon, and that for mid-sized semiconductor firms lacking large dedicated packaging teams, automated exploration tools help bridge substantial resource gaps.

Advanced semiconductor packaging has become the primary mechanism for computational scaling as monolithic silicon approaches photolithographic reticle limits and rising wafer defect costs. Disaggregating system-on-chip architectures into modular chiplets such as compute cores, high-bandwidth memory and analog I/O controllers enables process-node optimization for each die. Assembling multiple dies onto high-density substrates creates an explosive combinatorial search space in which engineers must evaluate thousands of spatial floorplans, inter-die bump patterns, routing layers and stackups. With leading-edge fabrication costs climbing at sub-3nm nodes, monolithic dies larger than 800 square millimeters face severe yield penalties. Industry consortia and commercial leaders including the Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express group have prioritized modular advanced packaging, while established commercial electronic design automation suites provide high accuracy for signoff verification but require hours or days of cluster compute time to evaluate a single package geometry.

Following validation on three-chiplet architectures, Hitachi is preparing broader industry rollouts. The articles leave open the results of the planned Proof-of-Concept engagements with commercial chip vendors, fabless design firms and packaging OSAT providers. The articles do not state when the platform will move beyond the verification stage to practical application. The articles do not give the outcome of efforts to extend surrogate models to higher die counts, emerging optical interconnects and UCIe standard specifications. The articles do not state the cost of the platform or when it will be commercially available.

stories.Headline: Wolters Kluwer shows legal teams how purpose-built AI speeds contract workflows
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, Wolters Kluwer released an on-demand session regarding how modern legal departments can be powered by artificial intelligence. Speakers Jennifer McIver and Stephanie Allison demonstrated how specific tools like Legisway Advisor, Legisway Analyzer, and Expert AI help corporate legal professionals work faster. These AI-powered solutions are designed to automate repetitive tasks and accelerate contract workflows to improve overall productivity. The presentation focused on using purpose-built AI to uncover critical legal insights and deliver greater strategic value to a business.

Implementing these tools requires a unified legal platform to streamline workflows and improve visibility across various contracts. This technology allows legal teams to review documents more quickly, identify potential risks, and improve general compliance. In a separate report from November 16, 2026, Keao Caindec of the California-based company Clarra noted that AI performs better when accessing consolidated information. Internal tests at Clarra showed that moving away from disconnected platforms improved AI performance sixfold and increased token efficiency by approximately 80 percent.

Keao Caindec, the CEO of Clarra, stated that many corporate legal departments are rushing into AI investments without making necessary operational changes. Raman Rai, an adviser on AI deployment, told attendees at the Law.com General Counsel Conference East that companies often invest heavily without first determining which problems the technology should solve. Additionally, Kira Ciccarelli of Diligent argued that legal departments must have a clearly defined role in AI governance to influence critical decisions early. Robert Rivkin, the chief legal officer for United Airlines, suggested that using AI to the maximum extent before hiring outside counsel will likely become a common practice.

The broader context shows that while some firms like Intuit have used AI to cut costs by 82 percent, others struggle with governance and accuracy. Researchers and judges have warned that while fake citations are decreasing, subtler errors where real cases are used to support wrong points are becoming harder to detect. Legal professionals are also turning to tools like CCH Jurisdictional Compare to streamline multi-jurisdictional analysis through AI-powered collaboration. Future efforts in the field will likely focus on balancing this rapid innovation with strict governance and human judgment.

stories.Headline: Nigeria's INEC removes 1.6 million AI generated profiles from official voter register
stories.Summary:
Artificial Intelligence has recently begun to interfere with election discourse by creating deepfakes, cloned voices, and misinformation to manipulate national voting outcomes. The Independent National Electoral Commission, known as INEC, discovered that AI was used to manipulate the official voter register recently. To address this, INEC removed 1.6 million AI-generated profiles and sanctioned staff members who were indicted for these irregularities. These events occurred as Nigeria prepares for the 2027 elections, where sophisticated disruptors may cause further electoral havoc. This technological interference has introduced new risk factors that could potentially destroy the integrity of future democratic processes.

The voter register saw an inflation from 93 million to 103 million entries, though INEC only flagged 268 initial irregularities. In February 2026, the Senate repealed the Electoral Act of 2022, rejecting real-time uploads to the IReV portal. This legislative change upheld the physical Form EC8A as the primary source for collation instead of using digital uploads. The 2015 elections featured the Smart Card Reader, which led to the Rivers State governorship dispute between Wike and Peterside. The Supreme Court later ruled that the card reader supplemented the voter register rather than supplanting it under law.

Professor Joash Amupitan, the Chairman of INEC, stated that elections can be undermined even before the first ballot is ever cast. He attended a national summit titled Beyond the Ballot, which focused on AI, FIMI, and the integrity of electoral information. Amupitan argued that INEC cannot police the truth alone and requires clear inter-agency escalation procedures to manage information crises. He called for institutionalised fact-checking channels and practical simulation exercises to prepare all stakeholders for potential AI-driven threats. This summit was held in partnership with the European Union, IPC, CEMESO, DAI, and other various strategic partners.

Social media users and opposition members flagged the database for duplicate profiles and inflated numbers after the preliminary register publication. Journalists raised alarms about the remaining 8 million AI-generated profiles that were not removed during the first cleaning process. Nigerians are now united in demanding a transparent forensic audit of all INEC databases to ensure future electoral credibility. Some politicians may use AI to their advantage while blaming the opposition or the electoral umpire if they lose. The public remains concerned that mischief-makers, scammers, and fraudsters will weaponise AI to cause an upset in 2027.

Before the AI threat, Nigerians relied on the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and the INEC Result Viewing Portal for transparency. These tools used fingerprint and facial recognition to provide real-time viewing of polling unit results after the 2022 amendment. However, a technical glitch during the 2023 presidential election broke public trust in the democratic institution and the system. The 2015 controversy over manual accreditation with card readers previously led many tribunals to annul various election results. Former President Goodluck Jonathan is noted for conceding defeat in 2015 rather than questioning the card reader's legal use.

INEC must now continue to clean its database and deploy available tools to fight against various forms of electoral malpractices. The commission needs to bridge the credibility gap by improving digital literacy and strengthening the nation's overall digital infrastructure. Future efforts should include signing memorandums of understanding with social media giants like TikTok, X, Facebook, and Instagram. The articles leave open whether the 8 million remaining AI profiles will be removed before the 2027 national elections. It remains unclear if Nigeria can achieve the same AI resistance seen during the recent United States midterm elections.

stories.Headline: Validix unveils Atomic Claim Architecture to govern and verify generative AI content
stories.Summary:
Validix, a Swiss company advancing governed claims for enterprise AI, unveiled its Atomic Claim Architecture on Nov. 17, 2026, according to PR Newswire. The announcement was published by The Manila Times on November 17, 2026, at 10 a.m. Validix AG is based in Zug, Switzerland. The Atomic Claim Architecture is a new patent-pending invention that changes how organizations govern content produced by generative AI. It is a secure governance layer, independent of and complementary to large language models.

The architecture constrains what large language models can generate and verifies content before it is released. The model itself is not modified, so organizations can apply the architecture to AI tools they already use or plan to deploy in the future. The architecture breaks evidence into Atoms, which are small, verifiable units of truth, each traceable to its source. Every claim is built from these Atoms, so it can be traced to the evidence behind it. If AI-generated content cannot meet this standard, it is withheld or sent for human review.

Validix provides continuous monitoring of the evidence, and if the underlying source evidence changes, every affected claim is flagged and sent to a human reviewer. Upstream control, pre-release checks and continuous monitoring of evidence sources form what Validix calls a Governed Claims Infrastructure. Lluis Pallarès, co-founder of Validix, said every organization using AI to communicate is putting its name behind what the technology says. Pallarès said that responsibility cannot be delegated to a language model. Pallarès said the architecture turns evidence into enforceable boundaries for what AI is allowed to assert and makes release a separate, controlled decision without requiring changes to existing AI models.

Pallarès said Validix is designed to accelerate expert review, not replace it, and that reviewers see the evidence behind every claim and keep the final say. In the pharmaceutical sector alone, companies have incurred more than $66 billion in recorded regulatory penalties and settlements globally since 2010, according to Violation Tracker Global. United States False Claims Act settlements and judgments exceeded $6.8 billion last year, according to the DOJ. Validix's first application, built for teams that create, review and monitor content in life sciences, is already in live use at a pharmaceutical company following a pilot project. Marketing and sales teams can verify communications through the Validix platform to check that the information is supported by current evidence.

Validix plans to launch its commercial platform in early 2027 and is opening a limited number of pilot partnerships across regulated industries. A video explainer on how the Validix Atomic Claim Architecture works is available at validix.ch/how-validix-works. HellerWeather released an upgraded version of its AI-powered Content Creator, a browser-based tool that uses forecast and climate data to generate first drafts for vertical videos, webcasts, digital shorts, blog posts, newsletter articles and other formats. Tim Heller, a meteorologist and chief developer of the application, said there is never a quiet weather day thanks to Content Creator. HellerWeather said the new feature is part of its broader AI Tool, which launched earlier this year.

HellerWeather said the browser-based system saves most meteorologists three to five hours of preparation time per week. Heller said it does not take a creative genius to write that today will be partly cloudy with a high of 78. Heller said allowing AI to take care of some of the necessary yet time-consuming work allows meteorologists to focus on tracking severe weather and producing more engaging content. Heller said more content means more revenue. The company said users enter a location and the system applies background prompts built from Heller's 35 years of on-air experience.

Heller said meteorologists keep full editorial control before anything is produced, published or shared. Heller said zero prompting does not mean zero input and that there is always a human-in-the-loop. HellerWeather said the AI Tool also serves as a meteorological and climate research assistant, with access to traditional forecast models and newer AI weather models, including Google's WeatherNext. The company said proprietary forecast confidence rankings and in-app alert-day notifications help weather teams finalize forecasts. HellerWeather said the same data powers more than 20 first drafts that meteorologists can use on air, online and on social media.

The company said the generated content appears in English and can be rewritten in conversational American Spanish, a feature added last summer. HellerWeather said the system is built for browser-based use, strict data privacy and hallucination prevention. The company said it does not require or store proprietary client data. Heller said his goal in building the application is to help his colleagues and coaching clients work more efficiently and communicate more effectively. Heller said Content Creator and the HellerWeather AI Tool do not replace meteorologists but empower them.

stories.Headline: GitHub and Microsoft pilot AI scans that yield 99 verified open source vulnerability reports
stories.Summary:
GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot called Codename MDASH to help open source maintainers fix security vulnerabilities, and the results were published on November 18, 2026. The system used Microsoft's MAI Cyber model to scan projects and propose fixes, while an AI triage agent from GitHub Security Lab filtered duplicates and validated high-impact bugs. Researchers from Microsoft FORGE Lab then manually verified each remaining finding before any report was sent. The multi-stage process produced 99 verified private reports across six participating projects. As of November 15, maintainers had fixed 55 of the vulnerabilities, with 14 already integrated into releases.

The pilot flagged 9,791 possible issues across the six projects, and after automated filtering and manual review maintainers received 99 private reports. The six projects were AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick and Netty, all alumni of GitHub's Secure Open Source Fund. Each report included a suggested fix and proof-of-concept material, and maintainers kept control over whether and when to patch. Caddy maintainers fixed all 22 reports they received within a week or less, and ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, generated 22 reports. The first fixes shipped roughly a week after the initial scans.

GitHub is now extending AI security scans to all alumni projects in its Secure Open Source Fund, with findings reviewed before being reported privately. The fund has supported 216 projects so far, and the participating repositories account for software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month. Each project in the fund receives USD $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors, alongside security training, and more than 300 maintainers have fixed more than 4,000 vulnerabilities. Broader data shows more than 850 secret leaks prevented or resolved and more than 1,500 vulnerable dependencies updated. GitHub said the support package for alumni will also include AI security scans and access to Copilot Max.

A maintainer named Grobmeier said a security advisory normally takes around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand and fix, and called that a huge difference. Grobmeier said Codename MDASH found unknown, obscure security bugs with succinct reports and filled gaps from prior reports that had not been noticed. Grobmeier also said the FastMCP scan provided unique insights above and beyond what AI scanners had provided in the past. Grobmeier said Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports. Wolf said maintainers do the fixing and that the job is to make sure they never do it alone.

The work addresses a growing problem for open source projects, whose maintainers increasingly deal with large numbers of AI-generated vulnerability submissions, including duplicates and issues that are not actually security flaws. Many of those maintainers are volunteers or work in small teams. The pilot was designed around two principles, to send only findings that matter and not to send unverified reports to maintainers. That reflects wider concern that AI has sharply lowered the cost of finding potential flaws but not the cost of validating and fixing them. The pilot remains limited in scale and still depends heavily on human review.

Seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers spent about two days per project checking findings by hand, a level of scrutiny that may be difficult to expand broadly without additional resources. That challenge is one of the project's main lessons, since AI can generate large numbers of possible findings cheaply while open source security still relies on careful human validation and maintainers' own judgment. GitHub plans to integrate the lessons into its private vulnerability reporting and security advisories. When maintainers publish a security advisory and it is reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert downstream repositories that rely on the affected package. The articles leave open how far the manual review can scale and what the alumni scans will find.

stories.Headline: Google launches AlloyDB Express to provide fast database provisioning for developers and AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Google launched AlloyDB Express in preview on November 18, 2026, for developers and AI coding agents. This new version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL addresses database bottlenecks for software teams using AI tools. The service allows for the creation of a PostgreSQL database in under two seconds. Users can provision these databases through the gcloud CLI, REST API, MCP, Terraform, or the Google Cloud console. The system pauses automatically after 15 minutes of inactivity and resumes when a new query arrives.

The service targets engineering teams needing fast provisioning for prototypes, internal applications, and testing while maintaining central security controls. Administrators can centrally set identity, network, and organisation policies that apply automatically to databases created by users or agents. Security features include public DNS endpoints that mask IP addresses and block incoming traffic unless it is explicitly allowed. Internal workloads connect through private DNS or Private Service Connect, with access managed by Google Cloud IAM and VPC Service Controls. Native PostgreSQL roles also manage access controls for these isolated environments.

Google stated that the service combines traditional transactional workloads with search, retrieval, and model-linked functions for AI application development. They built AI features directly into the service, removing the need for external tooling or a separate vector database. The company provides natural language-to-SQL generation through AlloyDB Studio and related APIs for developers and AI agents. Users can access Gemini models inside SQL queries to run semantic filtering, ranking, summarisation, and generate embeddings. The service supports vector search using Google's ScaNN index and pgvector HNSW to store vector embeddings.

Engineering teams and AI agents are affected by this shift toward balancing AI speed with infrastructure and data access controls. Other reports show threat actors using AI agents for live intrusions, including a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent. The FBI issued a FLASH alert on November 13 regarding the ARTEX framework used against government and financial sectors. Other tools like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI are being used by financially motivated actors and China-nexus espionage outfits. These attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities and change tactics based on the target's response.

The background shows a paradigm shift where intrusions occur at machine speed through the automated chaining of complex attack paths. Google Threat Intelligence Group found that disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026. Zero-day exploits jumped to 22 in August 2026, compared to a 2025 average of 8 per month. Mandiant responded to LLMJacking incidents in 2026 where attackers burned through compute quotas, with some fraudulent charges reaching $1 million. North Korean actors used AI to create fake recruiter profiles and deploy the SOMBERMEME backdoor.

AlloyDB Express uses consumption-based pricing with active compute at USD $0.115 per Compute Unit hour and storage at USD $0.30 per GB-month. Google offers a free tier with 50 free Compute Units each month and charges USD $0.00 for paused compute. Customers can upgrade to full AlloyDB with one click, keeping data, schemas, users, and connection strings unchanged. This upgrade provides access to disaster recovery features, read replicas, and high availability for production applications. The articles leave open how defenders will counter the increasing stealth and sophistication of AI-driven attacks.
