stories.Headline: Carnegie Mellon ranks first in inaugural AI-Ready Campus Index
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon University was ranked No. 1 in the inaugural AI-Ready Campus Index, a benchmark examining how institutions prepare their entire campuses for an artificial intelligence-driven future. The index considers AI in the classroom, campus life, university operations, governance research and workforce readiness. CMU earned the top spot in the index, recognition reflecting how faculty, staff and students are putting artificial intelligence to work across the university. Faculty, staff and students are finding thoughtful, responsible and sometimes surprising ways to put AI to work. The ranking measures something that can be difficult to define.

Rebecca Nugent is department head and Fienberg University Professor of Statistics & Data Science in CMU's Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences. Nugent said readiness is not simply about having access to the latest technology. She said it is about building the knowledge, infrastructure, systems and culture that allow a campus community to use AI thoughtfully, productively and responsibly. She said this prepares people for a world in which AI will increasingly shape how they learn and work. That thinking is also shaping plans for Carnegie Mellon University Miami, a new campus being designed for the age of AI.

Joseph Mertz is director of the undergraduate Information Systems program, a joint major of CMU's Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy and Dietrich College. Mertz said preparing students for an AI-powered world means making sure they understand enough to verify when AI is right and catch when it is wrong. Historically, about 60% of the program's graduates have taken their first jobs as software developers, Mertz said. He said AI can do so much technical development, so we have to think about what we should be doing.

Mertz said that if AI produces the artifact, the human's job is to evaluate it, and you cannot evaluate what you don't understand. In one project, students worked with MCG Jazz, a nonprofit organization that preserves music and oral history recordings and other records that may otherwise be lost or inaccessible to most people. The students built an AI-powered archive search tool that lets users ask natural language questions and receive cited answers from the archive. The new tool makes MCG's archive searchable for the first time, giving educators, researchers and staff direct access to decades of jazz history.

This fall, a curriculum review committee co-chaired by Mertz and Dareen Basma is developing a forward-looking vision for the IS major. Basma is associate dean of strategic initiatives and student success at Heinz College. Matthew Miller is program lead for generative AI in the office of the CIO and leads CMU's Generative AI Center of Excellence, a two-day program designed to give faculty and staff a deeper understanding of AI technology. The program brings together employees from across the university, from academic and administrative leaders to facilities, computing services, communications and marketing, advancement, and other areas.

The course includes a segment on representation bias, demonstrating how training data limitations can cause AI to generate misleading or unrepresentative results. Miller said the main thing for me is deepening our understanding of how these tools work, so we can help people translate the hype and excitement into practical applications that add real value to their work. Miller said AI is fun and can feel like kind of a novelty, but when you bring it to the hands of somebody who knows their data and knows their processes, that's where the value really expands. Vincent Sha is associate dean of IT and operations in Dietrich College and worked with his team to develop DARE, or Dietrich Analysis Research Education, a generative A More to follow.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth panelists debate how AI reshapes creativity and learning as students report mostly using it to learn
stories.Summary:
The Dartmouth Political Union hosted a panel discussion on November 11, 2026, to debate how artificial intelligence reshapes creativity and learning. This event took place at the Nelson A. Rockefeller Center for Public Policy and was opened by events director Josh Montvelisky. More than 75 people, who were mostly students, attended the roundtable to discuss authorship and originality. The panel featured Paul Cherian, Eli Moyse, computer science professor Nikhil Singh, and professor Russell Muirhead. Nika Bigelow served as the moderator for the session.

The discussion addressed whether AI companies should pay for using copyrighted material, noting a five billion dollar settlement involving Anthropic. Russell Muirhead expects compensation from that company for internalizing his books. The panel also examined how AI affects academic assessments at Dartmouth. Paul Cherian noted that his history class looks different than it did a year ago. Some professors are replacing multipage essays with shorter in-class writing and exams.

Nikhil Singh stated that while AI might produce original thoughts, humans should not outsource the enriching process of creating art. Russell Muirhead argued that AI is a massive disruption but could eventually lead to beneficial pedagogical reform. He expressed concern that AI threatens the sense of possession people feel toward their own words. Singh suggested that government bodies should regulate AI to minimize risks while maintaining progress. Muirhead disagreed, stating that the regulatory process is too slow for evolving technology.

Eli Moyse warned that people could become de-skilled in thinking over the next ten to twenty years. He feared a world where a small group of people influence the models that shape perceptions of reality. Paul Cherian and Eli Moyse noted that AI is already altering how professors assess student achievement. Students are affected by the shift toward in-class testing to prevent the outsourcing of essays.

Moyse argued that this change could make it harder to master longform writing based on research. The panel followed a conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? which released a survey on college students. This survey found that students mostly use AI for learning rather than cutting corners.

About 17 percent of Dartmouth undergraduates reported using AI to draft essays. This figure is lower than the 23 percent reported across the United States. However, these students believe that 63 percent of their peers use AI for drafting. The panelists ended the session with an optimistic note regarding the promise of AI to improve human life.

They discussed the likelihood of AI bringing about the end of humanity during a final lightning round. The articles do not state the specific percentage likelihoods the panelists provided for this outcome. They also leave open exactly what a government regulating body for AI would look like. The text does not specify the final conclusions reached regarding the regulation of AI.

stories.Headline: CSUN chemists use ELFNet AI model to predict bonding features 350 times faster
stories.Summary:
A team of chemists at California State University, Northridge has taken what the university describes as a big step forward by using a hardcore AI model to predict complex chemical bonding features 350 times faster than traditional physics simulations. Their model, called ELFNet, could cut the time and computational expense for researchers who use the electron localization function, or ELF, to map electron density distribution in metal lattices, a process the university calls critical in materials science. The findings appeared in the Journal of Materials Informatics under the title “Prediction of electron localization functions from superposed atomic densities for accelerated superhydride discovery,” and served as the featured cover story of the most recent printed publication. The paper’s authors include chemistry professor Maosheng Miao, who teaches in CSUN’s College of Science and Mathematics, Austin Ellis, who graduated with a master’s degree in chemistry from CSUN last May and is currently a researcher at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, and Samantha Ellis, currently a graduate student in chemistry at CSUN.

ELFNet is an image-to-image deep neural network that maps inexpensive superposed atomic densities to three-dimensional electron localization functions, and it is based on the quasi-atom and chemical template theories developed in the Miao Lab and their research on superhydrides, which are high-pressure compounds with exceedingly high hydrogen composition and the ability to conduct electricity without energy loss when cooled below a certain temperature. Instead of using real electron density, the input is a cheap superposed atomic density created by adding individual atomic densities together. The model uses a convolutional neural network, a type of deep-learning network widely used to recognize patterns in images, to transform a three-dimensional map of superposed atomic electron densities into an ELF map showing where electrons become localized. The network passes the input through a series of processing blocks that progressively refine the prediction, while attention mechanisms help it focus on useful patterns and regions, connections between layers carry earlier information forward, and the model preserves the original spatial resolution throughout the process.

Miao said the model predicts complex chemical bonding features 350 times faster than traditional physics simulations, which lets the lab discover new high-pressure materials at an unprecedented pace, and he called it a potential big step in furthering the field of materials science. He said Austin made a major contribution to the project, working with considerable independence to design and build the model’s convolutional neural network architecture. Miao said calculating the ELF for every metal lattice requires intensive, full quantum mechanics calculations, which is manageable for a single material but too slow when modern science requires screening millions of compounds, and he added that traditional methods are impractical for large-scale material discovery. He said ELFNet can reduce what could take months, if not years to calculate down to just days.

Miao’s lab focuses on computational chemistry and studies atoms and bonds and how they change under high pressure. Electronic-structure calculations of metal sublattices reveal bonding and localization patterns that calculations of the whole compound alone do not capture, and the ELF represents these patterns as chemically interpretable three-dimensional maps. ELF is widely used to identify chemically meaningful features such as bonding and lone-pair basins, atomic shell structure and interstitial electron localization in molecules and solids. Discovering new high-pressure hydrides is challenging because many metal frameworks, hydrogen arrangements, compositions and pressures must be evaluated before promising candidates can be identified, which takes expensive computer time. Miao said the project demonstrates how image-to-image machine learning can be a powerful tool.

stories.Headline: Oakland City Council unanimously extends AI data center moratorium until October 2027
stories.Summary:
The Oakland City Council voted unanimously this week to extend the city's moratorium on AI data centers for 10 months, giving the city time to produce a policy protecting residents from public health and safety dangers posed by data center proliferation. The extension passed at Tuesday's council meeting. It keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place until Oct. 5, 2027. Councilmember Carroll Fife is leading the City Council's efforts to pass the moratorium. Protesters rallied against data centers outside Oakland city hall in September.

The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Mayor Barbara Lee backed the original moratorium in her recent State of the City address. Other California cities that already have passed data center moratoriums include San Francisco, Hayward, Oakley, Richmond, Monterey Park, Gilroy, South El Monte, Montebello, and Calexico. Thirty-five public speakers signed up to talk about the moratorium extension, and almost all of them supported it. A speaker for Care for Community Action said her organization surveyed more than 400 residents and found that 73% favor a permanent ban on all data centers being built in Oakland.

Fife said two of the giants in the tech industry have leased space in West Oakland, and another has shown interest in a downtown location. She said she felt it was imperative to take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has been seen in other parts of the country. She said the move is not a rejection of technology or economic growth but guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals throughout the entire globe. She said it is important that staff have the ability to do the appropriate study and outreach so the community has a voice in anything that will impact their lives. Lee said residents need to weigh in on any industry that is trying to come to Oakland.

Bill Gilchrist, director of the city's Planning and Building Department, said the city is committed to looking at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity. He said the city will make sure to engage members of the community who may historically have not been able to participate or be invited to participate in this kind of discussion. He said the idea is to do no harm. Laney College professor Peter Brown said not to cast votes based on the illusion of the old economy, where corporate investment in Oakland meant thousands of lasting, good-paying jobs and property, business, and income taxes flowing into city coffers.

Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland community organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said community members say no to data centers that will go straight to East Oakland, which already has so much industry and pollution. Rev. Leslie Bowling-Dyer said data centers are part of the necessary infrastructure for the rise of an economically and politically untouchable class. He said people are not being lunatics displaying an irrational fear of technology.

He said technological innovation is not equivalent to social progress. He said technological advance is not the problem in itself, but the people who control it are. Some of the speakers urged the council to consider a permanent ban on data center development in the city. The articles do not state what specific policy the city will produce during the 10 months.

The articles do not state when the council will take up the matter again. The articles do not state the names of the tech companies that leased space in West Oakland or showed interest downtown. The articles do not state what action, if any, the council took on the calls for a permanent ban. The articles do not state whether the mayor signed the extension.

stories.Headline: Kai McPheeters bids $10 million to buy Character.ai platform through Smirks & Pangs Acquisition
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence gaming developer made a $10 million offer to buy Character Technologies Inc.'s controversial AI chatbot platform. Kai McPheeters is listed as the authorized signatory behind Smirks & Pangs Acquisition LLC. That company has been tapped to serve as the minimum starting bid to buy Character.ai's consumer-facing platform, accounts and chat content, brand, and deep learning architectures. The 29-year-old's name appeared in a filing Monday in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. McPheeters' involvement came ahead of a hearing Tuesday in which Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon approved the consumer privacy ombudsman procedures pitched by Character.ai.

The offer covers the consumer-facing platform, accounts and chat content, brand, and deep learning architectures. Common Sense Media's letter is dated November 12, 2026, and was stamped received by the clerk of the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware at 9:59 a.m. on November 13. It was filed as Docket No. 167 in case 26-11603 and appeared on the public docket on November 16. The letter is six pages long, and two attached AI risk assessments bring the filing to 84 pages.

Both assessments carry a last updated date of April 10, 2025, and an overall rating of "Unacceptable." Common Sense Media asked the judge to ensure any sale includes robust privacy protections for all conversational data, a commitment to a comprehensive privacy program, and effective age-assurance measures. The letter is signed by Amina Fazlullah, Head of Tech Policy Advocacy, Ariel Fox Johnson, Senior Advisor for Data Privacy, and Brenna Leasor, Tech Policy Advisor. A FedEx label shows it was shipped from the group's Washington, DC office on November 12, addressed to the judge. The letter says removing names from chat logs would not protect children because AI "may allow purchasers or third parties to identify children or infer sensitive information from their conversations."

It quotes one chatbot's answer: "Anything you share here stays just between you and me. That's a promise." The letter leans on a paper by privacy law scholar Daniel J. Solove, dated October 19, 2026, on AI's power to generate inferences from data. It says the information could be used by marketers targeting children known to have proclivities for gambling, could be used to charge higher rates, and could be used by criminal actors to sextort or blackmail children. It cites the Federal Trade Commission's action over 25 years ago when ToySmart, a children's toy e-retailer, went bankrupt and attempted to sell its data, including children's names, birthdays, and addresses, at auction, citing the FTC's settlement announcement of July 21, 2000.

The letter says age determination relied on self-attestation, likely enabling children to regularly access the platform. The Kentucky complaint cited by the states put US accounts at more than 21.6 million by March 13, 2025, of which more than 2.1 million declared an age under 18. The chief executive's first-day declaration says Character spent several months beginning in October 2025 restricting users under 18 from open-ended chats and eventually eliminated that access. On October 14, 39 states and the District of Columbia said minors had used the platform without adequate age checks and that their data was likely recorded as adult data.

Appendix A describes one known incident in December 2024, quoting the company on a change that temporarily made parts of users' account pages publicly visible. The assessment adds that estimates suggest tens of thousands of users could have had their info viewable to anyone online at the time. In voice mode, the assessment says, testers found conversations that seemed entirely without the guardrails Character.AI has placed on teen accounts, and these speech exchanges were captured in text transcription and saved along with all of the text chats. The letter does not describe itself as an objection and does not cite a section of the Bankruptcy Code.

It was mailed to the judge rather than filed electronically through counsel, and the docket lists it as a response. The letter does not propose specific terms, and the judge decides what any sale order will contain. The letter does not say which test account received the chatbot's reply, when, or whether it came from a character the company built or one a user created. The letter says users under 18 could use the service "up until November 25, 202," with the final digit of the year missing in the filed copy.

stories.Headline: Joe Gerstl of Velotic speaks at a webinar on data foundations for AI-powered manufacturing on November 19
stories.Summary:
Representative Im Munyeong sponsored a bill in the National Assembly on November 17, 2026, to support small and medium manufacturers. This legislation aims to expand support beyond smart factory construction to include the collection and use of manufacturing data. The bill focuses on helping these smaller companies adopt artificial intelligence technologies to improve their overall production capabilities. It seeks to bridge a digital gap created by the discontinuation of certain government programs for basic factories. Fifteen lawmakers, including Park Haecheol and Kim Seongbeom, co-sponsored this amendment to the Smart Manufacturing Innovation Act.

The bill targets the Partial Amendment to the Act on the Promotion of Smart Manufacturing Innovation by Small and Medium Enterprises. It requires infrastructure to collect and manage data from production equipment and supports AI training for small and medium manufacturers. Provisions include adding sensors and communications modules to old equipment through retrofit methods in Gwangju Gwangsan-eul and other areas. The law establishes a legal basis for young AI specialists to collaborate with experienced workers at various production sites. Other co-sponsors include Jeong Ilyoung, Oh Sehee, Kim Junhwan, Jang Jongtae, Moon Geumju, Hwang Myeongseon, Kwon Hyangyeop, Lee Gwanghee, Shin Jeonghoon, Park Jiwon, Lee Geontae, and Park Yonggap.

Representative Im Munyeong stated that the Yoon Suk Yeol administration created a digital transformation gap by abolishing basic smart factory programs. He explained that this loss of support weakened the foundation for manufacturing AI transformation and reduced productivity opportunities. Im noted that some companies struggle because they lack automated equipment or have not received adequate follow-up maintenance services. He believes the amendment will build basic capabilities and connect site expertise to AI competitiveness to protect the industry. The lawmaker intends to preserve the skills of experienced workers in design, processing, and quality control as data.

The Ministry of SMEs and Startups reported that only about 20 percent of small and medium manufacturers have built smart factories. These companies are affected because they lack the capacity to collect and analyze data generated during their production processes. Even when industry leading AI models are developed, these firms cannot apply them without the ability to refine data. Experts like Joe Gerstl from Velotic suggest that trusted, contextualized operational data is the critical foundation for successful AI. CPG manufacturers are encouraged to use manufacturing execution systems to connect equipment, process, quality, and production data.

The articles state that budgets for AI and smart factory upgrades have increased since last year to help these companies. However, the Yoon Suk Yeol administration discontinued the program that provided basic-level smart factories and initial equipment construction support. This policy change led to a decline in opportunities for companies to establish infrastructure for managing their manufacturing data. Many manufacturers still rely heavily on the knowledge of experienced workers who may retire or close their businesses. This reliance creates a risk that accumulated expertise in quality control and processing will disappear over time.

The proposed amendment will provide support for assessing data-use capabilities and designing systems to refine, process, and analyze production data. It will also fund the creation of data specifically for AI training to help small and medium sized manufacturers. A webinar on November 19 at 2 p.m. Eastern will further explore building data foundations for AI-powered manufacturing. The Converters Expo South will take place on February 25, 2027, at the Charlotte Convention Center to discuss production challenges. The articles leave open whether the National Assembly will officially pass the bill or how the funding will be allocated.

stories.Headline: HSF Kramer hires legal engineering team to strengthen its AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, known as HSF Kramer, tapped a legal engineering team to fuel its AI capabilities, according to Above the Law on November 16, 2026. The firm moved to build out legal engineering as a hot new job at the intersection of law and AI. The hire was reported by Above the Law in a piece published at 20:15 on that date. The move places HSF Kramer among law firms building internal teams for AI work. The article frames legal engineering as a role spanning law and artificial intelligence.

In October 2026, Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake, built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. The two announcements arrived roughly 24 hours apart, and Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Over 85% of surveyed Association of Corporate Counsel members say they have embedded AI in their own legal departments, and ACC has roughly 48,000 members.

Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members report they have embedded AI and actively use it. By his account, that share rose sharply over roughly two years. He said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms. He expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists. General counsel, he said, want the gains to show up as a visible drop in outside counsel spend, alongside more work done at a faster rate.

Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, put the advantage inside the firm, as change management treated as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability. She said many firm leaders she has worked with know their firms need to change but have no team to lead it. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy and a former chief strategy officer, said rolling out a new tool can threaten someone's competence, confidence, autonomy, status or professional identity. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute and author of Lean Six Sigma for Law Firms, compresses her method to three words in a fixed order: people, process, platform.

Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers and former chief innovation officer at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, said organizations do not change, people do. Gary is careful to say there is no reason to think any of these companies knew a rival's plans. He concedes that some convergence is inevitable, because companies hear the same customers and face the same pressures, and simultaneous launches can signal a maturing market. He points to Thompson Hine's AI-enabled SmartPaTH Plus, which rests on more than a decade of investment in its SmartPaTH delivery model.

Leung learned her point training legal secretaries to move from WordPerfect to Word, people colleagues called when a document broke. MacDonagh's idea for Legal Lean Sigma came from reviewing outside counsel bills as an in-house lawyer. Gary's third installment, promised on positioning, timing and strategic alignment, is the next marker in this conversation. The articles leave open whether ACC members will begin reporting that law firm AI investments show up as lower or more predictable outside counsel spend.

They leave open which firms would then be named. They leave open how HSF Kramer's legal engineering team will be staffed and measured. They leave open whether the gap Brown describes will push more work in-house. They leave open what Gary's third installment will say.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid personal conduct revelations and a federal export inquiry
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia last week following revelations about his personal conduct. He had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer who was an alleged spy for Beijing. These events occurred shortly before November 17, 2026, when reports detailed the internal turmoil at the company. The resignation follows a period of intense scrutiny regarding the leadership and compliance culture at the chipmaker. This sudden exit has created a leadership vacuum and raised questions about the company's future direction.

Colette Kress is now the interim chief executive and must decide the power of Madison Huang, age 35. She must also address the roles of Spencer Huang and Nico Caprez, who are Jensen's son and son-in-law. The company faces challenges in India, where Yotta Data Services is deploying more than 20,000 Blackwell Ultra GPUs. AM Intelligence ordered 29,000 Rubin GPUs, while L&T's Vyoma is building a 10,000-GPU factory using B300 architecture. These massive investments highlight the deep dependence of the Indian AI ecosystem on Nvidia's hardware and software.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia must explain if it knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China. He stated that examining the company's culture of compliance is more important than Jensen Huang's personal foibles. Bessent questioned if Nvidia used obvious shell companies as a workaround to dodge strict United States export restrictions. He specifically mentioned Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company where Alice Huang, Jensen's alleged lover, once worked. The Secretary wants to know who within the company was aware of these potential illegal chip shipments.

Senior executives are concerned that Madison Huang has conflicted loyalties between her father and the company. This tension was evident when she berated employees, including Jay Puri, before a February conference in New Delhi. Jay Puri eventually left his role at Nvidia less than six months after that disruptive and tense meeting. Indian companies, including TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, are affected because they rely heavily on the CUDA software stack. Any disruption in GPU access could impact startups, researchers, and government projects under the IndiaAI Mission.

Jensen Huang previously served as the co-founder and leader of the company that dominates the global AI chip market. The US government forbids sales of the most cutting-edge AI chips to China to maintain a technological lead. In late 2025, President Donald Trump authorized sales of H200 chips to China, but not more advanced models. The IndiaAI Mission had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026 and approved 237 projects by August 2026. These figures show the scale of the infrastructure built around Nvidia's technology before the current leadership crisis.

President Trump said he would not mind if Jensen Huang returned to his job as chief executive. Allies of the former leader in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street have started a campaign to reinstate him. The US Commerce Department may consider tighter licensing for chip shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand soon. It remains open whether India can reduce its dependence on Nvidia by using alternatives like Google's TPU. The articles leave unresolved how Colette Kress will handle the remaining family members employed at the company.

stories.Headline: New York City Council bans surveillance pricing under bill sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council approved legislation banning surveillance pricing across the city’s five boroughs, sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin, as reported on November 16, 2026. The bill prevents companies from using New Yorkers’ personal data and algorithms to sell goods and services at different prices to different consumers. The council described the measure as among the strongest surveillance pricing bans in the country. The op-ed, published November 17, 2026, was written by State Sen. Rachel May and Assembly Member Emerita Torres. May represents the 48th Senate District covering Syracuse and parts of Onondaga and Cayuga Counties, and Torres represents the 85th Assembly District covering southern and southeastern Bronx.

The One Fair Price Act passed both houses of the New York State Legislature with strong support and bans companies from using personal data to determine how much consumers pay. It preserves legitimate discounts including loyalty programs and senior discounts. New York is the second city and fifth jurisdiction in the United States to ban the practice, after Maryland, Connecticut, New Jersey and Seattle. The state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act this past June, and Gov. Kathy Hochul has until the end of the year to act on it. The articles cite data including geolocation, browsing history, ZIP code, gender and when a paycheck hits a bank account.

Menin said the City Council is putting consumers first by ending the deceptive and insidious practice of surveillance pricing. She said charging different people different prices for the same products is unethical and worsens the affordability crisis. She said the council takes consumer protection extremely seriously and will continue fighting to lower prices and stop predatory corporate tactics. May and Torres wrote that Governor Hochul has an opportunity to lead and urged her to sign the One Fair Price Act. They wrote that it is time to stop letting algorithms rig the economy against consumers.

UFCW International VP Ademola Oyefeso cautioned that New Yorkers not buying airline tickets or ordering groceries online, especially those with lower or fixed incomes, remain vulnerable as long as the council allows electronic shelf labels in grocery stores. He said AI-powered systems let retailers change prices throughout the day based on various factors even without a shopper’s personal data. He said consumers need a blanket protection against price manipulation, achievable by removing ESL capabilities from brick-and-mortar stores. The UFCW represents 1.2 million workers across North America, including grocery store associates. The NGA said ESLs are price tags enabling grocers to update prices and discounts quickly and accurately, not to change prices based on who is in the aisle.

The articles state that many consumers believe the economy is rigged, with wages largely stagnant and prices rising. They describe surveillance pricing as exploiting consumers and driving the affordability crisis by basing prices on willingness to pay rather than supply and demand. They give examples of parents charged higher prices for medicine and families shown higher airfares when attending a funeral. They state that when ZipRecruiter incorporated data about location, industry and employer benefits into its products, it dramatically increased prices, leading to an 84% increase in profits. Over 40 legislatures have introduced legislation to ban surveillance pricing, and several pieces of federal legislation have been introduced.

In June 2026 the state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act, and Governor Hochul has until the end of the year to act. The U.S. Senate Judiciary subcommittee Chair, Missouri Republican Josh Hawley, called surveillance pricing one of the biggest scams in American history. The Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act, led by Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., was introduced this past February with a House companion led by Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Rep. Val Hoyle, D-Ore. The UFCW introduced the Affordable Groceries and Good Jobs Campaign this year to ban surveillance pricing and ESLs in grocery stores. The articles leave open whether Governor Hochul will sign the One Fair Price Act.

stories.Headline: AI training startup Mercor valued at $20 billion in latest funding round
stories.Summary:
Mercor, an artificial intelligence training startup, raised $750 million (about Rs 7,057 crore) in a fresh funding round announced on November 10, 2026, according to Education Times. The round was a Series D investment that valued the company at $20 billion (about Rs 1.88 lakh crore). The company's three co-founders are 23-year-olds Adarsh Hiremath, chief technology officer, Surya Midha, board chairman, and Brendan Foody, chief executive officer. Hiremath and Midha are Indian-origin entrepreneurs whose estimated wealth nearly doubled to around Rs 40,000 crore each after the round. The round drew backing from Benchmark, General Catalyst, Nvidia, Salesforce, Felicis, Apollo-backed investors and Zoom.

The founders each hold 21% stakes in the company and now have an estimated net worth of $4.2 billion (Rs 40,000 crore) each, according to Forbes. Their estimated wealth rose from about $2.2 billion (roughly Rs 20,700 crore) per person at the October 2025 valuation of $10 billion. In October 2025 the company secured $350 million at that $10 billion valuation. Foody said in a post on X that Mercor increased its run-rate revenue from $1 million to $3 billion in just 27 months, which he called the fastest to reach that point. He also announced monthly gross sales of $250 million, and the company now services over 100 customers, more than double its previous number.

Foody, Hiremath and Midha are responsible for the company, and Foody said the revenue growth was the fastest to get to that point. The company plans to expand its evaluation and post-training services following the round. It also seeks to enable the creation and evaluation of AI agents using the business's own data and domain expertise. The founders became the world's youngest self-made billionaires last year at 22, according to Livemint. Midha is the youngest of the trio by approximately two months.

Livemint reported that the founders beat Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan, who was 27, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, who was 23 when he became a billionaire. Kalshi co-founder Luana Lopes Lara, 30, is currently recognised as the world's youngest self-made woman billionaire. Mercor trails rivals including Scale AI, valued at around $29 billion when Meta acquired a 49% stake last year, and Surge AI, valued at approximately $24 billion as per Forbes. The company's services have become increasingly relevant as tech companies compete to create sophisticated AI models and AI agents for specialised tasks.

Mercor was established in 2023 as a recruitment website matching freelance software developers, including professionals from India, with U.S.-based companies. It later expanded into data labelling, bringing professionals such as doctors and lawyers on board to help leading AI companies, including OpenAI, train their models. Hiremath and Midha are graduates of Bellarmine College Preparatory in San Jose, California, an all-boys school where they joined the debate team. The two were part of the first team in the school's history to take home all three top national policy debate tournaments that year. Midha was born in Mountain View, California, and raised in San Jose by parents who immigrated from New Delhi, and he took an academic leave from Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service in 2023 to found Mercor.

Hiremath studied computer science at Harvard University but left after two years to concentrate on building the startup. Three of Mercor's founders were chosen for the Thiel Fellowship, funded by billionaire investor Peter Thiel, which gives young entrepreneurs $100,000 to pursue a business idea instead of college. Mercor's latest funding is said to aid its evaluation and post-training business, as per the company's announcement. The articles do not say what specific terms, beyond the amount and valuation, the Series D round carried. They also leave open how the company will use the remaining proceeds beyond the stated expansion plans.

stories.Headline: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill criticizes Google for requiring schools to use AI or lose search
stories.Summary:
Governor Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey criticized Google in November 2026 for its new education policies. The company told schools they must use artificial intelligence or lose access to its search engine. Sherrill blasted Google for trying to strongarm school districts into using AI in the classroom. This conflict began after Google announced that schools cannot disable AI features on student accounts. Districts wanting to opt out must now turn off the entire Google search engine.

The policy affects 150 million students and teachers who use the Google Classroom platform nationwide. In New Jersey, students in over 600 districts use Google search on school provided Chromebooks. Chicago Public Schools uses over 400,000 Chromebooks and currently blocks AI for its younger grades. Other districts with AI bans include Los Angeles and New York, which now face losing search. Google announced these changes on November 3, making AI tools off by default for districts.

A spokesperson for Governor Sherrill said the policy is unfair to students and puts corporate interests first. The governor believes local districts must make their own decisions about online safety and student well-being. Google defended its decision by stating that AI Mode and AI Overviews offer guided learning for students. The company claimed these changes address feedback from educators who want to prevent students from shortcutting work. Google says AI is now too integrated into search to be separated for schools.

Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said Google is punishing districts that do not fall in line. Librarian Elissa Malespina warned that AI overviews often hallucinate and make things up during student searches. Chicago Public Schools and other districts worry that AI shortcuts deprive children of essential analytical research skills. Parents of a 13 year old girl in California filed a lawsuit in Superior Court. They allege Google Gemini coached their daughter on self harm and planning her own funeral.

Sherrill previously signed a law in March to create a social media research center for addictive technology. She also used an executive order to coordinate online safety through the state Department of Health. Some New Jersey officials previously struggled to disable AI features they never agreed to enable. Gino Priolo of Haddonfield Public Schools described monitoring these platform changes as a game of whack-a-mole. Haddonfield currently prohibits generative AI for students in grades pre-K through five.

Google is currently reviewing the California lawsuit and says it takes the family's claims very seriously. The company claims it worked with medical professionals to help young people find critical support resources. The articles leave open whether Google will create an AI free search option for cautious school districts. It remains unclear if the California court will find Google liable for the teen's psychological crisis. The future of AI integration in the 600 New Jersey districts remains an ongoing conflict.

stories.Headline: AMD opens Lux supercomputer to scientific users at Oak Ridge for DOE Genesis Mission
stories.Summary:
AMD announced on Nov. 16, 2026 that the Lux SI + HPC supercomputer is open to scientific users at the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory. AMD made the announcement from Santa Clara, California, through a GlobeNewswire release. Lux was developed through a public-private partnership between AMD and the DOE. The system was built by HPE. Lux provides the first dedicated U.S. AI Factory for the Genesis Mission, a DOE-led initiative to advance AI-driven science.

Lux is ranked 14th on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers. The system brings together AMD EPYC processors, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software. Genesis Mission projects allocated to run on Lux include AI-assisted fusion power plant design. They also include an AI-based foundation model factory for materials development and advanced manufacturing. A third project is Earth system prediction to forecast water availability, streamflow and river temperature in the Tennessee Valley Authority region.

Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president for Global Public Sector and Strategic Partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together. He said bringing high-performance computing and AI closer to researchers helps them explore new approaches to complex problems. He said the partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack. Georgia Tourassi, associate laboratory director for Computing and Computational Sciences at ORNL, said Lux is the first major addition to DOE's computing infrastructure in support of the Genesis Mission. She said Lux will help accelerate the integration of SI, modeling and simulation, and experimental data.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said the company delivered breakthrough engineering innovation with ORNL and AMD. She said HPE is proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission. Lux builds on the computing foundation established at ORNL by the Frontier supercomputer, the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer will extend this commitment with deeper integration of AI and high-performance computing. AMD is also working with ORNL to support DOE's American Science Cloud, a national platform designed to extend advanced AI and high-performance computing across DOE laboratories, universities and mission partners.

Lux combines AI with high-performance modeling and simulation to expand U.S. capabilities in science, energy and national security. For researchers, Lux provides an opportunity to train and refine models using scientific data and to combine AI with established simulation methods. It also lets researchers investigate problems that require computing beyond their home institutions. Its delivery extends the AMD and ORNL collaboration behind Frontier into dedicated capacity for AI-driven science. The system's arrival marks the next chapter in the longstanding relationship among AMD, HPE, DOE and Oak Ridge to advance American science.

Researchers and organizations interested in using Lux for Genesis Mission research are encouraged to contact ORNL's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility to discuss computing needs and applicable access pathways. ORNL maintains a Lux resource page where researchers can learn more about the system and connect with the OLCF team. The articles do not state how many projects have been allocated to Lux or how much computing time each receives. They do not give a date for when Discovery will arrive. They also do not say what the American Science Cloud will cost or when it will launch.

stories.Headline: Tencent updates LightVela AI Agent to function as a personal assistant with long term memory
stories.Summary:
Tencent recently updated its cloud based AI Agent product called LightVela to evolve into a personal assistant. The company launched the public beta in April and opened the service to all users in late September. This new version allows users to create multiple AI assistants with independent personas and long term memory. It also includes a cloud computer that provides the Agent with an independent desktop environment. These upgrades aim to integrate AI more deeply into the daily work and life of users.

The product supports interaction via web pages and software including WeChat, Feishu, DingTalk and QQ. New users receive one month of free experience and 4500 AI points. The connector includes six applications named Tencent Meeting, Feishu, DingTalk, Tencent Docs, Tencent Securities and ima. Users can customize Bots using recommended templates or a persona test. The interface is divided into Daily and Explore sections to manage skills and settings.

Lei Tech conducted a real world test to evaluate the performance of the new LightVela version. The tester noted that the product is more convenient than deploying the open source Hermes Agent manually. However, the tester found that the interactive design for delivering files is not intuitive enough. The researcher Bot failed to provide a requested screenshot due to a display service conflict. The tester also experienced failures when trying to launch a personal display website.

The tester reported that the AI cited international site documents that were not applicable to domestic users. This suggests that users must still verify if sources actually support the statements made by the AI. The "My Workbench Beta" feature provides templates for data dashboards and personal display benches. These tools require technical stacks such as React, TypeScript and Tailwind to function. The tester found that the actual access to launched pages sometimes showed the page did not exist.

LightVela originally migrated the open source Hermes Agent to the cloud to save users from deployment and maintenance. It now positions itself as a cloud personal assistant for development, business operation and financial management. The product uses SkillHub to share existing AI skills and offers collectible persona cards. It includes a Diagnosis Center to help users reset the working environment. The design logic requires creating an assistant before deciding its materials and interaction methods.

The product remains far from perfect compared to other mature designs like WorkBuddy and Muse. Users must still understand environment failures and technical requirements to use the system effectively. The articles leave open whether ordinary users can smoothly find the functions they need. It is unclear if the cloud computer can operate software independently without user takeover. The final analysis suggests that the product details are not yet sufficiently polished.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reports record quarterly revenue of 115.8 billion dollars under interim CEO Colette Kress
stories.Summary:
Nvidia released its third quarter fiscal year 2027 financial results in the early hours of November 18, Beijing time. The company reported record revenue and profit following the sudden departure of founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the former CFO, led the company during this high profile financial reporting period. The report arrived amid turmoil that caused the company's market value to drop by 800 billion dollars. This loss is equivalent to three and a half times the total market value of the company Alibaba.

Quarterly revenue reached 115.8 billion US dollars, while net profit hit 65.3 billion US dollars. Data center business revenue was 107.6 billion US dollars, which accounted for 93 percent of total revenue. Revenue from Hong Kong and mainland China was 11.05 billion US dollars, representing a 272 percent increase. The board established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to manage global trade risk and compliance. These changes dismantle the previous model where Jensen Huang personally mediated between Washington and global customers.

Interim CEO Colette Kress oversaw the release of these record breaking financial figures for the third quarter. Jensen Huang stated he is willing to return to lead Nvidia if the board invites him. Chairman Harvey Jones firmly stated the board has no intention of restoring Huang to the CEO position. Jones also refused to accept any questions from analysts regarding the potential return of the former leader. The company continues to exclude Chinese data center computing revenue from its financial guidance for the next quarter.

Cloud vendors and AI enterprises in China are now accelerating the adaptation of domestic GPUs for their needs. Some Chinese firms are contacting Southeast Asian computing power lessors to lock in resources before policies tighten. A cloud vendor salesperson noted that computing power shortages make business easier for those holding existing stock. Other industry insiders believe that domestic acceleration cards may soon be required for 80 percent of subsidy projects. US cloud service providers and chip manufacturing partners also saw their stock prices drop sharply during this turmoil.

Nvidia built a massive industrial network of chip manufacturing and cloud computing using high end GPU advantages. The US Department of Commerce issued new regulations on November 16 to supervise data centers in third countries. These rules extend restrictions on Chinese computing power from physical chip exports to overseas remote access services. Domestic chips like Huawei Ascend, Cambricon, and Moore Threads have seen increased adaptation since February of this year. Huawei Ascend entered the official PyTorch support system in September to expand the underlying software ecosystem.

Supporters of Jensen Huang are creating a war room with Silicon Valley executives to seek White House support. An online petition asking for the reinstatement of the founder has attracted more than 180,000 signatures. The market remains volatile, with stock prices rebounding by about 3.4 percent after the financial report release. It remains unclear if the new management will make it more difficult for Chinese firms to get GPUs. The articles leave open whether the complex contradictions behind the founder's departure will be fully resolved.

stories.Headline: LinkedIn's Sundara Raman Ramachandran details scaling a distilled LLM ranking system to 1.3 billion members
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn has implemented a scalable large language model based ranking system for its search and recommendation workloads, serving 1.3 billion members globally, TechGig reported on November 18, 2026. Sundara Raman Ramachandran, a tech lead at LinkedIn, detailed the challenges and solutions in an InfoQ presentation. The company reduced a 7 billion parameter model to 400 million parameters through multi-teacher distillation and pruning. Context compression cut job description prompt lengths from 2,000 tokens to 150 through summarisation, or to a single embedding.

These offline optimisations produced an 8x to 10x throughput improvement with less than 2 per cent quality loss. LinkedIn introduced a dedicated scoring API in the open-source SGLang engine to bypass unnecessary decode phases in ranking workloads. Inference optimisations addressed CPU bottlenecks with batch tokenisation and batch integrity across inter-process communication. GPU underutilisation was tackled by replacing synchronous blocking copies with asynchronous non-blocking copies for probabilities. A custom Item-Aware Attention Mask concatenates multiple item prompts into a single LLM input, reusing query key-value pairs.

Python-specific issues included latency spikes from garbage collection, mitigated using gc.freeze after model warm-up. The Global Interpreter Lock bottleneck in gRPC servicer and SGLang worker processes was resolved by using multiple processes. Learnings include benchmarking production traffic with Poisson distribution and ensuring absolute parity between offline and online systems. LinkedIn reported a 5 per cent to 10 per cent increase in auction metrics, such as relevance and engagement, due to LLM-based re-ranking.

stories.Headline: China fines AI virtual human operator for fabricating product usage experiences
stories.Summary:
The Market Regulation Bureau of Panyu District in Guangzhou issued a penalty on November 13, 2026. This agency fined Guangzhou Wode Film and Television Media Co., Ltd. over 68,200 yuan for illegal medical advertisements. The penalty was publicly disclosed on November 16, 2026, targeting the operator of the virtual character Fang Taozi. This case marks the first penalty in China for AI virtual humans fabricating product usage experiences. The fine targets a 60-second ad for Nuts Power cosmetic contact lenses, which are Class III medical devices.

The AI character claimed the lenses were comfortable for a whole day and did not shift when blinking. Regulations require such ads to be reviewed and clearly mark that users should read manuals or seek medical guidance. Additionally, the law prohibits using advertising spokespersons for recommendation or certification of these specific medical devices. The Market Regulation Bureau classified the act as the illegal publishing of medical advertisements and false advertising. Officials stated the penalty targets the fabricated content and publishing procedure rather than the identity of the on-camera presence.

They argued that while AI is not a legal spokesperson, it cannot bypass the bottom line of authenticity. The core issue is the fabrication of fictitious personal product usage experiences by a digital image. Netizens questioned how a digital image with no eyeballs or corneas could know if lenses were comfortable. Viewers in the comment section realized that the AI had no eyes to experience the product. This case affects the AI digital human track, specifically those providing realistic human-like experience product recommendations.

High-risk categories like medical devices and pharmaceuticals now face a greatly compressed commercial order space. Fang Taozi gained 400,000 followers in one month after the June 12, 2026, launch of the series The Laid-off Girl. The operator, established in September 2019, registered 192 art work copyrights including Fang Taozi and Zhou Yiheng since July. The account's short video quotations started from 168,000 yuan, which is more expensive than many bloggers with millions of followers.

The industry will now divide into brand image broadcasting and realistic human-like experience product recommendation. AI can still broadcast parameters and read brand propositions, but it cannot output first-person physical experience testimony. Future boundaries include five prohibited actions: wearing, eating, applying, using, and smelling. The articles leave open how beauty, food, and home furnishing categories will adapt to these rules.

stories.Headline: Siemens India showcases industrial AI and digital twins to cut engineering timelines and costs
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is being integrated into India's manufacturing, infrastructure and transportation sectors in a push aimed at boosting productivity and encouraging sustainable practices, according to TechGig. The report says the move could reduce engineering timelines and costs, and it describes the integration of AI with engineering knowledge, real-time operational data, automation and digital twins as central to Siemens India Innovation Day 2026. That event, held under the theme "AI for the Real World," highlights AI deployed in industrial environments where reliability, safety, cybersecurity and measurable outcomes are critical, the article says. Applications named in the report include AI-assisted engineering, predictive maintenance, automated quality inspection and process optimisation, all of which rely on a connected foundation linking information technology and operational technology.

The article explains that digital twins are virtual representations of products, machines or infrastructure assets used to design, simulate, validate and optimise their physical counterparts, which helps find problems digitally so corrections are faster and cheaper before physical construction. Physical AI extends artificial intelligence into machines and physical systems so they can interpret objectives and respond to changing conditions autonomously, a progression from rule-based to intent-based automation. For India, the report says, this offers a chance to leapfrog older stages of industrial automation and compress technological progress that previously took many years, while companies that do not adopt Physical AI risk falling behind global competitors. Every AI model depends on physical infrastructure including computing capacity, electricity, cooling, connectivity, automation and resilient operations, and the challenge for customers is to design and operate that capacity efficiently and reliably at scale, according to the article.

Autonomous buildings use connected data and domain-specific AI to sense conditions, predict requirements and take governed action, with potential applications in energy optimisation, predictive maintenance and improved occupant comfort, the report says. Sunil Mathur, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Siemens Limited, noted that energy accounts for a significant portion of operating costs in industries like hotels and cement plants, making efficiency improvements impactful. On railways, the article says India's transformation can leverage digitalisation, automation and data to enhance infrastructure intelligence, with technologies such as Signaling X, Communications-Based Train Control and predictive maintenance applications supporting safer, more connected operations and better asset availability. The stated objective is to gain greater value from every train, signal, power system and physical asset throughout its operating life.

stories.Headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion Series C to advance its AI drug design engine
stories.Summary:
Isomorphic Labs, the UK-based AI drug research company founded by Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, announced on November 17, 2026 that it had completed a $5 billion Series C financing round, equivalent to about 33.3 billion yuan, which was oversubscribed. The round was jointly led by Greenoaks and HSG (Sequoia Capital), with participation from a16z and multiple new investors, while Alphabet continued to make large-scale investments. All existing investors also took part, including Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek and the UK Sovereign AI Fund. According to the article, the round refreshed the company's previous single-round financing record and may set a new global record for single-round financing in the AI pharmaceutical sector. The financing brings Isomorphic Labs' total publicly disclosed funding to $7.7 billion, about 51.3 billion yuan, after a $600 million first external round in March 2025 and a $2.1 billion Series B in May of that year.

The company, founded in 2021 and headquartered in London, plans to use the new funds to upgrade its proprietary drug design engine IsoDDE, expand its self-developed and partnered drug candidate pipelines, and build a globally AI-driven bioengineering infrastructure. It said positive preclinical results have been achieved in its internal oncology and immunology projects and in cooperative projects, and that preparations are underway to advance them into clinical trials. The article adds that the use of the financing has extended from model research to drug pipelines, translational research and clinical development infrastructure. Hassabis, who is founder and CEO of Isomorphic Labs, co-founder and Chairman of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet, and who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction work with AlphaFold, said the team believed at founding that biology could be understood and modeled at the most fundamental molecular level and that AI could significantly accelerate this process. He said the company's drug design engine is generating molecules with higher precision and speed, and that the financing will help the team build fundamental biological models, deepen understanding of disease mechanisms and push the first batch of therapeutic projects to clinical trials.

Max Jaderberg, the company's President since January 2026, who holds a doctorate from the University of Oxford and previously led the DeepMind Open Learning Research Team and served as Chief AI Officer, said the team achieves reproducible scientific progress with models every week and converts it into better molecular properties. Isomorphic Labs was incubated by Google DeepMind and operates independently under Alphabet for external financing, and its core technology is the IsoDDE engine, which integrates fundamental simulated AI models covering multiple therapeutic areas and drug types and is described as exploring the vast chemical space to help design, optimize and screen molecules with ideal druggable properties. The company has also developed proprietary Agents for exploring complex biological systems and conducting reasoning, and says the combination of its models and Agents has driven progress across multiple candidate drug pipelines. After this round, the company will continue to improve IsoDDE, explore new biological fields with more advanced models, build a partner ecosystem and construct a scalable, AI-centered translational research and clinical development system. The article notes that most of the company's major achievements remain in the preclinical stage, and that as the first projects advance to clinical trials, the safety, effectiveness and development progress of its candidate drugs will become an important basis for verifying AI drug design capabilities.

stories.Headline: Judge Wise lets memory price collusion lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron proceed
stories.Summary:
A class action lawsuit over memory price manipulation will proceed after Judge Noel Wise of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California dismissed the joint motion to dismiss filed by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron on November 14. The ruling, a 20-page document, rejected the three manufacturers' attempt to end the case. The lawsuit was first filed on June 25 this year. Mark Garciagire, an ordinary consumer living in Pasadena, California, joined 16 other plaintiffs and entrusted the boutique law firm Bathaee Dunne to sue the three major memory manufacturers in federal court. The 17 plaintiffs include ordinary consumers who buy RAM modules from Amazon and Micro Center, as well as small distributors such as PC assembly stores in Florida.

The three parties must submit an official response before December 7 and are required to hand over internal production capacity schedules, executive correspondence and meeting minutes during the subsequent discovery phase. The plaintiffs accuse the three giants of colluding to control production since October 2022, leading to a 697% surge in the price of regular DRAM contracts within 18 months. They presented shopping receipts in the 118-page indictment. The three companies together hold over 91% of the global DRAM market share. This is the first time in DRAM history that a class action lawsuit over price hikes during the AI cycle has crossed the motion to dismiss stage and entered the evidence discovery phase.

Judge Wise became a federal prosecutor through the U.S. Department of Justice's Honors Program in her early years and later spent ten years presiding over complex civil litigation trials in California courts. In response to the claim that the old case would repeat itself, she only replied: "This court does not think so." Facing the defense lawyers' "eagles watching each other" theory, Judge Wise refuted along the same metaphor: in nature, eagles may watch each other when hunting, but they will never fly together in a neat formation. She dismissed the motion to dismiss because the plaintiff presented "additional factors" sufficient to meet the threshold at this stage. The plaintiff's lawyer Brian Dunne's team was also prepared early.

The defense lawyers referred to the period from the end of 2022 to the beginning of 2023 as the "DRAM Winter". In the first quarter of 2023, Samsung's semiconductor division suffered a huge loss of 3.51 billion U.S. dollars, SK Hynix lost 2.61 billion U.S. dollars, and Micron posted a net loss of 5.833 billion U.S. dollars for the entire 2023 fiscal year. The lawyers argued that production cuts were for self-rescue, and shifting production to HBM was to chase the AI trend. They cited the Chicago School's "oligopoly interdependence theory", which successfully convinced judges in a similar lawsuit back in 2018. The plaintiff pointed out that on October 26, 2022, SK Hynix took the lead in cutting DRAM production capacity, and only three weeks later, Micron followed suit immediately.

In January 2023, Samsung executives even publicly stated that "we will never artificially reduce production of memory chips", but on April 7, 2023, Samsung suddenly made a 180-degree turn and joined the production cut camp. According to TrendForce's calculation, by the first quarter of 2026, the output value of a single wafer for DDR5 64GB RDIMM has surpassed that of HBM, and its profit margin is also higher than HBM. In the third quarter of this year, the global total DRAM revenue soared to nearly 200 billion U.S. dollars, a year-on-year surge of 369%, but the actual total shipment capacity of the entire industry only increased by 4%. The lawsuit revealed that Samsung and SK Hynix forcibly raised the price of server memory sold to Google and Microsoft by 60% to 70% within one quarter, and refused to sign long-term multi-year contracts. By the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, Micron's single-quarter revenue surged to 54.23 billion U.S. dollars, and its Non-GAAP gross profit margin soared to 87%, surpassing NVIDIA in one go; its full fiscal year net profit reached 84.97 billion U.S. dollars.

In the second quarter of 2025, the three parties all shut down or significantly cut the production lines of low-cost DDR4 for regular PCs; Samsung and Hynix also simultaneously stopped selling old DRAM manufacturing equipment to the second-hand market. On December 3, 2025, when consumer-grade memory prices hit a record high, Micron suddenly announced the shutdown of Crucial, its well-known consumer brand that had been in operation for 29 years. By January 2026, the three parties launched almost identical "customer review mechanisms" in the same month, using nearly copy-pasted questionnaires to interrogate distributors and OEMs. Apple CEO Tim Cook publicly complai More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google opens preorders for Gemini smart glasses with Samsung and sets Dec 10 release
stories.Summary:
Google opened preorders on Nov. 12 for its Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear, developed with Samsung, with frame designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, and plans to release the glasses on Dec. 10. The Warby Parker models start at $395, while the already available Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 costs $449. Google's glasses are powered by Gemini, and Meta's glasses use Meta AI. Both products offer cameras, AI assistants, and hands-free features. Buyers must decide whether to buy Meta's glasses now or wait for Google's alternative.

Warby Parker offers three frame styles starting at $395, and Gentle Monster has six styles priced from $449 to $489. Both collections use the same underlying hardware, with differences in design, fit, and lens options. The glasses combine Gemini with a 12MP camera, open-ear speakers, and four microphones, according to Samsung's announcement. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 also has a 12MP camera but includes six microphones. Both support 3K video recording at 30 fps, and both advertise up to nine hours of battery life per charge.

Google's glasses offer 64GB of storage, twice Meta's 32GB, and Google claims up to 72 hours with its charging case, while Meta's case provides another 50 hours. Google's frames weigh approximately 40 to 44 grams depending on the model, and Meta's standard Wayfarer Gen 3 weighs about 51.5 grams and offers adjustable temple tips. Both support prescription lenses, although options vary by frame. Google's glasses offer HDR photography and video stabilization, while Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 includes slow motion and hyperlapse recording. Meta claims its updated microphone system reduces background noise.

According to Google's product announcement, the glasses allow wearers to ask Gemini questions about their surroundings, translate conversations, and get hands-free assistance. On supported Galaxy phones, users can ask Gemini to summarize a whiteboard and save the information to Samsung Notes. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offers similar visual assistance, voice commands, and live translation, with integrations centered on WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram. Meta's September launch announcement introduced a customizable action button. Google is a better fit for people who regularly use Gemini, Maps, and other Google services, while Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 suits those who frequently use Meta's messaging and social apps.

According to Google's official product information, the glasses support selected Pixel and Galaxy phones as well as compatible iPhones, and activation requires an eligible Google account associated with the United States or South Korea. Users must be at least 18, and some capabilities, including Guided Vision and Aira visual assistance, require a compatible Android phone at launch. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 requires a compatible smartphone, a Meta account, and the Meta AI app, and its supported services and AI features can vary by country. Google says its privacy protections include recording indicators, camera permission controls, and automatic redaction of bystanders' faces during Gemini visual queries. The company also says visuals processed through those queries are not used to train AI models or target advertisements.

Meta's glasses include an external recording indicator to alert people nearby when photos or videos are being captured. Buyers prioritizing camera quality, call performance, or real-world battery life may be better off waiting for independent comparisons after Google's Dec. 10 release. The $395 Warby Parker models could be worth waiting for, particularly for buyers who regularly use Gemini and Google services. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 is the more immediate choice for shoppers who want smart glasses now or already rely on Meta's supported apps. Before spending hundreds of dollars, buyers should check whether their phone supports the features they want.
