stories.Headline: Helient earns Microsoft Data and AI partner designation and launches AI advisory service for law firms
stories.Summary:
Helient, a technology solutions provider serving the legal and other security-conscious industries, announced on November 17, 2026, that it earned the Microsoft Solutions Partner designation for Data & AI (Azure). The Haddonfield, New Jersey company also introduced a new AI Advisory service designed to help law firms adopt Microsoft Copilot and related AI capabilities with greater security, confidence, and control. The designation reflects Helient's continued investment in helping organizations modernize data platforms, strengthen analytics, and prepare for AI adoption with Microsoft technologies. It builds on Helient's broader expertise across cloud infrastructure, security, data, and AI. The announcement was issued through PRNewswire from Haddonfield, New Jersey.

The AI Advisory service focuses on four key areas, starting with strategy, which means identifying where Microsoft AI can support meaningful business and workflow needs. Readiness covers reviewing data access, permissions, infrastructure, and the firm's Microsoft environment. Adoption means helping firms incorporate approved AI capabilities into everyday work. Security addresses information protection, policies, permissions, and risks associated with unmanaged AI use. The service is available to law firms considering Microsoft Copilot and related AI capabilities or looking to improve an existing deployment.

Brad Bono, Chairman and CEO, said earning the designation means a great deal because it recognizes the expertise and commitment of Helient's people. He said Helient has always believed deep technical knowledge matters most when applied in practical ways for clients, and that clients' way of working is changing quickly. He said Helient wants to make sure clients' technology evolves with them, giving them the foundation to use AI in ways that make sense for their business. Bono said there is a lot of noise right now and law firms are being asked to make decisions quickly. He said Helient's job is to slow down the right parts of that conversation, covering where AI is genuinely useful, what needs to be addressed before it is introduced, and how firms maintain control of their information.

Separately, Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake about a day apart in October 2026, both built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year, and Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members now report they have embedded AI in their legal departments and actively use it. Brown said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms, and he expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists.

Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, places the source of advantage inside the firm, in change management treated as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability rather than a one-time rollout. She adds that many firm leaders she has worked with know their firms need to change but have no team to lead it. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy and a former chief strategy officer, argues that rolling out a new tool can threaten someone's competence, confidence, autonomy, status or professional identity, and she learned it training legal secretaries to move from WordPerfect to Word. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute and author of Lean Six Sigma for Law Firms, compresses her method to three words in a fixed order: people, process, platform, and she sees many firms running it backward. Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers and former chief innovation officer at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, calls the gap between announcement and action "innovation by press release."

Gary concedes that some convergence is inevitable, because companies hear the same customers and face the same pressures, and simultaneous launches can signal a maturing market. He points to firms that stand apart through their history, noting that Thompson Hine's AI-enabled SmartPaTH Plus rests on more than a decade of investment in its SmartPaTH delivery model. The ACC has roughly 48,000 members, the in-house buyers whose expectations those surveys reflect. The gap between Goodwin's Regina OS launch and Davis Wright Tremaine's firmwide AI expansion was 4 days, and the gap between Harvey's and Legora's launches of products both named Intake was about 24 hours. Gary's third installment, promised on positioning, timing and strategic alignment, is the next marker in this conversation.

Helient is a Microsoft Solutions Partner helping organizations modernize, secure, and manage complex cloud and hybrid environments with practical expertise and a long-term perspective. With deep experience across Modern Desktop, Azure, infrastructure, security, and managed services, Helient helps organizations reduce complexity, improve operational stability, and move work forward with confidence. The articles leave open whether ACC members will begin reporting that law firm AI investments show up as lower or more predictable outside counsel spend. They also leave open which firms that staffed the change work would be named if that happened. The articles do not say what Gary's third installment will conclude.

stories.Summary:
Standing vice chairman Ha Jung-woo of the National AI Strategy Committee visited several research sites in Daejeon on November 17, 2026. He toured the National AI Science Research Center, Daejeon Tipstown, and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology to discuss industrialization. This trip followed previous regional visits to Daegu-North Gyeongsang and Gangwon that took place during October. Ha met with various officials from academia, industry, and research to review ways to apply artificial intelligence in the field.

The committee is focusing on the K-Moonshot project, which uses AI across twelve mission areas including nuclear fusion, semiconductors, and new drugs. This effort is supported by the National AI Science Research Center, which was established in May to integrate AI into the entire research process. Additionally, the government is promoting K-Factory, an intelligent unmanned factory system that utilizes digital twin technology and robots. Ha reviewed the KAIROS platform at KAIST, which is an unmanned operating system built with domestic technology to control logistics and humanoid robots.

Ha Jung-woo and other officials discussed the necessity of strengthening industrial competitiveness to help South Korea become one of the top three AI powers. During a talk concert at Innovate Korea 2026, Ha exchanged views with Yoon Kuk-jin, Jin Yohan, and Hong Won-hwa regarding corporate survival and future talent. He also spoke with investors and startups at Daejeon Tipstown, a facility established in 2021 that currently hosts thirty companies. The participants focused on the tasks required for entering global markets and exporting the K-Factory system overseas.

stories.Headline: Tangzheng Lian and coauthors post BlinkOPD, a distillation method that cuts training data 12-fold
stories.Summary:
Tangzheng Lian, Hang Zhang, Guanyu Hu, Renjiu Hu, Zhensong Zhang, Jiankang Deng and Jifei Song posted a paper on arXiv on 17 November 2026 describing a method called Blink On-Policy Distillation, or BlinkOPD, for training multimodal large language models. The work targets on-policy distillation, a post-training approach that improves fine-grained perception by folding costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. The authors report that vanilla on-policy distillation is inherently susceptible to what they call linguistic momentum, in which the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes and thereby weaken corrective supervision. Their proposal has the teacher blink at every token, reading the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed.

The method adds a first-glance gain that further strengthens the correction on rollouts which conflict with the teacher, so that more effective supervision is extracted from each on-policy trajectory. Using only 500 training images, which the authors say is 12 times less data than existing on-policy distillation methods, BlinkOPD reaches state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks. Beyond fine-grained perception, the paper reports strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination and multimodal reasoning abilities. The abstract lists the code as a URL on the paper's page.

The seven authors are credited with the method and its results, and their abstract states the claims about the benchmarks and the training data without attributing them to any other party. The paper appears under the identifier 2611.16402 and is dated 17 November 2026, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The abstract describes on-policy distillation as an effective post-training approach and frames BlinkOPD as the response to the linguistic momentum problem it identifies. No further statements from the authors beyond the abstract are given in the articles.

The context the articles supply is the arXiv listing itself, which also describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features directly on the website. The listing says both individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have embraced its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv is committed to working only with partners who adhere to them. It also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next with the paper beyond its availability in the listed formats.

stories.Headline: Han Seong-sook bans smart devices and deploys extra staff to stop AI cheating in college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Tuesday that the government would activate an interagency emergency response team, ban the possession of smart devices during the exam and deploy additional personnel to test sites to root out AI cheating in this week's college entrance exam. She made the remark during a Cabinet meeting, as concerns deepened that AI-assisted cheating could be used in this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, which is set for Thursday. The concerns followed the confession by the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam that he cheated with the help of AI. Han called such cheating a social evil and said the government would root it out completely.

Han said all smart devices, including smartphones, must be powered off and turned in, and that authorities would thoroughly inspect all glasses and watches worn by test takers. She said items such as collars, sleeves and buttons would also be carefully checked. The government will tighten the management of Wi-Fi networks around the test sites, and all bags belonging to examinees must be stored outside the examination rooms, such as in hallways. Checks will be conducted to ensure that no smart devices are active among the personal belongings stored outside the examination rooms.

Han said the government would deploy additional proctors and apply a zero-tolerance policy to strictly penalize any instances of cheating. She said any suspected case would be thoroughly investigated and met with stern action, including invalidating the exam, revoking eligibility and filing criminal complaints or requesting police investigations. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's exam, including a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or about $75,000, for tips. The article did not say what happens next beyond those measures.

stories.Headline: Fractal evaluates 20 to 25 startups for acquisitions to strengthen enterprise AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
Fractal is evaluating 20 to 25 startups for potential acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering, according to a Reuters report cited by TechGig on 17 November 2026. The company is looking to strengthen its enterprise AI capabilities ahead of an expected scale-up in enterprise AI adoption. CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said the merger and acquisition focus is on acquiring specialised engineering talent. The company also aims to strengthen relationships with large cloud computing firms and frontier AI labs. Fractal is open to deals worth up to ₹1,000 crore, with a preferred acquisition size of $50-100 million, Velamakanni said.

The company evaluated around 800 potential targets over the past 12 months. Fractal reported record revenue from operations of ₹956.5 crore in Q2 FY27, up nearly 20 per cent year-on-year, while net profit more than doubled 139 per cent year-on-year to ₹79.2 crore in the same quarter. Earlier in November, Fractal acquired Geneva-based analytics firm PricingOne for 1.32 million Swiss francs ($1.57 million), which Velamakanni described as an acqui-hire providing a foothold in Europe. Velamakanni expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper. He noted the cost of fixed intelligence from a foundation model could fall 93 per cent over a year.

This shift should make large-scale AI deployment compelling for enterprises, with impact becoming meaningful as early as FY28. Fractal aims for acquisitions that accelerate its ability to build and deploy complex enterprise AI solutions. The company reorganised its business in April around three pillars: AI-led Transformation, AI Foundations, and AI Work & Workforce. This structure enhances its enterprise AI offerings and builds capabilities in agentic AI governance. The articles do not say when any acquisition might be completed or which specific startups are in talks.

stories.Headline: IBM chairman Arvind Krishna plans $10 billion quantum investment and predicts AI will displace 10 to 20 per cent of jobs
stories.Summary:
IBM spends approximately $3 billion every year in India, and the company plans a $10 billion global investment in quantum computing over the next five years, according to Chairman and Chief Executive Arvind Krishna, as reported by TechGig on November 17, 2026. Krishna also predicted that artificial intelligence could displace 10 to 20 per cent of jobs over the next decade, with the business process outsourcing industry likely to face the biggest reductions in employment. IBM has continued to expand its workforce in India, hiring an estimated 5,000 to 10,000 people over the past year, and it is increasing recruitment in chip design, software development, testing, site reliability engineering, and AI. Nearly half of the code written at IBM is already generated by AI, Krishna said, and he predicted that programmers would evolve into system engineers who tell AI what to write rather than writing code themselves.

Krishna estimated that AI could add around $500 billion to India's gross domestic product by the end of the decade, and he urged the country to accelerate AI adoption across businesses and government rather than focusing disproportionately on developing large language models. IBM research indicates that over 90 per cent of Indian enterprises recognise AI's potential, but more than 75 per cent have made little progress in adoption, a gap that reflects challenges in data readiness, skills, and willingness to redesign business processes. Unlike earlier technologies, AI delivers full benefits only when it is integrated across entire business processes, according to the article. IBM is working with the Andhra Pradesh government and Tata Consultancy Services to establish a quantum computer in Amaravati by early 2027, and Krishna expects quantum computing to generate significant revenues by 2028-29 as commercial and scientific applications emerge.

Krishna favoured a light-touch approach to AI regulation, arguing that excessive government intervention could undermine innovation, and he said existing laws already address several potential harms associated with the technology. He advised the Indian government to scale existing initiatives in semiconductors and AI deployment before pursuing additional technology bets. Krishna predicted that open models would account for 80 per cent of all AI tokens before the end of the decade, which could limit the pricing power of a small number of large model providers. He also warned businesses against becoming overly attached to existing products and models as technological change accelerates, according to the report.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix invests 1.4 trillion won to support domestic chip suppliers and fund Trinity Fab
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix announced on Monday that it plans to spend 1.4 trillion won, or about $1.05 billion, over the next five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment. The South Korean chipmaker said the programme is meant to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the AI chip market. The company also gave details of a jointly funded testing facility called Trinity Fab, which will cost 874.6 billion won and will sit at its semiconductor complex in Yongin, south of Seoul. Smaller suppliers will use the facility to test products under conditions similar to commercial chip production lines, and it is scheduled to begin operations in May 2027.

SK Hynix will put 443.2 billion won into Trinity Fab, the central government will contribute 373.6 billion won and local governments will add 57.7 billion won. The facility will be housed within the first chip plant at the Yongin cluster, where the company plans to invest 600 trillion won to build four fabrication plants. The supplier support programme covers four stages, namely research and development, testing, mass production and sales, and its aim is to help smaller companies overcome financing and technology challenges. Under the research support programme, SK Hynix will provide up to 50 per cent of initial development costs in advance and will compensate suppliers for work done even if a project does not meet its targets. SK Hynix and financial institutions will further provide 2 trillion won in financing, backed by the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation.

SK Hynix is responsible for the investment and for the Trinity Fab partnership, which it runs with the central government and local governments. The company said the programme is intended to assist smaller companies in overcoming financing and technology challenges, and it will pay suppliers for work undertaken even when a project falls short of its targets. The articles do not name any individual executive or give any further direct comment from the company. The context the articles give is intensifying competition in the AI chip market, which the investment is meant to address by bolstering the supply chain. The articles do not say what happens after the five year programme or after Trinity Fab opens in May 2027.

stories.Headline: UNESCO finds AI models answer climate science questions well but average 33.8% on policy interactions
stories.Summary:
UNESCO released a report titled Can We Trust AI on Climate Information?, developed with the UNESCO Chair in Artificial Intelligence at University College London, on 17 November 2026, testing how reliably AI models handle climate-related questions. The number of models varied by test, with up to 33 assessed overall, five in the multilingual assessment and 15 in the conversational-pressure assessment. Leading models answered 88% to 96% of established climate-science questions correctly, and the best scores on tasks asking whether a source supported a claim were 71% to 77%. The best score for judging the direction of a single policy's effect was 94.5%, but across models accuracy on how two policies interact averaged 33.8%, close to the 33.3% chance baseline.

The multilingual assessment tested five models in 13 languages, and average accuracy was 88.6% in English, 83.6% in Hindi and Bengali, and 81.4% in Urdu, with only about half of the tested questions receiving identical answers across all 13 languages. In staged conversations, sustained pushback reduced the accuracy of initially correct answers by about 31 to 35 percentage points across 15 models, with many concessions occurring at the first expression of disagreement. For the policy test, researchers compared model answers with En-ROADS, a climate-policy simulator, asking whether the combined temperature effect of two policies would be greater than, less than or equal to the sum of their separate effects. The report says this measures agreement with the simulator on a defined task rather than the real-world success of any particular climate policy.

The report distinguishes two uses of AI that call for different standards of validation, namely public climate information, where services in Indian languages need language-specific testing including whether answers stay consistent and withstand misleading follow-up prompts, and policy analysis, where assessments of interacting measures need checks against validated modelling tools and scientific expertise. It says strong performance on factual questions is insufficient evidence for the policy use. The report's direct India-relevant evidence is the measured performance in Hindi, Bengali and Urdu, and its wider implication is to test a model for the specific task, language and conversational setting in which it will be used. The article names the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and the report notes that poorer performance in a language is not inevitable, since differences varied by model.

stories.Headline: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill pushes state-led AI and privacy rules as federal regulation stalls
stories.Summary:
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill pushed for state action on child safety and Big Tech privacy during a November 2026 interview. She acted because federal regulation on AI and social media has stalled while power shifted toward state governors. Sherrill believes states must now lead on data center oversight and the protection of children online. She argues that the current political climate requires governors to exercise powers that have not been tested recently. This shift occurred as President Donald Trump concentrated power within the executive branch of the federal government.

The governor signed a data center plan in May 2026 and related build-out bills in August 2026. New Jersey received a 525 million dollar share of the Meta settlement to address these tech issues. Sherrill noted that New Jersey put every port on notice that importing Russian diesel is illegal. She mentioned a data center fine exceeding one million dollars as part of her state's regulatory efforts. The governor also expressed her openness to joining the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact for future elections.

Governor Sherrill stated that power moves into vacuums left by the federal government in Washington. She said that states are now the laboratories for AI and privacy because no federal statutes exist. Sherrill believes that state data center plans are converging on pillars like energy and water reporting. She argued that this convergence and litigation could eventually produce a de facto national standard for the country. The governor claimed that being a strong leader requires being accountable and transparent about government problems.

Nilay Patel noted that tech billionaires now control huge swaths of local and national broadcast media. He mentioned that influencers like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani are shaping a new brand of politics. Sherrill said that voters are furious and scared because of the actions of billionaires like Elon Musk. She believes that working families are most empowered when Democrats fight for affordability and accountability. The governor noted that some communities are affected by noise and water issues caused by data centers.

Sherrill began her campaign in November 2024 immediately after Donald Trump won the presidential election. She ran on themes of affordability and accountability to secure a huge win in the midterms. The governor observed that corruption became a top issue for voters according to a Guardian poll. She linked this anger to tech CEOs visiting the White House and Trump's personal financial gains. Sherrill also discovered that the previous administration failed to clear non-citizens from the state voter rolls.

The state will continue to allow local towns to decide if they will host data centers. Moratoriums on these centers will likely spread until operators can prove they will not harm communities. Sherrill expects more Big Tech litigation to occur as states continue to fill the federal power vacuum. The articles leave open how the industry will demonstrate a model that convinces towns to cooperate. It remains unclear if influencer politics is a permanent shift or just a temporary moment in time.

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley rightsholders add over 100 AI tracks to Suno lawsuit
stories.Summary:
Rightsholders of Elvis Presley amended a lawsuit against the AI music generator Suno on November 13, 2026. This legal action was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The plaintiffs added more than 100 AI tracks that allegedly imitate Presley's voice or infringe songs. This amended complaint follows an original lawsuit that was first filed on November 6, 2026. The legal team is led by Richard S. Busch of the firm Adams and Reese.

The suit involves Elvis Presley Enterprises, ABG EPE IP, Raleigh Music Publishing, Abilene Music, and various trusts. It seeks 128.85 million dollars for copyright infringement across 859 songs, including Let's Twist Again by Chubby Checker. Elvis Presley Enterprises seeks over 50 million dollars, potentially tripled to 150 million, under Tennessee's ELVIS Act. Additional claims include 21.475 million dollars for stripping credits and 2,147,500 dollars for bypassing access controls. The filing cites 58 reproduced songs and 40 tracks using Presley's voice or likeness.

The plaintiffs allege Suno trained its AI on Presley's recordings without a license and willfully violated the Copyright Act. They claim Suno stole Presley's likeness and voice without care, calling the company's public denials unequivocally false. A spokesperson for Suno stated the service helps people create original music and prohibits unauthorized use of work. Suno claimed it does not allow prompts for specific artists and uses third party providers to screen files. CEO Mikey Shulman previously wrote in a blog post that the company never allowed prompts for copyrighted songs.

The lawsuit affects Suno, which raised 400 million dollars at a 5.4 billion dollar valuation in June. Other musicians, including Jason Isbell, are involved in a separate proposed class action lawsuit filed in Boston. Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment are also currently suing the AI company for similar issues. Warner Music Group settled its dispute with Suno and reached a licensing deal in November 2025. The plaintiffs argue that Suno's claims about prompt restrictions are false based on evidence provided to Billboard.

Suno admitted in an October 20 answer that users could include artist names in prompts as of January 2026. The company argued that it converts artist names into style descriptions rather than replicating a specific voice. The Presley plaintiffs cite a track called Recording session that allegedly infringes six different songs, including Hound Dog. Another exhibit is described as a complete reproduction of the hit song Can't Help Falling in Love. The complaint also includes 72 outputs of songs Presley recorded that the plaintiffs do not actually own.

The plaintiffs want a court order barring Suno from using Presley's voice and the destruction of training datasets. The case tests if the ELVIS Act applies to AI services to hold companies liable for their tools. The court must decide if Presley's army service from 1958 to 1960 allows for tripled damages. It remains to be seen if the court will grant the request to impound internal model weights. None of the allegations in either version of the Presley complaint have been tested in court yet.

stories.Headline: McKinsey and BCG say banks must adopt AI fast and at scale to capture $370 billion in annual profit by 2030
stories.Summary:
Global banks are entering a critical era of artificial intelligence adoption according to reports published in November 2026. McKinsey and Boston Consulting Group state that financial institutions must now implement these technologies speedily and at scale. The industry is facing a rapid shift as clients increasingly adopt AI agents for their own financial needs. This transition follows a decade of using AI primarily for fraud detection and raising operational efficiency. There is no longer a grace period for banks to pace their technological adoption.

Retail banks globally could gain US$370 billion in annual profit potential from AI by 2030 and beyond. This figure is over 30 per cent higher than potential gains from business as usual, according to Boston Consulting Group. In 2025, the banking industry achieved a record net income of US$1.3 trillion, but savings revenues fell nearly 35 per cent. Revenue growth for retail banks is expected to slow to 2 to 4 per cent annually through 2029. McKinsey surveyed 46,000 retail banking customers and found that awareness of generative AI tools is almost universal.

McKinsey says the AI disruption dividend will go to banks that move with precision and speed. They note that the conversation shaping transactions is increasingly happening outside of the bank. Boston Consulting Group claims that becoming an AI first organization is now a mandate rather than an aspiration. They state that AI significantly reduces costs for servicing and acquiring clients. Praveen Raina of OCBC says innovation must make banking easier for customers and people more effective.

Nearly a quarter of the 46,000 surveyed retail banking customers already use generative AI tools for their finances. S&P Global analysts Miriam Fernandez and Nicolas Charnay say the next three to five years are critical. They believe leaders in AI adoption will gain enduring advantages over laggards in the banking industry. Neobanks and fintechs are mentioned as efficient new entrants that could pressure traditional banks. S&P Global Ratings expects AI adoption to eventually weigh into the assessment of credit quality.

Financial institutions began using AI more than ten years ago to improve efficiency and detect fraud. Recently, deep pocketed banks have committed more capital to newer forms of artificial intelligence. Larger banks have an advantage because they can apply technology to a larger customer pool and cost base. However, smaller entities with less legacy infrastructure might find it easier to adopt AI solutions widely. S&P Global warns that hype could lead to poor investment decisions if budgets are not monitored.

Banks must now prudently allocate AI budgets and monitor returns to avoid scaling challenges. The industry is seeking to embed advanced capabilities into customer interfaces and various operational aspects. S&P Global suggests that efficiency gains only become substantial at high levels of investment. The articles leave open how specific banks will balance deposit profit falls with overall profitability. It remains to be seen which firms will successfully avoid creating overhead instead of real value.

stories.Headline: Uber's legal AI agent cuts contract review time by over 20 per cent at 91 per cent accuracy
stories.Summary:
Uber's Legal Redlining Agent has cut the average contract review time by more than 20 per cent while reaching 91 per cent accuracy in its AI-generated decisions, the company said in a report dated 17 November 2026. The system sits directly inside Microsoft Word, where it analyses proposed contract changes and assesses the legal risks they carry. It then recommends policy-aligned responses by drawing on retrieval-augmented generation, historical lawyer feedback and deterministic rules. Lawyers stay responsible for reviewing and approving every recommendation the agent makes. The agent spots edits made by external parties, works out their intent and compares the changes against legal policies.

It suggests whether a clause should be accepted, rejected or modified, and it writes comments explaining each recommendation. Uber began building the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025. An initial RAG setup pulled relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide the language model's responses, and a later feedback loop captured lawyers' decisions, reasoning and final edited text. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions down to about 20 candidates, and a second language model-based filtering stage checks their relevance.

Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life set to 365 days, gives priority to recent decisions. The architecture pairs a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph, while OpenSearch stores vectorised legal rules and historical feedback and Redis keeps session state for follow-up questions. A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and can override the model's recommendations. Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows.

stories.Headline: Kodivo launches free interactive lessons to help developers direct and verify AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Kodivo launched free, browser-based interactive lessons on November 17, 2026, to help developers work effectively with AI coding agents. The platform's AI Coding path teaches developers how to give agents clear tasks, select the necessary context, and verify the work the agents produce. The lessons include examples and practice questions that show how to turn vague requests into verifiable tasks. One scenario shows an agent changing code for a Save button, after which the saved note disappears when it is reopened.

The lessons present explanations in short, interactive cards that let developers practice the decisions they make while coding with AI. Users can try a lesson without creating an account, and the platform supports connecting external agents such as Codex or Claude Code through MCP. Developers who prefer learning with their own tools can use their own provider account for those connections. The free lessons do not include an external AI subscription or provider usage.

Kodivo is responsible for the platform, and its lessons focus on giving clear instructions and verifying agent output before developers trust the results. The stated aim is to improve developer proficiency in AI-assisted coding workflows. The lessons teach that verifying a requirement means following the interaction through saving and reopening, rather than solely inspecting the code. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Texas bill requires AI developers to report rogue incidents within 72 hours
stories.Summary:
A bill filed Tuesday in the Texas House of Representatives would require developers to report any rogue artificial intelligence incidents to the state, and it would let the state attorney general investigate any failures to report. House Bill 1201 was authored by Rep. Salman Bhojani, a Democrat from Euless. If passed, the law would govern frontier models developed or tested in Texas, along with incidents that happen to a person or computer system in Texas. The bill defines a frontier model as an artificial intelligence system, or the model it is based on, that is trained on a broad set of data, designed for generality of output, adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks, and trained using more than 10 to the 25th power integer or floating-point operations.

The incidents covered by the bill include accessing a computer, network or system without the owner's consent, disabling, circumventing or deceiving a human oversight process, and preventing an authorized person from rejecting, modifying, overriding or terminating the model's decisions or actions. They also include modifying, deleting or disclosing data without owner consent, and any action beyond the model's permissions that creates a foreseeable risk of death or bodily injury, substantial property damage, disruption of critical infrastructure or government service, or compromised information system security. Developers would have to report such incidents to the Texas Department of Information Resources within 72 hours, and that deadline shortens to 24 hours with law enforcement notified if there is an imminent threat of substantial harm to people. The penalty for failure to report would be at least $10,000 but no more than $100,000, though penalties could reach up to $1,000,000 per incident if a developer knowingly conceals information or submits materially false or misleading reports.

The bill would create some protection for developers, since a report would not be an admission of liability and would be confidential. HB 1201 would also make it illegal for an employer to retaliate against an employee who files a report in good faith. The Texas Department of Information Resources would be required to publish an annual report with an aggregate summary of rogue AI incidents. If enacted, the bill would take effect on Sept. 1, 2027, and the department would have to implement rules and a reporting system by Dec. 1, 2027. The legislative session starts on Jan. 12, 2027.

stories.Headline: UC Law San Francisco launches a three-day certificate lab for building legal AI tools
stories.Summary:
The legal technology hub known as LexLab at UC Law San Francisco announced a new educational program on November 13, 2026. This initiative is called the Law and AI Certificate Lab, which is designed as a three-day course for building legal tools. The intensive program will take place from December 1 to December 3 for a small group of participants. It provides a condensed version of the AI curriculum that the law school typically offers its students over a full semester. The course requires the participation of up to 24 individuals, including lawyers, government officials, academics, and technologists.

These attendees will use specialized technology provided by companies such as Legora, Harvey, and the website builder Replit. The curriculum focuses on the actual development of artificial intelligence tools while addressing important ethical considerations. This training allows professionals to build and evaluate their own software solutions within a short timeframe. Adjunct professor Damien Charlotin, who created the AI Hallucination Cases database, is directing the program alongside adjunct professor Erin Fraser.

Fraser also serves as an associate at the firm McDermott Will & Schulte while helping to lead this lab. These directors intend for the course to support professionals in navigating the complexities of modern legal technology. They aim to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and the practical application of AI in legal settings. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on sensitive computer chip smuggling
stories.Summary:
Former Commerce officials allege that Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to act on sensitive computer chip smuggling. These ex-employees describe his tenure as being marked by chaos and micromanaging. The allegations involve a refusal to use national security tools over the last year. This situation came to light as scrutiny heightened in November 2026. The controversy follows the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The department stopped adding firms to the Entity List after October 9, 2025. This created the first yearlong gap in additions since 2008. In May 2025, Lutnick rolled back a January 2025 rule blocking adversaries from AI chips. A new rule on Monday requires licenses for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This aims to close loopholes used to route chips to China.

Howard Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, are accused of blocking enforcement. Former staff claim Kessler micromanaged every minor decision and created a bottleneck. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed frustration that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip bans. Bessent stated that President Trump clearly wanted to stop China from receiving sophisticated Nvidia chips. The Commerce Department did not respond to requests for comment.

Four anonymous former officials fear professional reprisals for discussing their government experience. They claim enforcement officers found suspicious activity at Southeast Asian sites where Nvidia chips were delivered. An OpenAI researcher found evidence that banned Nvidia chips trained top Chinese AI models. Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025. These chips provided a quarter of China's acquired computing power.

The Biden administration first issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023. In February 2025, Lutnick started running the department and let go of veteran officials. These included Matthew Borman and Eileen Albanese, who were highly respected experts. An exodus of up to 50 skilled staff members followed over 18 months. This resulted in a loss of institutional memory regarding AI and diversion.

Key roles in the Bureau of Industry and Security currently remain vacant. These include the chief of staff and the principal deputy assistant secretary roles. The department claims the new licensing rule was directed by Treasury and the National Security Council. Reports suggest $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips reached China via Alice Huang. The articles leave open whether the White House will address these failures.

stories.Headline: Geetanshu Gulati and Tim Han urge readers to practice preemptive skepticism online
stories.Summary:
The Daily Trojan published an opinion article titled "Everyone should practice a post-AI mindset" on Nov. 17, 2026, written by Geetanshu Gulati and Tim Han. The article argues that readers should employ "preemptive skepticism" as they search for humanity and truth online. It says our generation is living through a technological revolution, and that millennials and Gen Z are often called digital natives or digital pioneers. It states that millennials and Gen Z are the most digitally literate generations, and that everything is done with smartphones nowadays. It gives ordering morning coffee and logging into Netflix or a bank account as examples of smartphone tasks.

The article says the digital world's most daunting thing is its lack of physicality or security, and that there is no such thing as concrete or absolute certification. It says everyone uses the internet and anyone can input information and modify it however they want. It says real information can be modified to mislead audiences, and fake information can be appealing enough to bring out real emotions. It says that with the rise of artificial intelligence-generated content on everyday media platforms, this is easier than ever. The article quotes Jelani Williams, a master's student studying digital social media, saying he has definitely seen a video he thought was AI.

It quotes him saying there are a lot of times he is just skeptical immediately, more so than anything, and asking whether something actually happened. It describes the liar's dividend as a phenomenon in which realistic AI and advanced technology allow public figures to falsely claim that authentic, damaging evidence against them is manipulated. It says the public figure then usually shifts the burden of proof to others, demanding even more concrete evidence despite having just stubbornly rejected the initial facts. It says the internet is permanently changing in ways one can't easily imagine, prompting us to keep engaging, stay up to date and leave marks. The article says people start acting overly intelligent, which makes the internet dangerous, and that one could easily fabricate false information to denounce another.

It says the one attacked could also easily accuse them of falsehood without verification, just because it criticized them. It says that in a world where fake can be mistaken for real and real for fake, simple claims and first impressions do not shift the entire burden of proof onto those presenting them. It says we should evaluate sources, corroborate evidence and demand support for claims of manipulation. It quotes Jelani saying a claim would just have to be backed up really well, and that people have to be taught how to interpret things properly so they understand it is not real. The article says guardrails are starting to be set up for AI transparency, and that the California AI Transparency Act requires generative AI providers to embed machine-readable disclosures in generated content and provide free diagnostic tools.

It says Article 50 of the European Union's AI Act ensures AI systems are developed so users know if they are interacting with an AI system. It says Coalition for Content Provenance and Authority credentials set standards and function as digital labels showing their origin of creation. It says these laws and standards try to keep online content credible and transparent, yet their effectiveness depends on whether companies, platforms and creators follow through. It says these can only be social contracts that lose their meaning if not followed, and that even with penalties in place they are nothing more than retaliatory actions after the consequence that cannot guarantee prevention. The article says one should practice "preemptive skepticism" for every single piece of content encountered, pausing to check where content comes from and what other evidence supports it before deciding whether to trust or dismiss it.

It says one must recognize the liar's dividend of public figures and demand more of their denials. It says skills in actively searching for and verifying the origins of content are a necessary, if not vital, skill for an individual in the post-AI age. It says we are too passive in understanding the changes these technologies bring to our lives, and that not a lot of us get to the nitty-gritty of how they shape behavior and what responsibilities come with using them. It says we often approach new technology as consumers prioritizing convenience, and few of us try to bear the responsibility of deciding what uses are ethical and what limits one should set. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Everyone should practice a post-AI mindset

stories.Headline: Pierre school officials draft AI classroom procedures after survey
stories.Summary:
The Pierre School District has spent the past several months working to address the growing use of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with district officials meeting alongside a staff committee to develop procedures for AI use after a community survey was conducted earlier this year. Superintendent Donavan DeBoer said he entered the role knowing that discussions about AI would be necessary as the technology becomes increasingly common, not just in schools, and he noted that AI has been a frequent topic at education conferences and professional retreats because of how quickly the technology evolves. Drawing a comparison to the introduction of cellphones in schools, DeBoer said educators learned that simply allowing students unrestricted access often created challenges that continue today, and he said the district needs to put guardrails on AI sooner rather than later because having some sort of plan is better than having no plan at all. District conversations began earlier this year with an AI-focused survey sent to staff, students and parents, and about 1,655 responses gave the district a starting point for committee discussions as members work toward establishing AI procedures for the 2027-28 school year. Eighty percent of students surveyed said they had used AI before, and nearly half of those students said they use it monthly or more often, while of the 832 student respondents, 309 said they use AI for homework help and 412 said they use it for research, with others reporting use for writing assistance and studying.

Of the 209 staff members who responded, about half said they had used AI for tasks including lesson planning, and most respondents agreed AI can help teachers save time, though many also expressed interest in additional training, recommended tools and established expectations for student use. Across all respondent groups, students, staff and parents expressed awareness that AI tools can sometimes produce inaccurate information, and DeBoer said many students also voiced concerns about academic integrity similar to those expressed by adults in the community. The district has since formed an AI committee that has met twice, and the group includes principals representing the elementary, middle and high school levels as well as Technology Director Bryan Linn, with DeBoer saying he and Linn are currently working to draft procedures and protocols for AI use. The committee plans to meet again in January to further develop those ideas before sharing them with building leadership teams for additional feedback, and DeBoer said he hopes to bring a proposal to the school board this spring and receive approval before the next school year. Currently, websites such as ChatGPT and Gemini are blocked on student devices because of privacy concerns, though DeBoer said the district may have opportunities to incorporate more secure AI tools into classrooms for activities such as project brainstorming or creating renderings in technical education courses.

DeBoer said he does not intend this to be a hard and fast policy because the world is moving at warp speed and the district's AI expectations and protocols will change as things change, and he said the district is looking at a set of processes and procedures to guide staff on consistent expectations for students rather than a policy that would constantly need revision. DeBoer said he expects AI use to be more common at the high school level than in elementary or middle school classrooms, particularly as students prepare for college, technical school and future careers where the technology is becoming increasingly prevalent, and he noted that AI-detection tools used during grading are not always accurate, prompting some teachers to return to pen-and-paper assignments to avoid concerns about misuse. While the district continues to develop expectations for classroom use, officials also hope to help teachers identify effective AI tools, provide additional training and continue evaluating the technology as it evolves, and results of the district's AI survey are available on the district website. AI policy is expected to remain a topic of discussion at Pierre School Board meetings, and the board meets at 5:30 p.m. on the second Monday of each month at the district administration building, with meetings open to the public.

stories.Headline: California passes first-of-its-kind law guiding attorneys on AI in discovery
stories.Summary:
The California legislature recently passed a first of its kind law to provide guidance for litigation attorneys navigating the complexities of artificial intelligence. This new legal framework was introduced to help legal professionals who are currently struggling to manage the rapid integration of AI into their daily practices. The legislation aims to offer a necessary flashlight for those foraging through the proverbial forest of emerging technology. It specifically addresses the challenges that arise when attorneys must handle discovery in an increasingly digital and automated environment.

The new law requires a shift in how attorneys approach the discovery process when artificial intelligence tools are involved in the creation of documents. It changes the landscape for litigation by offering specific assistance to those who find themselves knee-deep in an artificial intelligence world. While the provided text does not list specific section numbers or dates of enactment, it establishes a new standard for the state of California. This regulatory change is designed to clarify the obligations of lawyers when using these advanced tools during legal proceedings.

Patrick Fanning of Lathrop GPM reported on the development and noted that the guidance was much needed for the legal community. He suggested that the legislature has provided a way for attorneys to better understand their roles in this new technological era. Fanning highlighted the difficulty lawyers face when trying to balance innovation with the strict requirements of the law. His analysis indicates that the legislation serves as a critical resource for those managing complex litigation.

The broader context involves a wave of litigation regarding whether prompts and chat histories in generative AI are protected from discovery. Courts are currently distinguishing between factual materials and litigation strategy to determine if work product protections still apply. There is a growing concern that using consumer AI platforms may defeat confidentiality due to existing privacy policies. Legal experts are now watching to see if this California law goes far enough to protect email communications from open AI engines.

Articles.Title: Calif.’s New, First-of-Its-Kind, AI Law Offers Attorneys Some Assistance in Navigating Discovery - Law.com

stories.Headline: US states enact nearly 30 AI laws in 2026 as federal deregulation lags
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CIO on November 17, 2026 and written by David Talby, says the administration has made reducing regulatory barriers a priority, arguing lighter oversight is essential to American innovation and competitiveness. It says states are passing new AI legislation, international regulators are enforcing increasingly complex requirements, and lawmakers are turning attention to how businesses use AI. It says AI may be getting deregulated at the federal level while becoming more regulated in practice. It says an AI application meeting requirements in one jurisdiction may trigger additional obligations in another. It says consequences of inadequate governance are growing as AI becomes embedded in more business-critical processes.

The article says the White House issued an executive order last year seeking to limit conflicting state AI regulations and establish a more consistent national approach. It says an executive order does not automatically invalidate state laws. It says California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53), effective this January, requires covered frontier AI developers to publish safety frameworks and report critical safety incidents. It says New York's RAISE Act establishes similar obligations beginning in January 2027. It says California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed 11 more AI safety bills into law in September, capping a 2026 legislative year that saw nearly 30 AI-related measures enacted.

The article says Illinois in July 2026 enacted the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), effective January 2027, requiring covered frontier model developers to implement safety frameworks, report serious incidents and, for the largest developers, undergo independent compliance audits. It says the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA) took effect this year and establishes an intent-based liability model rather than a broad pre-deployment risk assessment requirement. It says Colorado in May 2026 enacted SB 26-189, replacing its earlier AI law with a framework governing automated decision-making technologies used in consequential decisions including employment, lending and housing. It says beginning January 2027 covered businesses will face disclosure and other obligations, while consumers gain rights concerning inaccurate personal data. It says Colorado also enacted the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements Act (HB 26-1263) in May, introducing requirements for conversational AI services including disclosures and protections for minors.

The article says the European Union's AI Act is moving into active enforcement. It says the EU in July 2026 adopted the AI Omnibus amendments, simplifying certain requirements and extending implementation deadlines for high-risk systems into 2027 and 2028. It says the underlying framework remains intact, with obligations addressing transparency, prohibited AI practices, general-purpose models and high-risk applications. It says the same application could face different requirements depending on where it operates, which individuals it affects and how its outputs influence decisions. It says the same underlying model might power a low-risk productivity assistant and a highly consequential employment application.

The article says organizations may have approved several enterprise AI platforms while individual departments independently integrate models into customer service, analytics, software development and decision-making workflows. It says third-party vendors continue embedding AI into existing products, often expanding an organization's AI footprint without corresponding governance processes. It says agentic AI systems are increasingly capable of accessing sensitive information, interacting with enterprise applications and taking actions versus generating responses. It says 280 laws were passed just this year, with weeks to go. It says David Talby is the CEO of John Snow Labs.

The article says federal lawmakers may eventually establish a national AI framework that supersedes some state requirements, and courts may also reshape the regulatory landscape. It says CIOs can't assume simpler, streamlined rules are coming. It says even with a unified federal approach, multinational organizations will face distinct international obligations. It says the best-prepared organizations will understand where their AI operates, understand its risks, continuously evaluate its behavior and demonstrate appropriate oversight. It says federal deregulation does not equal enterprise deregulation.

Articles.Title: The AI deregulation illusion: Why CIOs face more rules, not fewer - CIO

stories.Headline: NATO cyber agency gives allies OpenAI models and uses up to 300 billion tokens a month
stories.Summary:
NATO's Communications and Information Agency gives NATO's core institutions access to OpenAI's cybersecurity models so they can help protect Allied networks, and the alliance has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens a month. That access comes through Daybreak, OpenAI's program for vetted defenders doing authorized work such as reviewing code, chasing suspicious activity and testing fixes. The exposure sits in software that European institutions run every day, and ENISA, the EU's cyber agency, used OpenAI models to find four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes out for all four. ENISA and CERT-EU reviewed 27 software projects using several frontier models, OpenAI's among them, along with tools such as the Codex security plug-in, and maintainers assessed 88 potential issues and confirmed 95% of them as real.

Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation uses Daybreak to defend civilian infrastructure, and France's ANSSI and national agencies in Germany and Poland also have access. At NATO's 2026 Crossed Swords exercise, run by the CCDCOE, participants built and tested AI agents for cyber operations in Daybreak, with an emphasis on keeping humans in charge. CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help find six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, the operating system on MikroTik's network gear, and its researchers directed the work and checked findings on real systems. MikroTik released fixes, and CERT Polska confirmed they stop the attacks it had seen.

Dr Dylan Browne, the NCIA general manager, said that as the alliance scales adoption it will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models. He said this insight will help NATO optimise costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions. The agency's work therefore ties the technical defense of Allied networks to a closer reading of what the models cost to run and how they compare with rival offerings. The articles do not say what procurement choices or further deployments might follow from that review.

stories.Headline: Democrats win Congress as voters reject data centers over rising power bills
stories.Summary:
Democrats won both houses of Congress during the midterm elections in November 2026. Some candidates won by criticizing the AI boom and the growth of data centers. Voters expressed a strong desire for relief from rising electricity bills. This blue wave occurred as people rejected the proliferation of gigantic data centers. The election results reflect a widespread public backlash against the AI industry.

Voters rejected 40 of 41 local data center measures across 10 different states. A March Gallup poll showed 71 percent of Americans opposed local data centers. Wholesale electricity prices near some centers rose 267 percent over five years. Cornell researchers found operators pay only 38 percent of linked infrastructure costs. The four largest cloud companies expect capital spending of 720 to 740 billion dollars.

Senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan stated that people really hate data centers. Representative Greg Casar wants AI CEOs to testify under oath during hearings. Senator Ed Markey warned executives about the many subpoenas the government will print. Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona called for a day one pause on AI. Senator Bernie Sanders advocated for democratic oversight instead of an outright ban.

Building trade unions view data centers as a bonanza for creating new jobs. Some Republicans distanced themselves from the president because of their own constituents. Voters are concerned about electricity, water, jobs, and various AI doomsday scenarios. Tech leaders have courted President Trump, including Elon Musk who spent 500 million dollars. The Magnificent Seven companies now make up about a third of the S&P 500.

ING estimates that AI investment accounts for 37 percent of U.S. GDP growth. Governor Kathy Hochul of New York froze hyperscale data center permits for one year. Texas Governor Greg Abbott halted new grid connections while pending a necessary audit. Microsoft pledged in January to cover its own power costs for its operations. Meta and Amazon created billion-dollar community funds in August and October of 2026.

The Create AI Act would make a National Science Foundation computing program permanent. The AI Whistleblower Protection Act and AI LEAD Act are other bipartisan bills. OpenAI rebranded its data centers as compute campuses two days after the election. State utility regulators may force data centers to cover their own grid upgrades. It remains uncertain if Democrats can demand accountability from these powerful tech executives.

Articles.Title: Voters want relief from rising power bills. Democrats must find a way to deliver without stalling the AI investment helping drive the economy

stories.headline_source: Voters want relief from rising power bills. Democrats must find a way to deliver without stalling the AI investment helping drive the economy

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could erase many jobs forever and urges lawmakers to act
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the 71 year old cofounder of Microsoft, published a 6,000 word essay earlier this year titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical,” in which he warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out careers over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. In the essay he called for certain jobs to be “human reserved” and said AI will take on work in law, customer service, medicine, software and manufacturing, adding that many jobs will disappear forever. He wrote that the transition to the AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history and that the world is not preparing adequately for that transition. He also said that if the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.

The warning arrives alongside new figures on job losses, as Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported on November 5, 2026, that AI has been cited in 121,401 job cut announcements so far in 2026, which is approximately 20 percent of all cuts. Gates had already raised his concerns in September, when he appeared on NBC News’ Meet the Press with Kristen Welker and was asked whether AI is powerful enough to end all of humanity. He responded that AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths and that there has never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools. He added that self regulation is not enough and that legislation needs to be passed, with politicians and law enforcement offering safeguarding and monitoring.

The essay sets out Gates’ view that the coming shift will be turbulent and that choices made now are critical, and it calls for some roles to be set aside for humans rather than left to machines. His September remarks place the responsibility for safeguards on lawmakers and law enforcement rather than on the industry alone, since he said self regulation is not enough. The Challenger, Gray & Christmas count of 121,401 AI cited job cut announcements in 2026, about 20 percent of all cuts, gives a measure of how far the disruption has already gone. The articles do not say what steps, if any, governments or companies have taken in response to his call for legislation.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates Issues Grim Warning That ‘Many Jobs Will Disappear Forever’ Due to ‘Turbulent AI Era’ - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: ICBC Chairman Liao Lin outlines three priorities for banks adopting artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Liao Lin, the Chairman of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Ltd., presented three key priorities for banks using artificial intelligence on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He delivered these insights during his appearance at the APEC CEO Summit to discuss how financial institutions can best capitalize on new technology. The Chairman emphasized that banks must focus on specific strategic goals to successfully integrate these advanced digital tools into their operations. He believes that the current era is being defined by these major transformative technologies.

The strategy requires banks to align their technological advancements with their existing organizational structures to ensure efficiency. Financial institutions must also coordinate their investment cycles to keep pace with the rapid speed of technological change. Furthermore, the Chairman stated that banks must find a careful balance between pursuing innovation and managing potential risks. These three pillars are intended to guide banks as they move from pilot programs into full production.

Liao Lin explained that the Asia-Pacific region offers unique opportunities for AI due to its diverse financial services and vast markets. He also pointed to the highly interconnected industrial and supply chains within the region as a primary driver for growth. The Chairman described artificial intelligence as one of the most significant transformative technologies of the modern time. He suggested that leveraging these regional strengths would allow banks to maximize the benefits of AI adoption.

stories.Headline: St. Paul student says Turnitin flag gave her a zero as district lacks AI policy
stories.Summary:
A St. Paul Public Schools student wrote in a MinnPost opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, that she received a zero on an English essay that Turnitin flagged as 32 percent AI-generated, dropping her grade to a D on the night before her last day of sophomore year. She said she had earned a 98 percent in the class before that and had not used AI for any part of the essay. When she offered the next morning to rewrite sections with pen and paper, her teacher said that was not necessary because she knew the student's writing style and believed the work was original. The teacher had previously raised concerns about Turnitin, an AI detection tool used by the district.

The piece says the district has no official school board AI policy, although Phil Wacker, the district's high school curriculum supervisor, acknowledged Turnitin's limitations in September 2025, particularly for students whose first language is not English, according to St. Paul Publishing. At that time nearly 30 percent of the district's students were English learners. The SPPS Board of Education recently announced a goal of adopting an AI policy by the end of the 2027-28 school year, with details still vague and the board saying the policy will include expectations for how the district prepares students and staff to use, question, evaluate and create with AI. Wacker said conversations about a policy are happening.

The student argues that administrators, not students, should fix the problem, and that she sees a lack of urgency. She writes that the time spent debating a policy means the conversation will take her class's entire high school career, and that some students use AI and have found ways to avoid detection. Turnitin assigns a score based on the percentage of suspected AI sentences, measuring burstiness, or spontaneity of word choice, and sentence length, and the company claims human writing tends to be inconsistent and idiosyncratic. The student notes that her flagged essay was about how high school writing structure strips individuality from students' work.

Articles.Title: Why St. Paul Public Schools needs clearer AI detection rules — now - MinnPost

stories.Headline: China-linked threat actors use autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations
stories.Summary:
China-nexus threat actors used autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations between August and September. These attackers targeted advanced manufacturing, defense sectors, and various civil and human rights organizations. The malicious activity was tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. This campaign represents the second documented case of China-linked actors using the open source framework called Cairn. The actors conducted twenty-five operations against at least nineteen organizations to achieve unauthorized access or data retrieval.

The campaign targeted seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain firms and three US defense and defense policy organizations. Attackers used Chinese large language models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro to weaponize Cairn. Victims included a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, an education nonprofit, a US teacher's union, and an industry standards body. A defense policy think tank was also targeted through an open back-end registration endpoint on its identity platform. These operations lasted anywhere from twenty minutes to more than fifty hours and occurred simultaneously across multiple organizations.

Unit 42 researchers stated that attackers supplied a target and goal, then Cairn planned and executed the results. They noted that the framework coordinates activities through a shared blackboard where agents write findings as a fact-intent graph. Rickard Carlsson of Detectify said Cairn has a shared record that allows it to build on earlier findings. Tyler Oliver of Huntbase said it does not matter to a victim if a human or AI is behind the keyboard. John Strand of Black Hills Information Security suggested that organizations use continuous attack surface management and cyber deception.

The successful attacks resulted in the theft of dozens of valid credentials and military and government identities. One organization suffered a mass exposure of personal data that exceeded one million records. Attackers created persistent administrator accounts in a production system and modified a live industry standards-ballot document. The victims were affected by password-spraying, brute-forcing of production credentials, and unauthenticated account-creation bypasses on content management systems. Other organizations were targeted through identity and configuration weaknesses and exposed cloud APIs.

The attackers exploited known security gaps including insecure direct object references and mass-assignment privilege escalation. They also used weak and default credentials as well as dated public CVEs to gain initial network exposure. Unit 42 noted that AI is changing the speed, volume, and expanse of attacks but not the complexity. This means that software patching, attack-surface reduction, and identity hygiene remain effective defenses against these AI tools. The articles explain that AI agents can now work with limited supervision to identify and exploit vulnerabilities.

The findings provide a blueprint for how threat actors can weaponize AI tools in future offensive operations. Organizations are encouraged to identify all services exposed to the internet and restrict access wherever possible. Setting up tripwires can detect attackers during reconnaissance and lateral movement before they accomplish their objectives. The articles leave open how other AI penetration-testing frameworks, such as Artex, will be used in future campaigns. It remains to be seen how defenders will adapt to the increasing volume of autonomous AI attacks.
