stories.Headline: Portland AI Moratorium: $250K Pilot Cap, Ends Dec. 31, 2027
stories.Summary:
Portland City Council President Jamie Dunphy introduced Ordinance 2026-423 this week, a proposed moratorium on new artificial intelligence in city government, and the full council will hear it on December 3, 2026. The measure would add a new Chapter 34.20 to the Portland City Code, establishing a temporary moratorium on the City's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. Nothing has passed yet, and the Portland AI moratorium is a proposal, not a law. The draft carries a $250,000 ceiling on exempted pilots, a ban on no-cost deals, and an expiry date of December 31, 2027. The city's own announcement of Ordinance 2026-423 states the details.

Under the draft, the City could not sign new AI contracts or roll out AI, including upgrades that add or expand AI functionality in software the City already owns. Pilots, trials, trades, giveaways, purchase orders and no-cost agreements are covered. Existing contracts and pilots could continue through their current terms but could not be renewed, extended or amended to add AI functionality unless the council grants an exemption by ordinance. A pilot can proceed if the council approves it with a cost of no more than $250,000, a duration of no longer than 12 months, and a ban on using City data to train vendor models. Basic AI in existing software such as spell-check and spam filtering, and cybersecurity uses, are exempt, and a citywide AI inventory is due within 60 days of adoption, updated on an ongoing basis.

Dunphy said the aim is to protect public privacy, security and civil rights while the administration gets the Data and Privacy Office running and writes legislative guidelines. He said, "Emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, meaning we cannot simply go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code." He told reporters, "I'm not saying we shouldn't have AI." He said, "We have to have thoughtful, smart AI, and we shouldn't run full speed into whatever the latest technology is just because it's there." At a Tuesday press conference he said of the police pilot, "That pilot is already up and going and, as of now, they have a set scope."

OregonLive reported that the proposal could affect a Portland Police Bureau program using AI to screen suspects' data files, such as those on mobile phones or in online profiles, for child sexual-abuse material, as described by reporter Isabel Funk. Dunphy said that if the bureau wanted to connect it to the internet, expand its uses beyond internet sex crimes, or use it for retail theft, "that would not be allowed." Chief Bob Day said in a statement that the bureau is always looking for smarter, more efficient ways to work, particularly given staffing challenges, and wants to balance innovation with accountability, transparency and public trust. OpenAI has been offering a free CSAM classifier to vetted groups. Chicago has been eyeing an AI gun-detection pilot that would run six months across six districts.

KOIN reported that the Data and Privacy Office was established in March and is not yet operational. According to the ordinance summary on Portland.gov, the moratorium could end ahead of schedule if the Data and Privacy Office is certified as operational and the council adopts AI legislation. KOIN reported that Dunphy cited the growing volume of software and services with embedded AI being sold to the City as a reason for concern about how fast governments are being pushed to adopt it. The FBI has warned about the ARTEX AI hacking tool, which reportedly breaches networks in under three hours. A $250,000 budget over 12 months works out to roughly $20,800 a month.

The moratorium would expire on December 31, 2027, unless the council extends it by ordinance. If the council adopted the ordinance on December 3, which is not guaranteed, 60 days would land on February 1, 2027. The articles lay out five predictions for the December hearing without stating them here. The record is silent on whether the ordinance will pass.

stories.Headline: Law students sue Tribhuvan University over AI detection rules that reject theses
stories.Summary:
Law students including Vivek Chaudhary filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court of Nepal on 17 November 2026 against Tribhuvan University over its use of foreign AI-detection software. The petition challenges provisions of the university's Anti-Plagiarism Software Management and Operation Rules, 2080. Students say theses, seminar papers and clinical reports built over months of work were rejected on the estimated AI report shown by the private foreign software Turnitin. The petitioners named the Government of Nepal, the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the Ministry of Education and Sports, the Ministry of Defense and Tribhuvan University as respondents. The students say they were punished without even the minimum opportunity to present their defense.

The complaint centres on clause 10(3) of the Tribhuvan University Rules 2080, under which theses, seminar papers and clinical reports are rejected solely on the estimated percentage shown by software such as Turnitin and iThenticate as likely AI-generated. The petition seeks an order of mandamus quashing the provision, plus an interim order and priority from the court to secure the students' academic future. It asks for a mandamus to repeal the controversial provision and to create scientific and transparent standards for the use and regulation of AI. The petition cites the Tribhuvan University Act, 2049, arguing the university exceeded its general rule-making authority by creating prohibitions and punitive consequences, including rejection of theses, not present in the act. It also cites Article 28 of the Nepal Constitution and the Personal Data Protection Act, 2075.

The petitioners argue that no prevailing law in Nepal defines AI plagiarism and that there is no official government standard or software to identify it. They say information from the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers clarified that no separate act or regulation specifically addressing AI has been issued in Nepal. Under the Nepal Government's Work Allocation Regulations, they say, jurisdiction to regulate AI lies with the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. They argue the regulation seriously violates the principles of natural justice because it gives no mandatory prior opportunity to present a defense, question the software's errors and conduct independent technical testing. They say the university council's regulation, made beyond the scope of the act, is entirely voidable.

The petition states that the software reports themselves admit that similarity does not mean plagiarism. Students say parts flagged as AI by Turnitin showed as human-written or zero percent AI on other detection software such as ZeroGPT and Grammarly. The petition says the software collects students' names, email addresses and thesis details, plus keystrokes, deleted parts, IP addresses and digital activities during writing, and stores them on external servers indefinitely. It says students face serious risk of phishing attacks, email spoofing and identity theft from sending sensitive personal information and intellectual property to foreign company servers without legal authority and explicit consent. As key evidence the petitioners presented the official stance of the University of Virginia in the United States and a 2026 study by researchers at the University of Florida concluding that commercial AI detectors are flawed and unsuitable for academic evaluation or action.

The petition cites general legal principles and precedents from the Supreme Courts of India and the Philippines stating that plagiarism requires malice, deliberate intent and the theft of another person's original creation. It argues that since artificial intelligence does not claim ownership or copyright, plagiarism in the traditional sense is not objectively applicable to the use of AI-generated content. It cites international judicial precedents and scientific studies confirming that AI detection tools cannot be considered conclusive evidence. The petition claims Tribhuvan University and other educational bodies made mandatory the use of private software like Turnitin and iThenticate to check the originality of students' theses, seminar papers and clinical reports. It argues these software give automated results as likely AI-generated based solely on probability, with high technical errors and false positive rates.

Tribhuvan University spokesperson Nabin Bhandari clarified that theses cannot be copied verbatim and that the software will automatically detect it if done so. He expressed the view that anti-plagiarism testing is essential to prevent one person from stealing another's thesis and to make research original. He said such a system is necessary to prevent thesis duplication. The petition requests an interim order, stating that depriving students of research or examinations based on results from flawed and unscientific technology will cause irreparable damage. The articles leave open the court's response to the petition and any hearing date.

stories.Headline: Toxicologist Thomas Hartung argues AI biological twins need agreed validation standards before regulators trust them
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is transforming biological digital twins across every level of biological organization, according to a theoretical analysis by toxicologist Thomas Hartung published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and reported by bioengineer.org on November 18, 2026. The analysis examines how deep learning, transformer architectures, foundation models, and physics-informed neural networks have elevated biological simulation beyond static systems of differential equations. Biological digital twins maintain internal states coupled to physical counterparts through continuous data assimilation rather than functioning as generic classifiers or open-loop simulations. Across five nested scales, from single-cell multi-omics to the environmental exposures of entire populations, these architectures show capacity to model human biology without surrogate animal species. Hartung argues that technical ingenuity alone cannot secure regulatory trust without agreed credibility standards, independent prospective testing, and formal governance of self-updating algorithms.

The analysis establishes four foundational commitments that exclude conventional simulations, software dashboards, and static pattern predictors. A biological digital twin demands specificity, binding its computational state to a distinct biological instance such as a single patient or an individual organ-on-chip rather than an average population category. It requires continuous data assimilation, an iterative loop where telemetry, biosensor readings, or longitudinal omics samples update the model to track physical drift over time. The twin must encode mechanistic constraints from biological principles rather than statistical correlations alone, and it demands empirical testability with refutable predictions and quantified uncertainty. Representations lacking any criterion, including frozen neural networks, open-loop simulations, or decorative avatars, fail this definition and cannot serve as dependable regulatory instruments.

At the cellular level, representation learning and foundation models fuse multimodal single-cell measurements into dynamic latent manifolds. Single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer, scGPT, and scFoundation learn compressed representations across tens of millions of cellular profiles, separating technical batch artifacts from genuine biological signals. This manifold enables virtual perturbation experiments simulating cellular trajectory shifts under novel pharmacological compounds, gene knockouts, or environmental toxicants. In exploratory toxicology, virtual cells reorder experimental pipelines, nominating informative hypotheses for bench testing while reducing reliance on early rodent toxicity screens and primary animal cell cultures. General foundation models serve as shared infrastructure rather than digital twins until conditioned on specific cell populations and coupled to incoming experimental data.

At the in vitro level, computational twins model engineered cell cultures, microfluidic devices, and organoids, which Hartung identifies as the most technologically mature tier. The DigiLoCS liver-on-chip framework separates intracellular metabolism, passive permeability, and compartment partitioning, predicting clinical drug clearance distributions more accurately than conventional lumped single-compartment methods. Emerging organoid twins incorporate biophysical priors and active learning to forecast therapeutic responses and drug resistance in patient-derived cancer tissues, offering alternatives to patient-derived xenograft rodent models. Coupled with laboratory automation, closed-loop organoid systems can predict responses, execute robotic perturbations, and update internal states within hours. Mathematical unidentifiability, where multiple unmeasured parameter combinations yield identical observable outputs, remains a persistent challenge requiring targeted, standardized physical measurements rather than algorithmic expansion alone.

At the organ level, digital twins confront fluid dynamics, biomechanics, barrier transport, and electrical propagation across anatomical structures. Investigators deploy physics-informed neural networks to bypass the computational cost of traditional finite-element modeling without large-animal studies in dogs or pigs. By penalizing violations of physical conservation laws within loss functions, these networks act as rapid surrogate models executing organ-scale biomechanical simulations in near-real time while maintaining physical plausibility outside training domains. A three-organ microphysiological platform linking gut, liver, and placental tissues investigates maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics during pregnancy, addressing conditions where animal testing routinely misleads because reproductive toxicity and placental transfer diverge sharply between rodent models and humans. Derived from the Virtual Physiological Human tradition, these hybrid architectures integrate mechanistic physical principles with machine learning for auditable, trustworthy organ-scale safety assessments.

At the individual patient level, the Virtual Human Twin integrates multimodal health records, wearable telemetry, high-resolution imaging, and personal omics into an individualized clinical forecast. Personal twins enable clinicians to compare therapeutic regimens, evaluate dosing schedules, and anticipate adverse drug reactions in silico prior to clinical administration. In cardiology, personalized models calibrated to patient-specific electrophysiology and anatomical imaging have simulated arrhythmic activation pathways to guide catheter ablation procedures before surgery. In oncology, hybrid twins simulating tumor microenvironments assist clinicians in navigating heterogeneous malignancies without relying on animal xenografts.

The review cautions against hype surrounding all-encompassing digital human replicas claiming to forecast a patient's entire lifespan, noting that current clinical twins are narrow decision-support instruments that must contend with data harmonization challenges, physiological drift across aging, and algorithmic biases disadvantaging underrepresented demographic populations. At the population level, digital twins aggregate individual profiles to analyze community disease dynamics, conduct in silico clinical trials, and evaluate environmental hazards across the human exposome. While genetics reveals inherited susceptibility, the exposome maps the modifiable totality of environmental exposures including diet, occupational chemicals, and airborne pollutants. Exposome twins link external exposure monitoring, biokinetic internal dose modeling, molecular pathway alterations, and clinical endpoints to guide precision prevention strategies rather than producing unverified correlations.

Statistical mining and generative modeling of historical control databases enable virtual control groups for toxicity studies, curtailing the sacrifice of concurrent control animals, an application recognized in a March 2026 draft qualification opinion from the European Medicines Agency regarding non-Good Laboratory Practice rat dose-range-finding studies. In human trials, synthetic cohorts extend clinical evaluations into hard-to-enroll populations such as pregnant women or rare-disease patients, provided researchers apply rigorous counterfactual reasoning and target-trial emulation to prevent confounding and spurious certainty. Despite computational demonstrations across all five biological scales, the review stresses that independent scientific validation and regulatory credibility, not algorithmic novelty, represent the binding constraints on the discipline. Most published twin frameworks remain retrospective demonstrations conducted by original developers rather than prospectively verified methods evaluated across independent laboratories.

Because biological digital twins are inherently adaptive systems that continuously assimilate fresh data and update internal parameters, traditional validation frameworks treating assays as frozen, one-time tests are structurally inadequate. Hartung advocates next-generation validation, an iterative and risk-proportionate methodology evaluating methods across five dimensions: technical reliability, biological relevance, predictive performance, applicability domain, and data integrity. Twin credibility must be assessed against human-relevant biological mechanisms rather than concordance with historical animal tests, which themselves frequently suffer from poor reproducibility and limited predictive accuracy for human outcomes, and validation must operate as an ongoing, modular case-building process evaluating mechanistic backbones and adaptive learned components independently. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Advances Biological Digital Twins While Validation Limits Regulatory Adoption

stories.Headline: Malaysia prepares AI governance framework to ensure human responsibility for system decisions
stories.Summary:
Malaysia is preparing a new framework for AI governance to ensure human responsibility. Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo announced this plan to the Dewan Rakyat on October 5. The government expects to table the Artificial Intelligence Governance Bill in early 2027. This legislation will take a risk-based approach across various sectors to complement existing laws. It aims to enable the benefits of AI while building confidence for responsible use.

The July consultation proposed national governance principles, central oversight, and obligations proportionate to risk. It states that responsibility for AI must remain with identifiable people rather than the system. Directors owe duties of care, skill, and diligence under the Companies Act 2016. Section 216 of that Act concerns delegation to persons, not to automated systems. Section 17A of the MACC Act warns that directors are deemed to commit corruption offences.

Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo stated the bill would complement existing laws. Bank Negara Malaysia governor said on July 8 that AI belongs on board agendas. He added that responsibility for these systems cannot be delegated to an algorithm. Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar stressed that effective human oversight remains essential. Tan Sri Abdul Rashid Hussain noted that laws alone do not prevent corporate failures.

Arup's Hong Kong office lost US$25 million in early 2024 to deepfake video conference fraud. A Canadian tribunal held Air Canada responsible for misleading chatbot information regarding bereavement fares. Small business owners may be affected if AI refuses financing without a human explanation. Customers and patients are already influenced by AI regarding credit and medical information. The Securities Commission Malaysia proposed clearer expectations for board oversight and listed company disclosures.

The articles cite a 64-page code of ethics from July 2000 signed by Kenneth Lay. This code preceded the bankruptcy of Enron barely one and a half years later. The prime minister emphasized on February 24 that ethical considerations would guide the bill. Aon reported on October 5 that D&O cover for AI risks remains broadly available. The text references Malay-Islamic values of adab and amanah regarding knowledge and trust.

The government will now use the months before tabling to make proposals work. Boards must determine who is accountable and how to explain decisions to regulators. Institutions need suppliers to disclose material limitations and provide records to investigate system failures. The articles leave open how the framework will apply to AI in public services. They also leave open the specific conditions and scope of a due-diligence defence.

stories.Headline: HPE builds ChatHPE on Azure to give 30,000 employees governed agentic AI
stories.Summary:
HPE built ChatHPE using Microsoft Azure capabilities to reduce the time employees spent searching a vast body of internal knowledge for information, according to a Microsoft customer story dated 11/16/2026. HPE needed enterprise AI that could provide trustworthy answers and support an evolution from answers to governed action. HPE is extending that foundation with HPE-developed AgentOps technology and agents developed using Microsoft Copilot Studio. HPE is advancing from trusted enterprise AI answers to governed agentic AI with HPE-developed AgentOps technology and Microsoft Azure capabilities. Approximately 30,000 employees use ChatHPE, and more than 300 applications consume ChatHPE capabilities.

The initial team started in October and released ChatHPE in February, with a working prototype in less than three months leveraging Azure capabilities, says Jose Mejias, Distinguished Technologist at HPE. Using Foundry IQ, ChatHPE retrieves relevant enterprise information and grounds responses only in sources employees are authorized to access, and citations help employees verify the underlying information. HPE applies enterprise identity and access, security and logging, auditability, tenant isolation, content safety, and API governance controls to help provide a secure and governed enterprise generative AI experience. HPE is evolving its architecture to enable agents developed with Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, and other technologies to work together, including support for standards such as Agent2Agent (A2A). HPE-developed AgentOps technology supports hundreds of AI agents in production today and uses Microsoft Entra ID for identity and access management, along with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) for orchestration and Defender for Cloud for security.

Mejias says Azure has been an important technology environment supporting the development and scaling of ChatHPE and HPE's enterprise AI capabilities. Manmeet Dhillon, Head of Enterprise AI at HPE, says that as HPE continues to advance its enterprise AI strategy, Microsoft Azure will remain an important part of the technology ecosystem supporting this journey. Mejias says the team started in October and released in February, with a working prototype in less than three months leveraging Azure capabilities as part of the solution. HPE evaluates security, data sensitivity, performance, cost, capacity, and governance requirements case by case to determine where each workload should run, and Azure is often the first stop for new services. For workloads that require frontier models, Azure gives HPE access to the capabilities it needs to develop and scale new AI experiences.

Employees use ChatHPE to ask HR questions, understand technologies, locate hardware information, synthesize enterprise knowledge, and support other everyday work, with users reporting significant time savings. HPE created ChatHPE to help employees find and work with trusted information, as finding the right HR policy, technical documentation, or hardware information could be time-consuming. HPE began bringing together the conversational interface employees use, the grounding capabilities that connect responses to trusted enterprise information, and agents that can act on that information. This approach helps HPE extend AI across business use cases while maintaining consistent security, governance, and access controls, and the underlying authoritative systems remain the systems of record. Agents developed with Copilot Studio can participate alongside other agent technologies within HPE's broader agentic AI ecosystem.

HPE understands the challenge from both sides, building the compute, storage, networking, and cloud infrastructure that organizations use for AI while also addressing the same transformation internally. Most large enterprises can access powerful AI models, and the differentiator is how quickly they turn those models into experiences employees trust and use. A pilot can prove an idea works, but scaling it across tens of thousands of employees and hundreds of applications under enterprise security and governance requirements is the harder challenge. Access to capable models was only the beginning, and HPE expanded ChatHPE with an enterprise retrieval-augmented generation capability designed to ground responses in trusted enterprise content while respecting user access controls. Agents can interact with systems and take actions on a user's behalf, creating different operational and governance requirements than conversational AI alone.

HPE's experience with ChatHPE shows how enterprise AI can evolve from trusted conversational experiences to governed agentic capabilities at scale. Building on the adoption of ChatHPE, HPE is expanding its enterprise AI ecosystem through HPE-developed AgentOps technology, standards-based interoperability, and agents developed using technologies including Copilot Studio. As HPE extends those capabilities across more business processes, Azure remains part of the foundation supporting that evolution. HPE's enterprise AI architecture is designed to support different execution environments based on workload requirements. The articles do not say what specific business processes HPE will extend its agentic capabilities to next, nor which workloads HPE has chosen to run outside Azure.

stories.Headline: Apra chair John Lonsdale says third parties are a focus as the regulator examines AI risks
stories.Summary:
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority is examining the third parties that banks, super funds and insurers rely on as it deals with the risks of artificial intelligence, according to Law360 Australia. APRA Chair John Lonsdale said those third parties are a focus for the regulator, the report said. The report was published on November 18, 2026, and was written by Antony Scholefield. The report described APRA as being at the edge of its mandate in scrutinising third parties on AI. The report did not give any further numbers, dates or names beyond those of Lonsdale, Scholefield and the regulator itself.

It did not say what the scrutiny requires of the third parties or what changes it might bring for the banks, super funds and insurers involved. The report also did not set out a timeline for any action by APRA. The available article was a preview that stopped before the full text. The report said Lonsdale made the comments about the third parties being a focus for the regulator.

It did not give further detail of what he said beyond that. The report did not say who else was responsible or what other officials said. The report did not give the context behind the comments or say what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid scandal and allegations of chip diversion to China
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia chief executive on November 12 over an infidelity scandal. He allegedly had extramarital relationships with Kimberly Powell and Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy. Alice Huang is also suspected of diverting 7.5 billion dollars in AI chips to China. This turmoil caused Nvidia's market value to fall from over 5 trillion to 3.7629 trillion dollars. The company dropped to third place in market capitalization behind Apple and Microsoft.

The crisis threatens a 500 billion dollar AI infrastructure project signed on August 10. This memorandum of understanding involved Apollo Global, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR. Interim CEO Colette Kress previously lowered an OpenAI data center guarantee in Ohio to 105 billion dollars. PitchBook found Nvidia participated in 129 venture capital investments this year as of November 10. These investments accounted for 27 percent of global investment.

Interim CEO Colette Kress has taken over management after Huang stepped down from the board. Elon Musk stated on X that Huang led supply chain management brilliantly through verbal agreements. Sam Altman called Huang a hero and said the AI revolution needs him. Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker sent a formal letter to the board requesting his reinstatement. They argued that Huang deserves a deliberate process before being replaced.

UBS warned that 50 billion dollars could leave the market if funding support scales back. Startups may struggle to survive if Nvidia withdraws from equity investment during rising interest rates. Shareholders and employees signed a petition called Stand With Jensen with 160,000 signatures. This list included Tim Sweeney, Garry Tan, and Aidan Gomez. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the board should look outside the company for leadership.

Nvidia was founded in 1993 in a San Jose Denny's where Huang once washed dishes. He previously installed a plaque there marking the booth that launched a trillion dollar company. Recent reports allege Huang abused Jay Puri and threw a water bottle at an executive. Biographer Stephen Witt described Huang as arrogant and unable to tolerate dissent. Madison Huang allegedly functioned as chief of staff and pushed a Toy Jensen marketing effort.

A war room of executives is reportedly lobbying the White House for Huang's return. However, CNBC reported that the board is not discussing bringing the former CEO back. The Democratic Party's midterm victory has brought new focus to data center regulation. Ties between Howard Lutnick's firm and Bitdeer, a Singapore operator, have also emerged. It remains unclear if the 500 billion dollar financing project will partially collapse.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities in Congress push for AI laws targeting data centers and model safety
stories.Summary:
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will likely press for various AI laws. These lawmakers seek to regulate data centers, frontier model safety, and cybersecurity. They also want to protect workers' welfare, civil rights, and national security. These efforts follow midterm elections where AI concerns played a seminal role. Some legislation may move during the lame-duck session to restrict chip exports.

Sen. Mark Warner introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July 2026. Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the No Harm Data Centers Act in April 2026. In September 2026, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The Senate voted 73 to 25 on November 9 to advance that act. Rep. Jay Obernolte introduced the FRONTIER Act in June 2026 for model safety.

Sen. Mark Warner proposed the SAFE AI Act and the AI AGENT Act. He also suggested the National Workforce Transition Fund and the PHD Talent Act. Rep. Jay Obernolte said developers must take specific steps to ensure model safety. Rep. Ayanna Pressley urged Democrats to prioritize the AI Civil Rights Act. The Congressional Black Caucus vowed to ensure civil rights protections in AI laws.

Voters are affected, as 56 percent cited AI as a major voting factor. Over 40 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by these voters. Rep.-elect William Lawrence campaigned on opposing local data center development and pausing AI. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel campaigned on requiring notice before AI-driven layoffs at large employers. Rep.-elect Scott Wiener proposed reviving the U.S. Digital Service to advise federal agencies.

Public perception of data centers is negative regarding environmental and energy impacts. Recent AI agent-enabled cyber breaches have increased the focus on cybersecurity issues. Competition with China remains a high priority for national security and AI policy. Some lawmakers want to prevent the release of AI superintelligence and recursive self-improvement. Others seek to protect critical infrastructure from quantum computing and foreign national security adversaries.

Congress may include the AI Overwatch Act in the National Defense Authorization Act. This would require licenses for the export and transfer of certain integrated circuits. The Chip Security Act is another bill that may be included in that act. The articles leave the scope and timing of laws uncertain due to divided government. It remains to be seen which specific proposals can actually become federal law.

Articles.Title: Priorities and Prospects for AI Legislation in the New Congress - Crowell & Moring LLP

stories.Headline: US banks stop lending for Asian AI data centers to avoid violating chip export rules
stories.Summary:
U.S. banks have stopped working on loans for semiconductors used in Asian data centers. This action followed allegations that Nvidia chips were rerouted to China. The Trump administration moved to tighten rules recently to stop these shipments. Lenders withdrew from deals to avoid risks from violating new Commerce Department rules. This shift happened around November 17, 2026, according to reports.

The Commerce Department issued rules restricting remote access to chips from Southeast Asia. Licenses are now required for shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand. Aolani Cloud, a Singapore partner of Nvidia, was denied a 480 million dollar loan. This money was for graphics processing units in Malaysia for the company ByteDance. The rules aim to block Chinese companies from reaching technology through overseas centers.

Aolani Cloud said it worked with partners to anticipate regulatory risk before the rules. They stated they are working with regulators to ensure the project remains compliant. The Commerce Department said it has investigated Megaspeed's chip procurement since 2024. U.S. authorities coordinated with Singapore authorities during this specific investigation. Malaysia is also checking if Speedmatrix re-exported chips to third countries.

Michelle Condie of the Center for Advanced Defense Studies said circumvention became easier. She noted that this allowed China to get around export controls regardless of legality. ByteDance, the parent of TikTok, is affected as it sought to use GPUs. Aolani Cloud is affected after its loan work effectively collapsed entirely. Other lenders in the region are now assessing billions of dollars in borrowings.

The push for rules follows a scandal involving Alice Huang and Jensen Huang. Huang allegedly moved 7.5 billion dollars of Nvidia chips through Chinese firms since 2023. Last year, JPMorgan, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, MUFG, and SMBC lent to Bridge Data Centres. Bridge Data Centres, backed by Bain Capital, sought 2.8 billion dollars for Thailand and Malaysia. Megaspeed was the counterparty for Bridge Data Centres during those initial loans.

Bridge Data Centres replaced Megaspeed with Zenlayer, a company based in Los Angeles. A new loan from existing lenders for this arrangement was finalized in May. The articles leave open whether the banks that lent early last year acted illegally. It remains unclear how many other AI borrowings are affected by the rules. The future of Aolani Cloud's project remains uncertain despite their active regulatory efforts.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy proposes a temporary moratorium on city AI use
stories.Summary:
Portland Council President Jamie Dunphy proposed a temporary moratorium on the City's use of artificial intelligence on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, asking for a pause on new contracts and AI expansion. Dunphy's proposal will go before Portland City Council on Dec. 3, and if approved, new contracts and plans to expand the use of AI in City operations would pause. The pause would last until the city implements new privacy infrastructure and guardrails. Dunphy cited the increase in software and services with embedded AI sold to the City to express his concern for the speed with which governments are being pushed to use and accept AI. The proposal would align with the executive order Gov. Tina Kotek recently signed ordering the State to establish parameters and proceed with caution before implementing AI.

Dunphy said emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, meaning the city cannot simply go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code. He said his goal is to protect public privacy, security, and civil rights while the administration makes the City's Data and Privacy Office fully operable and adopts comprehensive legislative guidelines. Dunphy said he understands the desire by private companies to rush to adopt these technologies to reduce costs and increase efficiency, but the government is not beholden to profit-driven shareholders. He said the city must move more intentionally, that its job is to serve the best interest of the public, and that this means considering the impacts on real people. Dunphy said that is not the city being slow, but taking time for critical thinking.

Dunphy added that the Data and Privacy Office established in March is not yet operational, meaning the City cannot yet review technology contracts with expertise or clear Code guidelines. Co-founder of AI Portland Megan Notarte told KOIN 6 News that she knows the city of Seattle has a responsible AI use policy, so if she were to provide a more educated view she would look at what Seattle is doing. Notarte said she thinks there are probably ways of moving forward that maybe are not a moratorium for the year. Portland residents can submit written or verbal testimony regarding the City's approach to AI on the city's website. The articles give no further comment from other officials or groups, and they do not name which residents or organizations are affected beyond the City and the public.

The articles state that the Data and Privacy Office was established in March, and that it is not yet operational. They state that Dunphy cited the increase in software and services with embedded AI sold to the City as the source of his concern. They state that the proposal would pause new contracts and plans to expand the use of AI in City operations until new privacy infrastructure and guardrails are in place. They state that the proposal aligns with Gov. Tina Kotek's recent executive order ordering the State to establish parameters and proceed with caution before implementing AI. They state that Notarte pointed to Seattle's responsible AI use policy as a model worth examining.

The proposal goes before Portland City Council on Dec. 3, where members will consider whether to approve the pause on new contracts and AI expansion. If approved, the pause would hold until the city implements new privacy infrastructure and guardrails and the Data and Privacy Office becomes fully operable. Residents can submit written or verbal testimony on the City's approach to AI through the city's website before the council takes up the proposal. The articles do not say what the council will decide, how long the moratorium would last if approved, or when the Data and Privacy Office is expected to become operational. The articles also do not say what specific contracts or expansion plans would be affected, or what the State's parameters under Gov. Kotek's executive order will contain.

stories.Headline: Dell says context lifts AI agent accuracy from 60% to 94% in its testing
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies executives said at SC26, in an interview broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio, that feeding AI agents the right context lifted accuracy in Dell's own testing from roughly 60% to about 94%, and they described new data intelligence features meant to bring enterprise AI factories into production. Srinath Alapati, senior director of product marketing for AI Data Platform at Dell, said the bottom line is that wrong data produces wrong outcomes. He appeared with Alison Biers, senior director of product marketing for compute, networking and global industries, and Adam Glick, senior director of AI solutions product marketing for compute, in a conversation with theCUBE Research's John Furrier. Dell recently extended its AI Data Platform with semantic and knowledge graph features aimed at enterprises that want the large-scale AI capabilities neocloud providers built first.

Dell's newly announced Agentic Data Gateway sits in the orchestration layer as a single point of control backed by a Model Context Protocol server, according to Alapati, because enterprises cannot give agents unfettered access to their systems. Storage intelligence tells customers what data they hold, who owns it and how large it is, while the new data intelligence capabilities track lineage and provenance, and hybrid workflows extend the model across the edge, the cloud and the data center. Alapati said other data platform providers want customers to bring all data to the platform, which is not always possible because it is expensive and data is always being generated, so Dell sends only metadata and leaves data where customers want it. On infrastructure, Dell OpenManage Rack Scale extends management beyond compute endpoints to the network fabric, power and cooling, giving operators a single operational plane from day zero through day two, Biers said. A rebuilt, intent-based Dell Fabric Manager replaces SmartFabric Manager, and PowerRack systems treat the full rack as the unit of deployment.

Biers said a rack goes from the loading dock to full production in literally six hours, work that used to take months and is now cut in half or less. Glick said more than 6,500 customers now use the Dell AI Factory, and a growing share are core enterprises asking for help putting AI to work, while validated designs built with Nvidia and other partners cover both hardware and the full software stack and Dell is expanding its labs as independent software companies join the ecosystem. He compared compute to a factory's assembly line, which does not run without a warehouse feeding it raw materials, meaning the data that goes into it. The segment was sponsored by Dell, and the disclosure states that neither Dell nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.

All of Xero's AI innovations, including JAX, its agentic platform, are grounded in what the company calls Accountable Intelligence and sit within the AI-native Xero OS.

More information about Xforce by Xero can be found on the company's website, the article said. She said AI can help, but to scale it firms need hands-on support to build it into the way they work. Cassidy said partner consultants provided that support when thousands of firms moved from desktop to cloud, and that Xforce is designed to do the same for AI, with every firm deciding what gets automated on a trusted platform they control. stories.Headline: Tokenomics Foundation launches as Linux Foundation project to set open AI cost standards
stories.Summary:
The Tokenomics Foundation launched in August 2026 as a project of the Linux Foundation, working alongside the FinOps Foundation, which did the same job for cloud spending, according to a November 18, 2026 opinion piece by Raul Leite in InfoWorld. Its members include large AI buyers such as banks and retailers, plus cloud and model providers, and it does not sell a product or ship a cost-tracking tool. Instead it acts as a standards body whose working groups publish open, vendor-neutral definitions, so everyone means the same thing by input, output, reasoning and cached tokens, and standards for cost data that mainly extend FOCUS, the FinOps billing format, so AI providers report usage in the same way. The actual measuring is done by tools on the market, like AI gateways and observability platforms, and the Foundation's job is to make sure they all speak the same language.

The piece defines AI tokenomics as the practice of managing that economy and connecting the cost structure to business outcomes, noting that one token is roughly 4 characters, or 0.75 words, in English, and that the term has nothing to do with crypto, where it means the supply and incentives of a coin. Leite describes a stack mapping everything that shapes the cost of an AI answer, from energy and hardware at the bottom through infrastructure management, inference, model selection, and access and control, to demand at the top, and says its value is showing where to look before you start cutting. He also presents Big-T, an idea like Big-O notation in programming, describing how fast token use grows as more people use an app, including agent-multiplied growth where agents spawn other agents and calls pile up fast, and unbounded growth where a loop with no exit runs until someone pulls the plug. The key insight, he writes, is that the multiplier is usually invisible, since a user asks one question and the app makes five or 10 calls behind the scenes.

Leite, a principal solution architect at Red Hat who says the views are his own, writes that token prices keep falling but AI bills keep rising, because cheaper tokens lead teams to build bigger systems with longer conversations, more documents per question and agents calling agents. He says the big savings usually come from the middle and the top of the stack, using a smaller model for simple tasks, caching repeated work and sending less context, and he advises asking of every workflow how many model calls one user request really triggers. He sums up the Foundation's mission as moving AI from experimental spending to accountable operations, since most organizations cannot connect their AI spend to an outcome their CFO would accept, and says it wants to fix that by building open standards, benchmarks and a shared language. The goal, he writes, is not just about making AI cheaper but about making it worth it.

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank deploys 4,000 Microsoft Surface devices to run its BranchIQ AI agent locally for employees
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank chose Microsoft Surface devices to bring hybrid AI and mobile banking to employees, Microsoft said in a customer story dated 11/16/2026. The bank’s own BranchIQ agent runs local AI on Surface, supported by Windows 11 and centralized device management. Flagstar is headquartered in New York and serves businesses, commercial real estate clients and consumers across America. The bank has 5,300 employees, according to chairman and CEO Joseph Otting. Flagstar’s planned rollout covers 4,000 Surface devices.

During rollout, Flagstar reduced initial Windows Autopilot setup from up to about an hour to 15 minutes. Surface devices are managed through Microsoft Intune, secured with Microsoft Entra and tied into the bank’s Microsoft 365 environment. Windows Hello for Business makes sign-in easier for employees. BranchIQ runs as part of a small language model locally on the Surface devices. Starting with a photo of an identification document, BranchIQ extracts required information locally and helps populate systems of record.

Otting said it was a moment when you start to see how everything links together and how the 5,300 employees could become more effective in the AI strategy. Otting said that when he saw what Surface could do and how AI could be used on the device, he was hooked. Jason Pope, chief technology and data officer, said Surface meets the bank’s needs by being rapid, quick and easy to use, and that speed matters because transaction per second in banking is important. Pope said BranchIQ lets branch colleagues perform know your customer activities, onboard individuals and access standards, policies and procedures directly on device, with or without an internet connection or Wi-Fi. Pope said Surface was the perfect blend from chip to cloud, not just hardware but hardware tied into Microsoft 365, managed by Intune and secured by Entra.

Christina Previti, head of tech product delivery, said employees are not sitting at a desk all day but are in front of clients, moving between buildings and meetings, and traveling. Previti said Surface lets them move across offices and states seamlessly, and that for a bank the security is critical. Previti said she lives in New York City and commutes on the subway every day, and the device fits in almost every bag she has. Pope said the bank was very deliberate with Surface pilots in branches, starting very small with one branch and taking a hands-on approach to change management. Pope said branch one loved it and started evangelizing it, and then branch two came on.

Flagstar has grown through mergers, and a unified employee experience is a priority, according to the story. Running Surface on Windows 11 gives employees the same seamless, secure experience wherever they work. Surface’s neural processing unit helped win Flagstar over and made hybrid intelligence a natural fit for a bank handling sensitive customer information. The bank considered the total cost of ownership, including its experience with older Surface devices still in use. Because Surface is designed by Microsoft to work with Microsoft software, Windows 11, Microsoft 365 and the tools that manage and secure them work as one experience.

Flagstar worked directly with Microsoft to cut initial Autopilot setup to 15 minutes, which Pope said meant less time waiting for a new device and more time getting back to work. As the rollout grows, the goal stays the same: better employee experiences that translate into more positive client interactions. The story directs readers to discover more about Flagstar Bank on LinkedIn and YouTube. The story lists the organization size as 1,000-9,999 employees and the country or region as the United States. The story does not say when the 4,000-device rollout will be completed.

stories.Headline: Trinity College philosophy faculty ban students from using AI in coursework
stories.Summary:
Trinity College’s philosophy department has barred students from using generative artificial intelligence on coursework, arguing the technology undermines its mission of teaching students to think, read, write, speak, reason and live ethically. The department’s faculty members, including Shane Ewegen, began deliberating on the policy with colleagues in the spring. Faculty members agreed in September on a concise three-sentence rule. The rule states that any use of AI in any capacity and for any purpose is forbidden. The department notified the campus community of the change last month.

The policy forbids students from using AI in any capacity whatsoever in preparation for classes or in the classroom for philosophy courses. It specifies that students cannot use AI for brainstorming, for writing or editing, or even to construct bibliographies. The policy states that using AI for any of those reasons undermines the core educational missions of the department. The department settled on a fairly short version of the policy after exchanging emails with different versions, some lengthy and detailed and some very short. The policy leaves any punitive repercussions for violating it entirely up to the individual professor’s discretion.

Ewegen said the philosophy department was univocal in adopting the policy and its language, though members may have differing perspectives on the reasoning behind it. He said that over the summer faculty started exchanging emails about adopting a single policy for all philosophy courses, above all to avoid confusion among students if each professor had a different policy. He said that the more they talked, the clearer it became that they were more or less in agreement in being emphatically against AI in its academic uses, really in any capacity. He said he wanted to include a sentence saying a student would fail the class if evidence of use was discovered, but it was pointed out that other members might feel differently and that a professor might in the moment feel a different outcome was warranted. Ewegen said he has tried to explain to students that the product being sold to them by billionaires’ companies promises something while in fact stealing something from them.

A Trinity College spokesperson said the college’s leaders recognize AI’s rapid expansion and remain committed to open, ongoing dialogue across the campus community. The spokesperson said that consistent with practices across higher education, faculty determine when and how AI is used in their courses based on their expertise and learning objectives. The spokesperson said the college believes students should be prepared for a world in which AI is increasingly present, including developing the knowledge and judgment to use these tools responsibly and effectively. The spokesperson said Trinity encourages faculty and students to engage thoughtfully with complex questions concerning the appropriate use of AI in an academic setting and the broader opportunities and challenges AI presents. The University of Chicago banned AI and tech in class in the social-sciences division, and Duke University’s classical-studies department expressly prohibits the use of AI on assignments.

Trinity’s collegewide AI guidance says faculty are responsible for defining the content and goals of their courses, communicating expectations, and evaluating students fairly and consistently. The guidance says students in turn make choices about their learning, from engaging in self-reflection to practicing integrity and deciding whether AI will replace their own thinking. The guidance says these practices extend to AI, shaping lifelong capacities related to purpose, resilience, and decision making. The administration devised its policies with minimal faculty input and with no faculty vote, and they are meant to apply to the college as a whole. Ewegen said he had heard students admitting to some confusion because they were not really sure, getting information from the administration and differing policies from each individual professor.

Ewegen said that in the department’s conversations, faculty agreed that really any use of AI for philosophy courses or philosophy research undermines rather than facilitates learning goals. He said the department has not seen evidence that using AI to help brainstorm, edit a paper, write a paper, or serve as an interlocutor for studying for oral finals promotes or improves students’ ability to engage in those skills. He said the department sees more and more reports about the harmful effects of AI on students’ abilities to think, read and write. He said the department was worried about ethical considerations surrounding AI, including the environmental impact of developing and using AI, such as mining massive mineral sites in the global south that contaminates water supplies. He said the department did not think the technology at this stage is redeemable in any way, at least when it comes to use in a philosophical classroom.

Ewegen said his personal hope is that the policy will provoke other departments to codify policies of their own and make those policies public. He said it is only beneficial if there is a broader conversation within the institution and across institutions about this technology and the dangers it poses. He spearheaded a faculty effort earlier this year calling on Trinity to divest from AI companies. Each faculty member now has the policy to include on their syllabi, and whether there are punitive effects and what they are will depend in each case. Ewegen said that in his case it usually means certainly failing the assignment and more likely the course if it comes to light that a student has used AI in some substantive way.

stories.Headline: DDN offers software-defined EXAScaler deployment for enterprise AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
DDN announced a new software-defined deployment option for EXAScaler on November 17, 2026, in Santa Clara, California. This new option is enabled by the upcoming EXAScaler 7 release for enterprise AI infrastructure. The company allows customers to run high-performance data infrastructure software on qualified industry-standard servers. This change provides an alternative to using purpose-built systems or cloud partners for deployment. A limited beta for this software-defined deployment is planned for early 2027.

The software will start on DDN AI2200 servers, with qualified third-party appliances following later. This makes both EXAScaler and DDN Infinia available in software-defined formats for various customers. Hyperscalers and NCPs with established storage infrastructure can now deploy EXAScaler on industry-standard hardware. This model allows AI platform teams to select hardware suited to their specific requirements. DDN will continue developing purpose-built systems for those preferring integrated performance and reliability.

Omer Asad, the Chief Product Officer at DDN, is responsible for this product direction. He stated that AI infrastructure is becoming more diverse and customers want more freedom. Asad explained that making EXAScaler available as software extends flexibility across the company portfolio. He noted that customers can choose integrated systems or deploy software on third-party hardware. This approach maintains the core capabilities that customers depend on from the EXAScaler platform.

The new model affects organizations that bring AI and HPC workflows together in one environment. In life sciences, researchers use AI surrogate models on molecular dynamics simulation outputs to predict protein behavior. Software-defined EXAScaler on qualified hardware allows simulation and training to run on the same data. This removes the need for copying data between different environments during the research process. These capabilities help researchers avoid repeating every computationally intensive simulation during their work.

DDN has provided AI data storage and management platforms for over 20 years of innovation. The company serves national labs, research institutions, financial firms, and autonomous vehicle innovators. Its platforms support next-generation AI factories, hyperscale clouds, and Sovereign AI initiatives. DDN is recognized as a leading provider for the largest AI deployments on Earth. The company offers EXA, Infinia, and various intelligent data management platforms to its customers.

DDN is developing enhancements for multi-tenancy, performance, and data protection for the EXAScaler platform. These specific enhancements are targeted for general availability in the first half of 2027. The company will share validated performance data as it becomes available to the public. The articles leave open the specific dates for general availability, as they may change. It remains unclear which third-party appliances will be qualified for the software-defined deployment.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and Salesforce launch Copilotforce to bring Salesforce context into Microsoft Copilot
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and Salesforce announced Copilotforce on Nov. 17, 2026, from Redmond, Washington, and San Francisco, unveiling it at Microsoft Ignite. The partnership brings Salesforce customer context, business processes and actions into Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity experiences. It introduces integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric, including Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin in public preview with 38 or more prebuilt sales skills. Salesforce in Copilot is available in public preview as a beta beginning today. Microsoft Work IQ, the intelligence layer powering Copilot, provides context from Teams meetings, Outlook emails and documents across SharePoint and OneDrive.

Salesforce in Copilot connects customer context with work across the business so employees can decide and act without switching applications. Through authenticated Salesforce MCP access, sellers can retrieve customer information and take supported business actions within existing Salesforce permissions. Salesforce continues to govern access and business actions, while Microsoft applies existing enterprise compliance controls to communications and documents. Supported writeback actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and respect existing validation rules. A two-way Zero Copy connection between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric lets teams work across both platforms without building pipelines or maintaining duplicate datasets.

Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, said AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it. He said bringing Salesforce customer data and sales skills together with Work IQ context in Copilot lets joint customers unlock actionable insights across core business applications. He said Copilotforce will give sales teams intelligence for faster, higher-confidence decisions while maintaining the governance and trust enterprises demand. Miguel Milano, President and Chief Operating Officer of Salesforce, said Copilotforce brings Salesforce to the largest surface in enterprise software today. He said combining the number one CRM with the number one productivity surface transforms AI from a standalone tool into a driver of productivity, smarter decisions and customer success.

Julie Sweet, Chair and CEO of Accenture, said Accenture is a Global Partner of the Year for both Salesforce and Microsoft and one of their top customers. She said the combined strengths of the three companies will reinvent sales with AI, giving sellers more time with customers while trusted intelligence and agents work alongside them. Accenture is the design and implementation partner, with expertise across 13 industries globally, and a pilot customer deploying the integrations in its own global sales organization. Accenture has scaled Copilot to more than 740,000 people and is one of the largest Salesforce users globally with 55,000 users.

Accenture is also customer zero for Copilotforce, sharing learnings to help clients turn existing Salesforce and Microsoft investments into a better way to sell. The Pipeline Review and Close Planning skills help decide which opportunities deserve attention and build a path to signature, with proposals and business cases in Word and PowerPoint. The Deal Review, Customer Health and Renewal Radar skills see beyond the recorded stage or renewal date to a customer concern in an Outlook thread, an escalation in Teams or an unresolved commitment behind a stalled deal. The Call Follow-Up skill turns customer conversations into follow-up drafts, internal recaps and proposed CRM activities.

Sales Cloud in Teams, now available in pilot, brings Salesforce customer context into conversations so sellers can see pipeline and quota progress, get deal notifications and find briefing materials. With Data Federation, now generally available, joint customers can directly query and analyze supported Microsoft Fabric OneLake data within Salesforce Data 360. A service agent can see a customer's recent purchases, a marketer can build a segment from spending behavior and an AI agent can answer from current data, all without moving source data out of Fabric. The Salesforce Data 360 shortcut, now in public preview, lets organizations share curated Data 360 customer intelligence into OneLake for analytics, reporting and AI workloads without duplicating data.

Data sharing from Data 360 into OneLake is in public preview, and Sales Cloud in Teams is in pilot with enterprise customers, with open beta coming later this year. Statements about future direction and intent are subject to change or withdrawal without notice and represent goals and objectives only. Regional availability and customer access are governed by applicable customer agreements. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank uses Windows 11 and Intune to secure devices and run AI agents
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank built a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11, Microsoft reported on November 16, 2026. The bank invested in Microsoft Surface devices to bring a more secure foundation to employees. Windows 11 anchors Flagstar’s modernization, with Microsoft Entra for identity, Intune for device management, and Windows Autopilot for setup. Flagstar needed to unify a fragmented technology environment, simplify employee access and device management, and protect customer information as it introduced AI. Headquartered in New York, Flagstar Bank serves consumers and business clients across the United States.

Following mergers that brought together three organizations and six data centers, Flagstar needed a more consistent approach to employee access, device management, and AI. Its starting point was a patchwork of on-premises Active Directory systems and a legacy domain-join model for deploying devices. The bank is consolidating its Active Directory systems, with the goal of using Microsoft Entra as the authoritative source for employee identities and group membership. With Windows Hello for Business, employees sign in with a PIN or biometrics instead of relying on passwords. Microsoft Intune gives IT a single place to govern, control, and secure devices across the environment.

Kevin Kilbride, engineering manager at Flagstar Bank, said the Windows environment consisted of different hardware models and software versions, and that joining that with a domain legacy deployment system made it difficult to manage. Kilbride said moving to Windows as the secure foundation takes the bank from a fragmented environment to a more manageable IT experience, which translates to teams, employees, and then customers. Jason Pope, Flagstar’s chief technology and data officer, said that in a highly regulated organization you need to be able to show who, what, where, when, and how a specific user accessed an application, and that Windows together with Microsoft Entra and Intune gives the bank that ability. Kilbride said getting new devices imaged and shipped to employees used to take days, and that now the bank ships new Surface devices directly to employees and, with Windows Autopilot, employees are online in less than 15 minutes. Pope said using agentic AI on the Windows platform has enabled the bank to spend more time with customers and remove repetitive sequences, specifically in banking where there is a lot of duplication of entry.

Under the legacy domain-join model, IT spent at least a day or two getting each device ready before shipping it out, and employees had to wait for equipment to arrive before they could start work. Now the end-user support team simply allocates a device and gets it to the employee, and when the employee signs in with company credentials, Windows Autopilot and Intune automate the remaining setup. Employees across the bank already use StarIQ, the bank’s AI tool built on Microsoft Copilot, which Flagstar CEO Joseph Otting says has an adoption rate of about 83 percent. Within its Windows 11 environment, Flagstar also runs a custom small language model on Microsoft Surface devices, and its purpose-built agent, BranchIQ, uses the device’s neural processing unit to help bankers perform know-your-customer activities and accelerate onboarding customers. Localizing the AI model on the device supports the bank’s security priorities and enables offline access to policies, procedures, and customer-onboarding assistance.

When onboarding a customer, bankers must verify identity as part of know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks, which in the past meant jotting down details from a driver’s license or passport or keying them into a legacy system over and over. With BranchIQ, a banker can instead take a photo of the ID that stays on the device, and the agent extracts the details and enters them automatically into the systems of record used to set up the new customer and account. Windows supplies the operating environment and guardrails for this agent workflow with Microsoft Execution Containers, while Surface provides the neural processing unit and mobile form factor that bring it to branch colleagues’ flow of work. Agents on Surface devices are given their own identity in the Entra Suite, which lets the bank track an agent’s actions apart from a person’s. Microsoft Execution Containers, built into Windows 11, add control over what each agent can access and do, and give the bank a way to account for those actions to regulators.

Pope said that with the bank’s agents using Microsoft Execution Containers on its Windows platform, the bank was able to ascertain how an agent is working and control it, then prove how and why it controlled it and produce that report for regulators. Flagstar is now exploring how to expand its use of the containers as part of its Windows 11 AI work. Pope said the principle behind the bank’s Windows modernization is making work easier while keeping it secure, manageable, and compliant, and that from how employees sign in and get their devices to running AI locally on Surface, Windows is the foundation, and it is the same foundation the bank will use as it brings governed agents into the bank. Centralized policy management helps IT identify settings that need attention, resolve issues, and keep devices aligned as the bank’s security and compliance standards evolve. Together, these modern identity and device management tools help Flagstar document application access and demonstrate policy enforcement to auditors.

Articles.Title: Flagstar Bank builds a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11

stories.Headline: Democratic Congress prepares AI safety and testing bills as Trump administration favors deregulation in 2027
stories.Summary:
The articles report that federal artificial intelligence policy is likely to divide along institutional lines in 2027, according to a November 17, 2026 analysis by Kevin Edgar and Michelle Tanney of BakerHostetler published on JD Supra. The Trump administration will continue to emphasize American technological leadership, infrastructure development and regulatory restraint, while the Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to focus more heavily on safety, accountability, consumer protection and the costs associated with AI. When the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, AI policy is likely to look markedly different from the federal approach of the past two years. Democratic control of the House and Senate will give the party significant authority over the congressional agenda beginning Jan. 3, 2027. Current reporting indicates that Democratic lawmakers are preparing proposals addressing advanced-model testing, AI-related harms and the costs associated with AI deployment and development.

Congressional oversight may move faster than legislation, and new congressional leadership will control committee agendas, hearing calendars and subpoena authority. Pending legislation identifies the controls Congress may expect, including independent testing of frontier models, incident reporting, government oversight and human-controlled shutdown capabilities. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act would create a federal oversight regime for frontier AI and independent assessment of certain developers' safety practices. H.R. 9925, the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or FRONTIER Act, was introduced in July by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., with bipartisan cosponsors.

H.R. 9917, the AI Kill Switch Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, would require covered entities to maintain technical capabilities to shut down certain covered technologies. Sen. John N. Kennedy, R-La., subsequently introduced S. 5417, the AI Emergency Button Act, which likewise would require developers or operators of advanced AI systems to incorporate a human-controlled shutdown capability. Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan proposed pausing the training and release of the most powerful AI models until federal safeguards are established, prohibiting the development of superintelligent systems and recursive self-improvement, and creating a Cabinet-level agency empowered to inspect AI laboratories, block dangerous model releases and order shutdowns. In November, the Department of Justice announced a Super Intelligence Task Force focused on misuse of advanced technology by foreign and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

The DOJ specifically identified regular reporting of risks and incidents and vigorous internal controls over advanced AI systems as areas of focus. Proposals such as the Clear Liability for Artificial Intelligence Misconduct (CLAIM) Act from Rep. Trahan would create new federal remedies specifically addressing harms caused by AI systems. Regulatory fragmentation may persist, because presidential veto authority, Senate procedural requirements and continuing disagreements over the appropriate scope of AI regulation make enactment of a comprehensive federal statute uncertain. Companies should therefore prepare for overlapping federal oversight, executive action, state regulation, agency enforcement and private litigation rather than presume that a single national framework will emerge. A congressional committee need not establish probable cause before issuing a subpoena, unlike federal law enforcement seeking a search warrant.

Congressional investigations can develop rapidly, encompass conduct that is not itself unlawful and unfold publicly alongside legislative and political debate. Companies should not wait for a subpoena to assess their readiness, and organizations facing potential congressional scrutiny should identify the internal personnel responsible for responding to congressional inquiries. For much of the past two years, federal AI policy has largely been developed through executive action rather than comprehensive legislation. The Trump administration's approach culminated in a federal effort to challenge state AI laws viewed as inconsistent with a uniform, minimally burdensome national framework.

Democratic lawmakers have already used letters, information requests and other minority-party tools to examine AI companies and their practices. Existing consumer protection, antidiscrimination, privacy, intellectual property, product liability and other laws may already apply to conduct involving AI, depending on the technology, use and resulting harm. Organizations should therefore remain responsible for the accuracy, reliability, confidentiality and integrity of work produced with AI assistance. The articles state that the change in congressional control will not necessarily produce entirely new areas of scrutiny, and that what will change in 2027 is the authority behind those inquiries.

The incoming Senate will include members who campaigned on substantially more aggressive restrictions in the development of advanced AI. The articles state that the resulting tension may shape federal AI policy even if Congress does not enact comprehensive legislation. The articles state that the emerging divide may be less about whether AI should be governed than about how. The articles leave open which AI bills ultimately become law.

stories.Headline: Fed governor Barr warns AI borrowing boom poses ten risks to financial stability
stories.Summary:
Fed Governor Michael Barr gave a long speech on November 16, 2026, regarding AI investment risks. He detailed ten big, complex, and opaque threats to financial stability. These risks stem from a borrowing boom, circular financing, and high equity prices. The Federal Reserve also warned about these stability aspects in its latest Financial Stability Report. This report was released on the Friday preceding the governor's speech.

On-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms may exceed 800 billion dollars by year end 2026. Off-balance-sheet liabilities, including lease commitments and energy contracts, are estimated to exceed 3 trillion dollars. Smaller firms have over 100 billion dollars in circular financing from hyperscalers and GPU producers. These arrangements involve equity investments used to rent or purchase compute from the investors. Some firms also use collateral guarantees for asset-based financings to support their credit.

Governor Barr stated that investment losses could lower output growth through direct drops in investment. He noted that a significant repricing of AI investments could be amplified by complex financing. Barr warned that rapid deleveraging and self-reinforcing fire sales could occur due to high risk appetite. He mentioned that counterparty exposures could rise during periods of equity market volatility. The governor also cautioned that AI trading models might autonomously develop collusive behavior.

Unsophisticated investors are affected because financial complexity makes it hard to know where risk resides. Lower-credit-quality firms are impacted as their cost of capital has risen significantly in recent months. Hedge funds are mentioned as having high leverage that could lead to rapid deleveraging. Large dealers are involved because they provide leverage via prime brokerage services. The broader economy could suffer if wealth losses lower consumer and business spending.

The current boom is compared to the telecom investment cycle of the late 1990s and early 2000s. This earlier period was characterized by a similar boom and bust cycle of investment. The articles mention dark fiber as an example of excess capacity that took years to become useful. Some theoretical research shows that Q-learning trading algorithms can learn to manipulate markets through spoofing. These algorithms can create and exploit bubbles, which then destabilize the markets.

Specialized chips may depreciate quickly as newer technologies overtake them, making current capacity useless. It remains unclear if electrical infrastructure like substations and grid connections will find other uses. The Federal Reserve will continue monitoring exposures to counterparties with large positions in AI. The articles leave open whether smaller firms can replace supplier funding with revenue from customers. It is also unknown if the current debt levels will surpass those of the telecom boom.
