KMicro is an AI consultancy based in Costa Mesa, California, that helps enterprises turn technology investments into business outcomes. Microsoft introduced ISOC in public preview on September 23, 2026, bringing SIEM and XDR capabilities together in the Defender portal. Existing Microsoft Sentinel customers who meet the licensing requirements are expected to be able to opt in to ISOC beginning November 15, 2026. The assessment is advisory and independent of any deployment commitment, so the recommendation follows the facts.

The assessment is aimed at eligible Microsoft 365 E5, E7 and Microsoft Defender Suite customers. It evaluates an organization's Microsoft security footprint, current Sentinel state, SOC workflows, data sources, technical prerequisites and governance considerations against its priority business outcomes. It confirms ISOC eligibility and identifies whether the environment is Defender-only, active Sentinel, inactive or orphaned Sentinel workspace, or a mixed security operations environment. It maps priority threats, analyst workflows and investigation friction to ISOC capabilities including case management, workbooks, user and entity behavior analytics, threat intelligence, natural-language playbooks, SOC optimization and unified hunting. It prioritizes Microsoft-native and third-party data sources with a high-level view of volumes, retention and cost, and reviews licensing, access, workspace, retention, data residency, ingestion and cost considerations.

The engagement begins with stakeholder discovery across executive, security operations and technical teams, so the recommendation reflects business drivers and decision criteria, not just technical configuration. It delivers a clear recommendation and a 90-day action plan on whether to activate available capabilities now, plan more deeply, continue the current Sentinel path, or address prerequisites first. Mazen Sadat, CEO of KMicro, said most enterprises already own more security capability than they are using. He said the question is not whether ISOC is impressive but whether it is right for the organization, and when. He said clients want a clear answer, not a sales motion, and that the assessment gives executives the knowledge to move with confidence and faster.

KMicro said the recommendation can include staying on the current Sentinel path where it makes sense. KMicro said security teams are being asked to connect more signals, investigate faster, cut tool and data costs, and get ready for AI agents in the SOC, all at once. KMicro said that for many security leaders the opt-in opens a decision with real cost, risk and operating-model implications, and a short window to make it well. The assessment shows leadership teams whether ISOC fits their current operating model, what value is already within reach of their existing licenses, and which gaps stand in the way. The articles do not name individual customers affected by the assessment.

Microsoft said ISOC in Defender is generally available for core capabilities and brings SIEM capabilities, user and entity behavior analytics, threat intelligence, and threat protection and disruption together. Microsoft said eligible Defender Suite, Microsoft 365 E5 and Microsoft 365 E7 customers receive all Microsoft Sentinel SIEM features, 90-day default data retention for Defender data, more than 500 connectors, reduced ingestion rates and a built-in data lake. Microsoft said the complete breadth of SIEM capabilities is now in preview. Microsoft said more than 96,000 vulnerabilities were published to the CVE Program in 2026, more than double 2024's roughly 40,000 and more than 20 times the level of 2010. Microsoft said only 26% of vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog were remediated in 2025.

Microsoft said that in a single week this fall PHP disclosed two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, and that tens of millions of internet-facing PHP services were running affected versions at disclosure. Microsoft said nearly two weeks later about 29 million services remained vulnerable. Microsoft said security researchers developed a working, weaponized exploit within roughly a day of PHP2Shell's disclosure, and that the research expanded to additional PHP versions and configurations by the following week. Microsoft said it announced new AI Readiness Initiatives in Perception, in preview in January 2027, that turn Secure Now guidance into actionable plans with shared progress tracking. Microsoft said the Posture Prioritization Agent is now generally available and the Risk Reduction Agent is now in public preview, with coverage spanning Microsoft, AWS and Google Cloud.

Microsoft said vulnerability shielding, available in preview, applies targeted, temporary protection to buy defenders time before a permanent patch. Microsoft said enhanced data classification is generally available in January 2027, and that grounding protection for Copilot and expanded data loss prevention controls for prompts to Copilot and local agents on Windows enter preview in January. Microsoft said four blue team agents are now generally available: Alert Triage Agent, Attack Investigation Agent, Detection Authoring Agent and Threat Intelligence Agent. Microsoft said the Recon Agent is now generally available. The articles do not say when KMicro's assessment will next be updated or how many organizations have signed up.

stories.Headline: ECB vice president Boris Vujčić warns rapid AI expansion threatens EU financial stability
stories.Summary:
European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujčić warned on Monday, November 16, 2026, that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence could threaten financial stability in the region. Speaking at Euro Finance Week in Frankfurt, the official noted that stock market valuations for AI remain stretched and the risk of a repricing has risen. He observed that a recent correction following the mid-term elections in America serves as a necessary reminder for the industry to remain cautious. Vujčić argued that system-wide stability is now threatened by a range of additional factors beyond simple market valuations. These risks include the expansion of external funding from equity to debt markets and the concentration of exposures across the sector.

The Vice President also highlighted the dangers of quickening AI adoption and the potential for devastating cyberattacks against financial institutions. He emphasized that a resilient banking sector is critical given current geopolitical headwinds and elevated risks to overall stability. Furthermore, he stated that supervision must be maintained over non-banks, specifically mentioning the rapid growth of the private credit space. Boris Vujčić explained that private credit warrants close monitoring because of limited transparency and growing interconnectedness with insurers and banks.

He expressed concern regarding potential liquidity mismatches that could arise within these less transparent financial environments. These warnings follow a report from the International Monetary Fund titled Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity in the Financial Sector. The organization argued that AI can accelerate the discovery of vulnerabilities and turn isolated incidents into correlated disruptions affecting many institutions. The report suggests that AI transforms cyber risk from a technical security concern into a broader issue of enterprise governance.

It questions how much autonomy these systems should receive and whether organizations can contain them when something goes wrong. The International Monetary Fund noted that AI does not need to invent new forms of attack to change the risk equation. Instead, powerful models can cause significant damage when they are given network access or credentials in poorly configured environments. More to follow.

stories.Headline: India opens Consent Manager registration as data board remains unstaffed
stories.Summary:
India's digital personal data regime entered the second phase of implementation, with a milestone under the Digital Personal Data Protection framework meant to let individuals manage permissions through registered Consent Managers, Trisha Shreyashi wrote in a November 17, 2026 opinion article. She wrote that consent is collected in seconds on a click, while withdrawing it can mean navigating a maze of settings. She wrote that the imbalance between giving consent and withdrawing it persists. She wrote that the upcoming milestone promises to address the imbalance. The article appeared on moneycontrol.com on November 17, 2026.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 set up a map for phased implementation through the DPDP Rules, 2025. The framework applies to processing of digital personal data within India or connected to an activity related to data principals within India, and includes foreign SaaS companies, e-commerce platforms and offshore businesses offering services or goods to individuals in India even if processing takes place outside India. The first phase, the DPDP Rules, 2025, put in place the Data Protection Board of India and its operationalization. A Consent Manager is an entity registered with the Board that allows an individual to give, manage, review or withdraw consent across businesses through a single channel, must be incorporated in India and must meet the Board's conditions including a minimum net worth of Rs 2 crore and stipulated certifications. Registration rules for Consent Managers are scheduled to commence this month, ahead of substantive compliance obligations due in May 2027, and applications for registration opened from November 13, 2026.

The article said the chairman and members of the Data Protection Board of India have not yet been formally appointed or staffed, posing major risks in implementation of the second phase. It said appointing the Board's Chairperson and Members is an immediate priority and prolonged institutional vacuum risks undermining the framework's effectiveness. It said Consent Managers, whose value lies in protecting individual choice and the right to privacy, must demonstrate that their incentives align with their roles and do not interfere with them. It said transparent governance and effective oversight of Consent Managers are essential to preventing misuse. It said the role of the regulator is pivotal in ensuring clarity and consistency.

The article said the commencement notification brings Section 6 (9) of the act mandating registration into force prior to Section 6 (7), which provides for management of consent through the Consent Manager, and Rule 4 of the DPDP Rules, 2025 governs entities operating as Consent Managers. It said registration of a Consent Manager does not by itself require a data fiduciary to immediately connect its systems to the Consent Manager's platform. It said the data fiduciary remains accountable for processing undertaken by it or on its behalf, and where consent is disputed the data fiduciary will have to prove requisite notice and valid consent under Section 6 (10). It said a Consent Manager only administers permission and manages conflicts without acquiring unrestricted access to the individual's underlying personal data.

It said the phasing allows data fiduciaries a transition period to reconcile data collected, processed and shared, followed by mapping the data, reviewing privacy notices and consent mechanisms, assessing internal accountability, vendor agreements and third-party sharing arrangements, establishing data retention, deletion and other security practices, preparing for breach response and setting up a grievance redressal mechanism. The article said the Act's compliance machinery rests on three limbs, accountability, proof of consent and consequences of failure in safeguards, all within the constitutional frame set in KS Puttaswamy Vs. Union of India (2017), which settled the right to privacy as a part of Article 21. It said consent must be continuing, not just a record that a button was once clicked.

It said the Consent Manager is expected to assist individuals in giving, managing, reviewing and withdrawing consent in an accessible and transparent manner, enabling greater continuing control over their data. It said businesses and other data fiduciaries might face immediate difficulty in integrating compliance requirements vis-à-vis vendors. It said data fiduciaries should begin preparing to fulfill their obligations under the Act and the Rules, and that the principal duties concerning notice, consent and processing will follow at a later phase. The article said phased implementation might be easily misconceived as simultaneous compliance, and doing so adds an unnecessary compliance cost.

It said the milestone is a significant development for the consent management ecosystem and businesses involved in building or using consent management mechanisms and vendors. It said compliance extends well beyond obtaining consent and updating privacy policies. It said India's data privacy regime will ultimately be judged by the extent of authority an individual's choice carries over her information, and that consent management ecosystems will count for little if a change in preference does nothing beyond the screen. It said the decisive test is whether the whole, including the data fiduciaries, can honour the right to privacy across the systems and commercial relationships, and prove that they have done so.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Anthropic's IPO day
stories.Summary:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol in the early hours of November 18, 2026, according to 36Kr. The launch came on the same day Anthropic rang the listing bell for its public debut. 36Kr described the release as a competitive strike against Anthropic on its IPO date. OpenAI positioned Astra for complex professional tasks and Sol for daily work. The article said Astra outperforms Claude Fable 5.2 on complex professional tasks.

In the Agents' Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 78.3%, 5.2 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra, at an average cost of $2.89 per task versus $60.05 for Claude Fable 5.2. Astra leads Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 percentage points at about 4.8% of its cost, and the comparison excludes 9 Claude tasks that used backup models. Astra's API input and output prices both dropped 20% and cached input dropped 60%, while GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. In OpenAI's GDPval v2, Astra rose from 44.2% to 50.4% while output tokens fell 22%, and Basis found long-range accounting task time cut 50% and the most complex tasks cut up to 73%.

OpenAI calls Astra "the best model for scientists", and it is 9 percentage points higher than the previous generation on Terminal-Bench-Science at under one third the task cost. Astra scored 68.4% on the Vals Science Index and rose from 62.6% to 82.5% on BenchCAD 2.1 Core. In Artificial Analysis's AA-3D it ranks first with 1318 Elo against Claude Fable 5.2's 1271 Elo, and Higgsfield found Astra hit the target in one go in 73% of 3D generation tasks. In Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 at max inference, Sol scored 43.8% and Astra 44.2%, with Sol's task cost about one fifth of Astra's.

In OpenAI's LifeVal, Sol scored 83.8% against GPT-6 Astra's 79.8% at about one seventh the task cost, and OpenAI said many internal employees use Sol as their default model. In Harvey's LAB-AA v1.1, Astra's pass rate was 15.0% against Claude Fable 5.2's 7.2% at about one sixth the cost, and on AA-AnalystAgent Astra answered all five independent answers correctly on 62.5% of questions. Legora found Astra cut token consumption 62% versus GPT-6.1 Sol in complex legal Agent tasks. In a DCF valuation workbook, Astra reorganized per-share, enterprise and equity value results, key assumptions and sensitivity analysis, and in comparable transaction analysis it noted Paychex's acquisition of Paycor at 21.7 times EV/EBITDA against a 27.5 times median for five positive-EBITDA transactions.

OpenAI's synchronized safety assessment found GPT-6.2 Astra is the first publicly released OpenAI model reaching the High risk level in AI self-improvement capability, meaning it shows ability to significantly accelerate next-generation AI R&D. 36Kr said model competition has shifted over the past year from answering questions to executing tasks, with enterprises caring whether models complete tasks of dozens or hundreds of steps and at what cost. OpenAI demonstrated Astra generating a 3D sports car model, writing a Python solver for tire and suspension dynamics, and finishing animation in Blender. It also reconstructed parts of a 1/8 scale fuel-powered remote-controlled off-road vehicle and an inline-six engine from photos and manuals, and converted Marina City's fan-shaped balconies into paper lamp designs. 36Kr noted the cost comparison uses average task cost under the specified evaluation configuration and does not mean 95% savings in all real business scenarios.

Theo, writing on X, said he spent a day writing OpenAI a letter about GPT-6.2 Astra and that OpenAI fixed a small handful of his complaints but not enough for him to recommend it. He said he would not choose it over Opus 5.5 for developer work, though it once helped him build a reverse proxy he said would save $25k/month. He said that on long tasks Astra pulls in subagents and then asks weird internal implementation questions, citing a request for a new Outer Wilds level blocked after 2 hours by a question about whether r24's reviewer writes clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4. He said GPT-5.6 Sol did not do this and that he set up other agents on crons to check whether Astra blocked itself, and he said he tried Codex and still hit the issues.

Theo said Astra has the most unparsable outputs of any LLM he used this year and that every explainer is so deep in details it borders on incorrect. He said he switches to Opus 5.5 at the end of long Astra runs for a readable summary and that prompt adjustments and begging it to "eli5" did not work. He said that when he asked why worktrees were slow on one machine but fast on three others, Opus 5.5 answered that the SSD is slow. He said no OpenAI model could break ground on his ts-rust project even after $300k+ in tokens, while Opus finished it in under 2 weeks for about $20k in tokens. He said he was sick in bed and posted the letter in full instead of filming a video.

36Kr said the cost gap exceeds 20 times and that Astra's per-task cost dropped to less than one third of the previous generation. 36Kr said the cost reduction comes first from pricing adjustments but that the more important change is fewer tokens generated through better task planning. 36Kr said enterprise Agents that run continuously may find the reduced steps and computing resources more valuable long term than lower token unit prices. 36Kr said Astra's improvements extend to computer operation and 3D engineering design, with the model delving into parts, connection relationships and motion constraints. 36Kr said developers must reconsider not only which model to use but which tasks are worth paying a premium for top-tier models.

36Kr said Astra is responsible for high-difficulty tasks such as scientific research, complex engineering design and professional knowledge work, while Sol handles larger-volume, cost-sensitive daily Agent work. 36Kr said the model no longer just generates content but tries to understand how industries define qualified work output. 36Kr said Astra's change in the safety assessment may have more far-reaching significance than its visible product features. The articles do not say when GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol will become generally available beyond the launch. The articles do not give OpenAI's response to Theo's letter beyond his statement that it fixed a small handful of complaints. The articles do not state Anthropic's response to the launch on its IPO date.

stories.Headline: Robert Izquierdo picks SoundHound AI over Rigetti Computing for 2027 on revenue growth and valuation
stories.Summary:
Robert Izquierdo of The Motley Fool published a comparison of Rigetti Computing and SoundHound AI on Nov 15, 2026, updated at 2:05PM EST. The article weighed Rigetti, a pure-play developer of superconducting quantum processors and cloud-based quantum services, against SoundHound AI, which scales a conversational artificial intelligence platform through software and voice solutions. Rigetti builds superconducting quantum computers and operates them through its proprietary Quantum Cloud Services platform. SoundHound AI focuses on voice-enabled artificial intelligence, powering natural conversations in situations such as in-car commands and restaurant drive-through ordering. The piece framed the choice as quantum hardware against conversational intelligence, two paths to commercial success.

Rigetti sells access to its hardware to global enterprise and research clients, including partners like Amazon and Microsoft. Nearly 90.2% of Rigetti's revenue last year came from U.S. government contracts. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Rigetti revenue reached nearly $7.1 million, a decrease of 34.3% from the previous year, with a net loss of $216.2 million. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Rigetti's current ratio stood at 37.4x, its debt-to-equity ratio was zero, and free cash flow was negative $77.2 million for the year. SoundHound AI, following its acquisition of LivePerson, integrated digital messaging and automation tools to broaden its customer reach.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, SoundHound AI revenue reached $168.9 million, an increase of 99.4% over the prior twelve-month period, alongside a net loss of $14.0 million that narrowed significantly from the prior year. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, SoundHound's current ratio stood at 4.6x and its debt-to-equity ratio was zero at the end of 2025. SoundHound's free cash flow for the period was negative $103.1 million as it invests heavily in acquisitions and platform development. Rigetti's stock traded at $9.62, down 6.87% or $0.71, with a market cap of $3.3 billion and a 52-week range of $9.19 to $30.21. SoundHound's stock traded at $3.49, down 3.06% or $0.11, with a market cap of $1.6 billion and a 52-week range of $3.40 to $13.19.

Rigetti's gross margin was negative 5093.24%, its P/E ratio negative 26.86, and its EPS (TTM) negative $0.36. SoundHound's gross margin was 30.55%, its P/E ratio negative 7.80, and its EPS (TTM) negative $0.45. On a P/S ratio basis, Rigetti stood at 251.1x and SoundHound at 6.8x, with forward P/E listed as n/a for both and valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep. Rigetti faces hurdles as an early-stage hardware developer with a history of substantial operating losses, depends heavily on a small group of government customers, and competes against well-capitalized rivals such as IonQ and D-Wave Quantum. SoundHound deals with a history of substantial net losses and negative cash flow from operations, operates in a crowded market where incumbents like Microsoft and Amazon have vast resources, and faces integrating several major acquisitions amid evolving global regulations on artificial intelligence and data privacy.

Rigetti management predicts quantum advantage, when a quantum computer performs a task more efficiently and at lower cost than a classical computer, is at least three years away. Rigetti's tech requires special cryogenic equipment that keeps its quantum particles at a state colder than outer space, and rivals are producing quantum machines that can operate at room temperature. In its third quarter report, SoundHound announced it expects to reach adjusted EBITDA profitability by the second half of 2027. SoundHound's Q3 revenue was $62.4 million, a 49% year-over-year increase, and it anticipates sales of at least $250 million in 2026, growing to a minimum of $350 million in 2027. Izquierdo wrote that he would invest in SoundHound for 2027, citing consistent revenue expansion, the move to profitability, and superior share price valuation.

The article noted Stock Advisor's total average return of 823% against 209% for the S&P 500, with returns as of November 15, 2026. Related Fool.com pieces listed were a Nov 15, 2026 prediction on Rigetti's stock price in one year, Nov 11, 2026 takeaways for long-term Rigetti investors, a Nov 10, 2026 Rigetti Q3 2026 earnings call transcript, Nov 9, 2026 best quantum computing stocks, Nov 7, 2026 where Rigetti stock will be in three years, and Nov 4, 2026 coverage of Rigetti slipping 23.4% last month. The article left open whether quantum advantage arrives on Rigetti's three-year timeline and whether SoundHound reaches adjusted EBITDA profitability in the second half of 2027. It also left open whether SoundHound hits at least $250 million in 2026 sales and a minimum of $350 million in 2027.

stories.Headline: FAA expands SMART AI system nationwide as officials deny link to ground stop
stories.Summary:
The airline ground stop that disrupted travel since Friday was not related to the FAA's new $875 million AI-powered system, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there was no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop were linked to the new computer system. The top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday. The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop was not caused by the SMART system, any product of ASI or its integration with FAA and air traffic control. The timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART system, raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails address potential problems.

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. That office sends recommendations to the FAA's command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration. SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics into one platform. SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers, three days before the ground stop.

The system's AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a comprehensive visualization of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise. The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system's recommendations. According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested.

The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals. SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster. Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as large, rectangular boxes, according to the fact sheet, which does not reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through. To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time, allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas. No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.

Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails. The Oct. 13 letter said the nation's front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART's development and had received limited training and information during the current deployment process. The letter said the use of artificial intelligence within SMART had rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information. SMART, however, is not, at least not yet, set up for AI to be in charge of flight control, rather it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

Mike O'Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that's doing the work. The FAA, he said, cannot afford to be wrong on this. O'Donnell said it is good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they are not giving wrong information to controllers based on what AI has come up with, and there has got to be a way to verify and validate what it is doing to make sure that it is not the wrong information. He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI until we know for sure that it has proven itself time and time again, and that is going to take a while. The AI system's launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. Experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job. In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace, and that the AI does the math and the computation, but it is ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system's recommendation, and they make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.

stories.Headline: Artist Olivia Tai collects confessions about using AI to write personal messages
stories.Summary:
Olivia Tai, an artist who has repeated a project called the Confession box more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, set up a purple box on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square that held dozens of secrets written by passersby. A sign on the box read “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret,” and among the confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages. The confessions included “I had AI write my breakup text,” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text,” and “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”

Tai said calling the project a confession suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty, but they used it anyway. The question the project raises is whether using a chatbot for personal messages crosses a line, and whether it is ever acceptable to use AI to write a holiday card, a birthday message, a love letter or wedding vows. Danielle Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia who conducted vignette-based experiments as part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who had not. Hass said everyone felt guilty and that the driver of this relationship was dishonesty, with people feeling like they were manipulating others.

Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK, said his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy, even when they are honest about their AI use. Claessens noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes, but something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off. He said what people really want in social relationships is for others to put effort in, because it shows as a signal that you are invested in the relationship. Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it is appropriate and when it is not.

Newman suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide, asking whether you would be comfortable telling your partner you used AI to write your wedding vows, and said personal messages do not need to be perfect because part of what makes them authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect. Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who does not share a native language, or people with learning disabilities such as dyslexia who could use it for help. Hass said she believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she is glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages. Hass said guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings and to show us where we are supposed to be human.

stories.Headline: Family physician Mara Gordon uses an AI scribe on her phone to draft notes but reviews and signs each one
stories.Summary:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., wrote in a piece published November 17, 2026, that a reader asked whether to worry about an artificial intelligence scribe recording private medical conversations. The reader said her doctor had started recording office visits with an AI scribe and that she said yes when asked if she was comfortable. The reader said that in hindsight she felt a little freaked out. Gordon wrote that AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Gordon wrote that doctors use them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

Gordon wrote that she first asks the patient if they are comfortable using the service. Gordon wrote that if the patient says yes, she starts recording using an app on her smartphone, usually set down on the desk in the exam room. Gordon wrote that the scribe uses "automatic speech recognition," which records the conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. Gordon wrote that sometimes, when a family member accompanies the patient, the app needs to distinguish between three or more voices. Gordon wrote that when the visit ends, the recording is transcribed and a large language model geared toward medicine converts the raw transcript into a medical note.

Gordon wrote that the notes follow a standard format specific to the specialty and the type of visit. Gordon wrote that the notes reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making. Gordon wrote that she is ultimately responsible for the content of the AI-generated note and always reads them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them. Gordon wrote that when the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, she almost always ends up editing them to make her clinical decision-making more clear.

Gordon wrote that she talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego who specializes in clinical informatics. Gordon quoted Kim saying that an overburdened doctor seeing too many patients has an AI tool offered that seems like a great solution but no time to adequately review everything. Gordon quoted Kim saying the note goes into the chart and another AI tool reading the notes propagates errors throughout the chart. Gordon wrote that she comes across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time and that it is hard to know how much is related to AI and how much to human error. Gordon wrote that many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients, and that health equity advocates fear this means unequal access that could further widen health disparities.

Gordon wrote that she has been an eager adopter in her own primary care practice. Gordon wrote that she uses an app on her phone that records her conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record. Gordon wrote that it saves her time and helps her focus more fully on her patient, so she can make eye contact rather than stare at the computer screen. Gordon wrote that she shares her patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship. Gordon wrote that she worries corporate health systems will pressure doctors to use time saved with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients, and that artificial intelligence might one day put her out of a job.

Gordon wrote that there are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Gordon wrote that most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, though some use a desktop computer or a separate recording device. Gordon wrote that she uses her personal smartphone, as do many physicians she knows, and that she once got notification pings from her book club's group chat while recording a patient visit, which made her put the phone in "do not disturb" mode. Gordon wrote that conversations are not stored on her device but uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note, and that most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time. Gordon wrote that HIPAA means the program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy, and that the software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step, encrypting it, controlling access, protecting against data breaches, and being liable if data is leaked.

Gordon wrote that she recently saw a patient with metastatic cancer who did not believe he had cancer despite multiple conversations with her, his oncologist, and his surgeon, and that she had even, with his permission, called his spouse. Gordon wrote that the AI scribe did not get this tricky situation right and that the note simply said the patient had been misdiagnosed rather than reflecting the nuances of the conversation. Gordon wrote that she often catches other errors, like mistaking a patient's gender or age, and that the scribes are known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not," where the difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe companies delete recorded conversations within a set period of time as a security feature, to protect patient privacy and protect doctors from lawsuits, and that there is widespread concern the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits. Gordon wrote that some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could assess the quality of AI-generated notes or study physician-patient communication, and that for now recordings of regular appointments, unless a patient is enrolled in a research study, are not used for research.

Gordon wrote that most of her patients readily agree to the AI scribe, but occasionally patients worry the data isn't really secure or could be used to identify them in the future. Gordon wrote that if a patient doesn't want the AI scribe, she just takes notes on the computer while they talk, as she did for years before the scribes became available. Gordon quoted Kim saying AI is "just everywhere" and it would be impossible to separate it, and that software relying on machine learning is used for billing, clinical decision-making, and communication between the doctor's office and patients. Gordon wrote that AI is often used in risk calculators, like tools that estimate a patient's risk of heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure, and in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis based on vital signs and lab values. Gordon quoted Kim saying it is basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you."

Gordon wrote that she asked Kim, a primary care doctor like her, whether AI would replace them in the coming years, and whether an AI scribe that could ask the same questions she does could generate a treatment plan as good or better than the one she recommends. Gordon wrote that Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care, possibly for the better if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer. Gordon wrote that the article ends there, leaving Kim's ultimate answer about replacement unstated. Gordon wrote that readers can send health questions to thrive@npr.org. Gordon wrote that she is happy to have robots help with her administrative tasks but still takes pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence.

stories.Headline: Senator Maria Cantwell accuses the Commerce Department of failing to stop AI chip flows to China
stories.Summary:
Senator Maria Cantwell accused the Commerce Department of failing to stop China from getting advanced AI chips in a November 15 letter. She claimed that Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to take action, which she argued undermined the national security of the United States. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also accused the department of weakening export controls by resisting the blacklisting of a Singaporean company. This company, called Megaspeed, is at the center of a scandal involving the export of Nvidia processors to Chinese customers. The accusations follow reports that the Commerce Department delayed action despite repeated warnings about risks to America's technological AI advantage.

Cantwell urged Lutnick to use the 2018 Export Control Reform Act to strengthen enforcement and prevent restricted technology from reaching barred companies. The dispute involves Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that US authorities suspect helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia chips subject to export controls. The Trump administration imposed a 25 per cent fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, creating a perverse financial incentive. Cantwell cited 1.2 billion dollars in Nvidia stock held by Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm controlled by the sons of Howard Lutnick. These financial conflicts raise questions about whether business interests were put ahead of national security during the export approval process.

Senator Cantwell stated that America cannot maintain AI leadership if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Treasury, Pentagon, State Department, and US Trade Representative's Office favored blacklisting Megaspeed for months. Bessent noted that the Commerce Department, which is in charge of the trade blacklist, had not been in favor of this. A spokesperson for Lutnick, Kristen Eichamer, declined to comment on the letter but confirmed that Lutnick agreed to testify soon. Cantwell alleged that the department suspended a probe into Megaspeed and resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as security threats.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday that a growing consensus in Congress now favors new restrictions on China's AI access. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Senator Jim Banks of Indiana argue that export decisions should face much greater congressional oversight. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is affected by reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive and suspected spy. Megaspeed is affected by the investigation, though the company denies the allegations and says it conducts a legitimate and lawful business. China has also denied the allegations that restricted chips were transferred to its customers through the Singaporean technology firm.

The New York Times reported in October 2025 that US authorities were investigating if Megaspeed helped Chinese customers obtain restricted Nvidia chips. Megaspeed stated on Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has not violated export rules. A November 9 New York Times report alleged that the Commerce Department may have delayed the investigation into the Singaporean company. The controversy involves the diversion of restricted American computing technology to China to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology. These events occur as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January of the coming year.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has summoned Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify before his committee in December. Senators Warren and Chris Coons wrote to Lutnick, Marco Rubio, and Stephen Miller to preserve all documents regarding Nvidia exports. These officials were given until November 17 to confirm that the preservation directives for communications and documents had been issued. US officials are also scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering. The articles leave open whether Megaspeed actually breached US export rules and how Washington will handle future semiconductor export decisions.

stories.Headline: Complaint filed against education minister for dereliction of duty over AI cheating
stories.Summary:
Lee Jong-bae, a former Seoul city council member from the People Power Party, filed a complaint against Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The complaint was submitted to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency following remarks Choi made during a National Assembly education committee session on Monday. Choi stated that it would be difficult for authorities to detect every instance of cheating involving artificial intelligence. This legal action occurred just before the College Scholastic Ability Test, also known as Suneung, which was scheduled for that Thursday.

The complaint alleges that the minister committed dereliction of duty by failing to implement effective countermeasures against AI-assisted cheating. Lee Jong-bae argued that the government could have prevented such misconduct by installing radio detectors in test rooms or postponing the Suneung. These demands come after several high-profile cheating incidents, including a case where the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam used a miniature camera. Public anxiety has increased due to these events and other reports of AI glasses being used in schools.

Lee Jong-bae claimed that Minister Choi consciously abandoned his official duties despite knowing the limitations of the current monitoring system. He urged the police to conduct a thorough investigation and strictly punish the minister for his perceived negligence. The former councilor believes the government possesses the necessary tools to stop AI cheating but has failed to use them. He maintains that the minister's admission of difficulty in catching cheaters proves a lack of adequate preparation.

The situation reflects a broader national scramble to crack down on AI-assisted cheating before the annual college entrance exams. Other recent reports indicate that students in middle and high schools have been caught using AI glasses this year. The government has vowed to maintain zero tolerance against such academic dishonesty to protect the integrity of national tests. Police are currently investigating the tax accountant exam case after the top scorer turned himself in and apologized.

stories.Headline: Tencent releases Hy4 flash to provide cost efficient AI for professional workflows
stories.Summary:
Tencent announced the release of Hy4 flash on November 17, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, to power high speed and cost efficient AI deployment. This new model is the latest addition to the Hy model family and is designed to support everyday professional productivity workflows. The company developed this tool to provide a stronger balance of intelligence and efficiency for real world tasks for its users. It aims to deliver exceptional cost performance while maintaining strong intelligence and practical utility across various types of professional digital work. The release follows the launch of Hy4, which joined the ranks of leading open source AI models on November 4.

Hy4 flash has 224 billion total parameters, including 64 billion Engram parameters, with only 12 billion active parameters and 1M token context length. It costs US$0.070 per million input tokens, US$0.281 per million output tokens, and US$0.003 per million cached input tokens for its users. The model is available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom, QQ, ima, and Marvis, with OpenRouter integration coming very soon. From now until November 30, users can access the model for free on WorkBuddy or get 50 percent off via TokenHub. It uses hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram features, with a KV cache size 1/24 of Hy3 and 1/6 that of Hy4.

The Tencent Hy team made specific engineering choices across the pipeline to achieve this level of cost performance and strong practical utility. They used megakernel, 4-bit quantization, and DFly techniques to reach decoding speeds that exceed 150 tokens per second for low cost deployment. The team built an internal benchmark called WorkIndex based on typical WorkBuddy tasks to focus on deliverable quality and task turnaround time. They stated that reinforcement learning was used to cut the average end to end task output tokens by 50 percent for efficiency. The team recommends Hy4 flash for everyday tasks like deep research, document processing, PowerPoint generation, simple front end displays, and computer use.

Internal WorkBuddy users participated in a blind evaluation of 259 tasks in 27 categories to test the effectiveness of the new model. These 85 users reported satisfaction levels close to Claude Haiku 5.5, while noting the shortest task completion time among all models. The model slightly outperforms Hy4 Preview, which has 770 billion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, in overall effectiveness for users. Per task costs are 1/13 of Hy4 Preview, 1/20 of Hy4, and 1/8 of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max tier peak hour pricing for tasks. Users are directed to the more capable Hy4 for complex tasks such as long horizon software engineering to ensure the best results.

Tencent was founded in Shenzhen, China, in 1998 and has been listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong since the year 2004. The company is a world leading internet and technology firm that develops innovative products to improve the quality of life for people. Its communication and social services connect more than one billion people globally to help them stay in touch and access transportation. The business also covers financial technology, including payment, credit, wealth management, and insurance sectors, to support partners and their digital upgrades. Additionally, the company publishes some of the most popular video games and high quality digital content to enrich interactive entertainment experiences globally.

Tencent Hy plans to open source Hy4 flash with frequent iterations to continuously improve its practical utility and efficiency for real world work. The company will continue to push the boundaries of intelligence while delivering exceptional cost performance for its various professional AI tools. Hy4 previously ranked second among Chinese models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and first among open source models on Agent Arena. The articles do not state the specific date when the open source version of Hy4 flash will be released to the public. They also leave open the specific details regarding the upcoming integration with OpenRouter and any future pricing changes after November 30.

stories.Headline: CloudKeeper reaches Select tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track
stories.Summary:
CloudKeeper announced on November 17, 2026, that it had achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track, according to a press release carried by The Manila Times. The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers, and the Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through four tiers, which are Certified, Select, Preferred and Global Premier. The recognition builds on CloudKeeper's existing relationship with Anthropic and adds to its capabilities in helping businesses implement and manage AI solutions.

Drawing on its expertise in cloud infrastructure, FinOps and AI, CloudKeeper will support organizations building with Claude, including implementing Claude through Amazon Bedrock and addressing their AI infrastructure, governance and cost optimization needs. The company says putting AI into production involves decisions beyond selecting a model, such as how applications connect with existing systems, where workloads run, how usage is governed and how costs are managed. With experience across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, and offerings such as FinOps for AI and Generative AI Launchpad, CloudKeeper helps customers navigate these considerations. The announcement builds on CloudKeeper's earlier appointment as an authorised Anthropic reseller, which lets customers access Claude models through Amazon Bedrock within AWS.

Deepak Mittal, the CEO of CloudKeeper, said the company has spent over 15 years helping businesses make better decisions about their cloud investments, and that AI raises important questions about infrastructure, consumption and long-term costs. He said CloudKeeper wants to help customers get the most out of what they are building with Claude while keeping the economics in view, and called the recognition a meaningful step in that direction. Aman Aggarwal, the COO, said the interesting work begins when a team takes Claude from a promising capability and makes it useful in its own environment, which means connecting it with existing applications, making sound architecture choices and putting the right governance in place. He said the company's engineering and cloud teams work across these challenges and that the recognition supports the work being done with customers.

CloudKeeper describes itself as an outcome-driven AI and cloud cost optimization partner that combines FinOps expertise, proprietary technology and hands-on execution. With over 15 years of cloud cost optimization experience, it says it has helped more than 500 global companies reduce cloud and AI spend by an average of 20% across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Its outcome-based model delivers ongoing savings without upfront costs or long-term commitments, according to the release. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the two relationships strengthening CloudKeeper's ability to support customers with both Claude access and implementation.

stories.Headline: South Korea's military screens smart glasses at entrances to block covert recording on bases
stories.Summary:
Military authorities in South Korea stepped up screening of wearable devices on Tuesday to prevent unauthorized equipment from entering military facilities. These officials targeted smart glasses capable of filming or recording to ensure that no such devices are brought onto bases. The Ministry of National Defense issued these instructions to all military units across the armed services during the previous month. These new security measures officially took effect on November 1 to block devices that can perform covert recording tasks. The military is now focusing on these wearables to maintain security across all of its various military installations.

All eyeglasses must now pass through an X-ray scanner if one is available at the specific military unit entrance. Guards on duty at units without scanning equipment must physically inspect the glasses to ensure they are not smart wearables. These guards will specifically inspect the arms and frames of the glasses for charging ports or hidden miniature cameras. Suspicious glasses must be handed over to guards to verify the model, serial number, and specific charging specifications. Guards will also check these suspicious devices for any speakers or control buttons to confirm if they are unauthorized devices.

A ministry official stated that they ordered all units across the armed services to increase inspections for visitors and personnel. This official noted that the military will tighten disciplinary standards by weighing factors like whether the device use was intentional. The ministry plans to revise internal directives soon to impose stiffer disciplinary measures on those bringing unauthorized smart devices. Officials said these steps are necessary to prevent the unauthorized use of recording devices within the secure military facilities. The ministry is coordinating these efforts across all branches of the armed services to ensure a consistent security standard.

The tougher rules follow growing scrutiny in South Korea over several cheating cases that involved the use of artificial intelligence devices. A top scorer on the tax accountant exam fueled this concern by confessing to using generative AI to cheat. This individual admitted to using a smartphone and a miniature camera to gain an unfair advantage during the professional test. These cheating scandals have affected the general public's trust and prompted a wider crackdown on AI devices across the country. Other government sectors are also scrambling to stop AI cheating ahead of the national college entrance exam for students.

The background of this military action is rooted in the rise of AI assisted cheating using miniature cameras and smartphones. South Korea is currently facing a series of high profile cases where generative AI was used to cheat on exams. This environment of scrutiny has led the government to consider disabling Wi-Fi at certain test sites to prevent cheating. The military is reacting to these societal trends to ensure that similar technology is not used for unauthorized recording. These measures reflect a broader national effort to root out the misuse of artificial intelligence in various professional settings.

No violations involving smart glasses have been reported from any military units since the tougher rules took effect this month. The military will continue to monitor the situation as they implement the revised internal directives for stiffer disciplinary actions. The articles do not state when the revised directives will be finalized or exactly how much stiffer the penalties will be. It remains open whether other types of wearable technology beyond smart glasses will face similar levels of strict security screening. The reports do not specify if these screening measures will be permanent or if they are temporary emergency responses.

stories.Headline: AI analysis of one echocardiogram clip plus H2FPEF score identifies 78% of hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF cases
stories.Summary:
Researchers applied an artificial intelligence model called EchoGo HF to resting echocardiograms from 280 outpatients who had been referred for suspected heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and each patient also underwent exercise hemodynamic testing as the diagnostic gold standard, according to research published in the November 2026 issue of the Journal of Cardiac Failure. Adding the AI analysis of a single routine echocardiogram clip to the H₂FPEF clinical score identified 78% of patients with hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF, compared with 48% using the score alone. The AI model added the most value for patients with low or intermediate H₂FPEF scores, the group where diagnosis is hardest, so the authors tested a two-step strategy of calculating H₂FPEF first and then applying AI only when the score is inconclusive. An AI-detected HFpEF result also independently predicted elevated filling pressures and reduced exercise capacity, which suggests the model reflects disease severity as well as diagnosis.

The November issue, focused on artificial intelligence in heart failure, also includes a study in which investigators used clinical notes from 599 patients seen in cardiology clinics to optimize a large language model, OpenAI's o1, that classified the documented reason for non-prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors with 84.7% accuracy. Physician-attributed factors were the most common theme at 28.7% of notes, and the leading specific reasons were deferring the decision to a future visit at 15.4% and the physician judging the patient low-risk or unlikely to benefit at 7.4%. A review in the same issue maps current AI applications across the heart failure care continuum, including AI-enabled ECG and imaging for opportunistic detection of low ejection fraction, HFpEF and structural heart disease, risk stratification based on electronic health records, clinician decision support, remote medication titration and wearable monitoring. The review's authors conclude that the strongest evidence favors AI built into active clinical workflows that guide targeted testing, treatment optimization and follow-up, rather than AI used only to send passive alerts.

In their Editor's Page, guest editors Jonathan W. Cunningham of Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School, Elena Donald and Nir Uriel of Columbia University Irving Medical Center, and Ankeet S. Bhatt of Kaiser Permanente San Francisco Medical Center wrote that heart failure's population burden is growing and outcomes are worsening while the number of heart failure physicians is flat and training spots go unfilled, and that AI could help close that gap. They wrote that promise alone is insufficient and that AI, like any innovation intended to change clinical care, must be rigorously studied to understand where it adds value, where it does not and how it can be implemented safely and effectively. The editors called on the heart failure community to move past retrospective and in silico demonstrations of model performance and instead want prospective studies, including randomized trials where feasible, that test whether AI tools improve clinical decisions, treatment delivery, outcomes, equity and clinician workload. They wrote that AI researchers will continue to advance these tools but that clinicians and patients must lead their translation into care, and the complete November 2026 issue is available online now.

stories.Headline: China offers open-source AI models to help APEC economies reduce the digital divide
stories.Summary:
Industry leaders and experts stated on November 17, 2026, that China can help APEC economies narrow the digital divide. They believe China's open-source artificial intelligence models and rapid deployment capabilities can accelerate technology adoption across the real economy. Collaboration on artificial intelligence has become a primary and closely watched priority for this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation innovation agenda. These experts argue that China is emerging as a critical testing ground for global development in robotics and intelligent vehicles.

Closing the digital divide requires more than just hardware, as developing economies often lack the local talent and governance frameworks to maintain imported tools. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reports that the country ranks first worldwide in downloads of open-source large language models. To support this, the China Center for APEC Cooperation on Cross-border Data Flows was established in Qianhai, Shenzhen, Guangdong province. This center manages the Shenzhen-Hong Kong cross-border data verification platform and a secure data channel for medical information.

Samantha Zhu of Accenture Greater China noted that 88 percent of Chinese enterprises have moved beyond the pilot stage of AI adoption. Jeff Shi of SenseTime explained that his company now serves over 430 companies in the Asia-Pacific region by offering industry-specific solutions. Liu Qingfeng of iFlytek mentioned that his company has 600,000 overseas developers across 220 countries and regions. He also noted that over half of the 29 countries that signed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization agreement on July 16 cooperate with his firm.

The regional supply chain is shifting toward computing power and algorithms as flexible manufacturing replaces old labor cost advantages, according to Zhang Shaogang. New trade chains involving robotics and industrial large language models are emerging to favor economies that can operationalize these tools. Lin Zhifeng stated that the cross-border data verification model has already been replicated in Singapore. Future efforts will extend this cooperation to more APEC economies and broader industrial fields like new energy and smart manufacturing.

stories.Headline: MiTAC Computing unveils full-stack infrastructure to scale agentic AI for enterprises
stories.Summary:
MiTAC Computing Technology Corporation unveiled a comprehensive AI infrastructure ecosystem at the SC26 event in Chicago on November 17, 2026. The company showcased these innovations at Booth 4615 to demonstrate how full-stack solutions overcome common enterprise AI deployment bottlenecks. This new ecosystem aims to scale agentic AI by addressing critical compute, thermal, and data challenges for modern businesses. MiTAC collaborated with several strategic partners including AMD, Canonical, DDN, Intel, NVIDIA, and Rafay to deliver these scalable architectures. The event took place at McCormick Place from November 17 through November 19 to present these high-performance server solutions.

The G8825Z5 server uses AMD EPYC 9575F or 9755 processors and AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs for the compute-intensive prefill stage. For the decode stage, the air-cooled G4520G6 uses Intel Xeon 6 processors and eight Skymizer HTX301-4S accelerator cards. Each HTX301-4S card has 256 GB of memory, providing 2 TB of aggregate memory to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model. The upcoming ORv3 44OU Helion solution will scale up to 32,768 AMD Zen 6 CPU cores for hyperscale environments. A 52U liquid-cooled rack integrates 12 G4826Z5 servers with 96 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs to increase GPU density by 50 percent.

Rick Hwang, the President of MiTAC Computing Technology, stated that scaling agentic AI requires cohesive infrastructure rather than fragmented systems. He explained that MiTAC provides the foundational full-stack solution necessary to make sustainable AI factories a reality for enterprises. The company also utilized the vision of AMD Chair and CEO Dr. Lisa Su announced at the OCP Global Summit. MiTAC aims to empower organizations to intelligently route complex workloads and maximize agents-per-watt efficiency through their new rack-scale architectures. These leadership goals focus on providing end-to-end capabilities from research and development to global manufacturing and support.

Enterprises are affected by the need for more than raw GPU power to handle the exponential surge in inference workloads. Canonical Ubuntu provides the certified operating system layer to ensure seamless deployment and enterprise-grade reliability for these AI factories. The DDN Infinia solution prevents accelerator data starvation by processing monumental data streams with ultra-low I/O latency for users. Rafay helps organizations maximize return on investment by providing dynamic GPU-as-a-Service orchestration to eliminate idling across distributed workloads. MiCoreView software grants data center managers deep telemetry and unified visibility through a comprehensive POD management solution.

MiTAC Computing is a subsidiary of MiTAC Holdings Corporation and has provided energy-efficient server solutions since the 1990s. The company specializes in high-performance computing, cloud, and edge computing using rigorous methodologies to ensure quality across all levels. They have unified their brand with TYAN server products and Intel DSG to stand out in the server technology industry. Their expertise covers barebones, systems, racks, and cluster levels to achieve high performance and integration for their global customers. The company provides customized platforms for hyperscale data centers and specialized AI applications to meet unique business needs.

The company is developing the Helion Agentic AI Rack to support next-generation rack-scale architectures for hyperscale and enterprise environments. A proof of concept with ZutaCore uses waterless two-phase direct liquid cooling to support thermal design powers exceeding 4,000W. This cooling technology achieves a heat flux over 250W/cm2 and enables an annualized pPUE of 1.03 for the G4826Z5 server. MiTAC also offers various server platforms like the G4827Z6, G2610Z6, TN85-B8261, R1917GC, R1610Z6, M2810Z6, and the liquid-cooled C2611Z6. stories.Headline: Marsh's Schnur links AI tools to a doubling of client cyber incidents
stories.Summary:
Marsh reported that its clients filed 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October, which is more than double the 48 incidents recorded in the final two weeks of May, according to data the insurance broker released and Reuters reported on November 17, 2026. Meredith Schnur, who leads the US and Canada cyber practice at Marsh Risk, told Reuters in an interview this week that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities, and she said AI could be attributed to a significant number of the incidents. She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, combined with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors driving the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. Schnur said AI is not a peril but an amplification of risk in all areas, and she said the technology lets attackers find and exploit longstanding vulnerabilities such as unpatched software, exposed systems and weak identity controls at a much faster pace. The rise in reported incidents requires businesses and their insurers to contend with attacks that spread faster and reach more targets, because AI tools that are becoming more widely accessible let attackers scale their operations with fewer resources.

GlobalData expects global cyber insurance premiums to rise 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026, before growth accelerates to 10% in 2027 to reach $18.3 billion, as businesses respond to rising attack frequency. The Marsh figures compare the final two weeks of October with the final two weeks of May, and the 105 incidents more than double the 48 recorded in the earlier period. The report ties the increase to AI adoption and to slower containment and response times, and it says the wider availability of AI tools is widening the pool of potential targets and putting pressure on businesses. Schnur, the US and Canada cyber practice leader at Marsh Risk, is the person the articles identify as explaining the data, and she attributed a significant share of the incidents to AI in her interview with Reuters this week. She said the signs that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities are happening, and she described AI as an amplification of risk in all areas rather than a peril in itself.

She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, together with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors behind the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. The reporting was by Noor Zainab Hussain and Manya Saini in Bengaluru, with editing by Shilpi Majumdar, and the story was published by Reuters and carried by Insurance Journal. The context the articles give is a cyber insurance market that GlobalData expects to grow faster over the next two years as businesses respond to rising attack frequency, with premiums reaching $16.6 billion in 2026 and $18.3 billion in 2027. The articles do not say what Marsh or insurers will change in response to the data, and they do not describe any new policy terms or claims figures beyond the incident counts and the premium forecasts. What happens next, according to the articles, is continued growth in cyber insurance premiums at a faster pace over the next two years, driven by the rising frequency of attacks that the Marsh data shows.

stories.Headline: AdMaven launches Mave AI assistant that prepares campaign changes for advertiser approval
stories.Summary:
AdMaven introduced an AI assistant called Mave that is built directly into its advertiser dashboard, letting advertisers launch pop campaigns, adjust settings, analyze live account data and get platform help in their own language, according to a company announcement dated November 18, 2026. The company said media buyers often spend roughly 26 percent of a campaign manager's time, or over 10 hours a week, on a tedious weekly checklist of monitoring results, tweaking bids, reallocating budgets and pausing underperforming ads. Mave was designed to handle that post-launch daily grind so media buyers can focus on strategy rather than repetitive tasks, and it never acts on its own. Whenever an advertiser asks to create a campaign, adjust a bid or change a budget, Mave prepares a confirmation card showing every detail, nothing happens until the advertiser clicks Approve, and cards expire after 10 minutes. With Mave, advertisers can set up to 5 pop campaigns at once through guided, clickable prompts, with support for CPM, Smart CPM, Smart CPA and Pure CPA where enabled, plus country, OS and device targeting and an optional daily budget before creatives go into standard review.

They can pause or resume up to 20 campaigns at once, update bids for one country or all countries, or adjust daily budgets with a $10 minimum, and they can ask in plain language for daily check-ins, weekly summaries, campaign comparisons and period-over-period breakdowns by day, country, device, OS, browser and source, with data refreshing roughly every 10 minutes. Mave can also identify sources that spend without converting or convert at a much higher CPA than average so advertisers know which ones to block, show running and paused campaigns, creative approval status, current bids by country, source lists and available balance plus credit line, and answer questions from AdMaven's help center of 35 articles, including setup guides for 13 trackers, tracking macros and policy rules. When an issue needs a person, such as a payment or creative-review dispute, Mave prepares a pre-written message so the advertiser can contact support in one click. Noam Cohen, Co-Founder at AdMaven, said most of what advertisers do in the dashboard is not launching something new but the same daily questions about how campaigns are doing, where they are overpaying and what should be paused.

He said Mave lets them ask those questions directly and get an answer or a change ready to approve, but it does not make the call for them, and the budget and judgment stay with the advertiser while Mave removes the clicking in between. AdMaven describes itself as a performance-driven global advertising network delivering over 1 billion daily impressions worldwide, specializing in Pop, Push, In-page Push and Interstitial ads, and offering publishers a brand-protected ecosystem with no minimum traffic barriers. Mave is currently rolling out on an invite-only basis, enabled account by account inside the AdMaven advertiser dashboard's chat panel, and read-only Q&A access is also available through the AdMaven API for pulling account answers without making changes. Advertisers interested in early access can reach out to their account manager, and the company invites interested advertisers to sign up as an AdMaven advertiser to get started.
