stories.Headline: Michael Garland and Gaurav Pal say shared savings lets government adopt AI with little financial risk
stories.Summary:
Michael Garland and Gaurav “GP” Pal wrote in a November 17, 2026 commentary that government can adopt AI quickly with little financial risk. They said the government has not been an early adopter of new technology. They noted the Cloud First policy arrived in 2010 and FedRAMP in 2011. They said agencies are still migrating workloads to the cloud more than 15 years later. They said the artificial intelligence revolution is a juggernaut.

They said Anthropic’s recent IPO filing reports revenue grew from $41 million in 2023 to $16 billion in the first half of 2026. They said Bloomberg reports OpenAI’s annualized revenue was about $50 billion at the end of September. They estimated the government spends about $20 billion a year on commercial software licensing alone. They cited the Congressional Budget Office putting the fiscal 2026 deficit at $2.0 trillion. They cited Pew Research finding the federal workforce fell about 10% in 2025.

They said the mechanism is shared savings, where the contractor funds the deployment and the government pays a percentage of verifiably delivered savings. They said Energy Savings Performance Contracts have let agencies pay contractors out of guaranteed energy savings for decades. They said Medicare’s Shared Savings Program rewards providers who hold costs below a benchmark. They said in September the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and AI Office signed a one-year agreement with Red Cell Partners with a ceiling of $100 million.

They said Red Cell projects $62 million in Air Force audit-readiness support contracts could be consolidated into an AI-augmented model costing about $24.8 million, with the vendor earning 30% of the verified reduction. They said the General Services Administration’s OneGov program supplies a known price. They said GSA recently set a 50% discount on OpenAI token usage under a 27-month agreement. They said as of Oct. 27 GSA set a 40% discount on token usage across Anthropic’s Claude models.

They said the E-Government Act of 2002 authorized share-in-savings contracts for IT. They said the Government Accountability Office reported in 2005 that implementing regulations had never been issued, only 21 acquisition employees had taken GSA’s training course, and no contracts had been awarded. They said the authority expired that September. They said the Anti-Deficiency Act forbids obligating funds before Congress appropriates them.

They said the Pentagon pilot is a one-year other transaction agreement that sidesteps the multiyear problem for now. They said scaling beyond one-year pilots will take legislation. They said a small office skilled in designing cost baselines could be housed at GSA. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Kevin Roose details the race to build artificial superintelligence in a new book
stories.Summary:
Christine Emba, a senior fellow and guest host of The Gray Area podcast, spoke with technology journalist Kevin Roose about his new book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence, in an episode published on October 26, 2026. The episode examined what is happening behind the scenes at America's largest AI companies and how the squabbles, ideologies and goals of their CEOs and engineers could shape the future. Roose's book offers a behind-the-scenes look at the engineers and tech leaders competing to build artificial superintelligence, according to the episode description. The conversation also explored the rivalries between frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, along with the philosophical roots of "p(doom)" and AI safety. The episode description states that the race to build artificial superintelligence has sparked a massive data center boom and has made a handful of people some of the most powerful decision-makers on Earth.

Emba and Roose also discussed whether recursive self-improvement could push superintelligence beyond human control sooner than many people think. The episode was published by the American Enterprise Institute as part of its Social, Cultural, and Constitutional Studies work and appeared under The Gray Area with Sean Illing. The page lists Emba as a senior fellow and does not give any further dates, figures or named companies beyond those above. The episode presents Roose's account of the engineers and tech leaders competing in this race, and it frames the rivalries among the frontier labs as a central part of the story. Emba and Roose explored the philosophical roots of "p(doom)" and AI safety as part of the same conversation about how the goals of the people involved could shape the future.

The description does not attribute any further statements to Roose or Emba beyond the topics listed for the episode. No additional remarks from the participants are given on the page. The page places the episode alongside other recent Gray Area installments, including discussions of the gender divide, the Cornell case and trauma as a status symbol, and it links to a related book event with Daniel A. Cox on Generation Uncoupled. The articles do not say what happens next in the race itself or what any company or regulator plans to do. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Philosopher Matthew Parish argues that minds may create heaven and that AI advances support dualism
stories.Summary:
The Lviv Herald published an article by Matthew Parish on Tuesday 17 November 2026 arguing that heaven may be what we make of it. Parish wrote that the afterlife, should there be one, is not a place to which we travel but a condition of existence that our own minds bring into being. He said the traditional theological question of what heaven looks like may be misconceived. He argued that heaven might look different to everyone because the human mind is itself the architect of experience. He said some of the strongest reasons for contemplating this arise from recent advances in artificial intelligence.

Parish cited the eighteenth-century German philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that the human mind actively structures the way the world appears to us. For Kant, space and time are forms of human intuition, and causation, substance and other fundamental concepts are categories through which the understanding organises experience. Parish said we cannot step outside our minds to inspect the universe as it might appear to a being whose faculties are entirely different from our own. He asked whether consciousness that survives bodily death must continue to experience space, time and causation as we presently understand them. He said heaven could be a radically different mode of consciousness in which the organising principles of experience have been transformed.

Parish said the development of large language models has made him increasingly sympathetic to dualism, the proposition most famously associated with René Descartes that mind and matter are fundamentally distinct. He said he does not suggest artificial intelligence has demonstrated the truth of Cartesian dualism, still less that we have discovered experimental evidence for an immortal soul. He said a large language model may discuss the poetry of Shakespeare, explain the metaphysics of Aristotle, analyse the emotional consequences of bereavement and compose an apparently moving meditation upon eternal life. He said such a system can do all these things without possessing a human body, human memories or a human biography.

He said there is no universally accepted scientific test for subjective experience and that the possibility of machine consciousness remains a serious philosophical question. Parish said physical explanations can describe neural activity, information processing and behavioural responses but cannot explain why any of this should be accompanied by the inward quality of experience. He said the explanatory gap remains and that the possibility consciousness constitutes a fundamental feature of reality rather than an incidental product of matter deserves renewed attention. He said a materialist may reasonably argue that consciousness emerges from certain forms of physical organisation, whether biological or artificial.

He said that if consciousness is in some meaningful sense distinct from the physical mechanisms through which it ordinarily operates, then bodily death need not logically entail its extinction. He said we would still require an explanation of how consciousness persists and what preserves personal identity. Parish said Christianity traditionally understands heaven not merely as the satisfaction of subjective preferences but as communion with God. He said the Christian conception of salvation presupposes that human desires may be mistaken, disordered or incomplete.

He said Saint Augustine understood human restlessness as a consequence of our incomplete orientation towards God. He said Dante's vision of the afterlife connects the condition of the soul with the structure of its desires. He said the damned are not merely punished by externally imposed torments but are, in significant measure, imprisoned by their own condition. More to follow.

stories.Headline: ArisGlobal caches shared prompt prefixes on Amazon Bedrock to cut inference costs and latency
stories.Summary:
ArisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology, developed NavaX, an AI engine built on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal productionized its first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic's Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal's internal production telemetry, the system has processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments. It has handled billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching.

As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months. Over that period the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens. Per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%. NavaX's Dynamic Data Extraction agent extracts around 130 fields, and source documents are often 10 to 200 pages. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request, and for Claude Sonnet 4.5 the minimum prefix size is 1,024 tokens.

ArisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request, which left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth. ArisGlobal uses one explicit checkpoint immediately after the shared prompt prefix, which is sent first. The per-case document follows the checkpoint and is processed on each request. ArisGlobal gave up limited document reuse within one case and gained prompt reuse across the fleet.

In production, 65% of input tokens on a typical request are served from the shared prompt cache. Caching the shared prompt prefix produced up to 25% lower end-to-end latency on cached production requests. It produced approximately 50% lower effective input cost and approximately 40% lower overall monthly inference spend at more than 19 billion tokens per month. Around 15% more enterprise tenants were onboarded without proportional cost increases, and EU geographic routing remained unchanged.

For most active accounts, cases arrive about every 5 minutes per tenant and multiple tenants run concurrently. ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue. The entire system runs on AWS.

LifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal's AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. Because case content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment, drawing on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. The default cache TTL is 5 minutes, and select models support a 1-hour TTL by setting "ttl": "1h". Longer-TTL entries must precede shorter-TTL entries.

ArisGlobal advises caching what repeats rather than what is largest, and placing stable content first. For sporadic traffic, ArisGlobal suggests evaluating the 1-hour TTL on supported models. Model availability varies by Region. All performance and cost figures reflect ArisGlobal's production metrics as reported to AWS, and results will vary based on prompt structure, traffic patterns, and cache hit rates.

stories.Headline: USD 435 approves guidelines for safe AI use by teachers and students
stories.Summary:
USD 435 has established guidelines for how teachers and students can use artificial intelligence safely and effectively, as AI becomes an increasingly common tool in education. Assistant Superintendent Rick Rivera presented the district's proposed acceptable use guidance for artificial intelligence to the Board of Education during its Nov. 9 meeting. The board later approved the guidelines. The guidelines are intended to establish expectations for AI use by both staff and students. They are also meant to protect student privacy and ensure compliance with state and federal regulations.

The guidance recognizes that AI can be used in several ways in the classroom. Teachers may choose to prohibit its use on a particular assignment, allow limited assistance, or encourage students to use it as a brainstorming partner. The district plans to provide professional development for teachers interested in incorporating AI into their instruction. Administrators have already begun evaluating platforms designed specifically for educational use, including School AI and MagicSchool, with particular attention to student safety and data protection. The evaluation process includes reviewing whether platforms meet federal requirements for student privacy and online safety, including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), and the Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA).

Rivera emphasized that AI should be viewed as a tool to enhance instruction, not replace teachers or the critical thinking skills students need to develop. He compared the technology to using a navigation app when planning a road trip, saying the driver remains in control of the vehicle and makes the final decisions. He said AI "just gives us that information." Rivera said School AI, one of the platforms administrators have explored, uses servers located in the United States and has safeguards designed to filter information before it reaches students. The platform also provides teachers with information about student interactions, including questions being asked and potentially inappropriate content.

During an evaluation exercise, administrators were asked to try to get the system to produce inappropriate responses. Rivera said he asked administrators to type something in that would possibly have a student land back in their office because of what they did. He said the platform redirected those requests and provided feedback to teachers about student activity. Not only did it flag it, it sent him an email about what the person did. Rivera said School AI does not use student data to train its models and believed MagicSchool has a similar policy.

Board members discussed the importance of providing training for both teachers and students, noting that some educators may already be using AI but feel uncertain about discussing it openly. The board raised questions about parental notification and consent, as well as whether information entered by students could be used to train AI models. Rivera said the district would share its guidelines and information about any selected platforms with parents. He said the acceptable use guidance would provide a foundation for staff training and help teachers understand which tools are appropriate for classroom assignments. Rivera said any platform used for student assignments would go through an approval process to ensure it meets district technology and safety requirements.

The list of AI platforms included in the district's evaluation is not intended to be exhaustive. Because the technology changes rapidly, the list may be updated as additional tools are reviewed. Rivera said "AI is not a human" and "AI makes mistakes." He stressed that students must continue to check the information they receive and rely on their own judgment and critical thinking. He said the goal is to use AI as a thought partner that can help students develop ideas and creativity without replacing human connection or decision-making.

stories.Headline: Bain analysts argue AI advantage comes from signals competitors cannot copy
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a Bain & Company report published on 17 November 2026 by Matthew Crupi, Sanjin Bicanic and John Hazan, arguing that competitive advantage from AI comes from signals competitors cannot copy. The report says AI advances fastest where a signal lets a company quickly and reliably check that the work is correct. It describes a mining company's capital projects team that spent an hour on a Monday afternoon setting up review of its most critical investment projects. By Tuesday morning, agents had reconciled tens of thousands of documents against cost and schedule data, and a first pass was on the table. The team then had to decide which of the problems the system flagged were real.

The report says work falls into three groups: work with a fast signal, structurally slow work, and a dangerous middle nobody has measured yet. It says companies move the frontier by building a proxy, encoding an expert's unwritten standard into a rubric, and using simulation to reproduce an environment and grade success. It cites Goodhart's Law, warning that once a proxy becomes the target it can drift. It says building a signal is slow and expensive, so it belongs where the work makes a company distinctive. It says durable advantage depends on owning the data, workflow and feedback loop that make the system improve with use.

The report cites a March 2026 cross-industry Bain survey of 196 respondents in which 91% said AI helps them be more productive and 53% reported higher-quality work. Only 27% said it helps them do new types of work. It says Anthropic reports that as agent-written code moved through its own organization, human review became the new limit. It says agentic AI concentrates judgment into four human responsibilities: intent, constraints, validation and stewardship. It says most failures it has seen were not AI model failures but traced back to one of these four responsibilities going unassigned.

The report says Stripe had to write down a rule that data from two unrelated customer contexts must not appear in the same analysis, even where one person is cleared to see both. It cites an experiment with 791 professionals at Procter & Gamble in which AI raised the quality of ideas generated and human judgment concentrated on selecting among them. It says stewardship takes roughly a third of the human effort in Bain's agentic work. It says OpenAI helped an accounting firm build a tax preparation agent, and the share of returns reaching a baseline quality threshold went from 25% to 86% in six weeks. It cites an Anthropic survey of more than 500 technical leaders in the US in which 57% were running agents on multistage workflows but only 16% across processes spanning teams.

The report says Climate Corporation was a crop insurance start-up that built soil and climate measurement data across US farmland where almost none existed. It says Monsanto acquired Climate Corporation for about $930 million in 2013, and Bayer inherited it when it bought Monsanto in 2018. It says more than a decade later Bayer traces its current AI capability to that deal, and its CIO argues the data, not the model, is the part competitors cannot copy. It says lenders with no credit files built a proxy from mobile operator data, reading airtime top-up patterns as an indicator of who could repay, and a mobile credit-scoring industry formed around the score. It says reversibility sets the autonomy frontier: where errors can be caught and reversed, let the system run and audit the exceptions, and where they cannot, use the signal to accelerate review rather than remove it.

The report says AI separates output from expertise, so firms book productivity gains immediately while expertise losses arrive later and without warning. It says protecting human judgment requires companies to deliberately redesign both work and learning. It advises starting where the value is, testing the signal, and breaking one of the most important workflows into tasks because the frontier runs inside a workflow rather than around it. It advises deploying where results are already checkable and not pouring agents into work no one can grade. The articles leave open how companies should build signals where none yet exist and how the expertise losses will be detected before they surface.

Articles.Title: Everyone Has AI. Advantage Comes from What You Build Around It

stories.Headline: FDA adopts super intelligence as its official term for AI across communications and documents
stories.Summary:
The US Food and Drug Administration announced on Monday, 17 November 2026, that it will use the term “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in all official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports and policy documents. The agency said the shift was prompted by an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in September, which directs all executive departments and federal agencies to make the change. The FDA said the term change will not affect existing guidance documents, regulations, Federal Register notices and other previously issued FDA documents. The agency also said that where a statute or regulation uses “artificial intelligence” or “AI”, the FDA will continue to quote and cite those terms as written.

The executive order applies only to executive branch agencies and does not affect private industry, Sydney White, an attorney with Wiley Rein LLP, told Focus, which means pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers will not need to make the terminology change. White noted that private-sector organizations could be affected if any of the order’s directives are enacted into law. According to the order, the term “AI” is considered outdated, and “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies. The order directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to provide the President with proposed legislative language that defines “Super Intelligence” within 60 days of the order.

Christina Silcox, the research director for digital health at the Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy, told Focus that she would consider this more of a semantic change than a meaningful change, because neither artificial intelligence nor super intelligence have particularly strong definitions. Silcox expressed concern that using the term “super intelligence” to describe all clinical and clinical-adjacent AI-enabled tasks might lead to an over-reliance on the results by clinicians and patients. She emphasized that health systems with effective governance should ensure that users understand what each specific AI tool does, when it should be used, and how to interpret and act on the results. The FDA said it will make conforming edits to its public-facing documents as part of each document’s next substantive revision and update web content on its regular maintenance cycle.

Articles.Title: FDA to refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ going forward

stories.Headline: North Dakota student senators pass bills on AI and technology use in schools
stories.Summary:
Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol. The students met on Monday and Tuesday to form committees, subcommittees, debate and vote on both topics as bill drafts were created from their work. The summit took place on Nov. 17, 2026, according to photo captions by Michael Achterling of the North Dakota Monitor. Students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January. The bills will be made available to state lawmakers as they begin the 2027 legislative session Jan. 5.

The bill outlining rules for artificial intelligence use in schools passed on a 40-8 vote. It would allow students to use artificial intelligence tools beginning in ninth grade, unless under the direction of a teacher during classroom instruction, but would not allow students to use the tools to complete assignments. The bill would require teachers to list when AI use is permitted and not permitted as part of course instruction. Teachers would not be able to use AI to input grades into a gradebook or assign final grades, but they can use AI tools to assist with grading assignments and to create lesson plans. A bill regulating the use of technology during the school day was approved on a 47-0 vote, requiring school districts to use technology as a support to learning and not a replacement for essential instruction, in a manner reasonably suited to a student's academic level, age, accessibility needs, and educational circumstances.

Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier said one of his favorite units as a state government teacher was the mock Congress and he thought he could recreate that type of environment at the Capitol with high school students. Bachmeier said he genuinely appreciated and learned so much from the students, and that hearing from thoughtful and passionate young people helped develop his thinking. He said the goals of the summit were to expose student leaders to the legislative process and to give the student perspective on issues state lawmakers may need to grapple with. Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, said the students are smart and engaged, and that she hopes they will stay involved and come back to Bismarck to sit with their representatives during the regular legislative session.

Hogan said the seeds are being planted to have good public servants and there is a whole Senate full of them right now. Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School in West Fargo, said there was a lot of debate, not heated discussion but respectful discussion around topics that truly matter. Said said it was a unique experience and he believes the students did a good job putting their viewpoints into the summit's bill drafts, and he hopes state lawmakers take their opinions to heart. He said parents and students do actually have a voice and their voices should matter, especially with AI that changes how education is viewed and how education is operated.

Kierstin Hurtt, superintendent of Valley-Edinburgh School District and parent of one of the participating students, said she was watching the next generation of engaged leaders in North Dakota in real time, calling it inspiring, hopeful and massive. Hurtt said she was impressed that students were asking each other for clarity on their different points of view and opinions, and she hopes student senators will be able to use the voting board and the proceedings will be live-streamed in the future. Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, said it is good for students to interact with others from across the state and that expressing viewpoints constructively on complicated topics is an important skill to learn. Kramer said he thinks the bills being talked about should be pushed into the legislative session and talked about there.

He said the committee work and debating with other students inspired him to consider running for public office. Thomas Unser, a student at West Fargo High School, and Hazel Albert, a student from Hope-Page High School, also spoke on the Senate floor during the summit, according to photo captions. The North Dakota Monitor is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Review authors say AI advances antibiotic discovery and design across five areas
stories.Summary:
Antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections cause more than 1 million deaths worldwide each year, according to a Review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology on 17 November 2026. The Review focuses on recent advances in small-molecule antibiotic discovery enabled by artificial intelligence. It presents innovative approaches that are substantially increasing the size and diversity of the explored chemical space. It highlights recent artificial intelligence-driven advancements in phenotypic antibiotic discovery, mechanism of action elucidation, target-based discovery, de novo molecular design and lead optimization. The authors say these promise to expand the repertoire of antibacterial agents and uncover bacterial pathways and vulnerabilities amenable to therapeutic intervention.

The Review states there is a critical need for new classes of antibiotics, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action. It cites a 2022 Lancet analysis by the Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators on the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019, published in volume 399, pages 629 to 655. It cites a 2024 Lancet analysis by Naghavi and colleagues on the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2050, in volume 404, pages 1199 to 1226. It cites a 2024 report from the EcoAMR Series by McDonnell and colleagues on forecasting the economic impacts of antimicrobial resistance in humans, from WOAH and the World Bank. The Review is a preview of subscription content, with access through an institution or a Nature+ online-access subscription at $39.99 for 30 days.

A journal subscription gives 12 print issues and online access for $259.00 per year, or $21.58 per issue. The article can be purchased on SpringerLink for USD 39.95, with prices subject to local taxes calculated during checkout. The Review includes five figures, on strategies for systematically exploring small-molecule chemical space, a workflow for machine learning-guided antibacterial hit identification based on phenotypic screens, experimental approaches for mechanism of action characterization, a structure-based drug discovery pipeline for target identification and hit validation with associated challenges, and multimodal design of antibiotics for lead optimization and candidate progression. The reference list includes Levy's 1992 book The Antibiotic Paradox, published by Springer, and Silver's 2011 paper on challenges of antibacterial discovery in Clinical Microbiology Reviews, volume 24, pages 71 to 109. It includes Walsh's 2003 paper in Nature Reviews Microbiology, volume 1, pages 65 to 70, asking where new antibiotics will come from.

It includes Stover and colleagues' 2000 paper in Nature, volume 405, pages 962 to 966, on a small-molecule nitroimidazopyran drug candidate for tuberculosis. It includes Eyal and colleagues' 2016 paper in Scientific Reports, volume 6, article 39004, on a novel pleuromutilin antibacterial compound, its binding mode and selectivity mechanism. The references also include Miller and colleagues' 2008 paper in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, volume 52, pages 2806 to 2812, on discovery and characterization of QPT-1, the progenitor of a new class of bacterial topoisomerase inhibitors. They include Bax and colleagues' 2010 paper in Nature, volume 466, pages 935 to 940, on type IIA topoisomerase inhibition by a new class of antibacterial agents. They include Yao and colleagues' 2026 paper in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, volume 70, e01706-25, on stepwise evolution and clonal enrichment of gepotidacin resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

They include Mukherjee and colleagues' 2026 paper in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, volume 234, pages e131 to e140, on genetic background modulating zoliflodacin and gepotidacin cross-resistance and fitness in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Further references include Wan, Wong, Collins and de la Fuente-Nunez's 2024 paper in Nature Reviews Bioengineering, volume 2, pages 392 to 407, on machine learning for antimicrobial peptide identification and design. They include Martins and colleagues' 2026 scoping review in Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, volume 179, article 103461, on artificial intelligence in drug discovery for fungal diseases. They include Fu and colleagues' 2021 paper in Nature Communications, volume 12, article 6497, on leveraging machine learning essentiality predictions and chemogenomic interactions to identify antifungal targets. They include Wensing and colleagues' 2026 paper in Nature Microbiology, volume 11, pages 2157 to 2169, on pooled CRISPRi screening revealing fungal-specific drug target candidates.

The references further include Behsaz and colleagues' 2026 paper in Cell Reports Methods, volume 6, article 101510, on a large-scale discovery platform enabling identification of peptides targeting drug-resistant candidiasis. They include Pitt and colleagues' 2025 paper in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, volume 68, pages 851 to 859, on real-world applications and experiences of AI/ML deployment for drug discovery. They include Bender and colleagues' 2026 paper in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, volume 25, pages 855 to 876, on artificial intelligence in drug discovery, what it is, where we stand and the path forward. They include Hutchings, Truman and Wilkinson's 2019 paper in Current Opinion in Microbiology, volume 51, pages 72 to 80, on antibiotics past, present and future. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Unesco and CodeAI host an online AI workshop for Latin American teachers on 19 November 2026

It focuses on the AI for Oceans activity from CodeAI, where teachers train a machine learning model by classifying images of fish and marine waste. This process allows educators to observe how systems make decisions and identify potential errors or biases without needing prior programming knowledge. The workshop aligns with the UNESCO AI competency framework for teachers to promote a human-centred and ethical pedagogical approach.

The organizers are responsible for providing teaching resources and guidance on adapting these activities to various educational levels and subjects. They stated that the goal is to help teachers replicate these experiences with their own students during Hour of AI activities in December 2026. This initiative seeks to strengthen digital competencies and foster a critical understanding of responsible technology integration. Product launches that harden AI agents and expand Falcon's use cases support the platform and Flex model thesis, while keeping pressure on execution and margin delivery that the Narrative flags as risks.

stories.Headline: New Florida Legislative Leaders Pledge Property Tax Relief, AI Oversight After Election Certification
stories.Summary:
Florida’s new legislative leaders took the gavel on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, after state election officials formally certified the November election results, and both chambers unanimously chose their presiding officers in Tallahassee. The House elected Clay County Republican Sam Garrison as Speaker, and the Senate elected Manatee County Republican Jim Boyd as Senate President. Governor-elect Byron Donalds attended the swearing-in ceremony ahead of his inauguration in January. The organizational session coincided with the Elections Canvassing Commission certifying the general election outcomes. Certified results confirmed victories for Donalds in the governor’s race, Republicans in every state Cabinet race, and Ashley Moody in the U.S. Senate race, while Democrats won majorities in both chambers of the U.S. Congress and Republicans retained control of Florida’s statewide offices and legislative branches.

At the center of the upcoming work is Amendment 3, a constitutional amendment approved by nearly 62 percent of Florida voters, which raises the state’s non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 next year and to $250,000 in 2028. Boyd said lawmakers will establish a framework allowing local governments to provide additional property tax relief, and he said the Senate will keep working to expand choices and lower rates in the property insurance market while keeping education and workforce training aligned with available jobs. Garrison called Amendment 3 both the single most transformative property tax reform in state history and the biggest fiscal challenge Florida has faced in a generation, and he cautioned that offsetting the lost local and state revenue across counties from Dixie to Duval and Miami-Dade will take time. He said his priorities as Speaker are a strong economy, safe streets, and quality schools, and he announced a new Advanced Technology and Digital Security Committee plus a reinstated House Public Integrity Committee. Criticizing Congress for failing to pass federal regulations on artificial intelligence, Garrison said it is time for Florida to lead on the issue.

Republicans maintained a 20-to-8 majority in Florida’s congressional delegation, a 25-member majority in the state Senate, and a 70-to-50 majority in the state House. Boyd framed the Amendment 3 vote as a directive from residents struggling with the cost of housing, utilities, fuel, childcare, and groceries, saying families have made hard adjustments and expect government to do the same. Garrison, describing himself as someone who never met a tax he didn’t want to cut, said the laws of economics remain undefeated and there is still no such thing as a free lunch, adding that failure is not an option. Both leaders signaled close cooperation with the incoming executive branch as Governor Ron DeSantis prepares to leave office, and Garrison said it is his responsibility to help make Donalds the most successful governor in the United States. Lawmakers return to Tallahassee when the regular legislative session begins on March 2.

stories.Headline: CommBank releases CodeCheck to help Australian businesses find software vulnerabilities with AI
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Bank of Australia launched a new cyber security tool and AI harness called CodeCheck on 17 November 2026, designed to help Australian businesses identify potential vulnerabilities in their online systems, and it is available for Australian businesses to download from that day. The launch came as global websites run by at least 178 major organisations were hit by a suspected malware attack overnight, with affected sites including Zoom, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, Ikea and the BBC, and Vodafone Australia, ASOS, Levi's Australia and HSBC Australia also identified as compromised. The banking and finance industry was hit hardest in the attack, with 32 organisations affected across the globe, and according to reports the attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely, a website-testing platform, then planted code designed to steal payment data, hijack crypto payments and target older iPhones. While the Australian arm of HSBC was hit in the alleged attack, CBA's website was not.

CodeCheck, developed by CBA security engineers, gives businesses an AI-enabled approach to software security that draws on the bank's own method, and it is specifically designed for businesses that write their own code using OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code. The tool will guide the AI through analysing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers assess each finding, and CBA said businesses can advise what information to share with the AI so it better understands the code and makes more appropriate assessments, though engineers remain responsible for reviewing the findings and determining what action is required. In 2025-26 the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre proactively notified organisations of potential malicious threats and activity more than 4,400 times, an increase of 80 per cent on the previous year, according to the ASD's latest Annual Cyber Threat Report. The ASD said it expects AI-driven tools to compress significantly the window for vulnerability exploitation, which mostly occurs within two weeks of a patch or mitigation advice being released, and it has already found instances where some vulnerabilities were successfully exploited within 48 hours.

CommBank Chief Security Officer Nicola Nicol said cyber security is a shared challenge and strengthening Australia's cyber resilience requires everyone to play a part, and that as cyber criminals increasingly use AI, AI also needs to be put to work on the defensive side. Nicol said that with thousands of engineers working across systems powered by around 2.5 billion lines of code, the bank has seen first-hand how AI can help identify potential vulnerabilities earlier, that it built the capability to strengthen its own defences, and that by making CodeCheck freely available it wants to share what it has learned and help more Australian businesses use AI to strengthen theirs. ASD Director-General Abigail Bradshaw said AI tools are needed to help automate defences and stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers, and that accelerating the modernisation of Australia's technology and cyber security foundations is critical to protecting the systems relied on every day. Bradshaw said giving businesses practical ways to identify potential vulnerabilities earlier and build security into software from the outset supports that effort.

stories.Headline: UAE joins US and eight others in signing San Francisco Declaration on AI safety
stories.Summary:
On Monday, the UAE joined the US and eight other countries in signing the San Francisco Declaration, which commits them to protect sensitive technologies and the critical infrastructure that underpins artificial intelligence systems. The declaration also focuses on safeguarding supply chains, software and knowledge, and it serves as a reminder that AI development cannot be left to tech companies and markets alone. The UAE has been expanding its ambitions in this field, and the editorial argues that a multi-pronged and multinational approach to regulation will be essential. This approach, it says, should ensure that innovation, while crucial, does not get too far ahead of responsibility. The UAE has made several other commitments, including signing the Children First Declaration at the annual Paris Peace Forum last week, which aims to protect minors from untested AI models.

In 2024, it was invited to join 49 other countries in the Hiroshima AI Process Friends Group, which is tasked with promoting safe, secure and trustworthy AI. The country has also adopted key global governance and management frameworks as part of its domestic and international alignment on AI safety and risk management. The editorial says these commitments reflect the breadth of the challenge, because AI has implications for national security, economic resilience, privacy, education, child development and the integrity of public institutions, each requiring a different set of protections. The urgency is reinforced by the extraordinary amounts of money being invested in the industry, including Anthropic's much-anticipated stock market debut this week at a valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Anthropic's prospectus has acknowledged risks ranging from cyberattacks and biological weapons to the possibility of powerful systems escaping human control, while uncertainty surrounding Nvidia, a significant supplier of advanced AI chips, has exposed the volatility of the industry's financial exuberance.

The editorial argues that regulation should be nuanced enough to encourage research and investment while establishing clear boundaries around high-risk applications, which means rigorous testing, independent safety assessments, protections for children and safeguards against cyber and biological threats. It points to Abu Dhabi's recent agreements with OpenAI as showing how adoption can be accompanied by traceability and human accountability, and it cites OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman saying during his visit to the capital earlier this month that there is no room for debate over human control of AI. The editorial says the recent declarations in San Francisco and Paris are vital contributions to the global effort to establish shared principles, because neither AI's benefits nor its risks will be confined by national borders or single-nation regulations. It says the task now for the countries involved, and eventually the international community as a whole, is to turn such commitments into coherent rules and meaningful oversight.

stories.Headline: UBS warns AI agents may disrupt internet business models as Ermotti outlines bank AI plans
stories.Summary:
UBS Group warned on 17 November 2026 that AI agents could materially disrupt the traditional internet business model that supports digital advertising and enterprise software revenues, and chief executive Sergio Ermotti laid out the bank's own AI plans at the same time. Those plans focus on product upgrades, efficiency gains and new client offerings tied to the technology, according to the article. Ermotti also flagged potential risks from U.S. political uncertainty as UBS evaluates how AI driven changes might affect broader economic conditions. The article describes UBS as a CHF118.4b wealth manager and bank in the capital markets industry, and it says the firm is using its global advisory and financing role to test how AI agents might alter client workflows, product delivery and demand for traditional internet based services.

The article ties the AI agent focus to UBS's wider effort to turn the Credit Suisse integration and heavy digital spend into a leaner, higher return wealth and banking platform. It says continued investment in AI tools and digital platforms already used by a large share of front office teams, alongside digital distribution channels in Asia, can improve adviser productivity and client experience. The article points to a CHF44.87 fair value for UBS Group and says the push speaks to the view that UBS can extract more value from its fee base through productivity gains and a lower cost per client. It also says the strategy sharpens the firm's advisory pitch versus peers such as Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, particularly for clients seeking guidance on which internet and software models could face pressure.

The article names the flipside as well, saying that if AI agents significantly accelerate a shift away from eyeball-based internet models, fee pools in parts of asset management and digital distribution could become less predictable. It adds that tighter Swiss capital rules and U.S. political risk related to AI infrastructure buildouts increase execution risk for the technology-focused strategy. The article says the same AI story can appear either as a productivity upgrade or as a new layer of uncertainty, depending on which narrative investors already lean toward. It notes that its analysis does not cover who is steering those calls or how their pay aligns with investor interests, and it states the piece was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St.

stories.Headline: Fei-Fei Li warns that high compute and data costs price public sector and universities out of frontier AI research
stories.Summary:
Stanford University Professor Fei-Fei Li warned on November 18, 2026, that public sector entities and academic institutions are being priced out of frontier artificial intelligence research. The co-director of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI argued that the massive costs of compute and data are creating a divide in the research landscape. She noted that the scale of infrastructure needed to train foundation models now exceeds the traditional budget capacities of public research agencies. This shift follows a period of rapid progress led by well-funded private corporations that set the benchmarks for performance.

The current situation requires thousands of H100 or next-generation GPUs, which can cost hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars for top-tier training runs. Researchers also face the prohibitive cost of acquiring high-quality proprietary datasets that are dominated by private firms through vertical integration. Furthermore, private companies offer massive salary premiums that draw top talent away from academic labs and hollow out the research pipeline. These barriers force academic researchers to depend on private partnerships, which may create conflicts regarding transparency and the overall research agenda.

Fei-Fei Li stated that the centralization of AI research power is a core issue that threatens the objectivity of scientific inquiry. She suggested that the reliance on private sector partnerships could stifle long-term exploratory research and limit the role of academia. The Association of American Universities added that universities risk falling behind in critical technology without significant increases in federal funding for infrastructure. Other stakeholders have called for a National AI Research Resource in the United States to democratize access to necessary compute power.

This crisis is the culmination of several years of expansion where the field shifted toward massive foundation models. Academic labs were previously at the forefront of innovation, but capital requirements for compute infrastructure have since grown exponentially. Federal agencies and policy bodies are now debating the next phase of initiatives to address these critical access gaps. Reports and policy recommendations from the National Science Foundation and the OSTP are expected in the coming year to outline sustainable paths for academic access.

stories.Headline: Reese Cooper accuses SSENSE of using AI images that misrepresent his designs
stories.Summary:
Designer Reese Cooper criticized the Montreal retailer SSENSE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, for using artificial intelligence to create product images. He shared a series of Instagram Story posts pointing out rendering errors and inconsistent garment details in the digital imagery. Cooper claimed that these AI generated visuals misrepresent his actual designs and create a disappointing experience for creators. He expressed concern that customers would blame his brand rather than the retailer when orders do not match the website. The designer also questioned the fate of the professional photographers and stylists who previously worked at the company.

This public dispute follows a series of corporate changes involving CEO Rami Atallah and his brothers, Firas and Bassel. In February, the Superior Court of Quebec authorized an agreement allowing the brothers to reclaim ownership of the business from creditor protection. During a company meeting in April, Atallah stated that the firm would embed AI into its DNA to transform core functions. By June, reports indicated that SSENSE had dismissed approximately a dozen creative staff members from the cosmetics, retouching, and photo departments. The company shifted its strategy to superimpose garment images from mannequins onto the images of professional models.

Chief commercial officer Christine Sio stated that the company is evolving its content production to increase scalability, agility, and speed. A spokesperson for the retailer further explained that the new studio operating model aims to accelerate production and strengthen product storytelling. These official statements contrast with the views of a former photographer who described the technical process of using AI for model imagery. Cooper argued that the resulting work is low quality and lacks the consistency provided by human oversight. He specifically noted that certain details, such as tape on a shirt, disappeared in the AI versions.

The retailer continues to implement these automated systems to replace traditional in house photography and retouching workflows. This transition has sparked a larger conversation about the role of human creativity in the fashion industry's digital presence. While the company views the shift as a necessary evolution for efficiency, designers like Cooper fear the loss of artistic integrity. The conflict highlights the tension between corporate cost cutting measures and the precise representation of luxury design. It remains unclear if the retailer will adjust its AI processes to satisfy the concerns of its brand partners.

stories.Headline: Supermicro cofounder Yi-Shyan Liaw seeks to dismiss US charges for diverting AI chips to China

It also asks the judge to evaluate whether the prosecution provided enough evidence to support the charges of chip diversion. They claim that the government failed to properly state an offense that would justify the ongoing criminal proceedings. The defense maintains that the location of the trial is incorrect and should be changed or dismissed entirely. These representatives are attempting to prove that the prosecution lacks the necessary legal grounds to continue the case. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Multilingual by Design awards $1.05m to three teams piloting AI tools for multilingual teaching
stories.Summary:
Multilingual by Design awarded three grants totaling $1.05 million to teams developing AI tools for multilingual teaching, the organization announced on 18 November 2026. Teams led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop and DSST Public Schools will each receive $350,000. Their pilots are planned for 2026, 27 and will involve teachers and schools in Wisconsin, Massachusetts and Colorado. The projects address following small-group math conversations, preparing accessible versions of existing materials and adapting math lessons to students' English proficiency. Teachers will decide how the tools are used, review their outputs and retain control of instruction.

The Wisconsin team is developing Content and Language with AI, or CLAI, to give teachers a live view of students' small-group math discussions. The project brings together The Responsible AI for Learning (TRAIL) Lab, the Multilingual Learning Research Center and the WIDA Consortium, all at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. CLAI builds on real-time transcription and translation and is designed to identify students' use of mathematical concepts, connections to experiences from home and moments when they may need help. Six teachers in rural, suburban and urban Wisconsin school districts will pilot the tool. Organizers say students will control their own audio recordings, which will be stored locally and remain under district control.

In Massachusetts, the Joan Ganz Cooney Center and Medley Learning will develop Medley Studio, a tool for adapting materials that teachers already use. The planned supports include dividing text into shorter sections and adding definitions within the material, with recommendations matched to students' language proficiency. Teachers will be able to review and customize those supports before exporting or printing materials. The pilot will focus on five schools in Taunton, aiming to reduce preparation time while maintaining access to grade-level instruction. Medley's existing product is a browser extension that adds vocabulary support, translation and other scaffolds to classroom content, and the funding announcement puts the company's existing reach at 12,000 students across 48 school systems.

In Colorado, DSST Public Schools and Scale Up Partners will develop Premo, which uses AI to help teachers plan and adapt grade-level math lessons. Premo is intended to align lessons with established English language development frameworks and suggest teaching strategies and supports matched to individual students' English proficiency. Testing will take place within DSST's network of 16 public middle and high schools in Denver and Aurora. According to the announcement, more than 65% of students across the network are current or former multilingual learners. The work focuses on helping students engage with math content while developing the language needed to discuss and understand it.

Throughline Learning, a Providence-based education nonprofit, will provide technical assistance and lead research across the pilots. Teams will use a common set of measures to examine how the tools work for teachers and students, with outcomes ranging from classroom discussion to student achievement. The initiative's partner information also identifies ETS as a research partner. Before testing begins, Throughline will help teams establish their intended outcomes and data plans, with findings later developed into case studies and public resources. Each team will pilot under data-sharing agreements with its partner schools, and alongside the grants, teams will receive coaching and support for bringing their tools to schools beyond the initial pilot sites.

Multilingual by Design launched in March 2026 and is managed by Social Strategy Associates. Its open call attracted more than 180 applications from education nonprofits and AI builders, and thirty organizations attended a June workshop in Washington, D.C., where teachers described challenges in supporting multilingual learners. The initiative is supported by the Bezos Family Foundation, Gary Community Ventures, the Gates Foundation, the Hewlett Foundation, the Robertson Foundation and Sobrato Philanthropies. National Center for Education Statistics data for 2020, 21 show that 67.3% of U.S. public school teachers taught at least one English learner. Multilingual by Design plans to share findings from the funded pilots with educators, developers and funders as the projects progress through development and classroom testing.

stories.Headline: European data protection authorities examine AI candidate screening in 2027 enforcement action
stories.Summary:
Europe's data protection authorities will spend part of 2027 examining how organisations use automated tools, including AI systems, to screen job candidates. The European Data Protection Board said on November 11, 2026 that the topic of its sixth coordinated enforcement action will be automated decision-making in recruitment. The same plenary in Brussels produced two other outputs. The board adopted Statement 2/2026 on the first review of the European Union's adequacy decision for the Republic of Korea, dated November 10, 2026. It approved the final version of its recommendations on processor binding corporate rules, known as BCR-P, after a public consultation that closed in March.

The action will concern automated decision-making, including AI-driven ADM, in recruitment, according to the EDPB. More specifically, it will focus on enforcement of the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and the related right of access, in the context of automated candidate screening tools, including AI-driven ones. DPAs will join this action on a voluntary basis in the coming weeks, and the action itself will be launched in the course of 2027, according to the EDPB. The board did not say which authorities proposed the topic, how many have already committed, whether the action will use questionnaires or formal investigations, or whether it will target employers, recruitment agencies, software vendors or all three. The wording is narrow, concerning screening and two specific rights attached to that stage, rather than AI in employment generally or the management of existing staff.

The Coordinated Enforcement Framework was developed as part of the EDPB's 2021-2023 strategy, according to the board's CEF page. Every year, EDPB members submit proposals for the topic of the next annual action, and all EDPB members vote on the topic at a plenary meeting. National data protection authorities decide whether to take part, on a voluntary basis, through fact-finding exercises, new formal investigations, follow-up of ongoing formal investigations, or a combination. The authority that proposed the topic coordinates the action with assistance from the EDPB Secretariat, and a questionnaire or audit guide is built. All participating authorities launch the action at the same time, each drafts a national report, and the coordinators then produce an EDPB report adopted at a plenary.

The 2027 action will be the sixth. The first covered use of cloud-based services by the public sector in 2022, the second the designation and position of data protection officers in 2023, the third implementation of the right of access by controllers in 2024, and the fourth implementation of the right to erasure by controllers in 2025. The fifth, compliance with transparency and information obligations under Articles 12, 13 and 14 GDPR, was selected on October 14, 2025, with a launch during 2026. The right to erasure action involved 32 data protection authorities and 764 controllers that responded, according to PPC Land's coverage of the EDPB annual report, and its February 2026 report closed with non-binding recommendations. France's CNIL later fined consulting firm EXTIA 300,000 euros after an inspection carried out within that same coordinated action, finding that 204 of 265 deletion requests received in 2024 were not processed, not answered, or answered months late, in a deliberation adopted on July 21, 2026 and published on September 9, 2026.

The EDPB gave no reasons for its choice. On August 21, 2026, the Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens fined Uber 824,990,000 euros after finding that software had deactivated driver accounts from 2018 to 2022 following fraud flags or persistently low ratings, with no human review, and Uber has appealed. Spain's Royal Decree 723/2026, in force since October 5, 2026, requires employers to tell staff in writing about workplace algorithms that affect pay, hours, tasks, promotion, place of work or termination. The Spanish data protection authority, the AEPD, issued a warning, reference AI-00009-2026, over a resume-screening tool that had not yet been deployed, finding that the formal presence of a person in the process did not by itself take the decision outside Article 22. Austria's Federal Administrative Court ruled in September 2025 that the public employment service's AMAS job-seeker classification system did not breach Article 22, because advisers could override the score, while Germany's Federal Court of Justice, on October 21, 2026, held in four SCHUFA judgments that calculating a probability value about a person can itself be a decision under Article 22(1).

Under the provisional agreement reached on May 7, 2026, Annex III high-risk systems, a category that includes employment screening, must comply by December 2, 2027, so the GDPR coordinated action will run in the same year that AI Act obligations for hiring systems are due to take effect. California approved SB 947 on September 30, 2026, which bars employers from relying solely on an automated decision system for discipline or termination from July 1, 2027, and in the United States the Mobley v. Workday case was expanded in July 2025 to cover applicants processed through HiredScore AI features. On December 17, 2021, the European Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/254, which found that the Republic of Korea ensures an adequate level of protection. The CEF page does not label the dates it shows, but they match the publication of each action's final report, and on that pattern a report on recruitment screening would arrive no earlier than late 2027 and more likely in 2028, although the EDPB has given no date.

Articles.Title: EDPB picks AI candidate screening as its 2027 enforcement target - PPC Land

stories.Headline: NASCIO report finds 46 states have named AI leaders but many lack staffing and policy authority
stories.Summary:
State governments have rapidly created dedicated leadership roles to oversee artificial intelligence, but many of those officials lack the staffing, funding and authority needed to manage the technology across agencies, according to a report the National Association of State Chief Information Officers published on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The report surveyed 33 states and territories to examine how governments are organizing AI leadership, developing governance policies and preparing employees to use the technology. NASCIO said that when it began tracking in 2023, less than 20 percent of states had a chief artificial intelligence officer or a similar title, and that just three years later at least 46 states have identified at least one person tasked with directing AI, with 25 states having someone with AI in their title. According to the report, 76 percent of survey respondents said they were the first person to hold their role as currently defined in their state, and most positions were established through a directive from the state CIO rather than legislation or an executive order.

The report found that AI leadership does not always come with the authority to set or enforce statewide policies, since while 72 percent of respondents said they have jurisdiction over all executive branch agencies, only 44 percent have the authority to independently establish enterprise AI policies and standards, another 16 percent share that responsibility with another entity, and just over half said they have the power to enforce compliance. Ninety-seven percent of respondents said their states have developed AI policies or guidance, 83 percent have created processes for agencies to submit proposed AI use cases for review, and roughly 75 percent cited the National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework, released in 2023, as their most commonly used governance model. Fifty-six percent of respondents said their states do not have dedicated AI budgets, and 75 percent identified insufficient staffing as one of their biggest challenges. The report also noted that Washington, D.C. became the first major U.S. city to mandate AI training for all employees and contractors in February, New York expanded its AI training resources to its entire workforce of more than 100,000 employees in April, and San José, California has trained over 1,000 municipal employees since 2024.

NASCIO recommended that states give AI leaders clearly defined authority, invest in dedicated staffing and sustainable funding, strengthen collaboration among technology, privacy and cybersecurity teams, and expand employee training, stating that full authority to establish and enforce enterprise AI standards would reduce agency and staff burden, increase interagency cooperation and unify agencies in the state. The report's findings build on NASCIO's 2026 State CIO Survey, which found that 78 percent of state CIOs now have an AI governance framework, up from 65 percent in 2025, and that AI ranked as the top technology priority among state CIOs for the first time this year. Looking ahead, 90 percent of respondents said agentic AI, which can complete tasks and take actions with less human involvement, would consume significantly more of their time over the next three years, with workforce transformation and scaling AI across agencies also major anticipated priorities. The report concluded that with the right foundation, states can navigate the evolving risks and challenges of AI while harnessing its potential to improve government operations and the services they provide to the public.

Articles.Title: As states move quickly to govern AI, dedicated oversight remains a challenge - StateScoop

stories.headline_source: As states move quickly to govern AI, dedicated oversight remains a challenge

stories.Headline: Puja Tayal suggests AI supply chain alternatives for investors following a decline in Nvidia stock
stories.Summary:
Puja Tayal wrote an article on November 17, 2026, about AI stocks for Canadians. She discussed how Nvidia stock has fallen 32 percent and pulled the Nasdaq 100 down 14.7 percent. The decline follows the departure of Jensen Huang and questions regarding the company's corporate governance. A ban on Nvidia chips to China also contributed to the current stock market downturn. Tayal suggests that investors diversify across the AI supply chain rather than focusing only on chips.

Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, and Celestica are mentioned as potential alternatives to Nvidia in the chip industry. AMD data centre chips and Google tensor processing units could take the place of Nvidia GPUs. Celestica helps Google manufacture these units, while Hammond Power Solutions supplies transformers for various power grids. Bird Construction is building AI data centres for BCE and reported a 13 billion dollar backlog. Shopify is developing AI tools for merchants and saw net profit rise 75 percent in late 2026.

Jensen Huang previously described artificial intelligence as a five layer cake consisting of energy, chips, and infrastructure. He also included models and software applications as the final two layers of this specific AI structure. Puja Tayal stated that performance matters most in AI and alternatives must prove their mettle to investors. She noted that Shopify will thrive in the software space with AI supporting the company's overall growth. Tayal believes the current dip in Hammond Power Solutions is an opportunity for investors to buy.

Investors hit hard by the Nvidia downturn are the primary people affected by these market shifts. Bird Construction is benefiting from booms in energy export infrastructure and nuclear power infrastructure alongside AI data centres. Shopify merchants are affected by new AI tools designed to help them target their audiences more efficiently. The Motley Fool Canada team identified ten top TSX stocks for 2026, but Nvidia was not included. They previously recommended MercadoLibre on January 8, 2014, which grew from 1,000 dollars to over 19,000 dollars.

Nvidia's dip is not related to the performance of its graphics processing units, but security concerns may persist. Bird Construction reported 36.7 percent revenue growth and 61 percent earnings per share growth in third quarter 2026. Shopify's strongest net profit growth occurred in the fourth quarter of 2024, when it surged by 97 percent. Hammond Power Solutions serves mining sites, transportation systems, commercial buildings, public infrastructure, data centres, and industrial hubs. The Motley Fool Canada reports an average return of 103 percent compared to 88 percent for the S&P/TSX.

Investors may now buy Bird Construction as it recovers from a dip that occurred in October 2026. The chip industry must provide alternatives as billions of dollars of AI infrastructure investment remain on the line. It remains a black box how much of Shopify's recent profit growth is attributed to its AI tools. The articles do not state if companies will actually pull back on buying Nvidia GPUs over security concerns. It is not clear if AMD or Google will successfully take the market share from Nvidia.
