stories.Headline: Microsoft 365 outage technical; phishing campaign exploited it
stories.Summary:
Microsoft confirmed that its November 12 Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a technical issue and not by a cyberattack, according to a SecurityWeek report. The disruption blocked access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook, and it may also have affected Teams, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft 365 Copilot. The company traced the failure to an earlier network capacity upgrade that a later network change exposed. Microsoft said it had fixed the underlying problem and was restoring services in stages to keep things stable.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence found that attackers used the disruption to run a phishing campaign against users. The fake emails posed as Microsoft 365 service health notices and referred to the real incident identifier EX1550543. Some messages falsely warned that emails held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient clicked a link to restore them. Subject lines began with the word Outage followed by a six-character code, and sender display names combined organisation-specific wording with Outage Notification or Service Health. Microsoft named moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com as the domains used to send these emails, and it said recipient-specific SendGrid tracking links redirected to reallifeaccounting[.]com.

Microsoft advised security teams to examine suspicious emails and links, to investigate any user clicks, and to review their Safe Links policies. The company also confirmed that its security products were blocking the campaign. The report did not say how many users received the phishing emails or whether anyone clicked the links before the messages were blocked. It also gave no details on when the phishing messages were first seen or how long the campaign lasted.

Articles.Title: Microsoft 365 outage technical; phishing campaign exploited it

stories.Headline: Harvey Nash lets non-IT staff build AI tools under guardrails, CIO Ankur Anand says
stories.Summary:
Harvey Nash has spent several months running an approach it calls Citizen AI, in which employees outside the IT department build their own AI tools, agents and prototypes inside clear guardrails, according to Group CIO Ankur Anand, who described the work in a case study published by Computing UK on 17 November 2026. The company says the method joins a growing group of businesses taking the same route, and it treats the effort as much as a way to build a culture of innovation as a technology programme. Anand said the aim is to put AI into the hands of the people who best understand Harvey Nash's clients, processes and business problems, and to let them experiment within defined limits. The article gives one worked example, in which a content manager built a content agent that lets recruitment consultants find approved posts and assets, personalise them to their role and tone, and publish them to their social channels.

The approach changes how ideas become systems at the firm. Anand said that turning an idea into a technology solution once required specialist skills, funding and space on a development roadmap, and that AI now lowers that barrier so people can test whether an idea solves a real problem before the organisation commits significant resources. The goal is not to create hundreds of unofficial production systems but to support experimentation, after which Technology takes a proven concept and makes it enterprise-ready by addressing architecture, security, data protection, integration, testing, resilience, support and ownership. Harvey Nash uses Microsoft Copilot as its approved general-purpose enterprise AI environment, and its policy requires other AI applications used for company business to be approved by Group Technology, with specific protection for company, client, candidate, supplier and personal information. The company separates general AI use, agent creation and more advanced capabilities so that access reflects what someone is trying to achieve, and it distinguishes simple agents business users can build themselves from complex ones involving integrations that need technology team support.

Anand said guardrails are essential but should not make experimentation so difficult that innovation stops, and he set out expectations around an approved environment, controls on sensitive information and appropriate human judgement. He said the most important capability for an AI citizen is not necessarily coding but understanding a problem well enough to describe it, knowing its context and data, and judging whether the result is useful, and that people still need AI literacy to understand data sensitivity, test outputs and know when human accountability is essential. He said anyone who uses AI owns the work that comes out of it, so a person who sends an AI output in a client proposal, candidate email or board paper is accountable rather than the tool, and he said managers must make clear what data can and cannot go into an AI tool and give people time to learn. Every agent that moves beyond personal use needs a named owner who answers for what it does, what data it touches and whether it still does its job, with owners reviewing access as roles change and switching off agents that are no longer used or safe. Anand also flagged cost as an easily overlooked guardrail, saying agentic AI increasingly has consumption-based economics, so Harvey Nash monitors usage rather than treating AI as unlimited computing.

Anand described IT's role as changing, saying his team does not need to originate every innovation or build every prototype but should create an environment where innovation can emerge safely, identify the proof points that matter and turn the strongest ideas into secure, resilient enterprise capabilities. He said Citizen AI is about dramatically increasing the number of experiments an organisation can run, giving people at the coalface the freedom and guardrails to turn ideas into proven concepts, with Technology stepping in to scale an idea once it shows real value. The article does not say what results Harvey Nash has measured beyond the ability to count posts created through the content agent, which includes a gamification element to encourage usage. It also does not say what happens next beyond the stated plan of moving proven ideas into enterprise-ready systems.

Articles.Title: How Harvey Nash is embracing ‘Citizen AI’ for faster experimentation and adoption - Computing UK

stories.headline_source: How Harvey Nash is embracing ‘Citizen AI’ for faster experimentation and adoption

stories.Headline: Genesis AI raises 500m dollars with Nvidia backing to build a general AI brain for robots
stories.Summary:
Genesis AI raised 500 million dollars in a Series A round during November 2026. The physical AI company received backing from Nvidia to build models for various robots. This funding follows a seed round of 105 million dollars from over one year ago. The startup now holds a valuation of 3.5 billion dollars after this latest investment. It represents one of the largest robotics funding rounds in Europe for the current year.

The company operates in France and the United States with support from Bpifrance and Ericsson. Other investors include Khosla Ventures, Neura Robotics, Samsung, and Zoom. The startup aims to create a general AI brain for robots to use. This system will allow robots to learn tasks through observation and a few examples. It seeks to move beyond the current need for specific, hand-coded instructions for every action.

The company is led by founders and executives including Ck ndpiu and q ixcm. They stated that the current approach to robotics is too specific and limited. They believe that AI should allow robots to learn from a few examples. The goal is to create a system that works across many different robot types. This approach aims to make robot training faster and more flexible for users.

The technology affects the robotics industry by reducing the need for manual coding. Other companies like Mosaico raised 7.5 million euros to help manage sensor data. Mosaico was backed by Connect Ventures, OpenOcean, and United Ventures in Italy. This Italian startup helps companies organize the vast data needed to train AI models. They aim to solve the data problem that slows down robotics development.

Genesis AI is part of a broader trend of high venture capital in robotics. Other firms like Bleu Robotics in Paris raised 5 million euros in pre-seed funding. Enact Intelligence also raised a large pre-seed round in Switzerland recently. TSMC is launching a 500 million dollar fund to support future chip titans. This fund targets startups and suppliers to broaden the ecosystem during the AI boom.

Genesis AI will now work to deploy its general AI brain across robots. The company plans to scale its operations in France and the United States. TSMC intends to find the next Nvidia or Broadcom through its new fund. The articles do not state when the general AI brain will be released. They also leave open how Mosaico will scale its data management tools.

stories.Headline: Liquid AI releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra decision models that accept text, images and audio
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI released two new decision models, d1.2 and d1.2-ultra, on November 17, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. A decision model does not write text, because it returns calibrated probabilities over a fixed set of answers instead. The d1.2 family now accepts text, images and audio, and it adds five new answer types. The d1.2-ultra model scores 75 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, which is the top score among decision models on that index.

The models run only on the hosted Liquid API, and no weights are available yet, though Liquid AI says it will open them at some point. Parameter sizes are not disclosed, and the models take up to 65,536 input tokens per question and 128 questions per call. The d1.2 model scores 69 on the same index, and Liquid AI reports a 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 benchmarks in its own test. The new answer types cover reading a value, finding every span, locating objects, estimating a number with a range, and picking every option that applies. Audio can be the subject of a question or the question itself, the API takes 16-bit PCM WAV at 10 tokens per second, and both models answer 95% to 97% of questions correctly on held-out ESC-50 and FLEURS recordings.

The index combines six evaluations, with AA-Paperclip carrying 30% of the weight, four others carrying 15% each and When2Call carrying 10%, and its Decision Score penalizes confident wrong answers. On the chart shared by Liquid AI, Drex Max v1.1, SubQ Snap 1.2 and GLiDE v1.2 follow at 73, and d1.2 at 69 is 2 points below the deprecated d1-ultra at 71. Liquid AI argues that no model scores higher than d1.2 for less money, and it says d1.2 is faster and costs less than half as much as d1.2-ultra. The earlier d1, d1.1 and d1-ultra models are now deprecated and do not support audio or the new tasks. The calibration figures come from Liquid AI's own test on held-out splits of public datasets, and no public benchmark exists yet.

Articles.Title: Liquid AI Releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra: Omnimodal Decision Models That Top the AA Decision Index

stories.Headline: IBM chief Arvind Krishna urges India to scale chip and AI ecosystems
stories.Summary:
IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna said in New Delhi on November 16 that India must scale its semiconductor and artificial intelligence deployment ecosystems to become a global player. He identified chip design and assembly as India's strengths because of its skilled workforce, existing infrastructure and technical capabilities. He noted that India's contribution to the trillion-dollar global semiconductor manufacturing industry is only about $3 billion, which shows a significant gap. Krishna also said that while India has a strong position in software exports, its role in other technology value chain segments is limited.

Krishna advised the Indian government to focus on scaling these initiatives, and he pointed to AI deployment for global companies as another opportunity India can capture. Estimates suggest that AI could add around $500 billion to India's gross domestic product growth by the end of the decade, but India needs to accelerate AI adoption to realise this potential. An IBM survey found that more than 75 per cent of organisations have made little progress in AI adoption, even though more than 90 per cent acknowledge its usefulness. Integrating AI at scale requires preparing enterprise data and re-engineering business processes, according to the report.

IBM is expanding hiring in design, software, testing, site reliability engineering and AI skills, the article says. The report does not say what the Indian government plans to do in response to Krishna's advice, and it gives no timeline for any policy changes. It also does not say whether IBM's hiring expansion is tied to India specifically or spread across its operations. The article ends by inviting readers to share their thoughts, and it provides no further details on next steps.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA releases NVKE and NVKR as open-source projects for managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released two open-source projects, the NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and the NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), for running managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure, and both were recently announced as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. NVKE serves as the control plane for a managed Kubernetes service, while NVKR builds the OS images, container images and packages that those clusters depend on. Both projects ship under the Apache 2.0 license and are currently in public preview. NVKE is written in Go, uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API, and has no runtime dependency on NVKR.

A local evaluation of NVKE needs 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of RAM and 100 GiB of disk with no GPU, while a full footprint calls for 3 CPU servers for the management cluster, 3 CPU servers per workload control plane and a pool of GPU worker nodes. The software runs on your own NVIDIA GPU bare-metal servers provisioned through NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo), and node images build for both amd64 and arm64. No throughput or provisioning-time benchmarks are published, and the quality signal is certification rather than speed, with conformance testing on Kubernetes 1.36. After install, the NVKE API serves plain HTTP on port 30080 with authentication off, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup procedure.

NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions that produces executables, container images, Helm charts and node images, and its Recipes define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. Hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references, and NVKR can also build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. A node must present an attested SPIFFE identity before it gets join credentials, and the README says SPIRE uses TPM for this, while per-cluster etcd encryption is available. An OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart exports logs, metrics and traces over OTLP, and three companion projects plug into workload clusters: AI Cluster Runtime for the GPU runtime, NodeWright for node packages and NVSentinel for break-fix automation.

The repo describes NVKE as a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters rather than a distribution, and it exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster. Customers get standard clusters and use kubectl, while the operator manages them through the NVKE API or the nvkectl CLI. Bootstrap begins when nvkectl bootstrap site starts a temporary single-node kind cluster on a bootstrap host, after which NVKE requests 3 servers from NICo, which boots them from the node image before the temporary cluster is deleted. Compared with Gardener from SAP and Kamaji from Clastix, NVKE uses a dedicated control plane per cluster with its own etcd and node pools, and the articles give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao sets out a framework for AI data retention
stories.Summary:
A November 13, 2026 post on X by Fireworks AI cofounder and CEO Lin Qiao set out a framework for understanding AI data retention, and MarkTechPost explained it on November 17, 2026 by describing two standard API designs that decide where control of the data lifecycle sits. In the first design, a customer uploads a file or dataset, runs jobs against it, and then deletes it, with the platform keeping the data stored and available until deletion is requested. In the second design, a customer sends data, the platform computes and returns a result, and no application state stays behind, which is the pattern called zero data retention. The article says data retention has become one of the most misunderstood terms in AI infrastructure, and that after a wave of AI security headlines many development teams now ask whether their AI provider keeps their data.

The article describes zero data retention as a per-endpoint commitment not to persist covered prompts and outputs after an eligible request, with eligibility depending on the endpoint, request flags and account settings rather than the vendor name. It says stored features such as batch, file and dataset features keep data until it is deleted or expires, and it advises preferring ephemeral endpoints because deletion is the customer's job after an upload. Among the examples it gives, OpenAI Batch requires uploading a JSONL input file and then creating the batch, Amazon Bedrock batch inference keeps input JSONL files in an S3 location the customer chooses, the Gemini Batch API runs jobs from an input file the customer provides, and Fireworks AI Batch requires creating a dataset and then submitting jobs against it. The article says OpenAI batch files last 30 days by default and Anthropic batch data 29 days, that OpenAI non-batch files persist until deleted, and that Fireworks AI managed training datasets have no time limit and are deleted by the customer, while Amazon Bedrock and Google batch jobs read and write the customer's own cloud storage.

On the ephemeral side, the article lists OpenAI Chat Completions, where store defaults to false, Amazon Bedrock Converse, where content is only used to generate the response, and Google Gemini text generation, which is stateless when store is false. It also lists Fireworks AI Chat Completions, direct or through Nexus, whose schema has no store field, and the Fireworks AI Training SDK including Serverless Training, where forward_backward sends tokenized batches per call, no dataset is uploaded, and training data is not stored at rest. The article says a synchronous response alone does not establish zero data retention, and it cites OpenAI's data controls as describing two layers, application state that a feature must keep, such as uploaded files, and abuse-monitoring logs held for safety review, noting that a platform can be at zero on one layer and not the other. According to the article, Qiao said Fireworks AI keeps nothing after a deletion request, and the article adds that the same split has shaped data processing systems for decades.

Articles.Title: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained

stories.headline_source: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained

stories.Headline: Perplexity adds Multiagent feature to allow up to 16 AI agents to cross-check complex tasks
stories.Summary:
Perplexity added a feature called Multiagent to its Computer research platform on November 17, 2026. This new system allows a lead agent to manage a team of up to 16 supporting agents to complete complex tasks. These agents work in parallel, share findings directly with one another, and cross-check each other's work. The lead agent plans the overall task, assigns specific parts to the team, and merges all findings into one final response for the user.

This update introduces the highest effort level available, sitting above the Ultra setting. It requires a Perplexity Max plan, which costs 167 dollars per month when billed annually, and is available only on the web. The default team utilizes three model families, specifically Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon. Users can name specific models in their queries, and the system allows agents to coordinate edits within shared files.

Perplexity stated that this tool is designed for large, interconnected work such as annual report reviews and year-end tax preparation. The company explained that the lead agent acts as the single point of contact for the user while coordinating the supporting agents. This builds upon effort controls launched on September 17, 2026, which previously offered Light, Standard, High, and Ultra settings. The company positions this diversity of models as a key difference from competitors like Kimi and Grok.

stories.Headline: UNESCO publishes a teaching guide to help educators teach critical thinking about AI-generated information
stories.Summary:
UNESCO published a teaching guide on 17 November 2026 to help educators prepare learners to question AI-generated information and understand how automated systems shape what people encounter online. The publication, titled AI Answers. You Decide. ,  Teaching Media and Information Literacy in AI-Mediated Information Environments, offers discussion questions, activities and examples for educators, teacher-training institutions and curriculum developers. It extends UNESCO's existing media and information literacy curriculum to address an information environment increasingly influenced by AI.

The guide addresses the reliability and authenticity of AI-generated content alongside questions about the systems, interests and data behind it. The guide's scope includes convincing synthetic text, images, audio and video, as well as the algorithms that influence which information people see. Five connected areas organize the material: AI in everyday life, AI and the media, AI, the human mind and knowledge, AI, power and human rights, and AI and the future. The knowledge strand focuses on critical thinking, informed trust and evaluating AI-generated information, while the media strand examines changes to journalism, content creation and access to information.

Questions about power and human rights bring algorithmic bias, inequality and sustainability into the curriculum, and the future-focused material encourages learners to participate in shaping inclusive, human-centered approaches to AI. The publication is a companion to UNESCO's Media and Information Literate Citizens: Think Critically, Click Wisely! curriculum, launched in 2021 and subsequently piloted and adapted in more than 40 countries. The new guide was developed with eight international experts and peer-reviewed by ten additional specialists.

Mariya Gabriel, Assistant-Director General for Communication and Information at UNESCO, said artificial intelligence is transforming how people learn, communicate and access information, and that people must retain the ability to think critically, question what they see and make informed choices. Anne Leppäjärvi, who authored the guide, said AI does not change the foundations of media and information literacy but the environment in which they are applied, and that the goal is to equip learners with critical thinking skills rather than keep up with every technological change. Educators can adapt the guide's conceptual explanations, discussion questions, practical activities and examples to their own educational settings. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that, and they give no further dates or plans for the guide's rollout.

stories.Headline: Michael Anello shows how Drupal developers cut AI token costs with browser models and metering
stories.Summary:
Sessions at NEDCamp 2026 explored how developers can manage the costs and keep control of AI features built into Drupal sites, and speakers said cost and control should be treated as design inputs from the very start of a project. Michael Anello, in a session on Drupal AI modules worth knowing about, said Chrome's built-in model can be reached through developer settings and used by Drupal through the AI Browser Provider module, which cuts token costs for everyday summarising and drafting. He also demonstrated AI Metering, a tool that tracks token usage, estimates costs and enforces per-user monthly quotas. That module allows a local fallback provider such as Ollama when limits are reached, which offers an alternative to blocking editor requests, and the choice between blocking and falling back has a significant impact on the user experience.

Jacob Rockowitz, in a talk titled AI ate my Work, and I'm okay with that, discussed optimising coding agents by giving them small and predictable toolsets. He uses Git worktrees and custom DDEV commands as isolated playgrounds for agents, an approach that avoids hardcoded paths and reduces token spending by keeping agent context light. Jim Birch presented a company-wide AI governance system in his session on guardrails, governance and proof that a team still owns the work. His agency uses a PREP framework, meaning purpose, risk, evidence and person, to scope each AI use case, and the system includes a harness for tools, approved tools that do not train on company data, and managed settings. Birch also introduced ownership, where each AI-assisted piece of work receives a delivery record, a YAML file detailing the producer, reviewer, approvals and model used, which answers client questions about verification.

Fredric Mitchell, in a session on defending budgets, addressed budget defence in an AI-driven landscape and noted that AI overviews are eroding organic search traffic, which makes it harder to justify platform budgets based on traffic metrics. He proposed the Web Operations Maturity Model, a rubric that scores platform health across six areas, as an alternative. Ethan Marcotte's keynote, The Work We Want, explored the broader societal impact of AI and framed it within Ursula Franklin's stages of technology. Marcotte argued that AI is institutionalising control with a few firms, likening it to the historical trajectory of the sewing machine, and he suggested that AI limits function best when editors help set them, which gives those editors more control over their work.

stories.Headline: Mercor raises $750m Series D at $20bn valuation as annualised revenue passes $2bn
stories.Summary:
Mercor, a San Francisco company that pays doctors, lawyers, bankers and engineers to teach AI models how real work is done, announced in November 2026 a US$750m Series D at a US$20bn valuation, after its annualised revenue passed US$2bn in June 2026, up from US$1m two years earlier. The company was founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody, who is CEO, Adarsh Hiremath, who is Co-CEO, and Surya Midha, as an AI recruiting marketplace, and it found its market when AI labs needed experts rather than crowdworkers to write tasks, grade model responses and build verifiers for post-training. Its network counts more than five million domain experts, and it was paying out more than US$2m a day by March 2026, with contractors typically keeping 60% to 70% of gross billings. The Information reported US$614m in gross revenue for the first half of 2026, up 70% from the year before, and the company has more than 700 full-time employees as of November 2026. Felicis led a US$350m Series C at a US$10bn valuation in October 2025, and investors in the Series D include Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, funds managed by affiliates of Apollo, G Squared, General Catalyst, Glade Brook Capital, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group, XTX Ventures and Zoom.

Mercor says it works with all of the top five AI labs and six of the Magnificent Seven tech companies, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta named in reports, and it is pushing into enterprises. In July 2026 it agreed to acquire Deeptune, an a16z-backed start-up backed by a US$43m Series A that has recreated hundreds of enterprise apps, including Salesforce, as environments, and whose team is joining Mercor's New York office. Its APEX benchmarks measure AI on economically valuable work, and in October 2026 AI outperformed 12 licensed CPAs on APEX-Accounting; Mercor also post-trained a 397bn-parameter open model with SkyRL, built at UC Berkeley with Anyscale, lifting its APEX-Agents score by 70% in relative terms, and released datasets and traces on Hugging Face. Foody said every job in the economy will need its own AI agents and every company will need a way to train and evaluate them on its own work, adding that Mercor spent the last two years building that infrastructure with the frontier labs and is now bringing it to enterprises. Hiremath said every company deploying AI needs to know whether it works and the answer is different for each one, because a model can score well on a public benchmark and still fail on the systems, policies and edge cases that define how a specific business runs, so Mercor builds custom benchmarks with each enterprise and uses them as the starting point for post-training.

The company's setbacks have been real: a late March 2026 supply-chain breach led Meta to pause all its work with Mercor while it investigated the security breach, according to WIRED. The next product is the training environment, a simulated workplace where an agent can practise a task and be scored, and Mercor said in a post on X that training AI to do real professional work requires covering the full distribution of apps, worlds and tasks across the economy, noting that Deeptune built the apps for the leading AI labs. Mercor's technology partners include Cognition, which co-launched the APEX-SWE software engineering benchmark with Mercor, Anyscale, Hugging Face, which hosts the datasets, model weights and evaluation traces released in September 2026, Modal, whose cloud infrastructure runs sandboxed agent trials, and Daytona, which provides sandboxed environments for agent training runs. The firm appears to have recovered from the breach and is pushing from frontier labs to enterprises.

stories.Headline: CERT-In flags low severity emBridge flaw and eMudhra removes file browsing functions to fix it
stories.Summary:
CERT-In issued a vulnerability note on November 13 about eMudhra's emBridge digital signature utility, a client-side application that lets web portals communicate with digital signature certificates and hardware tokens installed on a user's computer. The agency said the flaw could let unauthorised entities on the same local area network access file and directory names on an affected device, and it classified the threat as low severity. Cybersecurity expert Karan Saini reported the vulnerability to CERT-In. CERT-In stated that file-browsing functions within the interface did not verify whether requests came from an authorised source, and that these functions operate with the highest system privileges on Windows.

An attacker on the same local network could use a malicious webpage to send requests to emBridge and map out file and folder names on the targeted machine. The affected versions are 5.9.1.x to 5.9.3.x on Windows, 3.2.4.x to 3.2.6.x on macOS, and 3.2.0.x to 3.3.0.x on Ubuntu and Red Hat Linux. CERT-In advised users to upgrade to version 5.9.4.x or later on Windows, 3.2.7.x or later on macOS, and 3.3.1.x or later on Linux. Several government portals, including the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA V3 portal, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade and the National Single Window System, rely on emBridge for DSC-based signing, and the Income Tax Department also recommends it for managing DSCs.

The agency confirmed that the flaw does not provide access to file contents, permit changes or deletions, allow code execution, or expose cryptographic keys or token PINs. eMudhra published its own advisory on the CVE and said it fixed the issue on November 11, two days before CERT-In's note, by removing the file-browsing functions from emBridge entirely. The company said that with these endpoints removed the file enumeration capability is no longer available through emBridge, and it rated the flaw's impact and risk as low. An attack would also require several conditions at once, including an affected emBridge version, a malicious webpage on the same local network, the user opening it, and a browser without Local Network Access restrictions.

The company added that its firewall and local-only request handling block direct access from other machines. Saini posted on X that while the bug was trivial, eMudhra's own advisory had further downplayed it. eMudhra told Inc42 that every digital signature certificate requires the user to enter a token PIN before use, and it pointed out that CERT-In's note confirmed keys and token PINs had not been exposed. A company spokesperson said identifying and fixing vulnerabilities is a routine part of responsible software development, and added that large global vendors like Microsoft, Oracle, Google and Adobe addressed thousands of vulnerabilities every month. The incident follows a major cybersecurity event in October where weak private keys for eMudhra's intermediate certificate authority certificates were reported.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud opens applications for a 15-week sovereign AI accelerator for European and Israeli startups
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud announced on November 17, 2026 an open call for applications to its Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI, which is available in Europe and Israel and supports startups building AI solutions for European regulatory environments. The announcement was made by Giorgia Abeltino, Head of Government Affairs and Public Policy for Google Cloud Europe, Middle East and Africa. The program is described as equity-free and runs for 15 weeks in a hybrid format with virtual and in-person sessions. Applications close on January 15, 2027, and founders can apply on the Google for Startups Accelerator page.

The accelerator is aimed at a small, high-touch cohort of late-seed to post Series A startups headquartered across Europe and Israel with strong traction that use AI for sensitive, regulated workloads. Target areas include government and public service technologies such as sovereign document processing and citizen service portals, with defense applications excluded, as well as healthcare and life sciences, regulated finance, and cybersecurity and data trust. Selected startups receive architectural mentorship, one-to-one pairing with Google Cloud engineers, and advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act Regulatory Sandboxes. Participants also get support to deploy across Google Cloud's tiered sovereign portfolio, from regional data controls and external key management to partner-operated clouds such as S3NS in France and Thales in Germany and fully air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments.

Abeltino wrote that artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe, and that enterprises and public institutions need advanced AI while meeting data governance requirements including the EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA, and national frameworks such as SecNumCloud and BSI's cloud security and sovereignty principles. She said the program wants founders to build in Europe with solutions made in Europe, and that digital sovereignty for startups should not mean settling for second-rate tools or lock-in to a single rigid stack. She described co-engineering with Europe's tech ecosystem so founders can scale on their own terms from day one, for instance by combining Gemini models, open-weight models like Gemma and Mistral, and verifiable data residency and cryptographic controls delivered with local European sovereign partners. Past participants, quoted in the post, said access to Google Cloud engineers who understand sovereign and regulated constraints saves young companies time and that the program helps build compliance answers into architecture from day one.

stories.Headline: Philippines residents protest planned US led AI and manufacturing hub
stories.Summary:
Local residents in the Philippines held protests on Monday against the upcoming visit of President Trump to Manila. These demonstrations center on a planned artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub located just north of the capital city. The project serves as the first major action for Pax Silica, which is an international initiative led by the U.S. State Department. This effort aims to secure high-tech manufacturing supply chains that do not rely on China.

The proposed industrial hub will cover more than 4,000 acres of land in the Philippines. This project follows the December 2025 announcement of Pax Silica, which has since attracted over 25 participating countries including India, Japan, Israel, and the United Kingdom. The Philippines officially joined this initiative in April, leading to the current plans for the manufacturing center. The Marcos administration claims this development could create between 100,000 and 130,000 new jobs for the local population.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. expressed great excitement in October, calling the hub a grand opportunity to move the country up the value chain. Conversely, advocate Maninging Vilog argued that the project only benefits the United States while grabbing local lands. Protester Kaiser Cortina questioned why farmers and bus drivers should care about artificial intelligence. Representative Antonio Tinio noted that opposition to AI data centers is a global issue seen across Southeast Asia, including Indonesia and Malaysia.

The U.S. government is pursuing this strategy because of long-standing concerns regarding Chinese access to advanced chips and hardware. Recent attention increased following reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Participants in Pax Silica signed a declaration on Sunday regarding the protection of critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies. President Trump is expected to meet with President Marcos on Wednesday during the ASEAN summit before he flies to China.

Articles.Title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub

stories.Headline: Academic librarians expect AI to drive change and want to lead AI literacy, Elsevier study finds
stories.Summary:
A global study from Elsevier found that 83 percent of academic librarians surveyed expect artificial intelligence to be the biggest driver of change in academic research, while 81 percent also named the misuse of AI as the greatest threat to the integrity of the scholarly record. The findings come from the Librarian of the Future report, which draws on responses from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders. The research highlights the increasingly strategic role librarians could play within universities as institutions respond to technological change, evolving research needs and growing concerns around research integrity. Almost all respondents, 95 percent, expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years.

The report says 82 percent of respondents believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers, and 76 percent believe librarians should contribute to AI governance. Despite these expectations, only 30 percent report that their institution has implemented an AI policy, which suggests a significant gap between the adoption of AI technologies and the development of institutional frameworks to manage their use. More than three-quarters of respondents, 76 percent, anticipate greater collaboration between libraries and other university departments over the next five years. The findings also point to the growing importance of leadership, influencing skills and the ability to navigate complex institutional decisions as librarians take on broader responsibilities.

Ann Gabriel, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Networks at Elsevier, said librarians have always been essential to research, but the study shows an opportunity for their expertise to play an even more strategic role. She said that as AI transforms how research is discovered, conducted and evaluated, librarians bring a unique combination of technical expertise, ethical judgement and trusted relationships across their institutions. She added that ensuring they have the skills, support and visibility to contribute fully will be important as universities navigate this next phase of change. Jim O'Donnell, University Librarian and Professor at Arizona State University, said librarians long thought they were in the book business, or perhaps the information business, and that the survey shows the community now broadly recognises it is in the research business.

The report suggests that librarians are increasingly positioning themselves as partners in the wider research process, rather than solely as providers of information resources. Alongside AI literacy and governance, demand is expected to grow for library expertise in open access, research data management and research integrity. The report identifies responsible AI adoption, trusted information and research integrity as areas in which librarians could play a more prominent role in supporting researchers and institutional leadership. Elsevier says it will continue working with the global library community to explore how the profession can respond to these changing demands, and the full report is available at Librarian of the Future.

Articles.Title: Academic librarians "see artificial intelligence as biggest driver of change"

stories.headline_source: Academic librarians "see artificial intelligence as biggest driver of change"

stories.Headline: Pearl engineering leader urges CIOs to measure cycle time and rework to gauge AI productivity
stories.Summary:
Nazar Yaremchuk, senior director of engineering at Pearl, wrote in CIO on Nov 17, 2026 that AI can write code in seconds but that is only the first stage of software development. He said AI-generated output can introduce errors, miss internal requirements or require extensive rework, so the time saved upfront can quickly disappear. Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. Yaremchuk said that if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren't so clear-cut. A report from Bain & Co found AI coding tools help developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%.

Yaremchuk said CIOs need to look at the entire process, from the initial idea to software in production, to understand whether AI is improving productivity. He said AI adoption metrics such as token usage and developer participation show how much a company is using AI, but not necessarily whether it is becoming more productive. He said a more useful approach is to track engineering cycle time, end-to-end lead time, review and rework time, and software quality. He said these measures are most useful when considered holistically, and leaders should assess whether quality is consistent or improving and whether review and rework are consuming too much time. He said establishing a baseline before expanding AI use, then tracking these measures over time, can help CIOs distinguish genuine improvements from shifts in where work happens.

At Pearl, Yaremchuk said, the team asked AI to help create pipeline automation, but it generated GitHub Actions workflows for an engineering environment that uses Azure DevOps and Jenkins. He said astute engineers caught the mismatch during review and had to rewrite the integration, and the code was plausible but didn't account for Pearl's actual infrastructure. He said Pearl has a quality-control process that combines AI-assisted review with human oversight based on risk, with lower-risk changes such as unit tests often reviewed primarily by AI while critical production-facing code still receives human review. He said Pearl's AI reviews identify an average of 16 errors per 10 pull requests, including security and architectural issues. He said the goal is not to remove humans from the review process but to use automation to catch issues efficiently and reserve human judgment for decisions where risk and complexity warrant it.

Yaremchuk said Pearl tracks engineering cycle time and has seen it decline month over month in 2026 as its use of AI-generated code has increased. He said that in September 2026, the average pull request Pearl released to production was 75% AI-generated, and 45% of all pull requests were written entirely by AI, with no line edited by a person before commit. He said savvy organizations have taken advantage of AI to automate repetitive tasks so that engineers can focus more on architecture, complex problem-solving and validating results. He said enterprises introducing AI agents that can execute multistep tasks and work together will need to rethink how they assign, supervise and evaluate that work, with clear permissions, defined responsibilities and appropriate oversight. He said of critical importance is determining where human judgment remains essential and how teams should adapt as more work becomes automated.

Yaremchuk said the priority for CIOs should be to redesign engineering workflows around the capabilities of AI, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing processes. He said this starts with establishing a baseline for development speed and software quality, then measuring how both change as AI adoption increases. He said it also means using the results to adjust workflows, review requirements and the allocation of engineering time. He said AI investments should be held accountable to the same business outcomes as any other technology investment, and more code, more tokens and broader adoption can indicate progress but can be misleading. He said the real measure of AI productivity is whether an organization can deliver better software faster, with quality and security intact.

Yaremchuk has nearly 20 years in software delivery and over a decade leading engineering organizations, and he oversees architecture, DevOps, security and AI adoption across a 280-person engineering organization at Pearl. He led a transformation that increased production releases from one to approximately 400 per week and now champions AI-native software delivery. He is completing an Executive MBA at Oxford Saïd Business School. The article was published Nov 17, 2026 and runs 5 minutes.

stories.Headline: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Ads to 44 countries through exclusive reseller Aleph
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 12, 2026, that it is expanding the market presence of ChatGPT Ads across 44 different countries. The company selected Aleph to serve as the exclusive reseller to provide local invoicing and in-person support for brands and agencies. This new arrangement allows advertisers in these specific regions to contract and pay for services through a local entity. These businesses can now access local market expertise and training while utilizing the advertising platform.

The expansion covers 14 Latin American nations, including Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Puerto Rico, and Uruguay. In Europe and Central Asia, the 16 participating countries are Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan. The Middle East and Africa include 10 nations, specifically Egypt, Kenya, Kuwait, Morocco, Nigeria, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates. This change does not affect the ability of global advertisers to target any country where the ads are available.

OpenAI stated that over one hundred thousand marketers have already used the platform, which has seen significant progress over ten months. The company explained that this announcement simply provides additional local ways for businesses to purchase advertising space. They mentioned a continued focus on broadening access to AI and protecting user trust while developing new measurement solutions. The organization intends to create more optimization tools and new formats as they build the full potential of the system.

The company noted that ChatGPT Ads are not available in mainland China or Hong Kong because the models are not available there. However, businesses based in those two markets may still advertise to users in other available regions through authorized partners. Advertisers can still choose to buy ads directly through the Ads Manager or via global technology partners. OpenAI will continue to improve the platform based on feedback from the businesses and people using the service.

stories.Headline: Stephen Ferrara launches AI + Nurse Academy to give nurse practitioners a foundation in AI
stories.Summary:
Stephen Ferrara, a doctor of nursing practice and family nurse practitioner, was named Medscape's Nurse Practitioner of the Month in a feature published on November 17, 2026, recognizing his work helping nurses navigate artificial intelligence. He is the chief executive officer and founder of AI + Nurse Academy, an educational platform that gives nurse practitioners a foundation in AI, which he launched in October 2025. Ferrara said his motivation comes down to trying to fix a system he feels is not working as intended for the people it is designed for. Early in his clinical career, he realized state law did not allow him to do things he had been educated and prepared to do, such as performing licensing physicals for people pursuing a barber career, and he turned his attention to overcoming barriers such as full practice authority laws.

The academy currently offers nurse practitioners and registered nurses a 60-minute continuing medical education module, and upon completion users receive a certificate of completion and one accredited hour of continuing education. Participants can also join a community of peers to ask questions, share concerns and exchange experiences, with responsible use as the company's guiding principle. Ferrara said the main goal is to expose every nurse to what generative AI is, what it means for their practice, and to prompt them to consider how they will integrate it thoughtfully into clinical practice. He explained that he wants nurses to understand where AI makes mistakes and how it can affect patient outcomes, stressing that keeping a human or clinician in the loop means AI does not make any decisions without a human or clinician reviewing it.

Ferrara said that in nursing school he was taught that at the end of the day it is your license to lose, and that if you adopt a tool it is your clinical judgment on the line regardless of whether you choose it or are told by administrators to use it. He pointed to flaws in the research large language models rely on, such as the lack of robust cultural, socioeconomic and ethnic studies in certain patient populations, and said he wants the human between AI and the patient to be able to discern whether a recommendation is pertinent. He said it is his core belief that AI can potentially make him a better clinician through rapid access to information and the ability to personalize it to patients, but that it is not magic. He said clinicians are ingrained to do no harm and asked how AI can be made to better anticipate things and patients rather than spewing things that are not necessarily helpful.

Before retiring from his Columbia appointments earlier this year, Ferrara served as inaugural associate dean of AI, spearheading strategy and programs to ensure nurses gained foundational AI literacy, and he moved from assistant to full professor of nursing at Columbia University in New York City. As associate dean of clinical affairs and chief clinical officer for the ColumbiaDoctors Nurse Practitioner Group, he expanded services to include house calls and integrated mental health services, achieving Patient-Centered Medical Home recognition. As president and immediate past president of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, he advocated for the Improving Care and Access to Nurses Act so nurse practitioners can practice to the top of their license and education. Ferrara reported receiving profits from AI + Nurse Academy, and the article says the path starts with a basic framework and AI literacy and ideally ends with improved patient outcomes, with nurse practitioners determining what happens in between.

stories.Headline: Revolut deploys ChatGPT and Codex to cut coding time and automate financial crime screening
stories.Summary:
Revolut has adopted OpenAI's ChatGPT, API and Codex across its global operations, OpenAI reported on November 16, 2026, in a customer story titled "How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar." Revolut was built to challenge the way people interact with money, and that ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets and 800,000 businesses. Its consumer base has grown by 23% in the last 12 months, according to the article. One of Revolut's largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models, which examines information, applies Revolut's rules and completes the defined process automatically. The release of GPT-5.5 was a turning point, when the models became capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent.

Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, from task start to feature merge, according to AI Lead David Abitbol. One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents. Revolut used one day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context. More transactions are screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one. Revolut also developed a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Abitbol said Revolut has a systematic framework so anyone building with AI follows the same standards across development, A/B testing and business metric prediction, holding every engineer to the same quality standard. He said the biggest problem AI can tackle today is the scaling of humans versus the demand Revolut gets. Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri said the result translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system customers can trust. Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik said he realised he did not need a whole team of developers and could launch different agents and assign each a particular task. Pitik also said every developer is responsible for the code they produce and that they do not blindly trust AI.

Amiri said the most critical decision is always about accountability, and that if an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand it well enough to stand by it. He said you earn real confidence in AI by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go. Global Head of Business Marketing Kim Maniovich said partnering with OpenAI enables Revolut to build solutions in a way that is lean, cost-efficient and tailored to how the company works. Maniovich said the average Revolut employee has three different jobs, and that month on month the targets get more aggressive but also more attainable. Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov said Revolut can shift focus from things that are important but hard to do without AI to things that matter for customers.

According to one report cited in the article, over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025. For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement protections for customers. The volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank. In a phishing investigation, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. Amiri said that with stronger AI tools, those connections can be uncovered instantly and investigators can dig deeper into the questions that really matter.

Abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks such as blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience, turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use. Maniovich said she hopes Revolut can take the values it operates by every day, its unapologetic ambition and desire to never settle, and enable people to apply them to their own lives through the products it builds. The article says Revolut's next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money. The article does not say when any of these future products will launch.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Sales with over 30 partner plugins
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Sales on November 17, 2026, according to a post on openai.com dated that day. The product is a new Sales experience built around a Sales plugin from OpenAI with dedicated skills for sellers. It also includes more than 30 new and enhanced partner plugins inside ChatGPT. OpenAI said the aim is to help every sales team understand customers better, spend less time on busywork and close more deals. The post said the tools let teams use information from the tools they already rely on to prepare for calls, tailor proposals and follow up faster.

The Sales plugin gives ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up. Partner plugins named in the post include Confluence, Guru and Seismic for learning sales processes and product updates, and ChatGPT Voice for rehearsing pitches and handling objections. Content tools named include ChatGPT Slides, Gamma, Figma and Canva, plus ChatGPT Sites for interactive demos or ROI calculators. Account tools named include Salesforce, HubSpot, Close CRM and monday CRM, and buyer-finding tools named include Apollo, Clay and Common Room, with Outreach and Salesloft for planning outreach. Call-note tools named include the Meetings plugin in ChatGPT, Gong, Otter.ai and Granola, Backstory is named for spotting deal risk, the Data plugin and Hex for analyzing sales data, and Docusign, Ironclad, PandaDoc and ServiceNow CPQ for quotes and agreements.

OpenAI said sellers can delegate work to their dot, an always-on agent in ChatGPT that can use the same plugins and customer context to prepare meeting briefs, track deal updates and bring relevant changes and proposed next steps for review. Sandeep Chellani, SVP and Head of Technology at The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, said the Salesforce Plugin for ChatGPT lets relationship builders uncover deeper insights about donor prospects and research partners and reduces the time and effort to gather and synthesize that information. Prof. Dr. Gunnar Gombert, Co-Founder and Managing Director of NeoBid, said the company uses HubSpot with ChatGPT for Sales to research real estate prospects, enrich CRM data, prioritize opportunities and prepare personalized outreach. Gombert estimated this reduces manual effort for these activities by around 65%, giving more time to help clients optimize energy procurement across their property portfolios. Sushanth Raman, CEO of Pallet, said ChatGPT for Sales and Rox are central to how the company operates and scales, and that Rox gives a clear view of the pipeline and surfaces deal risks early.

JR Harrell, EVP, Business Execution at Datasite, said Atlassian provides the connective tissue that allows OpenAI's frontier models to reason across the entire enterprise, and that grounding ChatGPT for Sales in the Teamwork Graph has democratized data. Jacob Tuwiner, Founder at Sculpted, said that in GTM the winners ship their best ideas before their competition, and that building in Clay for years meant clicking through menu after menu. Tuwiner said anyone can now use ChatGPT for Sales and Clay to ship a play in minutes that used to take an expert hours, days or weeks, and that Workflows shows every step instead of a giant table while Audiences takes the same play to a whole enterprise market. The post said availability of partner plugins and features varies by plan, region and workspace settings. It said ChatGPT Business and Enterprise admins can enable ChatGPT for Sales by opening the Admin Console, selecting their workspace and selecting Plugins, then making the Sales plugin and relevant partner plugins available for members to install or installing them by default.

The post said admins should review access to the required apps and the actions they can use, and that workspace members can complete any required account connections when prompted. It said OpenAI is continuing to build ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugin ecosystem around the work sales teams do every day. OpenAI said its goal is to bring more of that work into ChatGPT, with connected tools and customer context that carries from finding an opportunity to preparing for a conversation and following through. The post listed related OpenAI announcements, including dots on September 29, 2026, the Admin plugin for ChatGPT Work and Codex on August 25, 2026, and an expanded Oracle partnership on October 27, 2026. The post said people can install the Sales plugin to get started and learn more about ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugins.

The post did not give prices for ChatGPT for Sales or say which plans, regions or workspace settings include which partner plugins. It did not say when the more than 30 partner plugins became available or list all of them by name. It did not give a date for the next update to ChatGPT for Sales or say what that update will add. It did not say how many teams or sellers use the product. It did not give figures for time saved beyond NeoBid's estimate of around 65% less manual effort.

stories.Headline: OpenAI gives NATO institutions access to cybersecurity models through Daybreak
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 17, 2026 that it is working with NATO’s Communications and Information Agency, known as the NCIA, to give NATO’s core institutions access to advanced cybersecurity models through a program called Daybreak, helping protect Allied networks. NATO has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens per month as part of this work, according to the company. OpenAI also supported the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise, which was organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence and included a new training stream in which participants built, deployed and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations using Daybreak in the technical environment. The training placed participants alongside AI agents as operators, with an emphasis on maintaining human oversight.

Beyond NATO, OpenAI said it has provided access to its cyber models to defenders in Europe, including the EU’s ENISA and national cyber agencies in France (ANSSI), Germany and Poland. The Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine is using Daybreak to strengthen the cyber defence of civilian infrastructure, aiming to help Ukrainian teams identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly amid persistent cyber attacks. ENISA used the models to identify four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four, and a November joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU describes a review of 27 software projects using frontier models including OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak and tools including the Codex security plug-in. Across the models tested, 95% of the 88 potential issues assessed by software maintainers were confirmed as genuine, and CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS and coordinated their disclosure with the vendor, after which MikroTik released fixes that CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it had observed.

Dr Dylan Browne, the NCIA General Manager, said AI-powered cyber defence models represent a generational leap in cyber security because they accelerate vulnerability discovery, detect emerging threats at machine speed and enable defenders to stay ahead of adversaries. He said these technologies strengthen NATO’s cyber resilience, enhance its operational advantage and reinforce its ability to protect critical digital infrastructure at unprecedented scale and speed, and that as adoption scales the alliance will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models. That insight, he said, will help NATO optimise costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions. Sasha Baker, Head of National Security Policy at OpenAI, said the people defending democracies should have the most advanced technology on their side and that Daybreak puts more capable tools in their hands to help find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

OpenAI said NATO’s early use of its tools shows how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work in support of NATO’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states. The company said the work also helps strengthen cyber expertise across multinational teams responsible for protecting Allied networks around the clock and creates lessons that can benefit defenders across Europe and the broader Alliance. OpenAI said it remains fully committed to NATO’s principles for responsible AI adoption and to delivering solutions that are safe and secure. The company said it will continue working with governments, national cyber agencies and international partners to turn frontier AI capability into stronger, safer and more resilient systems, helping defenders find weaknesses, fix them faster and protect the services people rely on every day.

stories.Headline: ILO study finds AI and streaming reshape pay and working conditions in media and culture
stories.Summary:
The International Labour Organization published a study on 17 November 2026 examining how streaming and artificial intelligence are reshaping pay and working conditions in the media and culture sector. The report, titled Trends in remuneration and working time: Recorded media and live performance, looks at how creative workers are paid, how their working time is counted, and how digitalization and AI are changing both. Streaming has moved recorded media from physical sales and downloads toward subscription and advertising-funded services, and in recorded music streaming accounted for about 70 per cent of global industry revenue in 2024. AI adds a further layer because voices, images and performances can now be replicated, translated and reworked in new ways, which raises questions of consent, control and remuneration.

The study identifies three main ways AI can affect pay and work. First, AI systems can use existing works and performances as input, as when a recorded voice-over artist's voice is used to generate new dialogue, which raises issues of licensing, attribution and payment. Second, AI can generate or modify content, helping small production firms cut costs through tools such as subtitling and translation, but it may also reduce demand for some types of work or increase competition from AI-generated content. Third, AI can change job tasks, as when an editor spends less time on an initial cut and more on reviewing and correcting AI-generated material, and the question is whether those new tasks are reflected in pay, working time and skills. The report also cites a United Kingdom survey in which 61 per cent of screen directors said they had not fully understood the rights they were granting when signing their contracts.

Workers' organizations emphasize transparency and the need for creative workers to share in the value of later uses of their work, while employers and producers stress upfront investment, uncertain commercial returns and clear rights to finance and distribute the work. Collective agreements can clarify how such uses are permitted and paid, and the report points to the 2023 United States TV/Theatrical Agreement and a 2025 German film industry agreement, which include negotiated provisions on consent and remuneration for some uses of performers' digital replicas. The ILO's human-centred approach emphasizes transparency, human oversight and social dialogue, and the report says social dialogue can support a negotiated transition that promotes adequate remuneration, human creativity and viable enterprises. The report also notes that the ability to benefit from AI is highly uneven, since smaller enterprises and workers in less connected markets are likely to have less access to finance, skills, technology and the systems to manage rights and payments.

stories.Headline: TrustYou adds SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder to its Customer Experience Platform
stories.Summary:
TrustYou, a hospitality technology company headquartered in Munich, Germany, announced on 17 November 2026 that its Customer Experience Platform now opens on three conversational entry points built around jobs hotel teams do every day. The first, SummaryAI, has already read every new review across all sources so each property starts the day with its priorities set. The second, Ask TrustYou, answers any question about guest feedback and lets users follow up and dig deeper within the same conversation. The third, Report Builder, is new today and handles reporting for hotel teams.

A team describes a report once, including the KPIs, the properties and the comparison periods, and CXP then builds it, keeps it on schedule and delivers it as a PDF or Excel file in each recipient's language. That delivery reaches owners and boards who never log in to the system. All three tools work on one principle, which is that a user describes the outcome and CXP delivers it, so hotel teams act on guest issues sooner and guest insight reaches every role without training or analyst support. Multi-property groups get back the days each month they now spend consolidating reports across dozens or hundreds of properties, where quality and operations teams produce reports for general managers, owners, boards and regional leadership, and each audience expects its own KPIs, format and language.

Benjamin Jost, Founder and CEO of TrustYou, said hospitality is becoming conversational on both sides of the front desk, with guests already talking to AI to plan and book their stays. He said that on the guest side the company already closes the loop, because its Customer Data Platform sends every message and its agents answer every reply. He said staff should be able to work the same way with every system a hotel runs, so that you say what you need and it gets done. He described SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder as CXP's biggest step yet toward that vision, where opening it means the reviews are read, asking gives the answer and describing the report means the board has it every month.

SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder are live for all CXP customers, according to the announcement. TrustYou describes itself as hospitality's memory, a platform that unifies what guests feel, what they do and what they ask in a single system, and it says more than 100,000 hospitality businesses have used it since 2008. The company says its AI Review Summaries turn guest reviews from all relevant sources into structured, benchmarked insight for over 2 million properties worldwide, and that the same verified insight reaches travel platforms, booking engines and AI assistants via API and MCP. TrustYou is headquartered in Munich, Germany, and serves hospitality brands in over 165 countries.

stories.Headline: National Insurance Crime Bureau reports AI mentions in questionable claims rise over 1,400%
stories.Summary:
The National Insurance Crime Bureau, a nonprofit based in Oak Brook, Illinois, published its 2026 threat assessment on November 16, 2026, reporting that mentions of AI in questionable claims rose by more than 1,400% from 2025 to mid-2026 across auto, liability, cargo and workers' compensation lines. The report identifies three converging threats: AI-enabled identity schemes, organized crime networks that mix digital and physical tactics, and professional networks of attorneys, medical providers and auto repair firms working together to inflate claims. Fraudsters are using widely available tools to generate fabricated medical records, synthetic identities and doctored accident photographs at a volume that existing claims workflows were not built to handle. A separate Verisk study published in March 2026, based on surveys of 1,000 US consumers and 300 claims professionals, found that 36% of consumers would consider digitally altering a claim image or document even if it broke insurer rules, rising to 55% among Generation Z. On the insurer side, 76% of claims professionals said manipulated media submissions had grown more sophisticated over the past year, while only 32% were confident their organization could identify a deepfake. The report also found more than 1,600 transnational, interstate and state-level organized crime rings operating in 2025, running schemes that span staged accidents, vehicle theft and complex multi-party fraud.

The NICB describes predatory legal and medical networks as systematically exploiting the litigation system, turning low-severity incidents into mass litigation and driving settlement values well beyond the underlying loss, and it has focused legislative efforts on fraud in litigation funding. The FBI estimates non-health insurance fraud costs the US at least $40 billion annually, and fraud losses inflate loss ratios, which in turn drive premiums. In commercial cargo, total supply chain crime incidents across the US and Canada held roughly steady in 2025 at 3,594 events against 3,607 in 2024, but estimated losses reached nearly $725 million, a 60% year-on-year increase, according to Verisk CargoNet's January 2026 annual analysis. The average value per theft rose 36% to $273,990, confirmed cargo theft cases rose 18% year-over-year, and California, Texas and Illinois accounted for just over half of all incidents, while New Jersey, Indiana and Pennsylvania each recorded significant increases. Pranay Mittal, vice president of Travelers Investigative Services, said in a statement issued alongside the NICB report that shared insight is the industry's strongest defense because every insurer holds a piece of the picture, and that working with NICB and other fraud-fighting partners helps investigators spot patterns sooner and focus investigations with greater precision as new threats emerge.

Aimee Stidham, president of the International Association of Special Investigation Units, a global nonprofit headquartered in Albany, New York, and claims SIU manager at Hiscox USA, said in a statement issued alongside the report that the fight against insurance fraud is no longer undertaken by any single organization, and that today's most effective anti-fraud initiatives are driven by collaboration, intelligence sharing and a shared commitment to protecting policyholders. The NICB is integrating business intelligence across its member companies, authenticating digital evidence and building infrastructure to flag emerging fraud patterns earlier, while its field agents work alongside law enforcement to disrupt cargo theft operations directly. For brokers placing cargo or logistics cover, the articles say policies underwritten against 2023 or 2024 loss assumptions may no longer reflect current exposure, and carriers are tightening terms, adding exclusions and demanding stronger chain-of-custody controls from clients, conversations that now fall to brokers to initiate. Policyholders and industry professionals can report suspected fraud to NICB at reportinsurancefraud.org.
