stories.Headline: HHS publishes an eight-page clinical AI roadmap proposing state sandboxes and risk-based FDA review
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services published a federal roadmap for clinical artificial intelligence, hosted by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and dated Friday 13 November 2026, according to Nextgov. The roadmap proposes state sandboxes, risk-based FDA review, outcomes-based Medicare payment and post-market monitoring. It sets a "better than today" safety bar that clinical AI researchers, academic medical centres and research offices will need to plan around. The document is titled "A Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap: Better Answers, Faster Care, and Lower Costs" and runs eight pages. It uses the term clinical Super Intelligence (SI) throughout and states that SI is the former "AI," while Nextgov reported it on 16 November 2026 as a roadmap to boost clinical AI.

The PDF is hosted on cms.gov and says it "does not mandate SI adoption," "does not create a new agency or duplicate an existing regulator," and does not authorize autonomy that has not cleared the "better than today" bar for its risk tier. The document is organised around four priorities: earn public trust, build the data foundation, establish clear rules of the road, and pay for what works. It cites OpenAI's o3 model ranking the final diagnosis first in 60% of complex cases against 15.9% for internal medicine physicians, and Microsoft's MAI-DxO diagnosing 85.5% of challenging cases against roughly 20% for practising physicians. The roadmap's "rules of the road" section lists a continued rapid path to market for consumer wellness and clinical decision support software, consistent with FDA guidance it dates to 2026. It lists FDA regulation aligned to risk, "potentially anchoring around a novel competency-based approach, similar to how physicians are evaluated for their credentials," for certain SI-enabled devices.

Nextgov reports that an FDA discussion draft would require chatbots and generative AI to pass doctor-like competency tests before marketing. The roadmap lists real-world surveillance and predetermined change control plans, with FDA and CMS collaborating on surveillance infrastructure. It lists partnership with states on SI sandboxes in areas of state-only regulation, and clearer regulatory pathways that it says will lead to clearer ownership of liability, with federal guidelines aiming to offer best practices for de-risking innovation. CMS anticipates extending its ACCESS model to primary care, creating structures for SI-led solutions to join CMS Innovation Center primary care and total-cost-of-care models, exploring outcomes-based payment in Original Medicare, and working with states, including in Medicaid, on alternative payment tests. SI-led solutions would need partnerships with clinicians and facilities for escalation to human clinicians.

The roadmap builds on the White House AI Action Plan of July 2025, OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22, and an HHS strategy in December 2025 followed by a request for information. It says the CMS Health Tech Ecosystem grew from more than 60 initial company commitments to over 800, and that patient digital data access rose from roughly 5% to 60% in a year. The Medicare App Library launched in 2026. The roadmap points to FDA's TEMPO pilot and a January 2026 clinical decision support guidance. FDA's December 2025 announcement describes TEMPO as a voluntary pilot from its device centre in which manufacturers may request enforcement discretion for certain requirements, such as premarket authorization, in exchange for collecting and sharing real-world performance data, and it runs alongside the CMS ACCESS model.

CMS describes ACCESS as a voluntary 10-year Innovation Center model that pays for technology-supported chronic care based on outcomes; it began on 5 July 2026 and adds heart failure, COPD, substance use disorder and tobacco cessation tracks on 1 April 2027. The roadmap also cites FDA work with ARPA-H on the ADVOCATE programme to develop ways to evaluate highly autonomous systems. FDA has separately adopted the Super Intelligence terminology. Nextgov reports that the roadmap says the federal government wants to work with states on "areas of clear state regulation" without defining that phrase, and notes that states regulate the practice of medicine and license clinicians. It points to Utah, which is testing through phased pilots whether AI can safely issue initial prescriptions and refills, and reports that the roadmap does not say whether FDA oversees those pilots. Utah's Office of AI Policy told Nextgov it "remains dedicated to actively coordinating with federal partners."

The roadmap says it "will not wait for flawless evidence to open pathways, but it will require evidence to keep them open." The roadmap does not specify a reporting mechanism for monitoring data, so any institutional monitoring plan should anticipate the FDA and CMS surveillance infrastructure it describes rather than a fixed template. Where tools reach patients through ACCESS and TEMPO, organisations must be Medicare Part B-enrolled and name a medical director, per CMS. The roadmap names patient control of health data and consent to its use in SI as a core principle. HHS has also filed a final HIPAA rule changing patient record access. The roadmap says some FDA actions may trigger express preemption of differing state requirements, and ACCESS accepts applications on a rolling basis and adds new clinical tracks on 1 April 2027.

stories.Headline: West Side School Board formalizes $9 hourly student pay and weighs Idaho AI guidelines
stories.Summary:
The West Side School Board held its November meeting in the library of Beutler Middle School in Dayton, where motion sensors that control the lights kept switching off because seven adults sitting still did not move enough to keep them on. While the lights were on, the board began with the superintendent’s report, which shows the district uses approximately 2,500 gallons of gasoline and 9,800 gallons of diesel. The school pays for half of the fuel costs on things like bus routes, with the state picking up the other half, but it pays the full cost of fuel on sports trips and other extracurricular activities. To help with the cost of fuel, the school is looking into building a larger fuel storage and depot so that it can make bulk purchases and save on the per gallon cost. Board member Chris Robinson raised concerns over fuel quality dropping over time and spoke of an unnamed fuel stabilizer that claims to work for seven years, and then the lights turned off.

After a quick wave of the arms overhead to get the lights going again, the board moved onto student payments, because students who work during school hours in the Career Learning Center, or as part of the janitorial staff, have been unofficially getting paid at $9 per hour for their labor. That night after some discussion the board formalized them getting those payments, and the lights timed out again. Another arm wave followed, and the board proceeded on to the Idaho State Board of Education’s new guidelines for using generative AI, a policy that does not cover students using AI for their homework but covers what the district can do with AI as an institution. There were three decisions that the board could choose, and the lights went out again.

Under the first decision, the ball is ultimately in the Superintendent’s court, and in this case Tyler Telford can decide which AI tools are available to district staff and faculty. Under the second, the board does not have to mark or otherwise indicate that an email sent by the school was automatically generated by AI. Under the third, the school must get the parents’ consent before letting a student use AI tools if the tool in question requires it. After that, the board called for the meeting to adjourn.

stories.Headline: Damac chairman Hussain Sajwani says his Anthropic stake earned more in under two years than 30 years of investing
stories.Summary:
Hussain Sajwani, the 72-year-old chairman of Dubai-based luxury real estate developer Damac Properties, said at the Bloomberg Invest Dubai forum that what he made in 30 years he made in Anthropic in less than two years, according to Livemint. His comment came as Anthropic, the AI startup behind Claude, prepares for a Nasdaq IPO on Wednesday at a valuation of $1.4 trillion. The listing is expected to make all seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Christopher Olah, Jared Kaplan, Jack Clark and Sam McCandlish, multi-billionaires, while around 50 early employees are projected to cross the $100 million threshold in stock wealth. Sajwani said he expects his investments in AI firms, including Anthropic, to draw billions in returns.

In July 2024, Damac Group announced notable investments in AI companies, including $50 million in Anthropic, as one of the top investors who bought into the company from the cryptocurrency exchange FTX. The group also invested in Elon Musk's xAI and in Mistral, a France-based AI company behind one of the best European open-source large-language models. Sajwani said at the time that the group was excited to be part of the AI revolution and to contribute to the growth of the industry, adding that its investments in Mistral, Anthropic and xAI underscored its dedication to fostering innovation. He said that between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, the group is making a few billion dollars of profit.

Sajwani founded Damac Properties in 2002, and according to Forbes he started out in the food services business, catering to the US military and construction giant Bechtel, before shifting to real estate in 2001 after Dubai allowed foreigners to own property. Forbes puts his net worth at $15.3 billion, making him the 185th richest man in the world. Damac Group, his multi-billion-dollar conglomerate, divides its investments into seven core areas: real estate, capital markets, hotels and resorts, manufacturing, catering, high-end fashion and data centres, with a footprint across North America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East and Africa. Its notable activities include Damac Properties, the acquisition of Italian fashion house Roberto Cavalli and Swiss jewellery brand de GRISOGONO, the 50-storey DAMAC Towers Nine Elms in London and a luxury resort in the Maldives.

stories.Headline: Taisei launches a 150 million dollar fund for AI and robotics startups
stories.Summary:
The Japanese construction company Taisei announced on Monday, November 16, 2026, that it is establishing a new investment fund. This 153-year-old firm is dedicating 150 million dollars to support various startups specializing in robotics and artificial intelligence. The company intends to use these technological advancements to find viable workarounds for a shrinking domestic workforce. This strategic move aims to modernize the business by integrating automation into its traditional construction processes.

The fund will be managed by Pegasus Tech Ventures, a firm based in Silicon Valley that serves as the general partner. This partnership will focus on searching for new investments in automation and related fields through the year 2036. Taisei also plans to target startups that provide liquid-cooling infrastructure and high-density power solutions. These specific investments are intended to support the company as it expands its efforts into the construction of AI data centers.

Anis Uzzaman, who serves as the founder and chief executive officer of Pegasus, explained the purpose of the venture. He stated that the primary objective is to transform a traditional construction firm into a leader enabled by robotics and AI. Uzzaman further noted that the fund will help the company secure the necessary infrastructure for modern data centers. Pegasus currently manages over 2 billion dollars in assets and has previously worked with other Japanese companies like Aisin and Japanet Holdings.

This initiative comes as Japanese businesses struggle with chronic labor shortages, rising wages, and a general backlash against foreign workers. These economic pressures, combined with sliding domestic spending, are pushing more companies to adopt robotic solutions. Taisei has already shown interest in this sector by investing last year in a fund run by Met Fund Advisors. That previous investment focused on emerging startups coming out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

stories.Headline: Kotozna secures two Japanese patents for conversational AI on its 10th anniversary
stories.Summary:
Kotozna Inc., a Tokyo-based B2B SaaS company led by CEO Genri Goto, announced on November 17, 2026, that it had secured two Japanese patents for its conversational AI technology. The announcement coincided with the company's 10th anniversary, marking a decade of work in multilingual communication and enterprise AI. Kotozna was founded in October 2016 with a mission to overcome language barriers, and it has since expanded from multilingual communication services to generative AI-powered digital concierges, enterprise chatbots and interactive AI avatars. Its solutions now provide customer assistance around the clock in more than 50 languages, which reduces repetitive staff inquiries. The two patents are JP 7898212, called a Prompt Creation System, and JP 7932206, called an Answer Generation System, and together they cover prompt optimization and knowledge retrieval.

Rather than sending large amounts of information to AI models for every question, the technology builds optimized prompts containing only the information needed to generate appropriate responses. Unlike conventional RAG systems that divide documents into fixed-length segments, Kotozna's approach organizes information into meaningful sections so that important context is preserved. The company says this reduces unnecessary processing and token consumption, which helps improve response accuracy, lower latency and optimize AI operating costs, while also supporting efficient knowledge base updates as information changes. Goto said the mission over the past ten years had stayed the same, which is to make communication easier through technology. He described the patents as an important milestone in the company's journey and as a reflection of its commitment to developing AI that is innovative, reliable and practical for businesses worldwide.

The company states that its technology addresses three critical challenges in enterprise AI adoption, namely accuracy, speed and cost efficiency, enabling businesses to deploy reliable and scalable conversational AI solutions. Kotozna's solutions are deployed at more than 500 hotels and over 50 facilities and organizations, including airports, tourism organizations, shopping malls and public institutions in Japan and overseas. As Kotozna enters its second decade, the company says it will continue advancing its conversational AI capabilities toward intelligent AI agents that can handle complex inquiries, execute tasks and automate customer service workflows. It aims to strengthen its global presence through new deployments and partnerships, bringing its AI solutions to more businesses in hospitality, tourism, retail and other sectors worldwide. Kotozna reported capital of 70,000,000 yen as of December 31, 2025, and its head office is on the third floor of Hulic JP Akasaka in Minato-ku, Tokyo.

stories.Headline: Jesse Rome tells CX Today that AI makes selling harder and salespeople must become industry experts and trusted partners
stories.Summary:
Jesse Rome of Aslan Sales Training spoke to CX Today's Sean Nolan in an interview published on 18 November 2026 about how sales teams can use AI without losing the human side of selling. Rome said selling has become harder since he and Nolan did it, and that AI is a big reason. He said buyers have more information than ever before and ask why they need a sales rep if they can learn things on AI. He said the shift to virtual has created more decision makers in the room, with leaders from APAC and EMEA able to join a video call together. He said buyers now look for a solution partner who can make sense of different tools, tariffs and socioeconomic factors.

Rome said Aslan surveyed a thousand people in the B2B space and asked what is the number one thing they look for. He said buyers no longer need somebody who is an expert on products but people who are an expert on the industry. He said 90% of them named understanding their industry and having a unique solution as the number one decision-making factor. He said selling is harder, AI has given more information than ever, and socioeconomic factors are crazy. He said salespeople need to be more of a solution consultant and a trusted partner, not just a product expert.

Rome said Aslan has been around for about 30 years as a global sales training consulting firm partnering with large, medium and small organizations worldwide. He said it helps implement sales methodologies, organizational change and the conversion of product experts into trusted partners through enablement and certification. He said the foundation is being other centered, putting the needs of everybody you interact with before your own. He said people forget 90% of what they learn within a week, so Aslan Plus reinforces it through certifications, knowledge checks and AI-powered exercises. He said the future of AI is that it will start to replicate close to 80% of our productivity at 20% of the cost.

Rome said Aslan Plus is an AI-powered enablement platform built to help sellers sell, managers coach and organizations train and scale their go-to-market more efficiently. He said it works across four functions: comprehend, apply, master and integrate. He said application is the meat of the platform, with AI role plays as the flagship product and the right content at the right moment. He said mastery covers product, coaching and training certification, tracking compliance and development, because too many people are quiet quitting and the top 10% are not being invested in. He said Aslan used to be just a methodology company and is now a full enablement partner, so the platform must sit in the flow of work in the CRM, communication tools, CMS and SSO.

Rome said he probably fits into the bucket of salespeople hesitant about AI and thinks of himself as maybe a little smooth talking. He said you need humility, and you are either getting better or getting worse, with no staying the same. He said change is imminent and it is about whether you are ahead of the curve or behind it. He said AI is helping with workflows and messaging now, and that if you are not growing the bottom line in an organization of 200 reps, they will look at how to optimize your role. He said the human side of selling will never be replaced, the world of account managers and solution partners is where a lot of the growth is going, and AI will duplicate and scale exactly who you are.

Rome said every person is motivated by purpose or profit, either wanting to make more money or help more people. He said those motivated by money should learn a tool that duplicates their efforts and makes them more efficient if it stays in their voice and the right process. He said those who care about customers should implement AI because it will make sure you do not forget Cheryl's birthday. He said it will make sure you know about a merger and acquisition two weeks ago in their industry that will affect the global economics of those warehouses before it gets to you. He said if you truly care about your customers you will implement this because it gives more insights on the industry. He said whether you are motivated by purpose or profit, this can help you either way.

stories.Headline: South Korean President Lee proposes AI cooperation initiatives with ASEAN and Mekong nations
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung proposed expanded cooperation with ASEAN and Mekong nations on Monday, November 16, 2026, during summits in Manila. He suggested new initiatives focusing on artificial intelligence, trade, and security to ensure that everyone shares in the benefits of AI advances. Lee met with leaders at the 27th ASEAN-Republic of Korea Summit and a separate gathering at the Philippine International Convention Center. These meetings occurred as part of a four-day trip to the Philippines and China with first lady Kim Hea Kyung. The president emphasized the need for solidarity amid deepening geopolitical conflicts and growing economic uncertainty in the current international landscape.

The ASEAN-ROK AI Companionship Initiative and the ASEAN-ROK Cultural and Creative Industries Initiative aim to create new opportunities for young people. Lee proposed achieving annual bilateral trade of 300 billion US dollars by upgrading the ASEAN-Korea free trade agreement through proactive global responses. He pledged support for the ASEAN Community Vision 2045, a road map adopted in Malaysia in 2025 for a resilient, innovative ASEAN. Cooperation with Mekong nations, including Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia, will now include critical mineral supply chains and transnational crime. Bilateral trade between Korea and the Philippines reached 21.3 billion dollars as of September, surpassing the previous annual record.

President Lee stated that Korea is an ideal partner for Mekong countries because of its journey from aid recipient to donor. He claimed Korea possesses full-stack AI competitiveness, which includes infrastructure, models, applications, and services, to support safe and reliable AI development. Lee described ASEAN as a key partner for promoting lasting peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and a regional cooperation pillar. He expressed firm support for ASEAN centrality, meaning Southeast Asian countries should drive the political and security architecture of the Indo-Pacific. The president promised that South Korea would serve as a reliable action partner to help realize the long-term ASEAN Community Vision.

Philippine President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. said the partnership is relevant due to strategic uncertainty, rapid technological change, and various cross-border challenges. He noted that deep-rooted ties are reflected in shared strategic goals and vibrant people-to-people connections across the entire Southeast Asian region. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul agreed with Lee to pursue cooperation in nuclear energy, the defense industry, and the protection of intellectual property. The East Timor president recommended that the Korean people receive the Nobel Peace Prize during a summit meeting with President Lee. Korean companies operating in Thailand and the Philippines are affected by Lee's requests for government support to expand their local operations.

The Mekong summit resumed after six years following the 2021 military coup in Myanmar, marking the 15th anniversary of Korea-Mekong ties. ASEAN and Korea established a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024 to strengthen their existing diplomatic and economic relations across the region. Last year, Lee proposed a vision of being a contributor, springboard, and partner to deliver tangible benefits to the people of ASEAN. Korea and the Philippines signed a memorandum of understanding on science and technology cooperation to expand collaboration into the field of smart farming. They also signed a framework agreement on grant aid for projects run by the Korea International Cooperation Agency in the Philippines.

Lee and Prime Minister Anutin agreed to swiftly conclude a comprehensive economic partnership agreement to address uncertainty in the global trade environment. Korea and the Philippines committed to advancing future-oriented cooperation in aerospace, shipbuilding, disaster management, nuclear energy, and artificial intelligence technology. The two sides welcomed a plan to hold a special summit in Korea in 2029 for the 40th anniversary of dialogue relations. Lee will next attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, to continue his diplomatic meetings with various world leaders. The articles leave open the specific timeline for the industrial complexes and the final results of the free trade agreement negotiations.

stories.Headline: Korean man confesses to using AI to cheat on tax accountant exam as government investigates 528 national tests
stories.Summary:
Anonymous posters and a top exam scorer admitted to using AI to cheat on national exams in Korea around November 2026. A 34-year-old man surnamed Han confessed to cheating on the 63rd tax accountant certification exam. Other anonymous users claimed to have cheated on the civil service exam and the College Scholastic Ability Test. One user admitted to helping three other people pass an exam by lending them cheating devices. These admissions sparked a government investigation into AI-assisted cheating across various national tests.

The Ministry of Employment and Labor and HRDK will investigate 528 national certification exams administered this year. This review includes 37 professional qualifications like tax accountants and 491 technical qualifications like electrical engineers. Authorities will check for unusually high scores and large gaps in rankings compared to the last three years. For the 2027 CSAT, the government will assign dedicated personnel to test sites to identify smart glasses. A rapid-response system will link the Ministry of Education with metropolitan and provincial education offices.

The HRDK will establish a cheating tip-off center to analyze reports and online allegations. Grading experts will review answer sheets from first and second rounds for any flagged suspicious cases. If experts find clear grounds for suspicion, authorities plan to refer those cases to the police. A KRX spokesperson said they invalidated a June exam result and barred an applicant for five years. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency is investigating Han after he submitted a written confession.

A medical student in the greater Seoul area claimed to achieve a 98.6 average percentile using a camera. A Grade 9 civil servant stated they felt no remorse because their job requires little specialized expertise. Singer Ateez's J-Hope encouraged students who worked hard while urging adults to strengthen safeguards. Other users criticized the anonymous posters for their lack of remorse regarding the alleged cheating. The identities and exam results of the anonymous posters have not been verified by authorities.

The controversy grew after Han admitted to using generative AI and electronic devices on his certification exam. HRDK already detected 12 cases of smart glasses cheating for fire protection and information processing engineers. A similar incident involving smart glasses occurred during a Korea Exchange recruitment exam in June. Training for smart glasses inspectors took place on November 11 at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education. These events have led to increased worries about AI-assisted cheating across the country.

The government will refer confirmed cheating cases to the police or other investigative agencies for further action. Authorities are currently tightening anticheating measures ahead of the annual college entrance exam scheduled for Thursday. The police Provincial Special Detective Corps is leading the investigation into the tax accountant exam scandal. stories.Headline: South Korea pushes a health data law that lets researchers use pseudonymized medical records without patient consent
stories.Summary:
The government is pushing the Digital Healthcare Act, which would let pseudonymized medical information be used broadly without individual consent to promote medical AI development and health research, and the plan has sparked controversy. The Ministry of Health and Welfare and the National Assembly are seeking to enact the law, with passage targeted within the year, according to the 16th report. The Lee Jae Myung government had presented as a national agenda the building of an AI expressway to leap into the top three AI powers. It stated that in the bio and healthcare sectors the government would collect and link data to create a data ecosystem. Critics say the bill lowers the threshold for data use without adequate personal information safeguards.

The core of the bill is to establish a legal basis for the secondary use of personal health and medical information and to build large-scale datasets on that basis. At present, pseudonymized medical data can be used for research when individuals are hard to identify, but data collection is restricted and external transfer must be approved by the medical institutions holding the data. Under the bill, the Minister of Health and Welfare may request data provision from the National Health Insurance Service, the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service, medical data-centered hospitals and participating medical institutions. Absent special reasons, institutions that receive requests must comply. For example, if the ministry requests from Hospital A the clinical information of patients who underwent cancer surgery in a given year, the hospital must provide it in pseudonymized form unless there are special reasons not to.

A Ministry of Health and Welfare official explained that a researcher who wishes to use health and medical data must undergo review at each individual institution. The official said review criteria and procedures differ across institutions, so it often takes more than a year just to collect the data. The official also said the government has no authority to oversee whether the reviews are being conducted properly. Lee Sang-yun, chief research fellow at Research Community Health and Alternatives and an occupational and environmental medicine specialist, said that if his medical information were to be used to advance the AI industry, many people would likely not agree.

He said there is currently no consent process in place that ensures individual autonomy. Civil society groups, labor circles and patient organizations are demanding supplements, saying protections for patient rights and personal information are lacking compared with the industrial use of medical information. The data provided may include genetic information or whether the patient has a rare disease, which can allow inferences about the patient and the family disease history. Information on rare diseases with only a few dozen patients may, when combined with other information, identify an individual.

Kim Sung-Ju, head of the Korea Severe Disease Alliance, said at a National Assembly forum held on the 2nd that if research achievements based on patient information come back as high-priced pharmaceuticals or treatment technologies, the costs will again be borne by patients and the public. The current bill does not specify a right for individuals to refuse the provision of their information. The UK and Germany institutionally guarantee a patient's right not to agree to the use of their health and medical information for research and similar purposes. In England, the National Health Service operates a National Data Opt-out system that allows patients to refuse the use of their medical information for research, policymaking and similar uses.

Patients can register or withdraw their refusal at any time via the website or by phone. Another issue raised is that even if particular researchers or companies obtain industrial benefits from research using medical information, there is no structure that allows the patients who provided the information or the public to share in those benefits. stories.Headline: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin admits Korea cannot guarantee detection of AI cheating before the CSAT
stories.Summary:
Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin admitted that authorities cannot guarantee the detection of AI cheating before the college entrance exam. This admission occurred on November 16 during a National Assembly Education Committee meeting held in Yeouido, Seoul. The minister spoke during a plenary meeting while answering questions from lawmakers about the security of the upcoming test. He acknowledged that countermeasures against miniature cameras and similar equipment would probably not be perfect for the examination. These statements were made just two days before the start of the College Scholastic Ability Test in Korea.

The government will now require candidates to surrender smart devices and block public Wi-Fi at all examination centers. Authorities also announced the formation of an interagency task force to handle the threat of AI assisted cheating. These new measures were announced on November 16 to protect the integrity of the largest annual national examination. The government is also ordering a retrospective review of 528 national exams following a major AI cheating scandal. These changes aim to prevent the use of sophisticated electronic devices during the high stakes university admission process.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told People Power Party Rep. Park Jeong-hun that he could not identify every cheating case. He stated that he did not think the government could guarantee the detection of all AI assisted cheating attempts. The prime minister demanded vigorous effort to prevent violations and called for harsh punishment for those who cheat. He emphasized that the nation must prepare carefully as it approaches the biggest test day of the year. The minister's candid remarks have led some to describe his current position as irresponsible given the timing.

Some students and parents are demanding that the CSAT be postponed because of the intense fear of cheating. These groups worry that the fairness of university admissions will be undermined if the government cannot stop AI. Other affected parties include candidates in professional qualification exams, university essay tests, and various school based academic assessments. The public confidence in the system that determines educational opportunities for young people is now at serious risk. Many feel that the government responses lag far behind the rapidly evolving methods used by those who cheat.

AI cheating became more apparent after the top scorer on the certified tax accountant examination made several shocking revelations. In May, a candidate in Gwangju was caught using AI equipped glasses during a fire protection engineering certification exam. Prosecutors sought a summary judgment against that candidate for violating the National Technical Qualifications Act during the May test. Other cases have emerged in the Law School Admission Test, English proficiency tests, and various national professional qualification examinations. Online vendors have openly sold cheating kits, and button camera sets have reportedly sold out to prospective examinees.

The government must now procure and install additional equipment, which presents considerable practical difficulties with only two days remaining. Authorities must decide if they can comprehensively restrict communication between the examination rooms and all outside parties. Other countries have already revised professional exams, prohibited digital devices, or introduced measures to block all wireless communications. The articles leave open whether the current interagency task force can actually ensure a fair testing environment for students. The Ministry of Education will visually inspect glasses before the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday, November 19, 2026. stories.Headline: Reporter uses AI glasses to solve difficult CSAT math questions in 22 minutes
stories.Summary:

The reporter tested the device on math and science sections to see if cheating was possible. This experiment showed that difficult math killer questions could be solved in one to two minutes. The reporter finished the entire math section in 22 minutes and scored 98 points. A tricky Korean language question was answered by the AI in only one second.

The reporter used Rokid Glass AI from the Chinese company Rokid, which was released last January. These glasses cost about 750 dollars, weigh 49 grams, and look like ordinary horn-rimmed glasses. The device used the Gemini AI model and required a 20 minute setup before starting. The reporter solved 30 math questions and 20 Life Science I questions using the device. The science section took 12 minutes and 44 seconds, resulting in a score of 34.

Senior Staff Reporter Jeong Ji-yun performed the test and found the AI produced answers very quickly. The reporter noted that the AI provided correct choices and explanations for each wrong option. It was observed that the display on the lens was not visible to nearby people. However, the reporter mentioned that unnatural head movements and touching the temple could look suspicious. The reporter also found that the battery drained from 75 percent to 30 percent quickly.

Education authorities are preparing to ban AI glasses from test sites because the CSAT is three days away. This follows cheating reports in national technical qualification tests and the certified tax accountant exam. A top scorer in the tax exam admitted to using an ultra-small camera for cheating. These technologies threaten the fairness of the CSAT, which is a key gateway in Korean society.

The Human Resources Development Service of Korea detected smart glasses in four of five cheating cases. Most of those cases involved the Rokid model used by the reporter in this experiment. General purpose AI models struggled with science subjects that require specific training like pedigree analysis. Major generative AIs gave conflicting wrong answers to the same Korean question only one year ago. This shows that AI progress has been steep and is becoming more sophisticated.

Authorities cannot deploy radio-frequency or metal detectors to every nationwide test site within three days. Current proctoring manuals have clear limits when policing these advanced AI devices. stories.Headline: A Lifecycle Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Construction Research
stories.Summary:
An international team of researchers from Australia, Finland, Morocco and Thailand systematically reviewed a decade of published research on how artificial intelligence can support climate adaptation and mitigation at every stage of a construction project, from material production through demolition. The review, published in the KeAi journal Risk Sciences, followed PRISMA guidelines and combined bibliometric and content analyses to map where AI is being applied, how mature those applications are and what barriers stand in the way of adoption. The authors propose a lifecycle-based framework linking AI applications to climate outcomes, technological maturity and adoption barriers. Buildings and construction consume vast quantities of concrete, steel and aluminum and account for a substantial share of global energy use and energy-related carbon emissions, and the sector faces growing pressure both to cut its climate impact and to become more resilient as extreme weather events intensify.

The review found that AI can contribute across the whole construction lifecycle, including lower-carbon and more resilient materials, greener procurement and supply chains, energy-efficient and climate-resilient design, optimized equipment and scheduling on site, smarter building operation and maintenance, and better recycling and waste recovery at end of life. The team distilled these contributions into a conceptual framework identifying three principal pathways: cleaner and more resource-efficient energy use, decarbonization of the built environment, and responsible production and consumption of resources. The evidence is unevenly distributed, with most studies focused on mitigation such as cutting emissions and energy use and far fewer exploring adaptation such as climate-resilient infrastructure or extreme-weather preparedness. Applications such as predictive maintenance, building energy optimization and computer-vision monitoring are relatively mature, whereas generative climate-resilient design and fully integrated digital twins remain largely at the pilot stage.

Corresponding author Fahim Ullah of Victoria University in Australia said AI should not be treated as an isolated technological application but as a lifecycle-wide enabling technology that works best when integrated with complementary tools such as building information modeling, digital twins and the Internet of Things. He said the presence of AI capability does not automatically produce a net-positive climate outcome, because training and operating the models requires computational resources and electricity, and the climate benefits of AI must be evaluated against its own environmental footprint. Ullah added that AI can make a major contribution to a low-carbon, climate-resilient construction industry but is neither a standalone solution nor inherently sustainable. The authors also identify key barriers including poor data quality, interoperability problems, high implementation costs, organizational readiness, regulatory uncertainty and cybersecurity concerns, and they stress that AI is not environmentally neutral.

stories.Headline: BusPatrol runs AI school bus cameras in Montgomery County that generate tickets but show little decline in violations
stories.Summary:
BusPatrol, a company that operates artificial-intelligence-powered cameras on roughly 35,000 school buses in 24 states and more than 350 school districts, began operating in Montgomery County in 2017, and by the 2019, 20 school year all Montgomery County Public Schools buses had been equipped with cameras, according to an investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek in partnership with Type Investigations. The investigation found that school bus cameras in the county have generated more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines, but that violations have remained relatively consistent, with little evidence that collisions near stopped school buses have declined. The number of citations per active camera barely changed over five years, averaging 36 per active camera in 2020 and falling only to 34 by 2025. The investigation also identified at least three children who were struck by drivers while getting on or off stopped school buses in Montgomery County since 2017, based on a review of local news reports and school bus camera footage.

There has been some more recent improvement in the numbers, with Montgomery County police reporting 40,854 citations for illegally passing stopped school buses during the 2025, 26 school year, a 19.1% decrease from the previous school year, though thousands of drivers continue to pass stopped school buses while their red lights are flashing and stop arms are extended. The BusPatrol cameras use artificial intelligence to identify vehicles that appear to illegally pass a stopped school bus with its stop arm extended, capturing video and images of the vehicle including its license plate and sending that footage to local law enforcement for review, and police determine whether a violation occurred, so the technology does not automatically issue a ticket. The county's Vision Zero program has defended the cameras as a tool for accountability and education, as well as a way to collect information about dangerous driving around school buses. The investigation raises a broader question about whether more citations are translating into fewer dangerous encounters for children.

Other communities across the Washington region also use school bus stop-arm enforcement cameras, although those programs were not included in the national investigation. In Falls Church, Virginia, the city issued 1,193 school bus camera citations in 2025, more than twice the 546 citations issued when the program began in 2015, while Fairfax County launched its own school bus camera enforcement program in 2025 and recorded more than 6,300 citations or warnings between April 2024 and Dec. 17, 2025. Washington, D.C., also installed stop-arm safety cameras on 25 school buses in 2024, and the District's program is separate from the BusPatrol system examined in the investigation.

The debate over school bus camera enforcement comes as Montgomery County continues to track pedestrian safety concerns, recording 336 pedestrian-involved crashes countywide during the first nine months of 2026, including 17 fatal crashes, figures that include pedestrian crashes throughout the county and are not limited to school buses or school zones. The central question remains whether automated school bus enforcement is doing enough to prevent children from being struck by drivers, or whether additional safety measures are needed beyond issuing citations.

Articles.Title: Do Montgomery County AI-powered school bus cameras make children safer?

stories.Headline: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Asan Medical Center in Seoul developed a deep learning model to identify a rare and aggressive kidney cancer called fumarate hydratase-deficient renal cell carcinoma. This study, published in npj Digital Medicine, tested the tool using 335 digitized pathology slides to see if it could help doctors distinguish this specific cancer from other renal types. Twenty-one pathologists, including seven residents and fourteen specialists, examined 30 challenging cases both independently and with the assistance of the AI. The results showed that AI assistance increased overall diagnostic accuracy from 60% to 73.3% and improved precision from 66.7% to 77.8%.

The AI model, built on the ResNeXt101 architecture, flags suspected cases and generates color-coded maps to highlight suspicious tissue regions for the doctors. It is designed to help pathologists identify patients who may require additional genetic analysis or immunohistochemistry testing for a final diagnosis. The study found that receptive doctors improved their accuracy but had a median overreliance rate of 80%, meaning they often accepted incorrect AI advice. Resistant doctors were less influenced by AI errors, but they showed no statistically significant improvement in their diagnostic accuracy during the tests.

Professor Yong Mee Cho stated that AI could help clinicians recognize rare cancers they might otherwise overlook to ensure patients receive confirmatory testing. Professor Namkug Kim noted that effective AI use requires skills independent of traditional diagnostic expertise, which suggests a need for tailored human-AI collaboration strategies. The researchers questioned whether conventional clinical training adequately prepares doctors to critically assess AI recommendations to avoid overreliance. Future studies in routine pathology settings will determine if specialized training can help doctors benefit from AI while reducing the risk of errors.

Articles.Title: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?

stories.Headline: Jennifer Wood says auditors must validate AI output and challenge it with professional skepticism
stories.Summary:
Jennifer Wood, a partner and the assurance service line leader at the Bonadio Group, wrote in a Bloomberg Tax article published on November 18, 2026, that artificial intelligence must test rather than replace auditors’ professional skepticism. She said the AICPA’s new guidance on using AI in financial reporting and auditing, published on October 13, 2026, arrived at the perfect time and is nonauthoritative but increasingly relevant to audit quality and peer-review readiness. She said the practice aid lacks guidance on how firms should consistently validate and document AI-assisted procedures, particularly when AI is used to identify exceptions or support audit conclusions, along with practical examples. She said the biggest challenge for audit firms is determining when auditors can trust AI output, how to validate it, and when their own professional skepticism requires them to challenge it.

Wood said AI does not change auditors’ responsibility to secure sufficiently appropriate audit evidence but changes how they fulfill that responsibility. She said the biggest misconception is that AI is simply a faster way to perform existing tasks, when it is actually an opportunity to rethink how audits are performed. She said an AI output can be accurate without being complete, and she prefers the expression “validate before relying.” She said her firm has used AI for financial statement tie-outs and document analysis, and that a tie-out involving more than 100 pages historically consumed nearly two days of staff time, which AI can accelerate while identifying inconsistencies a human reviewer might overlook, though the auditor must still confirm the results. She said that in a hypothetical example of using AI to review 1,000 revenue contracts and identify unusual recognition provisions, the tool flags 25 contracts and all 25 are legitimate exceptions, but it might have overlooked another 10 contracts containing problematic provisions, so every exception identified was accurate yet the analysis was incomplete.

Wood said professional skepticism has historically focused on challenging management’s assertions, estimates, and representations, but now auditors must also challenge the technology that helps them evaluate those assertions. She said AI-generated work can look remarkably polished and authoritative, which can create a false sense of confidence, and auditors should instinctively ask what evidence supports a conclusion, what assumptions were made, and what might have been missed. She said AI creates additional responsibilities for engagement partners and reviewers, who need to understand how AI is being used on their engagements and whether appropriate validation has occurred, without needing to understand every technical aspect of the underlying model. She said firms need clear policies defining approved AI tools, permissible uses, confidentiality requirements, and expectations for validation and documentation, and that documentation for AI-assisted audit procedures should identify the tool used, the purpose of the procedure, the relevant inputs and outputs, how results were validated, and how the work influenced audit conclusions.

Wood said firms should distinguish between AI used for administrative efficiency and AI used to support audit evidence, which warrant different levels of oversight, and should incorporate AI governance into their existing system of quality management rather than treat it as a separate technology initiative. She said AI can improve audit quality and reduce the risk of human fatigue associated with repetitive procedures, citing financial statement tie-outs and document analysis as examples, and that AI can quickly summarize key provisions in a lengthy lease agreement or debt agreement so the auditor can focus on evaluating the accounting implications. She said the goal should be better audits, not just faster ones, and the greatest opportunity is reinvesting time saved in higher-value audit activities including risk assessment, investigating exceptions, and challenging management’s assumptions. She said that over the next three to five years, the firms that succeed will be those that integrate AI into their methodologies, invest in quality management, and fundamentally rethink how they develop their people, and that the firms that differentiate themselves won’t necessarily be using AI the most but will be demonstrating that AI is making their audits better.

Articles.Title: AI Must Test, Not Replace, Auditors’ Professional Skepticism

It said the catalyst would require extraordinary coordination among major TradFi companies and the Aster ecosystem, which is currently highly unlikely. It said interested parties in Bitcoin's expanding Layer 2 ecosystem are eagerly anticipating Hyper's market debut before it becomes available on centralized exchanges. The article did not say whether Meta AI or Mark Zuckerberg commented beyond the prediction itself. The article left open whether any institutional partnership, token utility upgrade or regulatory tailwind would actually materialize for Aster.

stories.Headline: Soros Fund Management reduces its stake in Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Soros Fund Management reduced its position in Nvidia during the quarter ending September 30. This move represented the largest disclosed reduction in the stock for the fund this year. The investment firm sold approximately 206,000 shares of the company. These shares were valued at as much as 47.4 million dollars. The action occurred as artificial intelligence hype began to cool.

The fund retained a stake worth just under 200 million dollars on September 30. This reduction of nearly a fifth followed earlier additions to the Nvidia position. At least a dozen family offices also reduced holdings, keeping combined positions above 1 billion dollars. Nvidia shares rose 22 percent through September 30, doubling the S&P 500 gain. The company is based in Santa Clara, California.

Dawn Fitzpatrick leads Soros Fund Management and previously served as an executive at UBS Group AG. George Soros is 96 years old and has an estimated worth of 9.7 billion dollars. The articles do not provide direct quotes from these individuals regarding the sale. They note that investors often reassess positions as new tools reshape their perspectives. These details came from required 13F reports for managers overseeing 100 million dollars.

Michael Platt of BlueCrest Capital Management also trimmed his stake in the company. President Donald Trump and some Silicon Valley backers are advocating for the return of the former CEO. Jensen Huang, age 63, was ousted on November 12 following disclosures of extramarital relationships. Some of these relationships were with Nvidia employees and a suspected Chinese spy. The Justice Department suspected the woman of being a spy.

Nvidia was a standout stock as investors chased the artificial intelligence boom. The market turned shakier after a late October New York Times report on Chinese espionage. That report suggested Jensen Huang might have been targeted in an espionage effort. Consequently, the stock has fallen more than 25 percent since that report. The company is now searching for a new chief executive officer.

Nvidia reports its third quarter results on Tuesday with Colette Kress stepping in. The articles leave open whether Jensen Huang will actually return to his role. They do not state if other family offices will further reduce their holdings. The future of the CEO search remains an open question for the company. It is unclear how the espionage allegations will affect future stock performance.

Articles.Title: Soros Fund Cuts Nvidia Stake as AI Hype Cools

stories.headline_source: Soros Fund Cuts Nvidia Stake as AI Hype Cools

stories.Headline: Denmark and Ukraine sign declaration for Danish forces to train military AI on Ukrainian battlefield data
stories.Summary:
Denmark’s Ministry of Defense announced on Tuesday that Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus and his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, signed a declaration agreeing to cooperate on the development of artificial intelligence, according to a Kyiv Post report dated November 18, 2026. Under the agreement, the Danish armed forces will receive large quantities of battlefield data and images from Ukraine, which they will use to train their own warfighting AI models. The deal gives Denmark direct access to Ukraine’s advanced Avengers Labs, which has built an extensive database drawn from millions of battlefield images and other information. Avengers Labs was initiated by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and uses the DELTA target detection system, which has created an annotated dataset obtained from more than 100,000 drone video streams each month. Denmark joins what the Danish ministry described as an exclusive club, since the United Kingdom was the first international partner to gain access to the platform.

The agreement requires Danish experts to work with their Ukrainian counterparts on the extensive dataset so they can train their own AI models and applications. That work is meant to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence into military operations in support of the defense capabilities of both countries. Denmark’s armed forces are also establishing their own AI Center, which will be the focus for implementing the new agreement. The center will coordinate cooperation with companies and research institutions that will enhance the country’s defense technology contribution. The Danish ministry said the cooperation would help develop the combat power of the Danish defense forces through knowledge of artificial intelligence and new technologies.

Bruus said technology on the battlefield is constantly developing and that Ukraine is at the forefront in this area. He said it is therefore very valuable that Denmark can learn from Ukraine through cooperation, though he acknowledged it rests on a sad basis. Bruus also said Denmark continues its unwavering support for Ukraine while strengthening the capabilities of its own armed forces through the sharing of AI and emerging military technologies. The Kyiv Post report describes the Danish ministry’s announcement as the source for the details of the declaration and the access it grants.

The report places the agreement in the wider context of Denmark’s support for Ukraine and its effort to build up its own military technology. It says the Danish armed forces are setting up an AI Center that will serve as the hub for the new cooperation and for coordination with companies and research institutions. The Kyiv Post, which describes itself as Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995, carried the announcement. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the establishment of the AI Center and the planned work with Ukrainian counterparts.

Articles.Title: Ukrainian Combat Data to Help Shape Denmark’s Next Generation of Military AI

stories.headline_source: Ukrainian Combat Data to Help Shape Denmark’s Next Generation of Military AI

stories.Headline: Israel can turn AI infrastructure constraints into opportunity through energy planning, article says
stories.Summary:
A sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections has raised investor concern that data center projects will face more local opposition and tighter restrictions, according to an opinion article by Lior Prosor published by The Jerusalem Post on November 18, 2026. The article says the market routing last Thursday showed that AI trade investors now worry about delays in electricity supply and computing capacity. It argues the market may be overstating the impact of these delays and that the period could be a buying opportunity. For Israel, the article says, the situation should also be a wake-up call.

The article says opposition to data centers stems from residents wanting to know who will pay to expand the grid and what communities will receive, such as tax revenues and local jobs. It points to BAAJA, a bipartisan permitting reform package whose sponsors released an updated version on November 7, which aims to streamline approvals and expand the transmission grid while requiring data centers to cover the costs they add. The package has not passed and would not eliminate local authorities' powers. The article also says a delay in a US project does not necessarily mean lost sales for suppliers, because another customer elsewhere may take the equipment, and it cites SpaceX building capacity outside the US, including a large project in Saudi Arabia, and renting compute through short-term contracts at market prices. It says SpaceX has reported that at current prices new deployments pay back their investment in less than a year.

The article says Israel can become a significant player without matching US investment levels, but the government and the national AI directorate need to connect computing ambitions to an energy plan they can execute. It lists immediate priorities as electricity generation, storage, transmission and grid connections, and calls for a multiyear plan with funding, clear accountability and delivery targets. It says microgrids and regional partnerships in energy and infrastructure should be added alongside expansion of the national grid. The article names Phinergy, which develops long-duration aluminum-air backup power as an alternative to diesel, Turbogen, which offers microturbines for local electricity generation including for smaller data centers, and Bezeq, which could see greater demand for connectivity between distributed computing sites.

The article says not every use of AI requires a giant data center, because inference can often take place in smaller facilities and local systems close to users and electricity sources. It says the difficulty of building AI infrastructure increases the value of those who can deliver it, and that investors may find opportunities in companies the market is punishing too severely. For Israel, it says, this opens a path to build domestic capabilities and sell the world solutions to a shortage everyone is facing. The article notes that its forecasts can prove wrong and computing prices can fall.

Articles.Title: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.headline_source: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.Headline: OpenAI adds computer-use agents and over 20 plugins to ChatGPT for Healthcare
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 16, 2026, that it is expanding ChatGPT for Healthcare with advances in computer-use agents, improved trusted clinical search, and more than 20 new healthcare plugins. The computer-use agents can navigate existing healthcare software by reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications. OpenAI said it is working with healthcare organizations including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together information care teams need. The announcement was reported by HCI Innovation Group on Nov. 17, 2026, in an article by Pietje Kobus-McAllister. The updates are intended to help healthcare organizations reduce time spent navigating disconnected software and streamline workflows from referral management and documentation to insurance verification and care coordination.

The computer-use agents include access controls and audit logs, and organizations can set which applications agents can access and which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models. In a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations, and in over 1300 reviews rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness. All of the more than 20 new plugins are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, including through ChartGPT, which brings ChatGPT into the EHR workflow.

The plugin list includes Aiva, Amion, Assort Health, Availity, Extend, Elation Health, Ferry, IMO Health, MCP Server, Infinitus, Relay, K Health, Luma Health, Metriport, Notable Integration Specs, Oracle HDI Overview, PenguinAI Medical Coding, Photon, Redox, Stedi, Subsalt, Trizetto, Turquoise, and UpToDate Expert AI. Elation Health's read-only beta plugin lets primary care practice managers use ChatGPT to identify patients scheduled for the following day who have gaps in insurance, registration, or contact information, and staff receive a list of issues to review and address in Elation's electronic health record before patients arrive. Kyna Fong, co-founder and CEO of Elation Health, said AI earns its place in primary care by helping the people who use it, and that the company earns it by being thoughtful about its use, maintaining control, and using it to make stronger systems. Infinitus is bringing its Relay agents into ChatGPT to support benefits verification and prior authorization workflows, and users can initiate a benefits verification, check the status of a prior authorization and identify next steps, or submit batch requests using a spreadsheet. Ankit Jain, CEO of Infinitus, said the next chapter of AI in healthcare won't be defined by how much information it can surface but by what it can actually accomplish.

The Elation beta is initially available to a limited group of Elation practices, and the company said the approach is designed to keep administrative work with AI while leaving clinical decisions and patient outreach under the control of practice teams. Relay is available to existing Infinitus customers using ChatGPT for Healthcare, and the integration is designed to let healthcare and life sciences organizations access Infinitus agents without leaving ChatGPT. Jain said healthcare is full of complex, interconnected workflows that require more than answering questions, requiring navigating systems, taking action, and following through, and that bringing Infinitus agents into ChatGPT combines frontier AI with specialized healthcare capabilities while maintaining the safeguards healthcare demands. The plugins let teams bring more of their work into the same conversation, including reviewing patient records and hospital protocols, preparing prescriptions for clinician review, coordinating patient outreach, checking insurance eligibility, and analyzing healthcare costs and operational performance. The new plugins join ChatGPT's broader ecosystem of plugins supporting work across industries, from healthcare data and research to documents, presentations, and software development.

OpenAI said healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, OpenAI is bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients. In a demo, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request, and the agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review. The articles give examples including a care coordinator using Luma Health to find tomorrow's appointments that still need confirmation and TriZetto to check insurance eligibility, and a primary care physician using Metriport to find a discharge summary and UpToDate to check follow-up monitoring. Other examples include an inpatient nurse using AIVA for a hospital's inpatient pump policy and Amion to find the covering endocrinologist, a care navigator using IMO Health, Stedi, and Turquoise Health to compare MRI sites, and a referral manager using Assort Health and Ferry Health for referral review.

ChatGPT for Healthcare customers have computer-use agents in ChatGPT Work and Codex and improved trusted clinical search available today, subject to workspace settings, and workspace administrators can enable new healthcare plugins. Individual clinicians have computer-use agents in ChatGPT Work and Codex and improved trusted clinical search available today, and select plugins are also available. ChatGPT for Clinicians is free for eligible, verified clinicians in the U.S. to review medical evidence and prepare clinical documentation, and both products offer customers a Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI to support HIPAA-compliant workflows. Computer-use agent capability is available in the OpenAI API, ChatGPT Work, and Codex, and customers can purchase ChatGPT for Healthcare directly or through an AWS Marketplace private offer by contacting the sales team. OpenAI said it is continuing to invest in the plugin ecosystem and inviting more healthcare companies to build with it.

stories.Headline: Nvidia cuts its Nokia stake by 56% while Nokia expands its AI and cloud business
stories.Summary:
Nvidia disclosed late Monday that it had sold 93.53 million Nokia shares during the third quarter, cutting its position by 56% and leaving it with 72.86 million shares worth $738.8 million on Sept. 30, down from 166.39 million shares at the end of June. The chipmaker had agreed in October 2025 to invest $1 billion in Nokia at $6.01 a share for a 2.9% stake, alongside a partnership to run Nokia's 5G and future 6G network software on Nvidia chips. Nokia shares fell 5% on Monday to $7.69, a third consecutive session in the red, and slipped another 1% overnight after the stake sale became known. Nvidia also cut its Intel stake by 25% and its Synopsys stake by nearly 10% during the same quarter.

In the same quarter as the stake cut, Nokia's sales to AI and cloud customers rose 123% from a year earlier and orders from those customers grew 118%. On Monday, Nokia teamed up with Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda to form AI Gigafactory Northern, which plans to bid for an EU contract to build and operate computing sites for European businesses, researchers and public agencies, with Nokia supplying the networking equipment. The partners have selected Oulu in Finland, Iru in Estonia and Valmiera in Latvia, and are still choosing a location in Sweden. Nokia also signed a multiyear agreement licensing its video technology for use in ASUS devices, resolving all related patent litigation between the companies, with financial terms kept confidential.

The partnership between the two companies continued after Nvidia reduced its holdings, and last month Nokia reported progress in using Nvidia chips to process radio signals and bring AI services closer to mobile users, citing work with European operators including BT, Deutsche Telekom, Elisa and Orange. On Stocktwits, Nokia retail sentiment has been bearish for a month amid a 1,250% surge in 24-hour message volumes, with several traders eyeing $5, about 35% below Monday's closing price and a dollar below what Nvidia originally paid per share. One user said $5 was their year-end target, another expects Nokia to fall back to $5 or lower, and a third flagged a possible slide to $6 and then $5 by year-end. Nokia's U.S.-listed stock has risen 20% year-to-date.

stories.Headline: FBI reissues advisory warning that criminals use ARTEX to automate business intrusions
stories.Summary:
The FBI reissued its FLASH advisory from the previous week about cybercriminals using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to target businesses globally, according to a Benzinga report published on November 18, 2026. The bureau said attackers can use ARTEX to automate intrusions and potentially move from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. According to the advisory, the framework was used during the October ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which exposed Microsoft 365 customer environments. The FBI directed companies and other organizations to monitor suspicious automated activity and to report potential compromises through the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Cryptocurrency bettors doubt that artificial intelligence caused the recent Federal Aviation Administration outage, even as the FBI repeated its warning about AI tools automating cyberattacks on businesses. Polygon-based Polymarket currently assigns only a 3% chance that the federal government officially attributes last week's nationwide flight ground stop to AI. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem appears tied to a router installation by an FAA contractor, with investigators still trying to pin down whether the failure was human error, a bad device or something else. Multiple outages over the last week have businesses and the administration on edge, including a Microsoft outage that disrupted access to Outlook and Teams.

Thousands of JPMorgan Chase customers reported problems accessing their accounts on Monday, and NSANet, the internal classified communications network for the National Security Agency, also went offline on Tuesday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said authorities found zero evidence of a coordinated cyberattack behind outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan, airlines and government agencies. Microsoft shares were sliding Tuesday as software stocks faced pressure from outage concerns, AI disruption fears and cybersecurity worries. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the FBI's call for monitoring and reporting through the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Articles.Title: FBI Reissues Warning About AI-Powered Cyberattacks on Businesses as Crypto Bettors Dismiss AI Link to FAA Outage

stories.Headline: Sujay Maladi wins first place at USC AI hackathon with QuestSC campus map platform
stories.Summary:
USC’s AI Strategy Committee collaborated with HackSC, a student hackathon organization, to host the first “AI@USC Hackathon” over the weekend at Ginsburg Hall. The event brought together over 300 student participants and several guest speakers, including industry professionals and University faculty. Students were tasked with designing an AI-powered solution to improve the USC student experience on campus, whether academically, professionally or socially. With $14,000 in prize money on the line, hundreds of students competed to reimagine the future of USC student life by leveraging artificial intelligence. Sujay Maladi, a master’s student studying computer science, won first place with a platform named “QuestSC.”

The hackathon was open to students of any major or school at USC, including graduate students. Competing teams formed groups by 11 a.m. on Saturday and had until 11 a.m. on Sunday to submit their final proposals, including a prototype, GitHub link, video demo and slide deck. Ten finalists were then chosen to pitch their ideas to a panel of judges, which consisted of faculty, professors, professionals and entrepreneurs. Prizes included $14,000, split between 3 finalists, as well as potential professional opportunities, including interviews and company visits. The winning projects will be considered by the Undergraduate Student Government and the University for possible implementation on campus.

Geoffrey Garrett, the chair of President Beong-Soo Kim’s AI Strategy Committee and special advisor to the president for global strategy and engagement, said students are at the frontier of technology, making them an “incredible resource.” He said the big theme of the hackathon is “For Trojans, by Trojans.” He said the organizers genuinely want to improve the student experience and know the best way to do that is to leverage the expertise of students. Maladi said he wanted to make something for USC and feels USC’s websites are completely disconnected. Maladi said he needs to find a way to integrate all of them into one thing and would really love to see this being used by all the fellow Trojans.

The second-place winner was Forage, a platform for students to efficiently navigate on-campus makers’ spaces by consolidating information like costs, required training and permission statuses. The Forage team won $4,000 in prize money. Ashwath Saravanan, a freshman majoring in electrical and computer engineering, competed with three of his friends, winning third place with “Trojan Arc,” a platform designed to help students manage their professional development by creating personalized career plans and matching students with curated internship and research opportunities. Saravanan said he joined the event just to gain experience and definitely got way more than what he was expecting out of it. Ethan Don, a freshman majoring in electrical and computer engineering, collaborated with Saravanan on Trojan Arc, and with $2,000 in prize money, Don said the team will most likely put it toward facilitation expenses as computing costs rise with more students using the tool.

Other finalists included “Same Page,” a tool that transcribes professors’ lectures to provide an accurate summary of their teaching styles for students who want a holistic assessment of a professor before choosing to take their class. “Kyros,” an AI agent reachable via iMessage, consolidates information on Brightspace, myUSC, engageSC and Handshake. Hasan Askari, managing partner at K1 Investment Management, spoke to contestants at the opening ceremony of the hackathon. Askari said there is this idea of having a will to do something that he wishes he could inject into more students every time he interacts with them. Askari said the magical thing about the world we live in right now for the students is they now are given the platforms and the tools where they’re not restricted by how things were done before.

Other guest speakers throughout the event included Jared Grusd, CEO of Gracenote and Nielsen, two separate technology companies; Holly Willis, a professor of cinematic arts; and Neha Jogani Narang, chief marketing officer at Replit, an AI-powered website and app builder. Grusd said we are living in a world where the act of creation, the cost to create, is coming down to the marginal cost of computing power. Grusd said the thing students build today will be infinitely better than what people could build last year. QuestSC is a 3D interactive map of University Park Campus, displaying live events, availability of gyms, libraries and other public spaces, as well as a live simulation of public transportation as it arrives and departs. Users of QuestSC can also see live locations of friends.

The winning projects will be considered by the Undergraduate Student Government and the University for possible implementation on campus. The articles do not state when that consideration will happen or which projects will be selected. The articles do not state the exact amounts of the first-place and third-place prizes beyond the $14,000 total split between 3 finalists, the $4,000 Forage prize and the $2,000 Trojan Arc prize. The articles do not state how many teams competed among the over 300 participants or the names of the judges. The articles do not state whether Maladi or the Forage team commented beyond what is given. The articles do not state any date for the event beyond the weekend and the 11 a.m. Saturday and Sunday deadlines.
