stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Accelerates Microbial Biosynthesis of Functional Bio-Based Nanomaterials
stories.Summary:
Microbial biosynthesis has emerged as an environmentally friendly alternative to traditional physicochemical nanoparticle production techniques, offering a versatile platform for generating functional nanoscale materials under mild reaction conditions. Conventional production routes, including chemical reduction, sol-gel processing, and laser ablation, routinely rely on hazardous reducing agents, toxic organic solvents, and high energy inputs that create environmental hazards and leave harmful surface residues. Microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, algae, cyanobacteria, and actinomycetes circumvent these issues by deploying enzymatic pathways, metabolic by-products, and active biomolecules to reduce metal precursors and stabilize nanoscale structures. Recent synthetic evaluations demonstrate that these biogenic nanomaterials possess superior biocompatibility and surface functionality compared with their chemically manufactured counterparts. However, translating microbial synthesis into industrial production has long been impeded by complex biological dynamics, unstandardized parameters, and erratic batch-to-batch variation, prompting researchers to integrate artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-driven materials informatics across every stage of the fabrication workflow.

Microbial nanomaterial generation operates through distinct biological mechanisms, primarily categorized into intracellular and extracellular pathways, alongside specialized biomineralization processes. In intracellular routes, metal cations traverse microbial cell envelopes through dedicated ion channels or electrostatic interactions with surface carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, undergoing reduction via intracellular enzymes, reduced cofactors such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, and thiol-bearing molecules like glutathione. Although intracellular synthesis yields smaller, highly monodisperse nanoparticles, product harvesting requires cell lysis that complicates downstream recovery. Extracellular synthesis circumvents this limitation by secreting reductive enzymes, extracellular polymeric substances, and redox-active metabolites into the surrounding culture medium, facilitating direct particle nucleation and capping without cellular disruption. Concurrently, biomineralization allows organisms such as magnetotactic bacteria to synthesize single-domain magnetic crystals of magnetite or greigite within membrane-bound magnetosomes, producing structures with tight size distributions and permanent magnetic dipole moments under strict genetic regulation.

The biochemical diversity across microbial classes dictates the morphology, yield, and catalytic activity of the resulting nanoparticles. Bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Escherichia, and Shewanella offer rapid growth and accessible genetic manipulation, using redox enzymes like nitrate reductase to yield metallic and metal oxide architectures. Fungi provide exceptional biomass yields and robust extracellular secretion rates, releasing high volumes of enzymes and secondary metabolites that simplify downstream purification while generating silver, gold, and zinc oxide nanoparticles. Photosynthetic microalgae and macroalgae utilize light and carbon dioxide to produce polysaccharides, polyols, and pigments that drive phyco-nanotechnology, yielding crystalline structures under sustainable cultivation regimes. Cyanobacteria contribute distinct phototrophic pathways that continuously supply reducing equivalents, whereas actinomycetes, particularly Streptomyces species, leverage diverse secondary metabolite profiles to assemble antimicrobial silver and gold particles with unique surface functionalization.

Despite the inherent flexibility of biological systems, native microbial synthesis remains exquisitely sensitive to extrinsic and intrinsic cultivation parameters. Small fluctuations in metal precursor concentrations, ambient pH, reaction temperatures, dissolved oxygen levels, nutrient feeds, and agitation rates trigger profound shifts in particle size, crystal structure, dispersity, and overall stability. For instance, alkaline reaction environments alter the ionization state of functional groups and boost biomolecular reducing capacity, favoring smaller, more uniform nanoparticles. Elevated temperatures accelerate reduction kinetics up to the threshold of thermal protein denaturation, while microbial physiological status during the logarithmic growth phase provides peak metabolic activity for efficient nucleation.

Because these environmental parameters exhibit complex, multidimensional interactions, traditional one-variable-at-a-time experimentation and standard response surface methodologies fail to resolve nonlinear interdependencies, leaving bioprocess optimization labor-intensive and frequently unrepeatable. Artificial intelligence and machine learning models are fundamentally transforming this landscape by replacing trial-and-error laboratory cycles with predictive modeling. Supervised learning algorithms, including artificial neural networks, support vector machines, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting regressors, can map multi-parameter inputs directly to nanoparticle size, yield, and morphology. Hybrid algorithmic frameworks, such as neural networks coupled with particle swarm optimization, have successfully isolated precursor concentrations, feed rates, and agitation speeds as primary drivers of particle dimensions.

Furthermore, convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and transformer-based architectures automate feature extraction from electron microscopy and spectroscopy imagery, quantifying structural properties without subjective operator intervention. Integrating these predictive algorithms with high-throughput multi-omics profiles, spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, allows researchers to anticipate cellular states and systematically dial in desired nanomaterial specifications with minimal experimental iteration. Beyond primary synthesis, post-synthetic surface functionalization is critical for adapting microbial nanomaterials to demanding technological environments, as native biomolecular capping layers alone rarely satisfy rigorous industrial or clinical benchmarks. Polyethylene glycol coatings provide steric hindrance that limits non-specific protein adsorption, extending circulation half-lives and preserving structural integrity even under extreme thermal stress.

Natural biopolymers like chitosan introduce reactive amine groups that promote mucoadhesion and support covalent drug conjugation, while targeted protein functionalization utilizing antibodies, transferrin, and cell-penetrating peptides enhances receptor-mediated uptake in pathological tissues. Researchers are also constructing hybrid nanocomposites by embedding biogenic nanoparticles within bacterial cellulose scaffolds or coupling them with graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide sheets, achieving synergistic mechanical strength, superior electrical conductivity, and amplified catalytic performance. Stimuli-responsive functionalization represents an advanced frontier in biogenic material engineering, enabling dynamic structural and functional adaptations in response to environmental triggers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Accelerates Microbial Biosynthesis of Functional Bio-Based Nanomaterials

stories.Headline: Gallup and Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab find one third of young people have AI companions
stories.Summary:
Gallup and the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab conducted a comprehensive study on how young people form relationships across sixteen different countries. The researchers used online surveys to gather data from more than 16,000 participants between the ages of 15 and 22. While 93 percent of the young people reported having at least one strong in-person friendship, 33 percent admitted to having an AI companion. The study found that 82 percent used AI for information and 68 percent sought advice, though interest varied by region.

Daily AI usage was highest in Brazil at almost 40 percent, followed by Japan and Italy at around 35 percent. In contrast, only 20 percent of young people in the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States used AI daily. The quality of these digital bonds differed by location, as nearly half of Australians rated their AI friends as high quality, while only 12 percent of Polish respondents did. Most participants globally gave their AI companionship a medium rating rather than a high or low one.

The researchers noted that people who used AI as friends reported higher levels of loneliness, but they could not determine the exact cause. They observed that 72 percent of respondents spend their time scrolling short form content on Instagram and TikTok. Six in 10 young people reported that they often scroll through this content when they feel lonely. The authors stated that the wider social context and the quality of relationships matter more than the specific form of connection.

The study concluded that having strong in-person friendships is the most effective way to reduce feelings of loneliness. Researchers found that not having a trusted adult outside the family was a significant characteristic for those lacking any friendship modes. They warned that assessments of AI should be compared cautiously with human friendships because expectations for chatbots are different. The authors emphasized that material conditions shape how young people form friendships more than their access to social media or AI.

stories.Headline: Ethics professor Domènec Melé argues AI shapes habits and desires but cannot replace human wisdom or communion
stories.Summary:
Dr. Domènec Melé, an emeritus professor of business ethics at IESE Business School and an emeritus member of the Royal European Academy of Doctors, published an article titled “Christian Spirituality and Artificial Intelligence: Discernment in a Global Technological Economy” in the journal Religions on 27 October, the academy reported on 16 November 2026. In it he reflects on how artificial intelligence and new technological environments affect the spiritual development of human beings. He writes that artificial intelligence has shown it not only expands human capabilities but also shapes habits, desires, attention and forms of relationship. He argues that processing information or generating plausible responses is not the same as wisdom, which requires integrating knowledge with experience, moral judgement and an orientation towards worthy ends.

Melé holds that fluid and personalised interaction may simulate attention or empathy but does not amount to communion, because communion requires reciprocal presence, vulnerability and the capacity for self-giving between persons. He notes that in an economy rewarding engagement or productivity, optimising means does not automatically settle which ends are worth pursuing. He says artificial intelligence can reduce repetitive burdens and broaden access to knowledge or assistance, but replacing activities whose value includes human participation, such as teaching, care, professional judgement or personal accompaniment, carries risks. He also warns of an unequal distribution of human presence, since those with greater resources may keep access to teachers, doctors or advisers in person while others increasingly receive automated substitutes.

The article further underlines the material footprint of the technology, noting that although it may appear immaterial to users, artificial intelligence depends on data centres, chips and electricity grids whose consumption of energy and water is considerable. Melé does not advocate rejecting technology or absolutising it, and he suggests technical creativity can be understood as a form of participation in the care and development of creation, while the power it confers is a responsibility entrusted to human beings rather than absolute dominion. In a context of concentrated infrastructure, data and capital, he argues that the social doctrine of the Church offers criteria of dignity, the common good, subsidiarity and solidarity to keep individuals and communities from becoming passive recipients of decisions taken elsewhere. He concludes that progress is genuinely human when directed towards the integral development of persons and, within the Christian horizon, towards communion with God and with others.

Over the past 30 years Melé has researched and written extensively on business and economic ethics, corporate social responsibility, Christian social ethics, spirituality in management, management philosophy and humanistic management. He has published more than 70 book chapters and scientific articles in journals including the Journal of Business Ethics, Business Ethics Quarterly, Business Ethics: A European Review, Business and Society Review, Philosophy of Management and Humanistic Management Journal. He is also the author of several books that have become reference works in humanistic economics, among them “Ethics in Business Management”, “Anthropological Foundations of Business Management”, “Business Ethics in Action. Seeking Human Excellence in Organizations”, “Christians in Society” and “Ethics in the Family Business”, the last co-authored with fellow READ emeritus member Miguel Ángel Gallo.

stories.Headline: Engineers must redesign legacy systems around event-driven flows and decoupled AI inference for real-time decisions
stories.Summary:
Modernising legacy systems for real-time artificial intelligence demands a fundamental architectural redesign rather than a simple lift-and-shift to the cloud, according to TechGig. The article, published on August 26, 2026, says enterprises increasingly expect software platforms to evaluate events, apply intelligence and respond in near real time. Legacy applications built around scheduled jobs and tightly coupled components often lack that responsiveness. A simple cloud migration is therefore insufficient, and engineering teams must adopt cloud-native patterns such as event-driven flows and decoupled AI inference.

The redesign involves several key shifts, the article says. Replacing batch dependencies with event-driven flows lets services publish changes and downstream components subscribe, which supports real-time decision flows and reduces unnecessary polling. Separating AI inference from application logic creates a cleaner boundary that is vital for model evolution, retraining, versioning and controlled rollouts without impacting core applications. Building for real-time context is also paramount, because fast predictions based on stale data are ineffective, so cloud-native platforms use streaming systems, low-latency stores, caches and feature services to assemble current information. Architects must identify data critical for immediate decisions and design for the required business latency.

Systems should be decomposed selectively, since microservices help when they create independent ownership or scaling boundaries but excessive decomposition can introduce latency and complexity. Meaningful boundaries for AI platforms include event ingestion, context enrichment and inference. Kubernetes serves as an operational foundation offering workload scheduling, horizontal scaling and health management for variable AI workloads, though containerising a poorly designed application does not make it cloud-native. Engineering for failure is critical in distributed systems, with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and idempotency designed into the platform and reliability measured across the entire business flow. Observability must be integral from the outset, with metrics, logs and distributed traces, plus AI-specific monitoring for model latency, prediction distributions and drift.

Built-in governance is equally important, ensuring traceability of model versions, data, rules and actions through model registries and decision logs. The article says modernisation should be incremental, introducing new cloud-native services around existing applications rather than disruptive full-system replacements. Durable cloud-native AI platforms are defined by characteristics that manage change, including loosely coupled services, event-driven communication, scalable compute, low-latency data access, automated delivery, resilience, observability and built-in governance. The core question for modernisation shifts from merely moving applications to the cloud to rethinking how systems should operate when intelligent, real-time decisioning becomes a core capability.

The expansion follows OpenAI's growing focus on India, including a previous $500,000 grant to IIT Madras for studying AI's impact on teaching and learning. stories.Headline: Amagasaki by-election candidates use AI-generated faces on posters as officials confirm no legal grounds to remove them
stories.Summary:
A city council by-election in Amagasaki, Hyogo Prefecture, on November 15, 2026, drew 12 candidates for one vacant seat, and at least four of them displayed posters with AI-generated faces rather than their own photographs. Former prefectural assembly member Hikoharu Konishi acknowledged that four candidates had used artificial images, and the Amagasaki City Election Administration Commission confirmed at least four posters were suspected of using generative AI. In one case, officials said the man depicted on the poster of candidate Hiroyoshi Hara was not Hara himself, and an election official who had met Hara said the person shown looked completely different. The controversy emerged during a closely contested race in which voters also chose a mayor on November 15, with incumbent Kazumi Matsumoto winning a second term and Hiromi Ikeshita securing the council seat. Some posters depicted men with tattoos on their arms, while others showed attractive, distinguished-looking older men alongside simple campaign messages.

Japan's Public Offices Election Act has regulated posters through requirements on dimensions and identification of responsible parties but has not required candidates to use photographs of themselves. After the July 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, when campaign poster boards displayed sexually explicit images of women and other material unrelated to candidates, lawmakers revised the law to require candidates' names to be clearly visible and to prohibit material damaging another person's reputation or violating public morals. The amended law contains no provision requiring a candidate's actual face to appear on a poster, and election authorities said they had no legal grounds to order the posters removed. Under the publicly funded election campaign system, public funding for poster production in the Amagasaki by-election was available up to approximately 610,000 yen per candidate, depending on reimbursement conditions. Each of the four candidates received enough votes to qualify for the return of the 300,000 yen deposit required to stand in the municipal election, though all four were defeated.

An Amagasaki election official said the commission could not intervene simply because a photograph or image was misleading, citing freedom of political activity and freedom of expression. Konishi, who with his secretary had submitted the candidacy registrations on behalf of the four individuals, reportedly responded that he found officials' requests for identity verification unpleasant. Speaking on behalf of candidate Koichi Sato, number 12, on November 14, the final day of campaigning, Konishi told voters the posters were the ones everyone in Amagasaki had been talking about and asked whether people genuinely felt suspicious about the images. He confirmed to Kansai Television that the images were produced using AI, saying of Sato's poster, "This was made with AI," and calling it "an image." Konishi said production costs were matters to be settled between candidates and contractors, that he had followed the Public Offices Election Act properly with the election commission's approval, and that outsiders should not make a fuss.

One Amagasaki resident said the artificial appearance immediately discouraged closer examination of the candidates' messages, and another said it made them wonder how committed the candidates really were and that it was difficult to sense any sincerity. Another resident said candidates should not engage in such unusual practices, while another questioned whether the individuals were seriously attempting to win office. Reporters searched Amagasaki for campaign vehicles and tried to contact the individuals by telephone but could not locate them or obtain interviews. Ono Planning Office, a local poster production company that has worked on more than 1,000 campaigns, restricts AI use to image correction and set its own guidelines in November. Company representative Satsuki Ono said AI can create a completely different face from the original material, that this is no longer simply correcting a photograph, and that charging nearly 600,000 yen for posters made with AI for practically nothing and paying only for printing could yield a substantial profit.

Election consultant Takuma Ohamazaki said that normally someone who runs for election incurs expenses and finishes with a financial loss, and that in this case he suspected some people may have ended up making money. Ohamazaki also warned that increasingly sophisticated AI could make future cases far harder to detect, saying the cat-and-mouse game between technological advances and the Public Offices Election Act will continue. Legal experts said Japan's election legislation has historically been designed to regulate specific, identifiable practices, making it difficult to anticipate abuses from new technologies, and that restrictions on political expression must be balanced against democratic freedoms including the right to participate in elections and communicate political messages. There has been no confirmation that the four candidates or their associates improperly received public funds or profited, and the allegations remain suspicions rather than established wrongdoing. Similar concerns circulated on social media, where users questioned whether obtaining publicly funded poster payments might have been one motivation for entering the election.

Further changes to the Public Offices Election Act are scheduled for March 2027, including a requirement to disclose when AI has been used in election-related materials. The planned disclosure requirement has drawn criticism because it carries no penalties for violations and does not necessarily require detailed explanations of which elements of an image were generated or altered. Experts questioned whether a simple declaration that AI was used would provide meaningful protection against misleading campaign imagery. Without clearer definitions of prohibited conduct or enforceable penalties, they warned, candidates may continue exploiting gaps between rapidly developing technology and election regulations. The Amagasaki controversy has highlighted a broader challenge facing Japan's democratic system.

Articles.Title: AI-Generated Election Posters Spark Controversy in Japan - News On Japan

stories.Headline: City leaders at Global AI Cities 2026 set out five priorities for making AI and digital infrastructure resilient
stories.Summary:
At Global AI Cities 2026, more than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester to discuss artificial intelligence and digital resilience. The event was organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Sarah Wray reported on the conference for Global Government Forum on 16 November 2026. The discussions were captured in the report Making AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities. The report draws on insights from the event and includes examples from Romania, Westminster and Alberta.

The report sets out five priorities for cities, including fixing the fundamentals and prioritising according to criticality. It also calls for governing AI throughout its lifecycle and making digital infrastructure itself resilient. The report says resilience depends on people and partnerships as well as technology. Global AI Cities 2027 is to be held in Manchester on 24-25 May. The report is available to download.

Alexandru Georgescu, senior researcher at Romania's National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics, said local authorities are not actually ready for AI in itself. He said generative AI and large language models are not comparable to traditional software and need new processes and new cybersecurity practices, including adversarial testing and red-teaming. He said many large organisations are not ready to do this, let alone local administrations that probably have not budgeted for it. He said cities are agglomerations of critical infrastructures that serve wider regions and become targets for criminals, rogue states or state-sponsored organisations. He concluded that many local authorities are not adequately prepared and do not have the level of support they need from central authorities.

Gurpreet Muctor, chief data and technology officer for Westminster City Council, said a late 2025 cyber-attack took five months to recover from and forced the shutdown of all systems. He said the attack was perpetrated by somebody who impersonated a council employee and was still a manual process, not an AI attack. He said AI increasingly adds a new layer to that threat in the form of deepfakes that can impersonate council workers, politicians or senior officials. Richard Henderson, corporate chief information officer for the Government of Alberta, said many local governments make it too easy for hackers because they are not getting the fundamentals right. He said Alberta built AI-assisted tooling to scan 400 million lines of government code for vulnerabilities, work he estimated would have taken a human 125 years of development time.

Henderson advised cities not to wait for the most advanced tools and said they can probably build their own reasonable facsimile relatively quickly for not a significant amount. He said the only way to survive the deepfake threat is through good governance and protocols, such as an agreed challenge phrase to ascertain that someone is genuine. Georgescu said there is too much focus on the cutting edge when good enough is often adequate for both attackers and defenders. He said his institute prioritises based on criticality, identifying which systems would cause the greatest harm if compromised and hardening those first. He highlighted the most basic AI-related risk as someone pasting citizen data into a public LLM to save time, and said the human factor and security culture matter.

Georgescu said there is not enough talk about the lifecycle of AI products and systems and how decommissioning will be handled. He warned of AI agents stuck in systems and attached to data that an adversary could exploit long after the department that built them has moved on. Henderson said staff are not interested in waiting for discussions about AI and will use it whether organisations like it or not. One senior leader at the summit described facing a pandemic, a major snowstorm and an energy blackout, which highlighted the difference between having technology and having resilience. The city is now strengthening resilience through a city brain supported by AI, improved cybersecurity, closer partnerships with telecom providers, resilient government buildings, district-level citizen refuges with power and connectivity, and new platforms providing real-time information on infrastructure.

The articles do not state what specific measures, funding or deadlines follow from the report's five priorities. They do not name the city whose leader described the succession of crises. They do not give the outcome of the Westminster attack beyond the five-month recovery and system shutdown. They do not say what action, if any, Romania's central authorities have taken in response to Georgescu's comments. They do not give details of the Global AI Cities 2027 agenda beyond its dates and location.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI systems act autonomously, forcing security teams to monitor five new surfaces
stories.Summary:
Agentic AI systems that can read repositories, query databases, modify code and start workflows are changing what enterprise security has to cover, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Unlike earlier AI that mainly produced content or recommendations, these agents build their execution plans dynamically, so security teams cannot predict the sequence of actions in advance. The report says this gap calls for a new class of security tools built specifically for autonomous agents. It lists five security surfaces that enterprise teams must address as these systems move into production.

The first surface is the agent estate, which means continuously finding every approved and unapproved agent, AI platform and extension, including shadow AI. The second is the agentic supply chain, where models, skills, plugins and tools can change what an agent is able to do. Identity and permissions form the third surface, because an agent holding legitimate credentials can still cause a breach if it combines permissions in unexpected ways. Runtime behaviour is the fourth, requiring controls with enough context to watch tool calls and data access as they happen. The fifth is intent, which traditional tools struggle to represent, making it important to detect when an agent's behaviour drifts from its original objective.

Several platforms are named as addressing these problems. Dash Security focuses on continuous discovery of the agentic layer, supply-chain risk assessment, and session- and intent-aware monitoring. Zenity secures AI agents across their lifecycle, with discovery, posture management, runtime detection and prompt-injection protection. Palo Alto Networks Prisma AIRS folds agent security into a broader enterprise AI security architecture, offering visibility and control as agents enter production. HiddenLayer extends visibility into autonomous execution through Agentic Runtime Visibility and Threat Hunting, while Check Point AI Security, enhanced by Lakera's technology, pairs controls over AI interaction with defenses for agent actions, especially tool use in workflows. Noma Security treats agentic AI as part of a wider AI and data security platform covering discovery, posture, supply-chain risk and runtime protection, and Prompt Security, now part of SentinelOne, provides visibility and controls across employees, applications and agentic systems, with a focus on sensitive-data exposure and prompt injection.

The report frames this as a shift in enterprise security requirements rather than a single product fix, since agentic tools act instead of only advising. It does not give adoption figures, pricing or a timeline for when companies are expected to put these controls in place. The tools it describes are presented as available options from the named vendors, and the article closes by inviting readers to share their thoughts on the subject.

stories.Headline: Los Angeles schools survey parents, students and staff to shape generative AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District is distributing a survey to parents, students and staff to help inform its policy on generative artificial intelligence in schools, LAist reported on November 16, 2026. The district wants to hear from community members about how the technology should be used in classrooms across the system. The survey is meant to gather input that will shape the district's formal policy on generative AI. The report was published by Elly Yu, who covers early childhood issues for LAist. The survey follows a surprise moratorium that LAUSD implemented in September on student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for this school year.

Before that moratorium, district policy allowed students 13 and older to use the technology under supervision. The school board has an ad-hoc committee on generative AI that examines the new technology and what its role should be in the classroom. The committee was formed as part of a resolution that was passed to limit screentime in the district. The ad hoc committee is scheduled to meet four more times this school year, on Dec. 9, 2026, Jan. 20, 2027, March 3, 2027 and April 7, 2027. The committee plans to make policy recommendations that the full board could vote on.

The survey of parents, students and staff is intended to help inform the district policy that emerges from that process. The committee's work and the survey together will feed into the recommendations the board may eventually consider. The context is a district still working out how generative AI fits into its classrooms after the September moratorium paused student use on school-issued devices. The ad-hoc committee's four remaining meetings this school year give the board a schedule for turning community input into recommendations it could vote on. The survey gives parents, students and staff a way to weigh in before those recommendations take shape.

stories.Headline: EU science and ethics advisors urge public AI evaluation capacity
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors and the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies issued a joint statement warning that traditional public policy guardrails cannot govern rapidly advancing artificial intelligence. The two senior advisory bodies called on the European Union to establish sovereign capacity to evaluate complex AI models rather than delegating safety assessments to commercial technology firms. The statement, titled ‘The next phase of artificial intelligence ,  Governing for safety, security and human agency,’ sets out four core principles for European policymakers. The advisors delivered the four primary recommendations to the College of Commissioners. The joint statement was published on 16 Nov 2026.

The first recommendation is to keep existing rules strong, with safety, cybersecurity and human agency remaining mandatory prerequisites for AI development. The advisors warn against regulatory backsliding and say political hesitation risks weakening statutory obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and that lobbying to dilute compliance deadlines must be resisted. The second is to calibrate development and deployment to degrees of danger, so the pace at which foundation models and autonomous systems are released correlates with potential hazards. Where models pose severe cybersecurity, biosecurity or critical-infrastructure risks, deployment must be contingent on verified mitigation rather than post-incident response. The third is to build independent public evaluation capacity, with the advisors urging the EU to develop public testing facilities and warning the bloc cannot remain dependent on self-attestations or proprietary safety benchmarks supplied by commercial developers.

The fourth is to establish an ecosystem for continuous learning, in which regulatory frameworks and scientific risk assessments evolve dynamically alongside advancing model capabilities, since static compliance checklists are obsolete and authorities must create adaptive monitoring loops that ingest empirical evidence from operational deployments. The Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, established under the Scientific Advice Mechanism, comprises seven eminent researchers appointed in their personal capacity to deliver evidence-based policy counsel. The European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies operates as an independent advisory body examining where scientific discovery intersects with fundamental European rights. Officials within the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation confirmed that the move reflects mounting concern that commercial market pressures threaten to bypass fundamental safety reviews. The GCSA and EGE argued that relying exclusively on commercial developers to determine whether their proprietary models trigger GPAI systemic risk thresholds introduces an inherent conflict of interest that undermines European safety objectives.

The advisors asserted that safety and market competitiveness are complementary, and that reliable, audited and trustworthy systems form the only durable foundation for widespread societal adoption in medicine, public administration and critical engineering. In independent coverage by Wisevoter, titled Scientists Urge Europe to Enforce AI Rules, observers underscored that the European advisory apparatus is pivoting attention away from theoretical rule-drafting toward concrete technical verification capabilities. European academic organizations welcomed the advisors’ insistence on public evaluation infrastructure. Policy commentators at European Interest had previously pointed out that public scientific research risks marginalization if access to frontier models and evaluation tools remains gated behind commercial licensing agreements.

University consortia emphasized that independent evaluation capacity within member states would provide academic researchers with transparent benchmarks and reproducible verification protocols. For universities, research hospitals and academic research offices, the recommendations highlight procurement due diligence and audit trails, expansion of research ethics committee remits, academic participation in public evaluation testbeds, and safeguarding scientific reproducibility. Both bodies have previously advised the Commission on computational technologies, delivering opinions on artificial intelligence in crisis management and publishing detailed guidance on the successful and timely uptake of artificial intelligence in science in the EU. The joint statement arrives as the operational burden of the AI Act, finalized in 2024, has shifted toward secondary rulemaking and practical enforcement.

Critical milestones currently under negotiation include the general-purpose AI Code of Practice and implementation frameworks that clarify downstream compliance obligations. The European Commission has introduced legislative proposals including the Cloud and AI Development Act (COM(2026) 502 final). The advisors warn that without substantial budgetary investment in public technical staff, automated evaluation tooling and independent laboratory verification, regulatory bodies risk becoming rubber-stamping entities for proprietary commercial claims. Following publication of the joint statement on November 16, 2026, the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation and DG CONNECT are scheduled to review the advisors’ recommendations.

Attention will center on whether the European Commission incorporates explicit funding for independent evaluation infrastructure into upcoming Horizon Europe work programmes and the implementation roadmaps for the Cloud and AI Development Act. In parallel, the European AI Office is preparing the final administrative drafts of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, where stakeholder negotiations over independent auditor access remain under way. Under existing voluntary frameworks, major model providers conduct internal red-teaming exercises and issue selective model cards. The articles leave open whether the Commission will adopt the recommendations and how the negotiations over independent auditor access will conclude.

stories.Headline: Bureau of Industry and Security requires licenses to export advanced AI chips to certain data centers
stories.Summary:
The Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on November 16, 2026. This rule requires licenses to export, reexport, or transfer advanced artificial intelligence chips to certain data centers. It targets facilities providing significant computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5 destinations. The rule also applies to data centers whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those same locations. These restrictions apply to chips anywhere in the world.

Licenses are now required for advanced computing items under ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090 shipped to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. The rule covers data centers providing more than 12 million in aggregate total processing performance to restricted customers. It formally rescinds the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule and its associated authorizations. The rule takes effect upon publication in the Federal Register. It uses the term Super Intelligence instead of artificial intelligence following Executive Order 14434.

The Bureau of Industry and Security is responsible for implementing these new export controls. Officials stated the rule relies on existing power over chip shipments rather than regulating remote access directly. They explained that serving restricted customers after chips arrive counts as a new in-country transfer. BIS noted that due diligence is meant to prevent evasion through corporate spinoffs or restructurings. They will review all license applications on a case by case basis.

Cloud providers, chip suppliers, and data center operators are affected by these new compliance requirements. Some companies, including Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance, reportedly used chips in Japan, Malaysia, and Thailand. The rule affects any party holding the chips, even those not involved in the original shipment. Exporters must now verify the know your customer checks of foreign data centers. Those already supplying restricted power must obtain a license within 90 days.

The Bureau of Industry and Security previously concluded in 2009 and 2014 that cloud computing was not subject to regulations. Remote access allowed Chinese companies to rent computing power in the United States or third countries. This created a loophole because the physical chips never had to cross any international borders. The current rule addresses this by regulating the chips behind the capacity rather than the activity. It uses Sections 1753 and 1754 of the Export Control Reform Act.

The Bureau of Industry and Security will accept public comments for 60 days after the rule is published. Congress is pursuing the Remote Access Security Act, which passed the House on January 12, 2026. This bill awaits action in the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. The Secretary of Commerce may add more high risk destinations to the license list. The articles leave open whether the Senate will pass its own version, S. 3519.

stories.Headline: Illinois reports say data center power demand delays coal plant closures until 2033
stories.Summary:
Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering Illinois plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change, according to a pair of state reports released Monday. Under a law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. But big new data centers require so much electricity that it has become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand. The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year, because cleaner sources including wind and solar are not being built quickly enough.

In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate, and the goal of shutting four of them down by 2030 remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed, and eleven so-called peaker plants that burn oil or natural gas as backups were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen, and peakers in Waukegan will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation.

Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at the Respiratory Health Association in Chicago, said fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people. Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County, called the recommendation disappointing and said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. She said her community is tired of dirty energy. Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants, but state officials said that is not being advised, and the state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants.

Illinois is not running out of power yet, but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, that the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity. Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city. State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month, and hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, and the Integrated Resource Plan released by the Illinois Commerce Commission.

stories.Headline: Malaysia plans full AI exposure in schools next year as PAGE urges a balanced approach
stories.Summary:
The Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia successfully conducted its 16th annual general meeting in September 2026 to continue its campaign for English language instruction. This educational lobby group previously advocated for the use of smartphones as teaching aids, though many teachers initially insisted that these devices remain at home. While some developed nations are now restricting technology, the Madani government has decided to implement full scale exposure to artificial intelligence within the Malaysian education system. This new curriculum is scheduled to begin next year for students entering Year One and Form One.

Several countries are currently spending significant funds to return to traditional learning methods to combat digital fatigue and protect cognitive focus. Sweden spent more than 2.1 billion krona, or 875 million ringgit, over two years to bring printed textbooks and teaching guides back into classrooms. Denmark committed 540 million Danish krone, which is 330 million ringgit, over ten years for physical books while making schools and after school clubs handphone free. Other nations including Finland, Italy, France, and Norway have restricted or banned phones, while Madrid, Spain, is capping primary student screen time to two hours per week.

Datin Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, the chairman of the Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia, expressed concerns regarding the eagerness to put screens in front of developing children. She argued that implementation must be guided by child safety, equity, and educational outcomes so that students do not surrender their ability to think independently. She noted that professors at Harvard University are increasingly banning laptops, as an analysis by The Harvard Crimson in September 2026 found such bans had more than doubled. She believes pupils still need physical books and handwriting practice to avoid being distracted by digital notifications.

The group suggests that Malaysia should learn from developed countries that have come full circle by finding a healthier balance between digital and traditional education. The author warns that excessive self promotion without adequate preparation could lead to failure, citing the recall of 8,878 Chery Omoda 5 cars and 600 other vehicles. The goal is for students to use technology to solve problems and make informed decisions rather than depending on it to think for them. The group will continue to serve as a channel between concerned parents, the Ministry of Education, and other stakeholders.

stories.Headline: Railway reports attackers stole AI keys and ran up $740,000 in usage
stories.Summary:
Attackers breached the cloud hosting platform Railway in October and used stolen AI provider credentials to run up an estimated US$740,000 in unauthorised AI usage, according to Railway's incident report published on November 10. The company said the attacker specifically targeted AI provider credentials and believes they were passed to distributed transfer stations for model distillation. The attacker decrypted stored environment variables for at most 1.85 per cent of Railway's workspaces, affecting about 100,000 accounts. Database logs showed queries selecting variables matching AI provider keys, favouring customers with many stored variables. Developers on platforms like Railway store app settings as environment variables, which can include secrets such as API keys, and an AI provider's API key works like a password tied to a billing account, letting anyone holding it charge usage to the owner.

Refund handling varies by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini have begun refunds under existing fraud policies, while OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing claims case by case through a shared channel with Railway. Railway committed to covering Anthropic-related costs while discussions continue, and said it would also cover OpenRouter, which enforced its no-refund policy. That commitment marks a shift from October 26, when Railway initially told customers it could not refund spend from compromised API keys. The decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, covering AI agents and GitHub OAuth tokens, and Railway reset all affected tokens, notified users, and found no logins to Railway accounts using the stolen credentials.

Railway's report identified similar thefts at OpenCode, Warp and Fireworks AI between October 6 and 23, describing the incident as part of a series of attacks on platforms holding AI keys. Fireworks AI disclosed two linked incidents: the first, on October 6, involved misused internal credentials exposing secrets for evaluation jobs for a limited number of accounts, and a November 9 update said attackers reached its development machines on October 24 via a third-party cloud provider breach, exposing customer account and billing information and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights. Fireworks believes a financially motivated group is selling large language model access through illicit routing gateways, a practice known as LLMjacking. The Fireworks breach also affected Notion, which used Fireworks for its Notion AI Insights feature; Notion said fewer than 1 per cent of its workspaces might have been affected, disconnected its systems from Fireworks and deleted its data by November 3, and has since disabled Insights and advised affected customers to rotate passwords or API keys used with Notion AI.

In both the Railway and Fireworks incidents, customer systems were not breached directly, and exposure occurred through platforms or vendors between customers and AI models. Railway filed a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center and engaged a forensics firm, while Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42.

stories.Headline: Razorpay expands Agent Studio to offer Indian merchants AI agents for cart recovery and EMI collection
stories.Summary:
Razorpay is expanding its artificial intelligence agent platform, Agent Studio, beyond transaction processing so that it can offer new merchant services to businesses across India. The company announced the expansion on November 18, 2026, according to a TechGig report published that morning. The platform is designed to help businesses recover abandoned carts, collect overdue loan instalments known as EMIs, and automate customer interactions. Razorpay is positioning Agent Studio as a marketplace and builder platform where businesses can deploy specialised AI agents for their daily operations.

Agent Studio recorded around five lakh monthly agent runs as of September and is live on 350 brands, according to Khilan Haria, the chief product officer at Razorpay. Voice-led commerce has gained momentum among customers, with an AI agent calling a customer on behalf of a business to complete a transaction or recover a payment. Haria said conversion rates in some voice-led use cases ranged from 8 to 10 per cent in most scenarios and reached as high as 20 per cent for dropped-off opportunities. Razorpay announced a partnership with Meta on November 17 to enable payments through Meta Business Agent on WhatsApp, letting customers discover products, interact with businesses, and complete purchases using UPI, cards, or net banking within the same conversation.

Haria said AI enables a decision layer across the buyer and merchant journey, moving beyond basic chatbots, and the platform lets businesses build customised agents by describing desired automated tasks without writing code. The initial applications included abandoned-cart recovery, subscription payment recovery, dispute responses, and cash-flow forecasting. In September, Razorpay launched RAY, an AI account manager on WhatsApp that lets businesses check payment information and initiate refunds through messages or voice notes. Last month, Razorpay also partnered with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT through its growth marketing platform, Engage, which assists brands in preparing product catalogues and managing advertising campaigns with an AI agent.

These initiatives are part of Razorpay's strategy to become more involved in merchants' day-to-day operations, extending the company's role past core payment processing. The expansion taps into the growing use of conversational and voice-led commerce among businesses, which the company sees as a significant application of its agent platform. The articles do not say what further products or markets Razorpay plans to enter next, or how the platform will be priced for merchants.

stories.Headline: US restricts AI chip exports to China as Australia joins technology security alliance
stories.Summary:
The United States administration announced new Commerce Department restrictions on November 18, 2026, to limit China's access to advanced AI accelerators from vendors like Nvidia. These measures specifically target chip smuggling and overseas data centres to increase geopolitical oversight of silicon flows and data centre capacity across the Asia-Pacific region. Simultaneously, Australia joined the United States and eight other allied nations, including India, by signing the San Francisco Declaration. This international agreement focuses on coordinating the security of critical technologies and infrastructure that support artificial intelligence supply chains.

The new restrictions require tighter control over advanced hardware, while the San Francisco Declaration establishes resilient corridors for compute, semiconductors, and AI infrastructure. These geopolitical shifts occur as Fujitsu research shows that 70 per cent of Australian firms are sharing data more widely than their governance frameworks allow, surpassing the 60 per cent rate in the United States. Additionally, BlueFlag Security reports that 83 per cent of organisations are running unapproved AI agents, many of which possess administrative privileges. These figures highlight a growing gap between the rapid deployment of enterprise AI and existing data sovereignty controls.

The US administration is responsible for the export controls, which they intend to use to monitor the movement of high-end silicon. Regarding the supply chain alliance, the participating nations aim to ensure that the infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence remains secure and resilient. In the private sector, TechnologyOne is challenging its research and development teams to double their output to avoid the AI-driven redundancies seen at companies like Canva and WiseTech. This approach seeks to combine higher engineering productivity with revenue expansion to combat competition from direct-to-consumer AI tools.

stories.Headline: Letta proposes a three-tier memory architecture to address stateless AI agents
stories.Summary:
Memory is the hardest unsolved problem in AI agents, and existing techniques offer only subtle trade-offs and incomplete solutions, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Modern large language models operate as stateless systems, which means all relevant information must be re-inserted into the prompt on every call. That stateless nature creates a structural problem for agents that carry out work across multiple turns, sessions, tasks or weeks. The Letta team, which developed MemGPT, proposes a three-tier memory architecture for agents that draws an analogy to an operating system's memory hierarchy.

That architecture includes core memory for persistent blocks within the context window, recall memory for searchable interaction history, and archival memory for structured knowledge held in external databases. Agents are designed to move data between these tiers using tools such as memory_replace, archival_memory_insert and conversation_search. The approach shifts memory design from simple prompt injection to an agent-managed hierarchy, which the report describes as a significant architectural change in stateful agent development. Working memory covers information an agent uses immediately within the context window, episodic memory records past interactions chronologically like a journal, and semantic memory stores durable, context-independent knowledge such as user preferences or team processes.

Common memory features often rely on vector stores for semantic search, embedding all user and agent interactions as vectors and retrieving the relevant ones. That method struggles in production with contradictions, retractions, salience and the decay of stale facts, the report says. Effective memory systems instead integrate layered approaches, including a scratchpad for current tasks, file-based memory for durable preferences, episodic logs of full conversation transcripts for on-demand retrieval, and recursive summarization that compresses older context into brief synopses. Vector stores suit searching large corpora for semantic similarity but are not ideal for precision, mutability or expiry.

The most robust design has the agent itself manage its memory, with tools for reading, writing, updating and deleting information, so it can decide what to remember and what to forget. The report notes this could potentially include sleep-time agents that consolidate memory between sessions. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce DeltaChargeNet to simulate electronic structures in materials and devices
stories.Summary:
Qingyun Zhang and twenty-one other researchers introduced a machine-learning charge density model called DeltaChargeNet on November 18, 2026. This new system integrates with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital method to simulate electronic structures and quantum transport in materials. The team developed this tool to predict electron density from atomic structures while maintaining a low linear-scaling cost. They specifically designed the model to handle complex devices that contain interfaces and disorder.

The framework requires an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict the difference between density functional theory and atomic superposition densities. This process includes a charge neutrality constraint and a secondary residual charge model to correct remaining potential mismatches. The researchers validated the system using bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. They found that the maximum band energy error for bulk HgCdTe remained below 10 meV. The charge neutrality constraint prevented electrostatic potential distortions of 0.68 to 1.88 eV, while residual compensation fixed errors of 0.16 to 0.46 eV.

The authors, who represent ShanghaiTech University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, stated that these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent density functional theory. They explained that the model allows for large-scale device simulations without needing the full self-consistent field loop. To demonstrate the practical application of this technology, the team simulated quantum transport in an infrared detector containing 11,220 atoms. This combination of first-principles accuracy and linear-scaling inference enables the study of much larger electronic systems.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude sees India downloads rise 15 times as ChatGPT falls 21 per cent
stories.Summary:
Claude, the AI assistant made by Anthropic, saw its downloads in India rise 15 times year-on-year in the September quarter of 2026, according to data from the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower reported by TechGig on November 18, 2026. Over the same period, downloads of OpenAI's ChatGPT fell 21 per cent, although ChatGPT remained the market leader among generative AI apps in India. Claude's revenue from in-app purchases climbed to third rank from fifth a year earlier, overtaking platforms such as Instagram and YouTube. On a sequential basis, Claude's in-app purchase revenue grew 75 per cent from the June quarter, while ChatGPT recorded 61 per cent revenue growth and Gemini's revenue slipped 31 per cent quarter-on-quarter.

The figures also show how the other apps performed. ChatGPT's India revenue from in-app purchases increased by 70 per cent since Q2 FY26, despite its slower download growth. Google's Gemini app reported a 44 per cent year-on-year rise in revenue in Q2 FY27, even as its downloads dropped 29 per cent. OpenAI India MD Prabhjeet Singh said last week that India is ChatGPT's largest global market for weekly active users, having doubled its user base since January. OpenAI has an office in Delhi NCR and plans to open additional offices in Mumbai and Bengaluru, while Anthropic inaugurated its first India-based office in Bengaluru earlier this year.

The report places these shifts inside a fast-growing market. India's AI market is projected to multiply 5.3 times by 2030 to reach $126 billion and to add $1.7 trillion to GDP by 2035, according to Inc42's Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026. Sensor Tower attributed Claude's revenue surge to its download growth, and the data points to a change in consumer preferences within the competitive Indian AI market. The articles do not say what steps the companies plan next in response to these numbers.

stories.Headline: Nvidia expects AI accelerator shortages to persist through fiscal 2028
stories.Summary:
Nvidia expects a shortage of its artificial intelligence accelerators to continue through the end of fiscal 2028, according to a report from Hanwha Investment & Securities on November 17. This prolonged supply constraint occurs despite a leadership transition and stricter United States restrictions on shipments to China. The company previously projected revenue growth of roughly 70 percent for that fiscal year, though former CEO Jensen Huang noted that demand could drive growth near 100 percent without supply limits. The current market situation requires a shift in supply distribution, as unmet global demand from sovereign AI projects and model developers may absorb chips originally meant for China. Nvidia has committed 36 billion dollars to cloud capacity as of the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and seeks to mobilize over 500 billion dollars through an external financing platform.

Additionally, proposed U.S. legislation like the MATCH Act, the Chip Security Act, and the AI OVERWATCH Act could restrict Chinese firms such as YMTC and CXMT from maintaining or expanding equipment. These changes are expected to benefit Samsung Electronics and SK hynix by reducing the risk of a global memory oversupply. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who has served as chief financial officer since 2013, is now responsible for the company's capital allocation and investment strategies. Nvidia has stated that it intends to honor all existing customer commitments during this transition, although the terms for new financial support may become more stringent. Hanwha analyst Park Jun-young explained that while regulations might alter investment timing or customer mixes, they are unlikely to damage the structural demand for memory.

He noted that limiting the growth of Chinese memory makers will likely provide a positive long-term outlook for the South Korean industry. The broader customer base for GPUs now includes AI cloud providers and enterprises, which account for 45.3 percent of data center revenue compared to 54.7 percent from traditional hyperscalers. This diversification helps sustain demand even if some neocloud operators experience delays in their financing. Analysts will continue to monitor whether some demand from China is being met indirectly through operators in third countries. If these transactions are blocked, it could affect some sales, but the overall trajectory for AI infrastructure remains strong.

stories.Headline: Jing and colleagues present provenance-gated tool invocation to defend LLM agents against indirect prompt injection
stories.Summary:
A paper by Jing, Chen, Sun, He and Si published on 18 November 2026 in Advances in Engineering Innovation, volume 17, issue 12, pages 1 to 7, sets out a method called provenance-gated tool invocation for defending LLM agents against indirect prompt injection. The authors are L. Jing, N. Chen, Z. Sun, C. He and F. Si, and the work appears under the EWA Publishing imprint in Oxford in the United Kingdom. The paper is open access, and the datasets used or analyzed during the study will be available from the authors. The statements, opinions and data in the publication belong to the individual authors and contributors and not to EWA Publishing or its editors. EWA Publishing and its editors disclaim responsibility for any injury to people or property resulting from any ideas, methods, instructions or products referred to in the content.

The paper sits among prior work it cites on tool use and prompt injection, including Toolformer by Schick and colleagues in 2023 and the indirect prompt injection study by Greshake and colleagues, also in 2023. It also cites a 2025 survey by Deng and colleagues on security challenges for AI agents in ACM Computing Surveys, volume 57, issue 7, pages 1 to 36. Zhan and colleagues are cited for InjecAgent in the Findings of ACL 2024, pages 10471 to 10506, and for adaptive attacks that break defenses in the Findings of NAACL 2025, pages 7101 to 7117. Yi and colleagues are cited for benchmarking and defending against indirect prompt injection in the KDD 2025 proceedings, pages 1809 to 1820.

The reference list also includes AgentDojo by Debenedetti and colleagues in the 2024 NeurIPS proceedings, pages 82895 to 82920, and PlanGuard by Gong and Deng at the 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks, pages 1 to 6. Debenedetti and colleagues appear again in 2026 for defeating prompt injections by design at the IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning, pages 587 to 618. Tang and colleagues are cited for a 2026 survey in Information Fusion, volume 127, article 103941, and Chen and colleagues for SecAlign at the 2025 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, pages 2833 to 2847. Wang and colleagues are cited for DataFilter at the 2026 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning, pages 139 to 157, and Abdelnabi and colleagues for catching task drift with activation deltas at the 2025 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning, pages 43 to 67.

Further references cover Shi and colleagues on prompt injection attacks to tool selection at the 2026 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium, and Jia and colleagues on the task shield in the 2025 ACL proceedings, volume 1, pages 29680 to 29697. Denning's 1976 lattice model of secure information flow in Communications of the ACM, volume 19, issue 5, pages 236 to 243, is cited, as is a 2026 critical evaluation of defenses by Jia and colleagues at the ACM Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies, pages 265 to 270. McNemar's 1947 note on sampling error in Psychometrika, volume 12, issue 2, pages 153 to 157, also appears. The copyright line names EWA Publishing, its licensors and contributors for 2026.

stories.Headline: Insurers offer CoreWeave effectively unlimited AI infrastructure debt as risk specialists flag concentration concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the Nasdaq-listed cloud infrastructure company, is drawing a growing pool of insurance sector lenders to finance its AI infrastructure build out, according to industry sources cited in a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance on November 16, 2026. Those sources describe insurers as offering CoreWeave what is being framed as effectively unlimited debt capacity tied to AI infrastructure projects. Risk specialists across insurance and tech finance are flagging concentration concerns as insurance backed AI debt structures increase in scale and complexity. CoreWeave runs cloud infrastructure across the US, Denmark, the Middle East and Asia Pacific, and it has a market cap of $29.5b.

For CoreWeave, insurers leaning in as a major lending base reinforces the bull story that large institutions are willing to fund its AI build out at scale, even while the business is loss making and carries less than one year of cash runway. The bear case gets sharper at the same time, because insurance backed structures increase balance sheet complexity, concentrate funding into one lender group and tie CoreWeave more tightly to fixed interest costs in a sector where its share price has already been volatile over the past three months. The article says the key marker from here is how 2026 full year revenue lands against management's guidance range of US$13.0b to US$13.3b. That single line item will show whether aggressive insurer supported capacity growth is being matched by customer demand or leaving more leverage resting on the same underlying cash flows.

The article does not name the insurers involved or the individuals who made the statements, describing them only as industry sources and risk specialists. It says the surge in insurer lending support is one piece of a much broader story about the business, and it notes that Simply Wall St has flagged two warning signs, one of them major, for CoreWeave. The article was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and it states that its commentary relies on historical data and analyst forecasts only.
